name: Connecticut Mirror
title: During Banned Books Week, librarians weigh threat of ‘soft censorship’
description: Connecticut libraries are seeing an uptick in “soft censorship” of books that receive complaints or informal challenges from patrons.
text:
Children’s librarian Sarah Quigley still remembers when the call came in earlier this year, midway through a mid-morning storytime packed with young children. She had just finished Tasha Spillett’s “Raven’s Ribbons,” a book about a young Indigenous boy who wants to wear a ribbon skirt, and turns to his grandmother for guidance. At the end of the book, Spillett writes about two-spirit people, who have an expansive gender identity that exists outside of a binary. 
Then a person from the neighborhood, who had heard about it via text from someone attending the story time, called the library. They were angry, and said the book pushed harmful gender ideology. On a round rug patterned with the ABCs in the library’s brightly lit children’s section, Quigley had moved from the book to a sing-along, unaware of the controversy.
Quigley, who is a children’s librarian at the Mitchell Branch of the New Haven Free Public Library, is one of an increasing number of people who work at Connecticut libraries who report noticing examples of “soft censorship,” a term that refers to books that are not formally banned or challenged, but have received complaints or informal challenges from patrons, parents, and “pressure” from special interest groups. 
As the American Library Association (ALA) observes its 44th annual Banned Books Week, many library staffers are thinking through how to respond to this new chapter of censorship, from open discussions with concerned parents to small, meaningful interventions like bookmarks that let a patron know that if they remove a book with the intention of restricting access to fellow readers, librarians will replace it.
Launched by the ALA in 1982, Banned Books Week is a celebration of banned and challenged literature that also seeks to bring attention to censorship in libraries and school districts across the country. A formal book challenge means that an individual or group of people have filled out paperwork asking that a book be relocated or removed. 
Last year, the ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom recorded challenges to a total of 4,235 unique titles, from Patricia McCormick’s “Sold,” which addresses child sex trafficking, to Malinda Lo’s “Last Night At The Telegraph Club,” which takes place in a lesbian bar in California’s Bay Area during 1950s era McCarthyism. According to the ALA, over 90 percent of those challenges came from “pressure groups” like Moms for Liberty, and elected officials on the municipal, state and federal level. 
Of those, Connecticut saw challenges to seven unique titles, including Maia Kobabe’s “Gender Queer,” Peter Brown’s “Fred Gets Dressed,” Edwidge Danticat’s “Mama’s Nightingale: A Story of Immigration and Separation,” Loren Grush’s “The Six: The Untold Story of America’s First Women Astronauts,” Yaakov Katz’s “While Israel Slept: How Hamas Surprised the Most Powerful Military in the Middle East,” Lucy Knisley’s “Apple Crush,” and Syed Masood’s “More Than Just a Pretty Face.”     

A tote featuring banned book titles for sale at Possible Futures in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The bookstore is observing Banned Books week with a daily read-in in her store. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“These book challenges are happening in every corner of Connecticut, and what I’m most concerned about is the quiet censorship that doesn’t make it into the news,” said Sam Lee, co-chair of the Intellectual Freedom Committee at the Connecticut Library Association (CLA), stressing how hard it is to track challenges in public schools that do not have a designated library and media specialist on staff. 
“This is especially nefarious in school libraries,” but also includes public libraries across the state where librarians may feel actively discouraged from collecting titles by LGBTQ+ authors and authors of color, Lee added. 
Because the CLA, which sends data to the ALA’s Office of Intellectual Freedom, protects the confidentiality of those reporting book challenges, Lee said that she could not disclose where in Connecticut those challenges are taking place, or from whom they originated. Including branch locations, Connecticut is home to 235 libraries, according to the CT State Library.  
She also noted that those numbers may be artificially low: librarians sometimes do not report book challenges because they fear retaliation from patrons, parents, and elected officials. It can also be harder to track challenges in schools where paraprofessionals or volunteers are running an understaffed or informal school library. Fifty-one percent of book challenges curently take place in public libraries, according to the ALA; 37 percent take place in school libraries, eight percent in curricula, and three percent in higher education. 
Across the state, “a lot of media specialists are being laid off on a town-wide level,” said Kym Powe, children and young adult consultant at the CT State Library. While CASL tries to track challenges across the state, “it’s like a game of whack a mole.” In 2025, for instance, Bridgeport Public Schools cut all district librarians, citing a tight budget year. Powe sees that pattern happening over and over again across Connecticut, meaning that formal challenges within schools become that much harder to track.
What is ‘soft censorship’?
In part, understanding what constitutes “soft censorship” also means understanding the policies and protections that already exist in Connecticut’s libraries. Last year, the state passed S.B. 1271, “An Act Concerning School and Public Libraries,” championed widely as an act that protected the freedom to read and based on eponymous legislation that passed in New Jersey in 2024.   
The legislation, which is now state law, requires both school and public libraries in Connecticut to create organization-wide policies around collection practices, programming and library displays, and material review and reconsideration. 
In practice, having those standardized policies in place strengthens protections for both public and school librarians at a time when many are seeing their peers and colleagues lose or risk their jobs in other states without the same laws on the books. In March, for instance, Rutherford County Library Director Luanne James was fired for refusing to move 132 children’s books to the Tennessee library’s adult section (she has since filed a federal lawsuit).
“I can’t be fired because of these things anymore,” said Jenny Lussier, a digital and media specialist in Connecticut’s District 13 (Durham and Middlefield) who works with students from Pre-K through first grade, and is the former president of the Connecticut Association of School Librarians (CASL). 
During her time as a school librarian, Lussier has only had one direct request for reconsideration, around a book in Rachel Russell’s popular “Dork Diaries” series. But during her time as the president of CASL, she observed “this onslaught,” which began before the Covid-19 pandemic and then escalated as schools returned to in-person learning after going remote. 
Now, she said, the most significant challenge to the legislation is school districts that have not created any sort of plan for implementation, either because they do not want that degree of oversight, or because they do not have enough, or any, library and media specialists working for the district.   
The legislation, meanwhile, does appear to be working. In the year that the law has been in place, the number of recorded challenges in Connecticut has decreased, from 17 unique book titles in 2024 (that took place over just seven attempted challenges, in what the ALA calls multi-title challenges) to seven challenges in 2025. Raymond Garcia, a communications specialist with the ALA, said that the organization does not yet have the state-by-state data for 2026. 

Banned books for sale at Possible Futures in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The bookstore is observing Banned Books week with a daily read-in in her store. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lee said this year, she personally has tracked three formal book challenges, as well as two library program challenges and one “Hide the Pride” maneuver, in which a person entered the library, emptied a Pride Month display, and hid the books around the library, including under pieces of furniture. She said she cannot comment on where those took place. 
“I didn’t come up with this phrasing, but when people are vocalizing their concerns [around books and literary content], it’s confusing public accountability with public control,” she said.
What she and colleagues are now increasingly concerned about, she continued, are “soft” or “quiet” challenges that don’t ever make it formally into the CLA’s records, but sometimes spook librarians into changing what books they request or recommend for a library’s collection. When a book gets taken off the shelf, or never makes it onto it in the first place, there’s suddenly one less story in which a reader of any age might be able to see their own lived experience, they said.
Both Lee and Powe said that the majority of these challenges, in keeping with the national trend, target children’s books, especially those that feature LGBTQ+ characters, characters of color, and other “folks with minoritized identities.” 
In recent years, that’s looked like everything from Mike Curato’s “Flamer,” which the Newtown Board of Education narrowly avoided banning in 2023, to Justin Richardson’s and Peter Parnell’s “And Tango Makes Three,” a picture book about two male penguins who adopt a motherless egg and raise the nestling after it hatches. 
“When I’m having these conversations from a public perspective, sometimes people don’t understand what challenging might look like,” Powe said in a phone call Monday. For instance, “moving a book from the teen section of the library to the adult section of the library” can constitute a challenge, but some of these acts never get reported. 
“It’s okay if a parent or a household or a person does not want to expose their child to a book or a topic,” Powe continued. “That is ok. That is your right. The issue is, as it has always been, making that decision for other people. That’s just not ok.”
Lee pointed to “the four R’s of censorship,” a concept that comes from Dr. Emily Knox, interim dean and professor at the School of Information Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.. Those include redaction (“when you remove a page or you draw pants on a naked baby,” Lee said), restriction, relocation and removal. 
In the past several years, she and colleagues have also seen pressure that comes directly from patrons, whether in the form of a parental concern or a group that asks the library to pull a program, such as a drag queen story hour, or a patron who takes it upon themselves to quietly hide or remove a book from the collection. 
“We are getting reports of this from library workers in the field and parents’ groups that we work with,” said Amelia Aldred, deputy director for state and local advocacy at ALA. “The issue and the problem, which is clear, is that it is silent. It’s not as transparent as a reconsideration process for a book. We see library professionals who are preemptively removing books, before they have been challenged. We also see librarians telling us that they’ve been told not to purchase books that have been banned or challenged, or are even similar [to those titles].” 
Hamden resident and parent Nijija-Ife Waters, who runs the educational advocacy, training and consulting firm Un1que2L3arn, pointed to the importance of parents remaining vigilant about what their children read. As an advocate for all students, she doesn’t support book bans, she said. In fact, she’s currently working with a few clients in Florida who are fighting for the right to keep books that address Black history in their schools.
At the same time, and as a mother to a now-teenager, she believes libraries could do a better job categorizing sensitive and controversial books, in the same way that video stores used to add a parental advisory label or that movie theaters restrict entry to R-rated movies. 
She added that parents need to remain active participants in their children’s lives. For her, this includes going with a child to the library and looking at the books they want to check out.
“It’s about having a conversation,” she said. In her own home, that often looks like picking up an extra copy of what her son is reading, reading the material herself, and talking about the book together. It both gives her a better sense of how her son is processing the material — she referenced Shakespeare’s “Macbeth,” for instance, which has several violent scenes — and lets her know he’s keeping up with it.
“Books are meant to give knowledge and not cause confusion,” she said in a phone call Friday morning. “I think if a parent feels that they’re not ready for their child to be exposed to a particular topic or global challenge, it shouldn’t be pushed onto them. There still should be some form of conversation around this. Certain topics should not be accessible to a certain age without adults’ supervision.” 
‘I feel furious & I feel heartbroken’
In New Haven earlier this year, Quigley experienced that firsthand.
In late April, she selected “Raven’s Ribbons” for a program celebrating America’s semiquincentennial, because it centers the role of Indigenous people in the story of this country. The book, which came out in 2025, tells the story of Raven, a young boy who loves round dances for the sense of community they weave through communal movement and the syncopated beat of hand drums. 
In the book, Raven is especially drawn to the bright, traditional ribbon skirts that dancers wear, and which his grandmother is particularly gifted at sewing. But when he asks his grandmother if he can have one, “she hesitates,” Quigley remembered, because she’s never seen one on a boy or a man before. After thinking about the tradition, and her love for her grandson, she stays up all night sewing a rainbow-colored ribbon skirt for him. The book ends with Raven dancing joyfully in a rainbow-patterned ribbon skirt, hand in hand with his grandmother. 

A page from Raven’s Ribbons by Tasha Spillett at the Mitchell Branch of the New Haven Free Public Library on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.  The library recieved complaints after Children’s Librarian Sarah Quigley read the book during a storytime this summer. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“It’s a beautiful nod to Indigenous tradition and the value and the beauty of those traditions, and the value and the beauty of saying when it’s okay to change a thing,” Quigley said. At the end of the book, Spillett includes a note about two-spirit people. When Quigley was talking through the note at storytime, “I said, and two-spirit is kind of like trans people,” she said. Quigley acknowledged that the phrasing may have been an oversimplification, but that she was trying to find a way for kids to understand the concept.
As a children’s librarian and an educator, Quigley said, it’s important to her to share a diverse range of lived experiences. Spillett, as well as illustrator Daniel Ramirez, are both Indigenous: Spillett is Cree and Trinidadian, and Ramirez has roots in the Saginaw Chippewa Tribe in Michigan. 
But after Quigley read the book aloud, a patron called the library, having heard about the story time from a parent who was there. Speaking to Quigley’s supervisor, Branch Manager Marian Huggins, the patron pushed back against the book, suggesting that it was indoctrinating children. The person also threatened “to go to the press,” both Quigley and Huggins remembered, leaving both librarians shaken. 
“This is unacceptable indoctrination and is completely inappropriate,” the person later wrote anonymously on SeeClickFix, a website on which people normally report problems with municipal infrastructure, like downed power lines, broken stoplights and potholes. Sarah from the library needs to be held accountable for pushing an agenda on children who have yet to start kindergarten!!”
It was ultimately the first of three complaints that was made. Quigley, who has helped the library organize wide-ranging children’s programming on themes that range from LGBTQ+ Pride to the hip-hop nutcracker to nail art, said that she absolutely considers the exchange an example of soft censorship. Since April, she hasn’t changed anything about her storytime choices, or the books she requests for the library’s collection. And yet, it’s given her pause every time she puts together a program or reaches for a title. 

Children’s Librarian Sarah Quigley poses for a portrait at the Mitchell Branch of the New Haven Free Public Library on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.  The library recieved complaints after Quigley read Raven’s Ribbons by Tasha Spillett during a storytime this summer. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Before Quigley was in New Haven, she was a school librarian in Austin, Tex., where she heard the same kind of challenges and concerns from parents much more frequently. In 2022, the same year she and her partner moved to Connecticut, Texas saw formal challenges to 2,397 unique book titles across 94 challenges, according to the ALA. 
Any time that a patron suggests she is somehow harming children, she takes it personally. She thinks a lot about the students she served in Texas, and the fact that they’re still there, as their libraries become increasingly restricted.   
“This is my community!” Quigley said. “I feel furious and I feel heartbroken. It feels like people are digging their hands into places where they’re not invited just because they can.” 
Quigley added that she feels empowered largely because she knows that as her supervisor, Huggins, has her back. As both Powe and Lee noted over separate interviews, that’s not always the case. 
“She’s the children’s librarian,” Huggins said in a phone call Wednesday morning. “She has an MLS, she has years of experience, she has enthusiasm for the kids. She loves the kids, and the kids know it and they appreciate it. I think a lot of librarians are librarians because they love books. Sarah is a librarian because she loves people.”
“You can only make decisions for your own kid,” she added, noting that she speaks from experience as both a librarian and a parent who ran a fairly conservative home when her own kids were growing up. “That’s the bottom line. You are in charge of your own child. If you come in and we say, ‘This is going to be the story today’ and you don’t like it, you can leave. There’s a door.” 
‘Knowledge is power’
That type of “soft” or “quiet” censorship was also a topic of discussion at Eastern Connecticut State University (ECSU) on Tuesday during a symposium on banned books and censorship that Hope-Marie Cook, ECSU librarian and director of the university’s curriculum center, has organized in some form since 2002. 
In a library conference room brightly decorated with banned book displays and signs printed cheerily with the words “I Read Banned Books!,” Cook said that she holds the event to bring attention to censorship that people may not even know is happening. That’s especially true as she observes nationwide trends — the use of AI in generating book challenges, for instance, and the shift from individual concerns to complaints made by political and religious pressure groups — and thinks about the impact they may have on a local level.  
“Knowledge is power and before people can protect the freedom to read, they need to be aware of these attempts that have been rampant in the United States,” she said as titles from Harper Lee’s “To Kill A Mockingbird” to Toni Morrison’s “The Bluest Eye” and “Beloved” added pops of color to the room. “Many educators are not aware of censorship of books in schools, classrooms, libraries and other publicly funded spaces until it happens to them.” 
That was Cook’s experience too. In the 1990s, when she was a student teacher at a school in Las Vegas, a peer brought in Tarō Gomi’s 1977 children’s book “Everybody Poops” to read to a kindergarten class. But just before he began, the school’s principal appeared, pulled the book, and asked the student teacher to leave the school, and return to his classes at the University of Nevada. 
“That event left us all very stunned,” Cook remembered. But it also put censorship very much on her radar, where it has remained for the last three and a half decades. 
In the last few years, she’s been particularly concerned to see a rise in banned books in schools, of which the literary advocacy organization PEN America reported 11,982 in the 2025-2026 school year. When a book is banned or challenged, the process “does not allow readers to have access to literature that they might identify [with],” she said. “If books are taken off the shelves, titles will not have a chance to be read.” 
Amy Slowik, head of youth and family learning at the Russell Library in Middletown and is the recipient of the CLA’s “Excellence in Public Library Service” award, echoed that message during a presentation on censorship in public libraries. 

Amy Slowick, head of Youth and Family Learning, poses for a portrait at Russell Library in Middletown on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

In seven years at Russell, she’s not received a formal challenge, which she credits in part to the formal review and reconsideration policy that the library has in place. But she’s watched them crop up across the state, from Colchester to Old Lyme to the Kent Memorial Library in Suffield just last year.  
“What we do experience is ‘soft censorship,’” she said. At Russell, that’s looked like “direct pressure by patrons on staff,” from concerns about religious reading materials (for which there is a dedicated section) to requests to move a book from one section of the library to another. 
Recently, she remembered, a parent came directly to her because they were concerned that their child was not ready for a book like Pan Cooke’s “Puzzled,” which was grouped with fiction appropriate for kids ages 9 to 12. 
The parent had seen that the book, the protagonist of which is learning to navigate OCD, anxiety, and intrusive thoughts, references suicidality on the first page. 
Slowik, who is a parent herself, took the concern seriously. She started reading about the book in context of what young adults were experiencing in their own, real lives. “All this research was coming out about kids dealing with anxiety,” she said. Not only did the book seem age-appropriate: it could be a mirror for a young person experiencing the same thing. She ultimately put it back on the shelf.
For her, there are two other kinds of soft censorship: instances where staff no longer feel confident in buying or reshelving a book, or when “controversial books simply disappear.” At Russell, as with national trends, those are often books with LGBTQ+ characters and characters of color.  
“There were two theories,” Slowik said of books that disappear from the shelves. “People don’t want other people to take them, so they steal them, or people are afraid” to check them out, perhaps because they come from one of those marginalized identities themselves, or don’t want a book title to show up on their borrowing record.  
At Russell, staff worked together to design bookmarks that remind patrons that if they steal a book, the library will replace it (not all libraries have the funds to do that, Slowik acknowledged), and if they are looking for a specific book but afraid to check it out, they can search for a digital copy, or work directly with a librarian to find a solution. Slowik credited librarians Stephanie Rush and Sue Honer with the final designs.             
In recent years, Russell has also faced informal program challenges, including a drag queen story hour hosted with Middletown Pride that drew pushback from the community. In that case, the censorship worked: Russell hasn’t hosted one in several years.  
“We still have censorship at Russell Library, but it doesn’t look the same way it does in the rest of the country,” she said.  
Where Connecticut is within a national context 
As she keeps one finger on the pulse of soft or quiet censorship, Lee and groups like the CLA are also tracking challenges to the freedom to read at the national level, where federal legislators have proposed multiple bills in Congress aimed at book bans and literary censorship. 
One, H.R. 7661, would amend the  Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 to pull federal funding from public schools that allow books with “sexually oriented material.” In a testimony before Congress earlier this year, Sam Helmick, the 2025-2026 president of the ALA, called the legislation “a smokescreen,” intentionally broad enough to cut off funding to any school that brings in, or teaches from, books with LGBTQ+ content and characters. 
Two other pieces of legislation, meanwhile, would expand protections for libraries and librarians on a national level. Lee said that these, S.4689 and H.R.6440, or the “READ Act” and the “Right To Read Act” respectively, “would help protect the right to read,” although neither has seen significant support from members of the Connecticut delegation in Congress. 
Meanwhile, Lee knows to expect the challenges to keep coming, including those that may go unreported or underreported. In addition to her work at the CLA, Lee and a network of volunteers have also launched the New England Intellectual Freedom Helpline, which tracks challenges across Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, and Connecticut.   
In the early hours of Wednesday morning, all of that seemed both urgent and a universe away, as the bookstore Possible Futures opened its doors on New Haven’s Edgewood Avenue a few hours early for a banned books reading group. On a table close to the door, a display of banned books invited readers to come closer, with titles for all ages that ranged from Allison Bechdel’s graphic novel “Fun Home” and Ray Bradbury’s frequently-challenged “Fahrenheit 451” to Sarah J. Maas’ “A Court of Thorns and Roses” (during the 2025-2026 school year, Maas’ books were banned 196 times, according to PEN America) to Jessica Herthel and Shelagh McNicholas’ “I Am Jazz.” Musician Emily King’s airy vocals drifted somewhere from a playlist and speaker at the back of the room. 

Owner Lauren Anderson and employee Jada Boggs talk at Possible Futures in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The bookstore is observing Banned Books week with a daily read-in in her store. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Bookseller Jada Boggs drifted around the sun-dappled space, shelving books and checking inventory as she waited for customers. Only when she was still behind the counter for a moment did she reflect on her own relationship with reading, which pulled her instinctively to Possible Futures after it opened four years ago.
When Boggs was still just a kid, she gravitated toward “The Lightning Thief,” a novel by Rick Riordan that tells the story of a mixed-race protagonist, Hazel Levesque, who is the daughter of Pluto. She became so enamored with the character that she ultimately named her first car, a 2018  Hyundai Elantra, after her. 
“As a mixed girl, I got to see an interracial relationship where I could also see myself,” said Boggs. Riordan’s work “is goofy,” she said with a smile, but it gave her a place to think about her own lived experiences.

Employee Jada Boggs works on a book display at Possible Futures in New Haven on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. The bookstore is observing Banned Books week with a daily read-in in her store. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

When she sees book bans, “we’re taking away kids’ opportunity to learn about other experiences,” she said. “Like somehow it’s [book are] this big looming threat that is just exposure to the information.”

description: Note: We will update this story as the situation develops. Isaias is now a Category 3 hurricane, a designation that puts it in the category of “major” hurricanes. text:
Store shelves at a Walmart in Pensacola were emptied of bread and canned goods on Thursday, Oct. 8, as Isais approached. Landfall was expected Friday evening. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Note: We will update this story as the situation develops.
Isaias is now a Category 3 hurricane, a designation that puts it in the category of “major” hurricanes.
The National Hurricane Center reports sustained winds of 120 mph and stronger gusts. The storm was traveling toward the northern Gulf Coast at 15 mph and could make landfall Friday night.
“We have the resources that we need in place, to be able to respond, to be able to help people in need, and to be able to rapidly get things back to normal, from power restoration to the economy,” DeSantis said Friday morning.
According to DeSantis, Florida Power & Light has 16,000 linemen and personnel mobilized.
“Assume you’re going to lose power,” DeSantis said — and how quickly it comes back on depends upon where damage is sustained.
People as far away as Central Florida should take precautionary measures, the governor said, as rain bands from Isaias could extend that far.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hurricanes are categorized by number between 1 and 5 assigned based on the storm’s maximum sustained wind speed. Officially called the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, Category 3, 4, and 5 hurricanes are considered “major.”
According to the he National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, during a major storm, “Devastating damage will occur: Well-built framed homes may incur major damage or removal of roof decking and gable ends. Many trees will be snapped or uprooted, blocking numerous roads. Electricity and water will be unavailable for several days to weeks after the storm passes.
The rainfall forecast for Hurricane Isaias as of early morning on Oct. 9, 2026. (Via NHC)
Meanwhile, Pensacola residents, businesses, and utilities have been heeding the governor’s advice.
The Emerald Coast Utilities Authority said it is temporarily shutting down water and sewer services on Pensacola Beach, a barrier island, beginning at 3 p.m.
The shutdown is being done to help reduce the potential for sewer backups and overflows during the storm.
Pensacola residents flocked to stores Thursday including the Wal-Mart in west Pensacola, where they scurried to buy hurricane supplies. Bottled water was being replenished on a rolling basis by the pallet-load by store employees.
Chips, bread, lunch meat, and other staples were nearly gone from the shelves. Toilet paper remained well-stocked.
Vienna sausages, canned chicken, and canned tuna were all nearly sold out.
Naval Air Station Pensacola planned to close at noon Friday to non-mission essential personnel because of the storm, officials announced via Instagram. NAS Whiting Field was moving aircraft off-base, too. Similarly, Eglin Air Force Base, the Panhandle’s enormous weapons range, evacuated airworthy aircraft and move non-flyable craft into hangars, according to its Instagram. Some service members and their families were ordered to evacuate.

title: Maine to receive $36M in early release of federal heating assistance
description: Maine is set to receive more than $36 million in federal funding to help low-income households and seniors afford rising fuel costs as nighttime temperatures begin to dip below freezing. According to a press release from U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office on Friday, this will mark one of the earliest releases of funds in the […]
text:
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. (Photo by gmnicholas/ Getty Images)Maine is set to receive more than $36 million in federal funding to help low-income households and seniors afford rising fuel costs as nighttime temperatures begin to dip below freezing.
According to a press release from U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ office on Friday, this will mark one of the earliest releases of funds in the history of the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, known as LIHEAP.
Last year the funding release was delayed by the government shutdown, and not available until December. 
The release noted that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Community Services will release $36,675,395 in LIHEAP funding for the State of Maine and $1,408,729 for the Wabanaki Nations.
Debate over energy costs highlights how differently Jackson and Collins approach governing

The recent spike in fuel prices, attributed to restrictions in the global supply due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine, on top of increasing costs for healthcare, food and other goods has become a key concern of Mainers and Americans more broadly, particularly as winter approaches.
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
According to the latest data from the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.97 per gallon on Oct. 5, up roughly 79% from last year. That is down slightly from Sept. 21, when the average price reached a record high of $6.02. 
“I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” said Collins, who along with independent U.S. Sen. Angus King, was among a bipartisan group of lawmakers who sent a letter to HHS last month requesting the early release.
The Iran War and rising energy costs have become a major issue in the U.S. Senate race. During a Thursday debate against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins touted her behind-the-scenes conversations with Trump administration officials to get both the assistance funds and reserve oil supplies released.

text:
A hurricane watch was in effect Friday morning for Mobile, Baldwin, Escambia, Covington and Conecuh counties as Hurricane Isaias strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane. (Alabama Emergency Management Agency)Hurricane Isaias strengthened into a Category 3 storm Friday morning hours before an expected landfall somewhere in the Florida panhandle.
The storm system had sustained winds of about 120 mph and was  245 miles south of Pensacola mid-Friday morning moving north at 15 mph. It is moving largely along the same track as before but shifted slightly east. Its path will continue north, with much of the storm expected to cover large portions of Alabama before moving on to Tennessee Saturday afternoon to evening. 
“We will continue to really see the same impacts that we talked about, damaging winds, a few tornadoes possible in those bands, particularly across the eastern and southeastern portions of the state will have a better tornado risk, and heavy rainfall will continue as advertised between one and a half to four inches generally, with maybe some spots getting five inches of rain that could cause flooding in low-lying areas,” said Jason Holmes, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service based in Birmingham.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A hurricane warning was in effect Friday morning for Mobile, Baldwin, Conecuh, Covington and Escambia counties.  Tropical storm warnings and watches were in effect for central and southern Alabama.
Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday declared a state of emergency in 40 counties in central and southern Alabama and on Thursday ordered mandatory evacuations of visitors in coastal Alabama. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall said in a statement Friday the declaration put the state’s price-gouging laws into effect. The law could subject people who raise prices of a good or service 25% or more over the average cost over the previous 30 days to fines of up to $1,000, unless the increase is due to a reasonable cost.
Places in south Alabama such as Evergreen and Greenville could experience up to six inches of rain. As it travels further north, places in northern Alabama could have between two to three inches of rain. 
Winds are expected to exceed 70 mph in Mobile and Baldwin counties.
According to the Alabama Emergency Management Agency, storm surges are expected to reach between six and nine feet along the coastal areas and four to six feet in Mobile Bay.
“People need to begin making preparations,” Holmes said.

description: The Alabama Supreme Court Friday upheld a lower court’s dismissal of a challenge to Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s residency and eligibility to run for governor. In a 13-page, unsigned opinion, the court said the Montgomery Circuit Court “lacked subject-matter jurisdiction” over the case. Tuberville has faced questions about his residenc[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama, the Republican nominee for governor, speaks to the crowd before President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The Alabama Supreme Court Friday morning affirmed the Montgomery Circuit Court's decision to dismiss a challenge to Tuberville's residency and eligibility to run for governor. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Supreme Court Friday upheld a lower court’s dismissal of a challenge to Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s residency and eligibility to run for governor.
In a 13-page, unsigned opinion, the court said the Montgomery Circuit Court “lacked subject-matter jurisdiction” over the case.
Tuberville has faced questions about his residency for years, which he has dismissed. Two plaintiffs who challenged Tuberville’s residency attempted to do so under what is known as a “quo warranto” action, meaning “by what authority.” Plaintiffs argued that as a party nominee, Tuberville was a quasi-public official and subject to quo warranto, but the justices said that a nomination did not give a party nominee “some portion of the sovereign functions of government.”
“We hold that a party’s nominee for election to public office does not exercise any public office,” the opinion said. “Thus, a quo warranto action is not authorized against a party nominee.” 
Messages seeking comment were left Friday with Tuberville’s campaign and Montgomery attorney Joe Espy, who represented Tuberville in court. 
Barry Ragsdale, an attorney representing the plaintiffs in the case, said in a statement Friday morning “we were obviously disappointed with the decision, but not particularly surprised.”
“There is simply no question that Tuberville is constitutionally ineligible to be governor,” the statement said. “Today’s decision opens the door to ineligible candidates, including non-U.S. citizens, to seek elected office so long as the political parties fail to do their jobs in ensuring that their nominees comply with the Constitution. It is another sad day for the rule of law.”
Montgomery Circuit Court Judge Brooke Reid dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hours-long hearing. Reid did not judge the merits of the case.

title: Dan Ahlers: Democrat seeking South Dakota’s top office says he knows how to win uphill battles
description: DELL RAPIDS — In a coffee shop on his hometown’s main thoroughfare, Dan Ahlers thinks back on his first run for elected office 20 years ago. There was a different Democrat running who needed to drop out, local party leaders said, and they wanted Ahlers as a replacement. “‘Don’t worry, it won’t be a big […]
text:
Dan Ahlers, a Democrat running for governor of South Dakota, stands in a building he owns that houses a coffee shop in Dell Rapids, South Dakota. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ahlers-Profile-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
DELL RAPIDS — In a coffee shop on his hometown’s main thoroughfare, Dan Ahlers thinks back on his first run for elected office 20 years ago.
There was a different Democrat running who needed to drop out, local party leaders said, and they wanted Ahlers as a replacement.
“‘Don’t worry, it won’t be a big deal. You won’t win anyways,’” Ahlers recalled them saying. “But I took that as a challenge, and I won.”
As a 32-year-old Democrat in a district where Democrats were outnumbered by Republicans, Ahlers was elected to one of the district’s two House seats. He went on to win election to the Legislature two more times and served a total of six years.
Larry Rhoden: Rancher, welder and three-decade politician makes his case to earn SD’s trust

By the time of his first campaign, Ahlers said, he was accustomed to exceeding expectations. He ran long distance track at Augustana University, after the team’s head coach told him he wouldn’t make the team.
“My sophomore fall semester, I took a PE class, and he saw me running, and he called me over,” Ahlers said. The coach asked why Ahlers wasn’t out for track, to which Ahlers responded, “‘Because you said I was too big.’ He said, ‘Be at practice at 4.’”
After graduating with a degree in government and international relations, Ahlers couldn’t find many South Dakota jobs that fit what he’d studied, but he wanted to stay close to home.
He decided to open a VHS video rental store in Dell Rapids, where he remembers a loan officer telling him the business wouldn’t last.
“And I remember the day that he signed up as a customer in my third store,” Ahlers said. “Not too bad for something that wasn’t going to work.”
Now Ahlers, 52, is running for governor — an office Democrats in the state haven’t held for 47 years, since 1979 — against Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden.
Ahlers faces an uphill battle running against a sitting governor in a state where Republicans outnumber Democrats. He said that doesn’t bother him.
“Whether it was business or running for the Legislature, over and over, I’ve been told that things are not possible,” Ahlers said.
Roots in local business, community
Ahlers opened his first video rental store in 1999 in Dell Rapids, a town of about 4,000 people located 20 miles north of Sioux Falls in eastern South Dakota.
He eventually added stores in Hartford and Tea, which he later sold. Ahlers maintained his Dell Rapids store until 2019 but closed it as it became increasingly difficult to get DVDs from studios.
Less than a decade after getting his video rental business off the ground, Ahlers purchased a building in downtown Dell Rapids.

Cars are parked along a street in Dell Rapids, South Dakota. (Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)

A small business loan officer told him a coffee shop wouldn’t sustain itself in a small town, Ahlers said, but authorized a $50,000 loan. That wouldn’t cover paying for the building, renovations and the equipment needed to get a coffee shop running, Ahlers said. So, he used profits from his video stores.
“That other business that they said would never succeed helped pay for it,” Ahlers said.
He was determined to make the coffee shop a success.
“I enjoy proving people wrong,” he said. “I think that I take those things as a challenge.”
For the next two years, he repaired the building’s damaged foundation and renovated the space before opening the shop in 2008. It became The Jabberwock — a coffee shop that also welcomed local musical acts, wedding receptions and graduation parties.
He sold the business a few years later, but still owns the building. He has also been a substitute teacher and led Dell Rapids’ before- and after-school program, and its Chamber of Commerce. Ahlers was hired in 2023 as the executive director of the state Democratic Party, but has taken a step back from his duties while on the campaign trail.
Ahlers lives in Dell Rapids with his wife of 28 years, Amy, and their two sons. He said the decision to run for governor came down to what his family thought of it.
“My wife, I mean, she had to think very hard on this,” Ahlers said. “She’s very thoughtful, very deliberative, and she eventually said, ‘I think you need to do this.’”



On the issues
Listen to host Meghan O’Brien’s Searchlight Report podcast interview with Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers, including questions on abortion, relationships with tribal nations, climate change, taxes and Medicaid. She also asked him to share a “big idea” for South Dakota. O’Brien asked Ahlers’ opponent, Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, the same set of questions for an episode that published prior to the June primary election.





Democrats ask, ‘Why not now?’
Republican former Gov. Kristi Noem ignited the race to succeed her in January 2025 when she resigned to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Her lieutenant governor, Rhoden, was automatically elevated to fill the remainder of her second and final term.
While serving as executive director for the Democratic Party, Ahlers asked other Democrats to put their names on the ballot for local and state offices. People around him asked why he wasn’t doing the same, he said.
Shane Merrill, chair of the state Democratic Party, was one of those voices.
“It just made total sense,” Merrill said, mentioning Ahlers’ legislative career and community experience.
Ahlers said his focus was on recruiting. He didn’t set out to run for governor.
“I think those opportunities for public service call you,” Ahlers said. “Some people do plan them. I mean, they go, ‘I’m going to do this, and then I’m going to do that.’ I’m a Democrat in a Republican state. I don’t have the luxury of laying out a plan like that.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Ahlers was the last candidate for governor to throw his hat in the ring when he announced his campaign in February. By then, four Republican candidates were running, setting up a primary election that ended in South Dakota’s first-ever statewide runoff election, won by Rhoden in July.
“I spent a lot of time listening, watching, doing the town halls, doing all that type of legwork to prepare for what was going to be a very quick, fast election cycle,” Ahlers said.
Merrill said a momentum shift toward Democratic candidates in other Midwestern states tells him that now might be the time for one to take office in the Mount Rushmore State.
“I think that the Democrats are poised to do very well,” he said. “It’s still South Dakota, it’s still a red state. It’s been 50 years, but eventually, in my lifetime, I guarantee it’s going to happen, and why not now?”
The Democratic Party hasn’t held a majority in either chamber of the South Dakota Legislature since the 1990s. Democrats had eight members in the 105-member lawmaking body this year.
Ahlers said he’s ready to work with Republicans.
“People will tell you we just don’t share the same values. I don’t believe that,” Ahlers said. “I don’t know a single Republican that says, ‘I want a bad education system for my kids or grandkids.’ I don’t know a Republican that says, ‘I want terrible healthcare,’ or ‘I love potholes in my roads.’”
Education an ‘incredibly important’ part of platform
Ahlers spent parts of his childhood in Dell Rapids and Rapid City, before his family moved to Gillette, Wyoming, where he spent the majority of his younger years. As a student of the public school system, Ahlers said an eighth-grade civics class caught his attention.
“I was inspired by a group of people from different backgrounds, with different ideas, who were able to come together and create something special like this country,” he said. “I want to be part of that. I want to go out and make life better, and have a positive impact for people.”
He returned to Dell Rapids as a senior in high school, but his time as a student in Wyoming taught him that “we can do better with education,” he said. There, students had more opportunities in STEM, or to prepare for skilled labor jobs after high school, he said.
“Education is incredibly important to me,” Ahlers said. “I know that when people get a good quality education, regardless of their abilities, they are better off in life, and we’re all better off for it.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a student in the school lunch line, he remembers carrying a different lunch ticket from the kids around him, because he’d receive a reduced-price meal.
“We didn’t ask to be where we were financially. It was a recession,” Ahlers said. “But walking up with a different-colored ticket said somehow that I was less than other people.”
He doesn’t want South Dakota students to feel singled out at lunch time.
“I don’t think that families should be charged for school lunches at all. I don’t understand why we treat it like an extracurricular activity,” Ahlers said. “It’s part of the day, you’re required to be there. Why aren’t we just feeding them?”
South Dakota lawmakers this year approved spending about $600,000 annually to cover the family share of reduced-price meals for students enrolled in the federal program. The legislation came from a Sioux Falls Democrat, Rep. Kadyn Wittman.
Legislative victories like those, Ahlers said, come from a willingness — and a need — to work with the majority party in the Legislature.
Ahlers ‘willing to learn’
As a freshman lawmaker, Ahlers said he was excited to use what he’d studied in college. He looked to more experienced lawmakers, like Paul Dennert, a Democrat from Columbia who served as assistant minority leader.
“He came in as a young man, was awestruck, like everybody,” Dennert said of Ahlers. “But, he was that young businessman from Dell Rapids, and was willing to learn and willing to ask a lot of questions to get familiar with the process.”
Ahlers was a member of the joint budgeting committee as a state senator in 2009 and 2010, and during his latest term in the House from 2017 to 2018. Also on that panel was Republican former Rep. Hugh Bartels, of Watertown, who ultimately served as speaker of the House.
Though he won’t be voting for Ahlers in the governor race, Bartels remembers Ahlers’ work on the committee favorably.
“He worked across the aisle,” Bartels said. “He knew appropriations is one of those areas where there’s only so much money to go around, and he realized that as an appropriator, and worked to get things through.”

Democratic candidate for governor Dan Ahlers talks with Democratic voters during the 2026 McGovern Day Dinner in Sioux Falls on June 5, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)

Ahlers said most of his legislation came from constituents, including parents from the community who shared their concerns about their children enrolled in special education programs.
During his most recent House term, Ahlers sponsored successful legislation that created an advisory committee of parents, educators and experts to improve language development for children who are deaf or hard of hearing before they enter kindergarten.
The state Department of Education initially spoke in opposition to the legislation, and no members of the majority party signed on as co-sponsors. But Ahlers “did the footwork” to get it passed, according to former state legislator Julie Bartling, a Democrat from Gregory.
He brought in students who would be impacted by the changes and experts in education and advocacy to show how the changes could benefit students who are deaf or hard of hearing, Bartling said.
“It was really pretty neat to watch how he could just start from something so simple,” she said, “and just take it all the way to the top.”
Ahlers remembers the day then-Gov. Dennis Daugaard signed the bill, making South Dakota one of the first states in the nation to enact such a law.
“It was great. It was a good day for those families. It was a good day for bipartisanship,” he said. “That’s when you get the best of what government can offer, when you find those moments where we can all figure out how to work on things together.”
As he looks at the path ahead of him, Ahlers considers everything else in his life that was, at one point, an uphill battle: a college track career, long-lived businesses, a legislative race he wasn’t supposed to win.
“I think those types of challenges drive me,” Ahlers said. “When people say that there are things that we just can’t fix, things that are too far gone, I’m like, ‘No, I know that we can do it.’”
