name: Nevada Current
title: Land use, luxury developers, and Lake Tahoe’s future are on the ballot
description: Yosemite made headlines and raised concerns among legislators when word got out that a private Nevada-based developer has been lobbying the current administration to intervene with a ‘public-private’ ask: a park land transfer that would enable construction of a private road connection to the famed national park. This occurred as Yosemite battled problems wit[...]
text:
"Luxury developers are rushing to exploit nature with no opposition from leaders in either political party." (Photo courtesy Pamela Mahoney Tsigdinos)Yosemite made headlines and raised concerns among legislators when word got out that a private Nevada-based developer has been lobbying the current administration to intervene with a ‘public-private’ ask: a park land transfer that would enable construction of a private road connection to the famed national park. This occurred as Yosemite battled problems with visitation safety, overcrowding, vehicle congestion, and ongoing wildfire challenges.
Lake Tahoe, another iconic Sierra Nevada jewel, is under equally tremendous visitor strain and wildfire pressure. Encompassing two states and five counties, Lake Tahoe faces even greater development threats without a commensurate level of concern by the Nevada (or California) candidates who will exercise control over the Lake Tahoe basin. This matters because:

Of the nearly 56,000 people who call Tahoe home nearly 16,000 live on the Nevada side. 
Greater Reno-Tahoe’s permanent population is more than 550,000; adding in commuter regions like Carson City and Douglas and Lyon counties pushes the number closer to 650,000. 
According to the Reno-Sparks Convention and Visitors Authority, 57% of the 3.9 million overnight visitors to Reno in 2025 traveled up to visit Lake Tahoe during their trip, with Washoe Tahoe’s north shore (including Sand Harbor State Park) the most highly impacted.
A 2021 analysis of Tahoe visitation projected the 15+ million annual visitors will increase by 25% by 2035.

Who looks out for Tahoe’s public safety and land management?
The Nevada governor chairs the board that oversees administration of the Nevada Department of Transportation (including the dangerously overburdened evacuation corridors SR-28 and US-50). The governor also appoints a representative to the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA) Governing Board as well as appoints the Director of the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR), another TRPA board member. DCNR’s director appoints the State Forester Firewarden to head the Nevada Division of Forestry, which together oversee Nevada’s thousands of acres around Lake Tahoe. Further, the governor has broad emergency powers. The top executive has authority to formally declare a state of emergency or disaster, often necessary during increasingly severe wildfire seasons, major blizzards, or infrastructure failures across the state.
The Nevada Secretary of State, meanwhile, holds a permanent voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board, whereas the state’s Lieutenant Governor serves as Chair of the Nevada Commission on Tourism (Travel Nevada). The commission sets the direction for recreation infrastructure grants and state tourism marketing that affect Tahoe traffic and visitation. The Nevada Attorney General serves as legal counsel for Nevada state agencies (NDOT, DCNR, State Lands) operating in the Tahoe Basin. 
Then there’s Nevada’s Congressional District 2, which encompasses 100 percent of Nevada’s Tahoe Basin across Washoe and Douglas counties as well as the consolidated municipality of Carson City. Through the current, but retiring, CD2 representative’s pivotal seats on congressional committees, this office holds great influence over millions in federal appropriations under the Lake Tahoe Restoration Act and exercises oversight of the U.S. Forest Service’s Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit’s (LTBMU), particularly regarding wildfire mitigation and forest health funding. LTBMU’s public land, some 156,000 acres, is managed as a single interdependent administrative unit. About one-third of its acreage is in Nevada.
Nevada’s Legislative Committee for the Review and Oversight of TRPA and Marlette Lake exercises formal legislative oversight over TRPA operations, regulations, and state funding. Like each of the elected offices noted above, all but one of the committee’s current members are on the ballot this year.
Public lands in corporate hands
State and local leaders in Nevada (and California), to date, have mirrored the transactions-focused administration in the White House and the first family. This summer saw a bipartisan embrace of “public-private” exploitation at this year’s bi-state Tahoe Summit at Nevada’s Sand Harbor State Park. Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen, who emceed the annual event, made a little noticed Freudian slip that set the stage for the event. 
While attempting to acknowledge the federal and state tax-payer-funded TRPA, Rosen inadvertently asked the developer-funded Tahoe Fund to stand. (The fund’s key members were, after all, prominently seated in front.) The senator’s faux pas wasn’t entirely off base since this powerful private entity is a major force behind the now captured TRPA, once a leading conservation and environmental agency formed to look out for the lake’s unique environment. 
The Tahoe Fund’s board is stacked with multinational resort and real-estate investors and a who’s who of hospitality and private equity interests who stand to gain by furthering Tahoe development. Operating as a private matching-grant powerhouse, the fund plays a central role in paving over, trail-ifying, and luxurifying the once-pristine Tahoe shores to cater to high-net worth visitors. Their reach now extends to the region’s forests. Through a sawmill project (covered by Bloomberg), the fund has helped legitimize commercial timber extraction in the basin. While marketed as a climate-adaption triumph, this is an example of how private capital directs public land management, allowing developers to manage the forest to protect their nearby resort investments.  
You could almost hear echoes of Ivanka Trump’s infamous quote about developing an unspoiled natural landscape “to realize its potential.”
Not to be outdone, Nevada’s senior U.S. senator, Catherine Cortez-Masto, took her plaudits a step further, “We can’t celebrate the 30th anniversary of this summit without acknowledging the public-private partnerships that have been essential to our work. That’s what Team Tahoe is all about.”
Inconveniently for the politicians, the Bug and Stallion fires in nearby Reno raged during the Tahoe Summit, shining an unwelcome spotlight on Reno-Tahoe’s increasingly dangerous roadways and strained infrastructure amid the push for greater development and tourism amenities. Despite the many speeches and photo ops, there was no discussion about out-of-date evacuation plans, one of which notably fails to account for the many thousands of tourists crowding Nevada’s shores. Also absent was any mention of air, soil, and water pollution. Total silence, too, on the overwhelming public opposition to the TRPA allowing controversial chemicals like glyphosate around Tahoe. 
What’s bad for Yosemite is good for Lake Tahoe? 
Amid this cozy ‘private-public’ milieu, luxury developers are rushing to exploit nature with no opposition from leaders in either political party. The same Yosemite-adjacent developer seeking a shortcut through the national park is also actively working to create a cruise ship-sized development in Placer Tahoe Kings Beach on a narrow two-lane road adjoining Nevada and overlooking north Lake Tahoe. Incidentally, this Tahoe development sits on a heavily trafficked road, which is also the main evacuation route for the many thousands who visit or live around the lake. 
An infamous blighted property in Crystal Bay, Nevada, which has gone through multiple luxury developer misfires, is back in the spotlight. Utah-based developers are seeking a five-year extension to control four public roadways. In November, the developers will ask Washoe County to abandon its interest in 60,291 square feet of public right-of-way as part of a massive rework of the formerly TRPA approved Waldorf Astoria.  
Meanwhile, at the southern end of Nevada’s Tahoe east shore another luxury developer has rights to remove several hundred trees (some estimated to be between 120 and 130 years old) and convert nine acres of habitat for local wildlife into what has been promoted on social media as a year-round luxury resort and event center. The developer also advertised the “developed campsite” or “glamping” property as a “shovel-ready”’ joint venture opportunity with all entitlements. 
Local opposition continues to raise concerns about the project’s many misrepresentations, land use, wildfire evacuation concerns, pending environmental damage, and added congestion in an already heavily visited area.
The commercialization and exploitation of nature isn’t new. We can trace the systemic displacement of native people, despoiled land, and rapacious destruction of ecosystems over centuries. 
Developers first re-imagined the TRPA and helped alter its focus to suit their needs in the early 2000s. In 2010 the agency laid off scientists to make room for economically minded staff members who prioritize rewriting strict ordinances and codes to favor developers and greenlight once unthinkable incursions into environmentally sensitive areas. Rather than hire more scientists, the agency’s latest addition is a celebrated “storyteller.” 
TRPA’s executive director, an award-winning PR pro herself, needs a top spin-doctor for a new development-driven lobbying effort: an update to the once sacrosanct Santini-Burton Act. Passed in 1980, it allowed the U.S. Forest Service to acquire thousands of acres of environmentally sensitive areas to protect Lake Tahoe. As if suffering from amnesia, both Nevada senators and their California counterparts have forgotten that the original Act decades ago was to ensure this land would not be controlled by private developers. 
Land set aside by the Santini-Burton Act currently serves as critical safety buffers in the Tahoe basin — providing defensible space, emergency staging capacity, and protection against the cascading risks of high-density land use, explained one resident who wrote about the proposed updates to the Act. She noted that legislators must not turn the original intent of land use conservation on its head. “Modernization must not become a euphemism for dismantling its core purposes. A law designed to stop development pressure should not be repurposed to manage it.”
Cruise-ship model: Extraction tourism
The fight to ensure more natural lands don’t fall under the control of corporate hospitality interests is practically a full-time occupation for volunteer grassroots groups within the Tahoe basin. 
Douglas Tahoe resident Elisabeth Lernhardt at a recent Nevada legislative meeting described Tahoe as the latest in “extraction-style tourism” and likened it to the cruise-ship industry: “The same interests own the ships, the ports, the shops, and the restaurants. The profits leave; the costs stay behind.”
Near Washoe County’s Tahoe watershed, local resident Steve Dolan with Friends of Third Creek has been actively involved in meadow restoration projects. He’s also monitoring the return of native beavers aiding in the repopulation of habitat attractive to the once over-fished Lahontan Cutthroat Trout. His latest concern is a determined push by tourism interests to disrupt the restoration work to make way for a new parking lot to accommodate visitors in the winter months.
“There’s a limit to what this beautiful emerald of the Sierra can accommodate,” he said. “There’s just a limit.”
Nevada officials owe their constituents some answers about Lake Tahoe’s future. One thing is for certain: the “story-telling” to justify all the development will continue.

title: Attorney passed over by judicial selection panel faces hearing master in election
description: Attorney Kristine Brewer, who came in first in June in the primary race for Clark County Family Court Department S, is not responding to questions about the Nevada Judicial Selection Commission subsequently passing on appointing her, the sole applicant, to the seat.  Brewer garnered just under 48% of the vote in the three-way primary, with […]
text:
Kristina Brewer, Randall Forman. (Candidate photos)Attorney Kristine Brewer, who came in first in June in the primary race for Clark County Family Court Department S, is not responding to questions about the Nevada Judicial Selection Commission subsequently passing on appointing her, the sole applicant, to the seat. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]Brewer garnered just under 48% of the vote in the three-way primary, with Hearing Master Randall Forman coming in second with 39%. 
A month later, Judge Vincent Ochoa announced he was retiring early, creating an immediate vacancy in Department S. 
The Nevada Commission on Judicial Selection announced in late July it was declining her application, leaving the seat vacant until voters decide in November. 
“Following its consideration of the applicant, the Commission declined to forward the candidate to Governor Joe Lombardo for appointment,” says a statement posted in July on the commission’s website. 
The move is unusual, as the governor routinely appoints candidates to the bench who are on the ballot at the time of their appointment. In June 2024, Lombardo appointed Tina Talim to the bench. She was elected to the post in November. 
The Nevada Constitution requires that the governor, presented with recommendations from the commission, fill a judicial vacancy within 30 days. However, the commission is not required to submit recommendations in the event there are no suitable applicants. 
It’s unknown why the panel declined to appoint Brewer. 
Federal bankruptcy court records indicate Brewer and her husband, Robert Blau, filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in November of 2025, citing assets ranging from $50,000 to $100,000, and liabilities between $100,000 and $500,000. 
Brewer, who spoke with the Current before the primary election, has not responded since. Her campaign consultant, Steve Sanson of Veterans in Politics, also did not respond to requests for comment. 
Forman says he considered applying for the appointment but decided against it, knowing that if he won but lost the election, he’d have to reapply as a hearing master. 
“That’s a pretty big risk to me,” he told the Current. “I like having a job, so I decided not to put in for that appointment.”
Department S hears divorce and child custody cases. 
Forman, who earned his law degree from UNLV’s Boyd Law School, spent 15 years in private practice, and has been a hearing master for five years, hearing juvenile delinquency cases and issuing domestic violence protective orders. 
This is Forman’s second run for the bench. He lost in the primary race for Dept. Z in 2020.  
He is endorsed by Culinary Local 226, SEIU Nevada, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, Laborers Local 870 and other labor organizations.
As of July, he’d raised just under $19,000 and had $5,000 in the bank.
Brewer received her law degree from Thomas Jefferson School of Law in San Diego.  She currently works for Leavitt Family Law Group. She says she’s practiced almost exclusively in family law since 2004. 
This is her third run for Family Court. She lost in the 2014 primary, and in a 2022 special election.  In addition to her 2026 application for appointment to the bench, she applied unsuccessfully in 2023. 
Brewer’s website lists endorsements from half a dozen individuals, including Nevada System of Higher Education Regent Patrick Boylan, who is known for making anti-transgender remarks. 
According to Our Nevada Judges, a website that tracks judges and judicial candidates, Brewer is also endorsed by Veterans in Politics, which is run by her campaign consultant Sanson. 
As of July, Brewer had raised roughly $19,000, including a personal loan of $11,000, and spent $24,000.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: In debate, Utah Rep. Kennedy says he’s ‘just getting started’ while Dem calls him a ‘lap dog’
description: Rep. Mike Kennedy defended his first term in Congress as Democratic challenger sought to cast him as a “lap dog” to the Trump administration.
text:
Candidates for Utah’s 4th Congressional District Democrat Jonny Larsen, left, and Republican Mike Kennedy participate in a debate at Snow College in Ephraim on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy defended his first term in Congress Thursday as his Democratic challenger cast the race for Utah’s 4th Congressional District as a choice between a “blue dog” or a “lap dog” to the Trump administration. 
Kennedy and Democrat Jonny Larsen met on the debate stage at Snow College in rural Sanpete County, sparring over issues including the Iran War, public lands and immigration enforcement. The debate was hosted by the Utah Debate Commission, moderated by Doug Wilks with the Deseret News and broadcast by PBS Utah.
The candidates are vying to represent a newly drawn, mostly rural and heavily Republican district covering the entirety of Tooele, Juab, Millard, Sanpete and Sevier counties, along with portions of southern Salt Lake and western Utah counties.



Kennedy, now representing Utah’s current 3rd House District under the state’s previous congressional boundaries, said he’s“just getting started making Washington smaller and Utah stronger.” 
Larsen pitched himself as a moderate Democrat focused on issues of fiscal responsibility and national security.
“We should be working on the 90% of issues that we all agree on instead of fighting over the 10% that we don’t,” Larsen said in his closing statement. “So I’d like to ask you: ‘Would you like a ‘blue dog’ or a lap dog to this administration?”
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

Kennedy didn’t directly respond to the characterization, focusing his closing remarks on Utah’s pioneer history and saying, “We have the opportunity to work together to build a brighter future here in this state.He told reporters after the debate that he’s worked with Democrats on eight bills he’s sponsored that have won approval from the U.S. House. 
“Every one of them is a collaborative effort with my Democrat colleagues,” Kennedy said. 
When asked during the debate about the cost of gas, Larsen condemned the Iran War, saying “we absolutely need to end this illegal war to bring order back” and drive down fuel prices. 
He criticized Kennedy for voting repeatedly against a war powers resolution that would stop the president from continuing military action without the approval of Congress. 
“As a veteran myself, who did two tours in combat, I understand that cost, and that price that we pay with American blood.”
Candidates for Utah’s 4th Congressional District Democrat Jonny Larsen, left, and Republican Mike Kennedy participate in a debate at Snow College in Ephraim on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)
Kennedy said he’s proud of President Donald Trump’s actions against Iran. 
 “They have to be dealt with. And I recognize that there’s pain in the short run, but there will be significant gain in the long run,” Kennedy said. He added that “to tie the president’s hands in the middle of a national security crisis is not the right thing for us to do.” 
Kennedy said he sponsored legislation that could help drive down gas prices called the License to Drill Act, which seeks to extend federal oil and gas permitting fees.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
When it comes to efforts to sell or transfer public land into private hands, Kennedy said, “there is an opportunity for us to use those lands in a responsible fashion.” He said he’s in favor of allowing a community with small tracts of land that are federally controlled to use those parcels for developing homes. 
Larsen disagreed, saying he’s concerned about mining, drilling, and effects of those projects on groundwater in rural areas. 
“Let’s not ruin the water supply that we are so desperately in need of right now, and protect our public lands for our indigenous people and tribes who absolutely deserve that,” Larsen said. 
He called U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s operations “very sinister.”
“Recently, within this own county, there was a turkey farm that was raided,” Larsen said, referring to reports that ICE officers detained people at a turkey processing plant in Moroni. “Families were separated. How can we do that and still say we have family values?” 
Kennedy said the first focus of federal immigration enforcement should be criminals and as a result of Trump’s policies at the U.S. border, “our citizens are safer. The second thing is we need to make legal immigration easier, and I’m dedicated to that.” 
While answering a question about energy during the debate, Larsen stopped speaking and said he lost his train of thought. He declined to finish his answer in that moment but returned to the topic later in the debate, calling the lapse a “brain fart.” 
Libertarian Taylor Wright and unaffiliated candidate Steven Burt are also competing for the 4th Congressional District, but they didn’t qualify for the debate stage based on a poll commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission.
Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: What on Earth is going on in Newark schools?
description: A new state audit reveals some troubling things about Newark’s school district. Are state officials paying attention?
text:
A new state audit reveals some troubling things about Newark’s school district. Are state officials paying attention? (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Newark’s school district is coming under intense criticism in recent days because of a damning state audit report that found evidence school officials wasted taxpayer dollars and inflated enrollment numbers to win more state aid.
Even worse, some unnamed matters have been referred to the state’s criminal justice division.
If you haven’t read about the audit, here are some of the findings:

The school district could have saved $18.7 million over two years by switching to the state’s health benefits program for public workers, but did not do so.
It did not perform criminal background checks for as many as 10 employees and did not make sure updated background checks were performed for another 199 district workers.
The district has spent $2.5 million to turn a district-owned property — one it agreed to sell in 2016 when it was under state control and then reacquired years later — into a museum, a project that “shows little progress.”
It also spent $566,000 to build, equip, and operate a gym in an administrative building that is used by an average of seven people a day.

The audit is bad enough. The school district’s response is loony.
“The state audit report concludes that the district’s financial transactions were properly recorded in the accounting systems, were related to the district’s programs, and were reasonable,” the district said in a press release.
That is indeed the beginning of the audit’s conclusion. But the very next sentence adds that there are multiple areas that merit school officials’ attention, including the millions in spending to build a museum and hundreds of thousands for a barely used gym, and the audit also says, again, that certain matters were referred to the state’s division of criminal justice. This is not good news for New Jersey’s largest school district and it’s hardly a moment for school officials there to crow.
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia, a Sussex County Republican and charter school administrator, said she thinks the audit shows that the state needs to take the district over again. The state relinquished control in 2017 after 22 years.
The district’s superintendent, Roger Leòn, is “absolutely out of control,” she said.
“Not only am I pissed off to all hell because my school districts up in cowtown get the shaft, I’m pissed off because I’ve been working with kids in urban areas for 19 years. I’ve been in Paterson. I’ve been in Jersey City. I’ve been in Kearny. I’ve been in the city of Passaic. I’ve been in Garfield. That’s where our charter schools are. We even have a school in the Bronx. I have been working with this population of kids and families for 19 years. And this guy is a special kind of special to exploit what those kids and their families need and literally bleeding the state dry,” she said.
Why León will remain Newark’s superintendent for four more years is itself worth investigating. The city’s school board in September 2025 rejected a move to extend his contract after parents raised concerns about student achievement and more. The vote fell one short of the necessary tally to keep León past June 2028.
Then in October, a board member who had initially abstained from voting on the contract extension had a sudden change of heart, and the board’s president, Hasani Council, decided that meant that León’s contract had been extended after all, as reported by Chalkbeat Newark. The board didn’t even take another vote. Just, poof!, contract renewed to 2030.
“I don’t know what this spell is that this man has over this district, what deals he’s worked out,” Fantasia said.
At the time of the apparent contract renewal, I asked the state Department of Education whether it was legal for a school board to renew a superintendent’s contract without voting on it. Spokeswoman Diana Pasculli said, “The New Jersey Department of Education cannot publicly comment on local school board matters.” The state can indeed comment on local school board matters; it just won’t.
Assemblywoman Vicky Flynn, a Monmouth County Republican and former school board member, wants heads to roll. When I asked her whose, she said, “Everyone — Roger Leon and up.”
 “Where is the state? They allowed this to go on, too, they share some accountability. The county superintendent, where are they?” Flynn said.
I asked the county superintendent, Joseph Zarra, to comment and he referred me to the Department of Education, which provided me with a substance-free statement that says nothing about the audit’s conclusions.
“The Commissioner firmly believes every student deserves access to the opportunities, resources and support they need to succeed, and that an effective public education system delivers this with a focus on strong academic foundations alongside responsible stewardship of public investment. That commitment is guiding the Department’s statewide school funding outreach, which is bringing together stakeholders from across New Jersey to help advance a funding system that is more transparent, predictable, accountable and sustainable while putting students first,” said spokeswoman Cecilia Williams.
I didn’t ask about changes to the state’s funding formula, which has nothing to do with Newark’s current troubles. But I think this shows that the state’s reaction to all this is, at least for the time being, to stick their fingers in their ears.
Newark school district spokesman Paul Brubaker said the district’s critics are using the audit to “tell a story other than the truth.”
“The truth is that Newark Public Schools has done more with less, and we have the receipts to prove it. The district has earned local, state, and national recognition based on multiple measures of achievement and progress. Annual independent audits comprehensively examine our finances, which are in order. And when communities are in crisis, they deserve leadership from their elected officials — not abdication of duty, deflection of responsibility, and repetition of the same old bitter, twisted lies,” he said.
Brubaker said the district is reviewing the report’s recommendations.
Newark schools may be showing incremental improvement, but test scores are abysmal. State data shows the district’s English language arts proficiency rate is 34%. For math, it’s 22%. Those same numbers statewide are 53% and 42%. Just 11% of Newark students are deemed proficient on a science assessment, compared to 27% for the state. Sixty-seven percent of the district’s 11th graders are graduation-ready in language arts (statewide, the number is 81%) and 40% in math (59% statewide).
None of this is going to be helped by a district museum or a gym for its administrators. I don’t think a state takeover would help either, because it didn’t the last time. It might be helped by a state government more interested in examining the district’s failures and trying to correct them. I’m not sure we have one of those at the moment.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Senate battleground pits Jon Patterson against Keri Ingle in Jackson County
description: LEE’S SUMMIT — Marching up and down the front steps of split level homes in a Lee’s Summit neighborhood on a recent Monday evening, Democratic state Rep. Keri Ingle was not the first to tell residents about the upcoming election. As her bright pink tennis shoes reached the stoop of the first house on her […]
text:
State Rep. Keri Ingle and House Speaker Jon Patterson are running in the Missouri Senate's 8th District. The race is one of two eyed statewide for its potential to turn a historically Republican seat blue. (Photos provided by candidates' campaigns)LEE’S SUMMIT — Marching up and down the front steps of split level homes in a Lee’s Summit neighborhood on a recent Monday evening, Democratic state Rep. Keri Ingle was not the first to tell residents about the upcoming election.
As her bright pink tennis shoes reached the stoop of the first house on her list, she saw a postcard with the face of House Speaker Jon Patterson — the Republican she is trying to defeat for Missouri’s 8th Senate District seat.
“We need a proven commonsense leader to defend our liberties and get things done. I am prepared to be a voice for hardworking families in the Missouri Senate,” the card reads alongside a photo of Patterson in a white doctor’s coat.
That both campaigns had already found their way to the same front porch was a small sign of how heavily contested the district has become. Ingle and Patterson are fighting for many of the same suburban Jackson County voters in one of the state’s few competitive Senate races, with millions of dollars and the fate of the Republican supermajority hanging over the contest.
Patterson, a former general surgeon who left the medical field a few years after entering the General Assembly, labels himself an “independent voice” on his campaign’s website, highlighting times he has broken with the Republican majority.
“I have not always voted along party lines,” he said in an interview with The Independent. “When I think there is something important, I’m willing to take the lead and vote how I think the district would want me to vote and what I think is best for the district and for Missouri as a whole.”
Last year, Patterson was one of 13 Republicans who voted against a plan to redraw the state’s congressional districts. The new map, which would have split Jackson County among three congressional districts, was ultimately blocked from use in this year’s election after a prolonged state and federal court fight. 
“I’ve been very clear on this from the beginning. I don’t think it’s a good idea,” Patterson said. “I would not support chopping Jackson County in three and having Kansas City be represented by someone from, potentially, Columbia.”
House Speaker Jon Patterson, a Lee’s Summit Republican, speaks at a press conference at the end of special session on June 11, 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
As speaker of the House, Patterson can prevent legislation from reaching the floor. But he said voters shouldn’t assume every measure passed by the chamber reflects his own views.
“For me to unilaterally veto things that a supermajority of the legislature wants, I don’t think would be appropriate,” he said. “In those cases, I just lead by example. I can go out, vote for my district, speak for what I think is right and have my vote.”
The 8th District covers much of eastern Jackson County, including, including the suburban cities of Blue Springs and Lee’s Summit, and stretches into Lone Jack, a city with more of a rural feel.
Alongside a Springfield-area race, the district is one of two Senate seats Democrats are targeting for a potential pickup. Winning both would cost Republicans their two-thirds supermajority in the chamber.
The race is also the most expensive among the 17 state Senate seats up for grabs, with television ad buys supporting the two candidates exceeding $1.6 million by the end of September.
Coming out of the Aug. 4 primary, Patterson had over $2.9 million on hand between his campaign and his candidate committee, according to Missouri Ethics Commission filings. Ingle had just over $500,000.
Despite the fundraising disparity, Ingle — who flipped her House seat when she was elected in 2018 — believes she has a strong chance.
“We’ve got the ground game,” she told The Independent. “We are talking to voters every single day about what matters to them and how to best reflect their values in Jefferson City.”
By late September, Ingle and a team of volunteers had reached 24,000 homes and planned to knock on 20,000 more doors before November. Patterson had his own coalition too, including former state Rep. Dan Stacy, who challenged him in the Republican primary.
Outside groups are also pouring money and manpower into the district. Americans for Prosperity, a conservative advocacy group, has spent nearly $90,000 in ads and canvassing for Patterson, according to Missouri Ethics Commission filings. A political action committee with ties to pro-labor groups called Will of the People PAC spent about $68,000 on pro-Ingle messaging as of its Sept. 3 filing.
Ingle told The Independent that outside organizations had committed to reaching 100,000 doors. As she walked down Magnolia Street late last month, there were signs some had already arrived: a pro-Ingle door tag sat in a flower bed at one home on her route.
 Taxes and schools

The 8th District seat has not been held by a Democrat in the past two decades, but Ingle believes the district has “moved considerably” to the left.
In the Aug. 4 primary, 17,000 voters pulled Republican ballots and voted for either Patterson or Stacy. Over 21,000 voted for Ingle on the Democratic ballot.
In the 2024 presidential election, a precinct-level analysis shows that approximately 51.7% of the 8th District voted for Donald Trump, compared to 58.5% statewide. And favor may be slipping.
A recent St. Louis University/YouGov poll found Trump and Gov. Mike Kehoe with net-negative approval ratings statewide.
The poll was administered around the time of the August primary election, when voters overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to phase out the state’s income tax with 83% opposed.
Progressive groups have put a spotlight on Patterson for championing and being one of the original sponsors of the proposal in the House. An ad by Will of the People dubbed him “Pay-More Patterson,” saying he “tried to play us with the Everything Tax.”
Following the ballot measure’s failure, Kehoe released a statement that the “work is far from over.” When asked if he would support a do-over, Patterson did not rule it out. Instead, he said the defeat offered a lesson.
“Voters are willing to look at things, but they want to know what it is going to be, how much and what is it going toward,” he said.
Patterson also said the amendment’s resounding defeat suggests voters are comfortable with current rates.
“I think that means that they are somewhat satisfied with the current system,” he said, pointing to tax cuts passed in 2022.
The cuts reduced the state’s top income tax rate from 5.3% to 4.95% in 2023 with a series of triggers that brought the rate down to 4.7% in 2025. The state’s fiscal analyses in 2022 predicted a loss of $764 million in general revenue annually.
Patterson voted in favor of the proposal in 2022. Ingle was absent from the vote with a health emergency.
In 2025, state lawmakers passed an additional cut, becoming the first state to repeal capital gains tax at an estimated cost of $625 million. Patterson voted in favor of the proposal while Ingle rejected it.
Pandemic-related economic conditions masked the effects of tax cuts, the liberal Missouri Budget Project wrote in July — but the state is beginning to feel the loss.
In June, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick warned that “the state is on track to completely run out of money in the (general revenue fund) and be forced to implement emergency budget reductions.”
“(Missouri Republicans) were spending beyond their means and then they were cutting taxes, knowing that those were one-time funds that they were relying upon,” Ingle said. “Now they are saying, ‘This is a crisis. We need to cut from public education.’ Well, it is a crisis you created, so you should be held responsible for it as well.”
In recent years, the cost of the formula that determines the amount of state aid for public schools has risen, and state lawmakers have declined to keep up with its growth. The budget passed by lawmakers in May underfunds the formula by $190 million, a budget Patterson voted in favor of and Ingle opposed.
Patterson told the Independent that he’s confident the local school districts are still “funded well,” and he wouldn’t support funding schemes that put too much pressure on local schools. But with the state facing potential budget reductions across the board, he thinks schools should find ways to scale back.
“I think the schools need to be more like businesses. When there is not enough money, they should first look at becoming more efficient before saying that somebody should give them more funding,” he said.
Lee’s Summit R-7 School District’s Tony L. Stansberry Leadership Center, as photographed December 30, 2022 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Last week, the Lee’s Summit School District’s board of education considered how to cut costs amid budget pressures from several directions. The board voted to claw back some of a voluntary operating levy rollback.
“The reality is that decisions made at the county level and some by some of our elected officials in Jefferson City have created a situation where our students, our staff and our community are paying the price,” said board Vice President Erica Miller. “Our district has been tasked with trying to make sense of a broken system.”
Voters in the Blue Springs and Lee’s Summit school districts seem to support investing in public schools and have a history of approving bond measures and levy transfers with a strong majority.
But local voters are far from writing a blank check to school districts. In 2011, voters in the Lee’s Summit School District turned down a proposed operating tax levy increase of 89 cents per $100 of assessed valuation.
Education is central to Ingle’s pitch to voters. The first impression of her campaign website is the bolded words: “lower costs, quality schools, strong communities.”
She has been one of the House’s most vocal opponents of the state’s voucher program, which uses state tax dollars to pay for private education and homeschooling expenses.
“I am not against private schools and private education,” she said. “I just don’t think they should be getting state funding.”
Patterson, by contrast, says vouchers are “a worthy investment” taking a “fraction of what we spend for the public school fund.”
“I think there is a lot of support for just getting kids the education they need, regardless of whether it is in public school, private school, homeschool, virtual school or a homeschool co-op,” he said.
There are 444 students currently receiving voucher funding in the eighth district, according to a St. Louis University PRiME Center report prepared for the State Treasurer’s Office. Over 32,000 students attend Lee’s Summit and Blue Springs public schools.
 Priorities

The race, while competitive, has strayed from personal attacks — though Ingle notes it has been a “bloodbath” with jabs at each other’s voting records.
Patterson’s campaign centers “property tax relief” as a priority, with him looking to lighten the burden of rising assessments. He sees potential in a property tax package that failed in the final hours of this year’s legislative session.
Rep. Keri Ingle speaks during House debate March 27, 2025 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Ingle was one of 61 in the House to reject the measure, though she had voted in favor of some of its elements in a separate bill. She also voted in favor of a bill in 2023 that allowed counties to freeze property tax rates for seniors.
“His attacks on me are me voting against property tax reform bills, which yeah, you’re right, I did,” she said. “Property taxes are what fund our law enforcement, our fire departments and what fund our schools.”
Beyond voting records, Patterson’s campaign has emphasized his humble beginnings and his adoption at age six. His parents raised him in Blue Springs, and he has made his family’s home in Lee’s Summit, giving him strong connections to the district’s largest municipalities.
“I’ve got a good perspective about the district because I’ve known both and I’ve lived in both and have been a part of both communities,” he said.
Ingle, raised in a military family, was accustomed to moving around before she settled in Lee’s Summit 17 years ago.
Before entering politics, she was a social worker and worked in child welfare in the Jackson County Children’s Division. She saw systemic problems, hopeful she could be part of the solution.
“When I look at pieces of legislation, I always view it through the lens of how this will impact the most vulnerable Missourians,” she said. “What will the impact be on someone who is on a fixed income that is maybe dealing with a disability or any manner of things?”
Both campaigns have drawn support from major interest groups. Ingle is endorsed by the Greater Kansas City AFL-CIO, the Missouri State Teachers Association and the Missouri State Council of Fire Fighters.
Patterson has endorsements from the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Missouri Fraternal Order of Police and the Missouri State Medical Association, among others.
Missouri Right to Life, an anti-abortion advocacy organization, declined to endorse a candidate in the eighth district.
Patterson, who says he wants to “make Missouri as pro-life of a state as it can be,” has spoken against a measure on November’s ballots that would make abortion illegal in Missouri with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and for survivors of rape or incest who end the pregnancy in the first 12 weeks.
Patterson said the rape and incest exception is too narrow.
“If you look at a state like Virginia, which has a 15-week limit exception for rape and incest, I think that’s the kind of place I would like to see us,” he said. “I think we’re getting there through the ballot process.”
Ingle does not think abortion should be further restricted in Missouri and has the support of abortion-rights groups like Planned Parenthood Great Plains.
Despite wide differences in positions on abortion and taxation, the two have some common ground.
Both co-sponsored legislation that would have created tax credit programs to expand access to child care. The proposal garnered wide support from Democrats and won over around half of House Republicans but ultimately stalled in the Senate this year.
Patterson believes his ability to find compromise between parties will be an asset to the Senate, which negotiates more and tends to move larger packages of legislation than the House.
“There are different constituencies that you have to work with other members, so that’s what I would really focus on: having good relationships, and doing things that are good for the district and not necessarily being in all the food fights,” he said.
If elected to the Senate, Patterson plans to mirror some of the style of the 8th District’s current Senator, Mike Cierpiot, a Lee’s Summit Republican.
Patterson filled Cierpiot’s House seat in 2018 and Cierpiot and his wife, Connie, mentors.
Cierpiot rarely participated in filibusters and largely negotiated behind the scenes. He wasn’t one for flashy disagreements on the Senate floor, though he did feud with the chamber’s far-right “Freedom Caucus” calling the group a “clown show” on one occasion.
Ingle has cultivated a different legislative style.  In the House, Ingle has routinely called out Republicans with accusatory and sometimes emotional floor speeches.
When some Republicans opposed a bill that sought to make child marriage illegal in Missouri in 2025, she said they “should be ashamed.”
“I am sick and tired of this body saying that kids, children need to be protected, but let’s force them to get married,” she said.
On the campaign trail last week, Ingle met voters with a softer side, asking how she could help.
One woman, who was initially hesitant to answer the door, said she just wanted someone who listens.
“I just want the people who are elected to take the concerns of the citizens as important,” she said.
Ingle told her she will “uphold the will of the people always.”
“That’s what we’re looking for.”

title: The Cornell case forced me to confront the sexual assault I buried for decades
description: I am Jane Doe. I was a freshman in college, second semester, when I got a call from my mom that my dad was in the hospital. I should find my older brother and we should come home. In the hour and a half it took me to locate my brother on campus (landlines, kids), […]
text:
Hundreds of Cornell students participate in a rally against the university’s actions after a student was sexually assaulted at a campus fraternity in 2024, on Oct. 5 in Ithaca, New York. The student, who is only being identified as Jane Doe, has alleged she was gang-raped inside the Chi Phi frat house in 2024 (Spencer Platt/Getty Images).I am Jane Doe.
I was a freshman in college, second semester, when I got a call from my mom that my dad was in the hospital. I should find my older brother and we should come home. In the hour and a half it took me to locate my brother on campus (landlines, kids), my father had ceased to be.
It was a Thursday. Valentine’s Day, 1985. My dad’s memorial was on the following Sunday and afterward we just… went back to school.
I did not weather it well.
I had never been a drinker in high school. I was a lame, in-the-band, desperate-to-be-accepted-but-never-actually-belonged geek of a thing. A goody-goody. But at college, alcohol was so accessible and I loved to dance. I had become a little sister at a fraternity and found a group of friends there that I had so much – too much – fun with in my first semester.
(It has to be said, though, I never missed my 8 a.m., four-days-a-week math class, no matter how scuzzy I felt.)
It was that second semester, though, the semester I lost my dad, that things went off the rails. I drank too much, cried too often, let my grades slip. Became an even bigger disappointment to my mom. And I was not a fun drunk.
It was during this time, during what amounted to a teary therapy session with one of the fraternity brothers, the person I probably trusted more than any other at that house, that I became Jane Doe.
I have a propensity for flying my so-called “dirty laundry” at full staff. Friends know about my unsuccessful relationships, my failed pregnancies and my work screw-ups – like the time I nervously asked Lee Greenwood what inspired him to write “God Bless America.” But I never shared this.
NEVER.
But it’s not my dirty laundry. It’s HIS. This man saw a vulnerable grieving person on the verge of being blackout drunk, and forced himself on her. Forced himself on ME. I protested the entire time, told him I didn’t feel “that way” about him, but it didn’t matter.
I was already crying when he started, but I remember crying harder.
I remember it feeling like an out-of-body experience, and as if I could not control my limbs. It never even occurred to me until recently that I might have been drugged. I’ll never know. We were sitting on a couch in a dark living room as a party raged downstairs and then I was on the floor, a floor covered in a color popular in the 1960s of sculpted wall-to-wall carpet that I would fundraise to replace in later years. My red shorts jumpsuit was down around my thighs and he was on top of me, grunting.
At some point the overhead light was flipped on, a man saw us on the floor, said “oops,” turned the light off and departed. I have wanted to assume he did not see my tears, hear me pleading for the man to stop or realize that the arms of a woman engaged in consensual sex might be embracing her companion as opposed to lying akimbo. But that’s not really a luxury I have any more.
After this happened, I continued to exist at school and as a little sister at that fraternity until I graduated. I just went on. I buried it. Because it was my fault, right? Because that’s just what you did, I guess?
My perpetrator – and that’s what he was (is) – was a man who everyone I knew would have described as “a really good guy.” I wonder if he even knows that what he did was wrong. Does he even remember?
I assume this is why the Cornell rape case — and the woman identified as Jane Doe at the center of it — has begun to plague me. I am doing everything I can to erase this man’s name and face from my memory, but suddenly it’s like he’s in the room with me all the time. I can’t escape him.
I’m almost certain I never cross his mind.
Maybe I’m wrong. Maybe the Cornell case has caused him to be haunted by my cries for him to stop. Maybe mine is the first face he sees in the morning and the last face he sees at night. Maybe he – a person I trusted implicitly – is consumed by regret for the harm he did to me.
But I bet not.
We are so trained to blame victims that I’ve blamed myself all these years. I just chalked it up to one of my many mistakes. But while we tell girls from an early age how to protect ourselves from assault, I fear we are neglecting to teach boys how not to assault.
We really need to fix this.
I never saw this man after he graduated. I am not connected with him on any social media, but I do maintain contact with a few folks from my college days who are. Would they believe me if I told them what happened?
I mean, he’s just such a good guy.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: How big a deal is the red-dyed diesel directive?
description: LINCOLN — Sixth-generation Nebraska farmer John Hansen leaned into baseball lingo to describe his take on dual diesel directives by President Donald Trump and Gov. Jim Pillen. He compared the impact to a bunt single. The swing was less than full and the outcome far from a home run, he said. “It’s somewhat helpful but small […]
text:
President Donald Trump tosses the pen he used to sign a new executive order just moments before waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. At left is one of his aides, Natalie Harp. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Sixth-generation Nebraska farmer John Hansen leaned into baseball lingo to describe his take on dual diesel directives by President Donald Trump and Gov. Jim Pillen. He compared the impact to a bunt single.
The swing was less than full and the outcome far from a home run, he said.
“It’s somewhat helpful but small in scale by far,” said Hansen, whose leadership of the Nebraska Farmers Union spans nearly 40 years. “We’ve got a much bigger hole to fill.”
A fuel pump on June 23, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Hansen said Trump’s executive order struck out in addressing “underlying systemic” issues,  including rising base fuel costs, tariffs, trade and other policies he said are driving up expenses and threatening the economic health of farmers and ranchers.
He and others interviewed about the diesel directives said they have lingering questions and were still trying to get a grip on apparent relief set to expire in a few months. Many saw the president’s move to temporarily (through December) allow use of untaxed red-dyed diesel for “any reason” — beyond the typical restricted use in farmland and construction equipment — as more of a break, in the short run, for long-haul commercial truckers. 
But the Nebraska Trucking Association, which represents roughly 900 companies, was skeptical and is cautioning members and partners not to fill up with the untaxed, tinted diesel fuel. 
“We’re being very clear,” said Kent Grisham, president and CEO of the state network. “Do not put dyed diesel in your tanks — at least not yet.”
 Ambiguity, concern

Grisham said he and industry colleagues see “a lot of ambiguity” in who can benefit from the federal directive and how it would work. 
However, he said they applaud the president’s attempt to find temporary relief, as “the world moves on diesel.”
“Every supply chain is diesel-powered, from the ships that cross the ocean to the trains that haul commodities to the trucks that move 88% of the tonnage in the state of Nebraska,” Grisham said. “So when the price of diesel is setting record levels, all of that is going to get into the pockets of you and me and everybody else.”
When announcing the diesel directive earlier this week in Grand Island, amid Midwestern farm and ag workers reeling from spiking diesel prices, Trump remarked that the action should cinch the elections of fellow Republicans Pillen and U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts. 
But as described in White House documents, details are yet to be hammered out by the secretary of the Treasury. The presidential action seeks to “defer” until later the payment of the federal diesel fuel tax without penalties, interest or addition to the tax. It tells the secretary to “explore” avenues that might eliminate, or forgive, the obligation to pay the postponed amount. The standard federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
A couple of weeks earlier, Pillen announced his own order to refund Nebraska’s state diesel tax — that’s 31.8 cents per gallon — on clear/undyed diesel fuel used during a similar 90-day period if the load being transported from field to market or storage involved Nebraska sourced commercial ag products. 
Intended as relief during harvest time, the Pillen directive also allowed the tax-free red-dyed diesel to be used for ag purposes on state public roads without penalty through December. Regular diesel mixed with a tint of red dye is meant to alert law enforcement if “off-road” fuel is being used unlawfully. 
 ‘Nothing burger’ vs. ‘welcome relief’ 

Kent Green, who farms about 3,000 acres in the Alliance area, said he hires five truckers who use clear diesel fuel to transport his sugar beet harvest to town. 
Green figures the combined executive orders could potentially result in a tax  savings of as much as 56 cents a gallon on roughly $6-per-gallon diesel during the few-month period. So far, he said, the contracted truckers haven’t bumped up the fees they charge Green.
“Maybe it’s been helpful to me in that way,” he said. But he called the relief short-lived, if at all.
“Taxes are like a balloon: You push on one side, it pushes on the other,” Green said, noting that clear diesel state tax revenues go to the Highway Fund to help take care of public roads and bridges.
Becky Potmesil and husband Scott raise calves and own or lease several thousand acres of ranchland around Alliance. She said tractors and machinery used on their property already were exempt from taxes and Potmesil viewed the president’s directive as a big “nothing burger.”
“It’s just a lot of noise,” Potmesil said, noting that she paid rising base diesel prices throughout the summer.




Quotation







It’s just a lot of noise.


– Becky Potmesil, rancher in the Alliance area



The Trump diesel order said that where states match his federal action, savings could “top $100 per fill, a real difference for the hardworking Americans who haul the freight and grow the food.”
Some groups reacted with glee. The president of the American Farm Bureau Federation earlier this week applauded the executive order to ease limits on the use of tax-exempt dyed diesel fuel.
“Allowing dyed diesel fuel to be used over-the-road will bring welcome relief for farmers because every cent per gallon matters when you’re running a fleet of grain trucks or hauling cattle hundreds of miles,” Zippy Duvall said in a statement.
The White House touted support from groups including the Alabama Farmers Federation, the Tennessee Farm Bureau Federation and the Louisiana Farm Bureau president.
“With about a dozen states easing enforcement of off-road diesel rules, President Trump’s executive order provides consistency across the country and ensures farmers and timber producers will not be penalized when they cross state lines to market their products,” said Alabama Farmers Federation president Jimmy Parnell in a statement.
Duvall noted a letter the national group sent to Trump last week, calling for efforts that would bring price relief for farmers as they complete harvest. The group underscored challenges, including that the national average on-highway diesel price had reached $6.38 per gallon. 
 ‘Don’t do it’ 

Sam Bradley, president of the Nebraska Petroleum Producers Association, said he was not at Trump’s Grand Island political rally nor had his board taken a position on the president’s order.
He said the group generally supports anything the administration can do to ease the cost of fuel and energy.
The Werner Enterprises building in Omaha. The international trucking and logistics company is a member of the Nebraska Trucking Association. (Naomi Delkamiller/Flatwater Free Press)
“Affordability is important to us,” Bradley said. “Our operations burn a lot of diesel. We have guys driving around in pickup trucks, we have maintenance crews utilizing equipment that burns diesel. We are very, very much affected by inflation.”
For Grisham, undecided details muddy the value of the president’s order. He said it could take numerous months for red dye to purge from an engine system, and penalty problems could arise for truckers who travel through states with conflicting enforcement policies. Experts said a minimum fine for unlawful use of red diesel is $1,000.
Grisham said his group had yet to receive assurance that truck warranties won’t be affected by dye use. “It’s another reason why we’re saying to our trucking partners, ‘Don’t do it.’” 
Hansen, who is also vice chair of the legislative committee for the National Farmers Union, said that while short-term relief might be in store for some Nebraskans, he described Trump’s action as “more perception than substance.”
“We’ve done a couple of things that are somewhat helpful, useful, but they’re not getting at the underlying structural problems around our energy policy, our trade policy — and the fact that the price of diesel is a few dollars a gallon higher than a year ago.”
Diesel fuel in Nebraska averaged about $6 per gallon today compared to $3.36 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Regulatory change opens door to one-stop mental and physical healthcare in NJ
description: New Jersey has awarded two contracts to nonprofits to make it easier for low-income patients to access mental and physical healthcare in one place.
text:
New Jersey has awarded two contracts to nonprofits to make it easier for low-income patients to access mental and physical healthcare in one place. (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey is working to make it easier for low-income patients to get mental and physical healthcare services in the same place, awarding two publicly funded contracts to nonprofit community health systems to expand these programs in parts of the Garden State.
The New Jersey Department of Human Services announced this week that it will provide some $391,000 to St. James Health, a community health center in Newark, and nearly $275,000 to Zufall Health, which serves patients in central and northern parts of the state.
The state said it wants to help the two federally funded clinic systems make it easier for people with substance use disorders, mental health issues, and chronic physical health conditions — diagnoses that can shorten lives by decades — to connect with both behavioral health treatment and primary care by offering multiple services at the same location, called integrated care.
Sarah Aleman, the senior VP who oversees behavioral health at Zufall, said integrated care reduces the need for referrals and visits to multiple health-care systems, something that benefits all primary care patients, but especially patients with mental health or substance use issues who face more barriers to care.
“The goal in integrated care is to ensure access to the right care, with the right team members, at the right time – all within a coordinated system of care,” Aleman said.
The contracts follow a spring 2026 regulatory change more than a decade in the making, which created a single state license for healthcare facilities to provide both behavioral and physical health treatments within the same office. These services were previously licensed through three separate processes governed by two different state agencies, creating red tape that made it hard for healthcare providers to offer both physical and mental health or substance abuse treatments at the same place.
“Too often people have to navigate multiple systems to get treatment for mental health conditions, addiction, and physical health needs,” Stephen Cha, the state human services commissioner and a physician, said in a press release.
The state Department of Health, which oversees the licensing, has issued one integrated care license under the new regulations, which took effect in April, to Zufall Health. A second application from Zufall is also expected to be approved shortly, according to communications director Dalya Ewais. Another 20 applications are under review, a volume she said reflects the growing interest in integrated care.
The contract funding comes from tens of millions the state receives annually from the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to address opioid abuse issues, and flows through a program designed to help federally funded primary care clinics also provide screening, assessment referral, and addiction treatments without the need for additional licensing, according to the Department of Human Services.
St. James now operates three locations in Newark and provides medical, dental, behavioral health, and pharmacy services. One of its clinics also includes a food bank.
Zufall offers a similar range of services at more than half a dozen sites in northern and central New Jersey, plus a mobile health unit and, as of May, a school-based clinic in Franklin Township that serves children and the community. Zufall also expanded its substance use treatment programs in recent years.
Outpatient integrated care does exist at some other venues in New Jersey, like Care Plus, based in Bergen County, and Integrity House in Newark, both large, established providers of mental health and addiction services that had the capacity to navigate the complex regulatory process to weave in primary care services. But the red tape has made it hard for smaller providers to do the same.
In addition, a federally funded program launched in 2017 made New Jersey one of eight states selected for a pilot that allowed community-based behavioral healthcare providers to get reimbursed through Medicaid for offering integrated care and case management. While funding first flowed to just a handful of programs, as of 2024 there were 19 certified community behavioral health clinics in the Garden State, according to a nonprofit that tracks this work.
“Integrated care programs help ensure that people are treated as whole individuals, not a collection of separate health needs,” said Human Services Deputy Commissioner Valerie Mielke, who oversees behavioral health programs in New Jersey.
