name: WyoFile
title: Railroad tie stacks raise stink in Laramie’s West Side neighborhood
description:
Local residents say the creosote-soaked ties are a health and fire hazard. 
The post Railroad tie stacks raise stink in Laramie’s West Side neighborhood appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—In the eight years since Kylene Claar and her family moved into a house with a brown picket fence on this city’s historic West Side, they’ve watched the Greenbelt, a river park adjacent to their block, come alive. 
“It’s been transformed,” Claar told WyoFile, giving credit to the local beavers for their riparian diligence. 
The family also regularly spots skunks, foxes and deer from the Greenbelt’s walking path that darts between cottonwoods and aspens as the trail crisscrosses the Laramie River. It’s a great place for Claar and her husband to raise their three sons, she said, including their adventurous 8-year-old, who rides his bicycle around the neighborhood. 
“He plays outside every day, and he’s outside all the time,” Claar said. “So I really worry about him and the toxic, pungent creosote smell. It’s overwhelming at times.”
This summer, Union Pacific Railroad began stacking creosote-soaked railroad ties on its property adjacent to the river and the West Side, a historic, working-class neighborhood sandwiched between the train tracks and Interstate 80. There’s now a small mountain of more than a thousand ties, according to estimates by locals. 

In this aerial photo provided to WyoFile, stacks of rail ties can be seen on Union Pacific Railroad property just east of the Laramie River and the city’s Greenbelt Trail. (Martha Jenkins)

Railroads, dating back to the 1800s, have used the pungent preservative creosote to protect wooden ties from succumbing to natural decay and pests. The stench, particularly on blistering days in July and August, raised concerns across the neighborhood. Residents, like Claar, say they want answers. 
“[Union Pacific] has tons of money. They own tons of land. Why are they stacking it right next to the river, right next to residential neighborhoods?” Claar said. “It seems like there’s a lot of other places they could put this. To me, it’s an outrage that they decided that this might be a good place.”
For now, the fate of the rail tie stockpile, as well as consensus on the possible risks it poses, is the subject of intense posturing among myriad interests that include residents, local and state officials, the Union Pacific Railroad, its contractor/lessee Omaha Track (represented by powerhouse law firm Holland and Hart) and the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality. 
It appears that, for now, stockpiling has ceased. However, a handful of residents formed Healthy Neighborhoods, a nonprofit that has threatened to sue Union Pacific and Omaha Track if the companies don’t remove the ties. The firms, meanwhile, are negotiating with DEQ over a disagreement about applicable regulations and permitting requirements.
“Why here?” Martha Jenkins, founder of Healthy Neighborhoods, told WyoFile. “Why somewhere surrounded on three sides by waterways on our little greenbelt where our beavers are, where our kids play, where people fish and swim?” 
“Our main concern right now,” she said, “is we need to get these moved.”
Martha Jenkins sits on her front porch in Laramie’s West Side. (Maggie Mullen/WyoFile)
The rail tie stacks, DEQ has said, may violate state “solid and hazardous waste” statutes, requiring a multistep review process that would impose extra measures and monitoring to protect against toxins entering soils and waters. It’s unclear whether such scrutiny might force actions to address the odor and air quality concerns. 
Omaha Track, however, maintains it doesn’t need a permit. 
“We understand the concerns about the ties at Laramie and have been working with various state and local officials and Union Pacific to ensure that we are in compliance,” Omaha Track President Jay Gowan told WyoFile via email. “As those conversations are ongoing, we cannot comment further until there is a resolution.”
Rail yard’s long history of creosote
The pestering odor is produced by creosote, a mixture of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons “derived from the distillation of tar from wood or coal,” according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Depending on exposure levels, it poses health risks, including cancer. It can linger in soils and pollute water. 
Union Pacific used the Laramie rail yard to treat railroad ties with creosote from 1886 to 1983. Because of creosote contamination, the Baxter/Union Pacific Tie Treating grounds along the Laramie River were deemed an EPA Superfund site in 1983, initiating forced cleanup and environmental remediation overseen by the EPA and the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality. It was removed from EPA’s superfund “priority” list in 1999.






A train loaded with rail ties leaves the Union Pacific rail tie treatment plant in Laramie in 1936. Creosote treatment took place on site from 1886 to 1983, when the grounds were deemed an EPA Superfund site forcing cleanup and environmental remediation. (American Heritage Center, University of Wyoming)






Stacks of rail ties are stocked along a railroad track at Union Pacific’s Laramie rail tie treatment plant in 1929. (American Heritage Center, University of Wyoming)


Despite that history, initial inquiries to Union Pacific, local and state officials about what might be done to address concerns were somewhat dismissive, said West Side resident and Democratic House District 45 Rep. Karlee Provenza. Union Pacific appears unmoved by locals’ concerns, she said.
“Union Pacific is like its own country,” Provenza told WyoFile. “They have their own police force, essentially. They have all the power in the world. I just get the impression that they don’t feel like they need to answer to the people of Laramie, and it bums me out.”
‘Truly depressing’
Jim Sparks, who lives directly across the street from the rail tie stack, said he doesn’t feel like he has many options to deal with the problem. 
Sparks recently retired as a city garbage collector, and has lived in the same home for the last two decades. But the rail ties have made him consider moving. Otherwise, he said, “that’s railroad property. And you can’t fight the railroad.”
This summer, the creosote smell gave Sparks regular headaches, he said, while dust was another problem. 
“I don’t have central air conditioning, so my windows were open,” Sparks said. “The dust and the smell is there constantly.” 
Sparks now wipes down the stove before he puts on a pot to boil, he said, “because the dust can be that bad at times.” 
Jim Sparks, alongside his dog, Tom, stand in front of their West Side home in Laramie (Maggie Mullen/WyoFile)
The arrival of the rail ties didn’t immediately worry Sparks, he said, but when he started noticing the smell and reading about creosote-soaked, rail tie piles catching fire, he started to worry. 
“Then Martha [Jenkins] approached me about getting together to start a nonprofit to try and get a lawyer to work on it,” Sparks said. 
Reed Zars, an attorney for the nonprofit, notified Union Pacific and Omaha Track in an Aug. 31 letter that the group intended to file suit if action was not taken. As of publishing time, the nonprofit had not yet received a written response, Zars told WyoFile. 
Jenkins said she can remember a morning this summer when the creosote smell woke her from a deep sleep in the early hours of the day. 
“It was truly depressing,” she said. “It was so beautiful in August, but we felt like you could smell it in our kitchen. You could smell it in the bedroom.”
Aside from the potential health effects, Jenkins said she also worries about the fire hazard the ties pose to the West Side. 
“It’s so close to the houses that, I mean, with this wind, the West Side would burn down,” she said. 
Robert Roybal sits on his front porch in Laramie’s West Side. (Maggie Mullen/WyoFile)
That’s something that also worries Robert Roybal. His house, where he’s lived for the last 43 years, is several blocks down from the ties, so he only really notices the smell when he walks his Scottie dog around the neighborhood, he said. 
Roybal, however, worries what would happen if “some stupid punk, or somebody,” threw a firework, or some kind of flare over the fence surrounding the ties. 
“If there’s a fire, it could go that way. It could go this way,” Roybal said. 
Like his neighbors, Roybal said, “for the life of me, I don’t understand why they brought them over here.”  
Regulatory stink
Provenza said she was stunned by initial responses from local and state authorities. Union Pacific, in addition to being a significant cog in the local economy, is a generous donor to community causes and events, one elected official told her. DEQ’s first response to her inquiries, Provenza said, was that the rail tie stockpile didn’t appear to violate any rules or pose risks beyond the agency’s on-the-books regulatory authority.
“The [DEQ Air Quality Division] has no regulations regarding the storage of used railroad ties,” DEQ officials wrote in a June 29 internal memo obtained by WyoFile. “The only applicable [air quality] regulations would be if Union Pacific begins burning the railroad ties, or if an excessive odor is noticed past the property line.” 
That same month, a DEQ inspector “walked the entire length of the trail where railroad ties were present and attempted to scent any noxious odors,” but “noticed no odors from the facility,” according to DEQ. “No concerns were noted for the facility at that time. Should concerns regarding odor continue, the [DEQ Air Quality Division] will revisit the facility for further investigation.”
Also based on initial inspections, the agency “determined that there is no immediate water quality threat to surface waters of the state from the stacked ties.”
Rail ties can be seen from the Laramie River Greenbelt Trail on Aug. 17, 2026. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
But there’s a question about whether the rail tie stack qualifies as solid waste, requiring a solid and hazardous waste permit. Wyoming DEQ in July met with city officials and representatives from Union Pacific and Omaha Track. Agency staff learned that not only did Omaha Track ultimately plan to stockpile about 5,000 ties, it proposes to shred the bulk of them to sell as fuel for industrial boilers and kilns.
“Based on the discussion, it appears that the current operation may violate the Environmental Quality Act and Solid Waste Rules,” the agency said in a July 27 letter to Omaha Track and Union Pacific representatives. DEQ added it “advises that no additional scrap railroad ties should be stored at the facility or at other unpermitted locations, and that no treatment (chipping/shredding, processing, etc.) of scrap railroad ties occurs until a solid waste management permit is obtained.” 
Omaha Track, via its lawyers, asserted that its intent to reuse the rail ties as a commodity precludes the stockpile and grinding operation from regulation under DEQ’s solid and hazardous waste program. “Omaha Track respectfully requests DEQ reconsider its determination that Omaha Track must obtain a solid waste management permit,” Holland and Hart attorney Jeffrey Pope wrote in a Sept. 16 letter to DEQ.
Reached by WyoFile, DEQ said it is still evaluating its positions on the situation. The agency declined WyoFile’s request for an interview, it said, because the matter is under review.
“DEQ is working with Union Pacific and Omaha Track to evaluate applicable regulatory requirements and determine what permits, if any, may be required through the Solid and Hazardous Waste, Air Quality, and Water Quality divisions,” Public Information Officer Jillian Scott told WyoFile via email. “DEQ continues to review information provided by the parties and assess the appropriate regulatory path forward.”
The former the Baxter/Union Pacific Tie Treating grounds along the Laramie River, highlighted in yellow, were deemed an EPA Superfund site in 1983. (Environmental Protection Agency)
Though aspects of the rail yard, including the handling of creosote-treated railroad ties, are subject to federal environmental laws, Wyoming DEQ has been granted “primacy,” or delegated authority from EPA, to enforce many of the federal environmental programs.
“Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality is the lead agency for governing the management and disposal of solid and hazardous waste under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act in Wyoming,” EPA Region 8 Public Affairs Director Katherine Jenkins told WyoFile via email. “EPA has provided and will continue to provide [Wyoming] DEQ regulatory and technical support in this matter.”
There is a federal regulation that applies specifically to railroad ties, EPA’s Jenkins added. Under federal code 40 CFR 241.4(a), “Railroad ties may be defined as non-waste fuel when they are processed according to the regulatory provisions and burned in specific types of combustion units,” Jenkins said. “That said, railroad ties are not exempt from regulation altogether and remain subject to applicable federal, state and local requirements.”
If the EPA is not satisfied with DEQ’s management of a particular federal program or environmental law, it can step in and override the state agency — an assurance that Provenza said she received from her former Wyoming legislative colleague Cyrus Western, who now serves as EPA’s Region 8 administrator. 
Western was unavailable for an interview for this story, Jenkins said.
‘Not a fun endeavor’
For all the debate among powerful authorities and companies, and deflection that Provenza and others have felt along the way, residents have no choice but to follow their instincts and demand that the railroad — physically and culturally ingrained in the community — be a good neighbor, she told WyoFile.
“What we’re seeing is people acting courageously with the powers that they have,” Provenza said. “And, you know, I get it: Taking on Union Pacific is not a fun endeavor. But my neighbors and the people who walk on the Greenbelt, and anybody who’s invested in the health of the river — there’s just a million reasons not to have [the rail tie stack] there. Union Pacific has plenty of land elsewhere that isn’t going to have the same impacts on people.”
And if state and federal regulatory officials decide that the letter-of-the-law provides legal space to allow what West Side residents and Greenbelt users have already endured, Provenza said, then changes are due.
“If this is fine,” Provenza said, “and yet there’s evidence — like scientific evidence — it is harmful, then it’s my job as a state representative to figure out, ‘Do we need to hold the agency [DEQ] accountable?'”
DEQ is to be commended for its evolving role on the issue, she added. 
“I’m pointing fingers at Union Pacific and Omaha Track to be better neighbors. We’ll use whatever regulatory pathway that might be available to try to protect the people of my community.”
Provenza and Healthy Neighborhoods are also pressing city of Laramie and Albany County officials. 
“There are ordinances you can put in place to stop the grinding,” Provenza said, “because while the ties are a problem just sitting there, we also know they become an even greater threat to the community if they start grinding up that wood.”
“Our greatest concern is the next phase of this operation; the grinding of the rail ties. We believe that presents a significant risk to the health and wellbeing of the City of Laramie, especially the West Side and Downtown area.”Sharon Cumbie, Laramie mayor
Provenza said she and others have implored local officials to hold a public meeting and make their positions clear to their constituents. But so far, the city has not done so. 
“This is where the push and pull of being a city councilor versus also a community member comes into play,” Laramie City Council Member Will Bowling, who represents the southern half of the West Side, said. 
To Bowling, it’s plain that the ties need to be dealt with. 
“As a neighbor and as a community member and as a concerned person, I’m like, ‘Those shouldn’t be as close to homes as they are, and they shouldn’t be as close to a water source, as they are,’” he said. “That’s pretty obvious. 
“Not only is that unsightly in this space, but we’re also talking about stuff that is soaked in creosote and can be environmentally hazardous,” Bowling said. “Then as a council member, I’m like, ‘let’s address all of those things,’ while also having to understand that currently, based on where they are, it’s industrial zoning, and under state statute, city ordinance, and according to DEQ, they’re not doing anything that they shouldn’t be doing,” he said. 
The city is waiting on an updated site plan, Bowling said, that may include moving the ties, “south of town, possibly into county land that’s down by the cement plant.”
After the ties are relocated, Bowling said, then comes the question of disposal and “what does that look like, and how is that done with the utmost concern for public safety and health in mind?” 
Ultimately, he said, “I think it behooves a transnational, multi-billion dollar corporation to want to maybe listen to public concern.”
In an email to West Side resident Martha Jenkins and her husband Mark, Laramie Mayor Sharon Cumbie wrote “The City is willing to fight, which may include significant legal fees.”
“Our greatest concern is the next phase of this operation; the grinding of the rail ties,” Cumbie wrote. “We believe that presents a significant risk to the health and wellbeing of the City of Laramie, especially the West Side and Downtown area.”
Still, Cumbie wrote, the city believes “there is a compromise: move the storage south closer to Mountain Cement. Then, any grinding activity must be housed in an enclosed warehouse with an advanced ventilation system that sucks out the particulate matter into receptacles, where the contents can be properly disposed of.” 
Union Pacific’s smokestack towers over the company rail yard and the adjacent West Side neighborhood May 23, 2026, in Laramie. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
But West Side resident Kylene Claar worries the damage has already been done. 
“The problem with the health thing is, we see this over and over, whenever there’s exposure to a toxin or chemical vapor, or things like that, it seems like it affects a person’s life down the road,” she said. 
In the meantime, she said her family has already been dealing with headaches, nausea and other symptoms that Claar worries are related to living two houses down from the ties. She also has lingering questions beyond the decision to store the ties on the West Side. She said she’d like to know whether there’s a neighborhood evacuation plan in case the ties catch fire. 
“I just feel like there’s no plan in place for how to deal with something if there were a huge emergency,” Claar said. 
From her family’s front porch, Claar can see a pole with a set of cameras that she said appeared this summer on the edge of the railyard. At night, she said, the pole’s flashing blue lights cast through her home’s windows, which feels “really invasive.” 
“Here’s the problem,” she said. “Instead of moving a dangerous, toxic fire hazard away from our children, whoever it is that’s putting in this camera is instead deciding to put our family under surveillance instead of just moving the railyard ties. 
“It’s that simple. That’s all we want done.”

title: Yellowstone’s historic fort gets a facelift
description:
Project underway in Mammoth Hot Springs amid mounting criticisms over federal infrastructure funding. 
The post Yellowstone’s historic fort gets a facelift appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Yellowstone National Park’s extensive assets of buildings, roads and trails are worth an estimated $8.5 billion, which brings massive maintenance responsibilities. 
Currently, park crews are working to rehabilitate the park’s oldest functioning structures. A two-year, $25 million project is underway to stabilize and restore the exteriors of several historic Fort Yellowstone buildings in Mammoth Hot Springs. All are currently used for employee housing. 
The buildings sit in a national historic landmark district that encompasses 35 structures dating to the 1890s and early 1900s. In the early years of the country’s first national park, Yellowstone’s resources were under siege by souvenir hunters, poachers and entrepreneurs setting up tourist businesses, according to the park service. When civilian park superintendents proved insufficient at protecting the hot springs and wildlife, the secretary of the interior tapped the military, and in 1886 Army troops moved in. 
Many structures in the subsequently built permanent post have endured, though the buildings pushing well over 100 years old have been due for some attention. The current project entails structural repairs, roof and exterior rehabilitation, window and door restoration, painting and hazardous materials mitigation, according to the park service. 
The project, paid for through the Great American Outdoors Act’s Legacy Restoration Fund comes amid mounting criticism of federal parks infrastructure funding. Earlier this year, the National Park Service shifted roughly 1,500 park projects, many already approved, to a new “low priority” list, the Associated Press reported in August. 
The projects span more than 200 sites and carry a combined cost estimate of more than $400 million, according to the Center for Western Priorities. They included 45 projects in Yellowstone, according to the Center, which range from contract fees for bison processing to dock repairs and a vault toilet.

title: Public land advocates: Be careful who you vote for!
description:
The Trump administration has taken an axe to regulatory safeguards of our public lands, writes guest columnist Earl DeGroot.
The post Public land advocates: Be careful who you vote for! appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

In the summer of 2025, the federal budget reconciliation bill included a provision to sell millions of acres of public land for low-income housing. After intense nationwide protest, the provision was removed from the bill. 
Millions of Americans breathed a sigh of relief, but the threat to our public land hasn’t gone away. The battle has shifted to federal land management. 
At the core of the battle is the Trump administration’s disregard for conservation values. This administration shows very little interest in balancing conservation with economic development. Instead, to promote their economic agenda, they’ve launched an assault on our land management infrastructure including budgets and personnel, as well as numerous laws and regulations that govern management activities.   
Because this threat is less visible than proposals to sell or transfer federal land, it often fails to grab the attention of public land users. That’s unfortunate, because a weakened management infrastructure has serious ramifications.
Budget and personnel cuts are especially concerning. They started with Elon Musk and his chainsaw, but continue long after his departure. 
According to the Conservation Lands Foundation, the administration’s proposed fiscal year 2027 budget for the Bureau of Land Management includes a 34% cut to the total budget and a 27% reduction in staff. It also includes a 61% cut to recreation management of trails, campsites and visitor services. A complete elimination of funding for cultural resources and wilderness management is proposed. 
The U.S. Forest Service is also under attack. In addition to proposing massive budget cuts, the Trump administration is in the process of moving the headquarters from Washington, D.C. to Salt Lake City. Numerous research facilities are being closed and their remaining functions will be centralized at a research headquarters in Fort Collins, Colorado. Because many personnel are unable to relocate for family reasons, institutional knowledge will be lost and research activities will suffer. 
The National Park Service is not being spared. The Trump administration has proposed a 32% budget cut for fiscal year 2027. In addition, President Trump has been redirecting tens of millions of National Park Service dollars to projects in Washington, D.C. (including the Reflecting Pool) while blocking numerous planned projects at national parks across the country.
Much of this is happening with the willing participation of agency leaders. That’s not surprising because the president nominated people who pledged absolute loyalty to his agenda. One of the most egregious examples is the nomination and confirmation of Steve Pearce to direct the Bureau of Land Management. Pearce has a long record of advocating for public land sales and unrestricted economic development.   
Regrettably, the unquestioning loyalty from high-level agency personnel almost always usurps the role of science when science contradicts the administration’s political agenda. A prime example is Trump’s insistence that global warming is a hoax despite overwhelming scientific evidence to the contrary. In a decision that directly contradicts science, the Environmental Protection Agency recently announced their intent to eliminate climate-related emission requirements for coal and gas burning power plants.  
Laws and regulations that govern public land management are also under attack. With considerable success, the Trump administration has attempted to revise, circumvent or eliminate the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Roadless Rule, the Public Lands Rule, the Waters of the United States Rule, the Antiquities Act and BLM Resource Management Plans. (For more details, click here and here).   
Much of this is going unnoticed by the average public land user in Wyoming. But it is certainly not unnoticed by our congressional delegation. They are complicit in supporting the destruction of our land management infrastructure. There is speculation that the ulterior motive is to build support for sales or transfer, born out of frustration with how federal lands are managed.   
In November, we have an opportunity to change the composition of our congressional delegation and elect people who support public lands. For many people in Wyoming that might mean putting loyalty to public lands over loyalty to party.

title: English is already Idaho’s official language. Voters can add it to the state’s constitution.
description: In 2007, Idaho lawmakers passed a law to make English the state’s official language. That law, which is still on the books, requires English to be used as “the sole language of government.” But it lists many exceptions to its requirement that government documents be in English, such as for law enforcement or for “public […]
text:
Ada County election workers sort hundreds of absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)In 2007, Idaho lawmakers passed a law to make English the state’s official language.
That law, which is still on the books, requires English to be used as “the sole language of government.” But it lists many exceptions to its requirement that government documents be in English, such as for law enforcement or for “public health and safety needs,” to ensure public schools can teach students who are learning English and to ensure colleges and so universities can “pursue educational purposes.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
In this year’s general election on Nov. 3, Idaho voters will decide on whether to amend the state’s constitution to declare English as the state’s official language.
But what isn’t immediately clear, some say, is whether the amendment will end existing exemptions in state law that allow languages other than English to be used by government agencies. The proposed constitutional amendment’s only exception allows the government to use other languages when required by federal law, such as in schools and, in some cases, election administration.
“It’s not entirely clear, honestly, how much it would change things,” said University of Idaho law professor Richard Seamon, who has taught at the school for 30 years.
The proposed amendment, passed by the Idaho Legislature to be placed on the ballot through House Joint Resolution 6 in 2025, calls for English to be used in “all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution of the state of Idaho.”
Here’s what the amendment will look like on your ballot:

        “Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho?”    
To pass, the amendment needs support from at least 50% of voters.

 In Idaho, a state with a high Hispanic population, amendment is meant to encourage learning English, according to Republican state lawmaker

In Idaho, an agricultural state with a high population of Hispanic people, some worry that the lack of clarity around the amendment could make it harder for some residents to run their businesses, know what’s going on in their children’s schools or to stay up to date about what’s happening in their communities.
“We see people working very hard to learn English, but learning a language takes time. And someone shouldn’t have to wait until they’re fluent in English to understand critical information — from their child’s school or interacting with local government or understanding information that’s already affecting their family, their health, their safety,” said Mari Ramos, CEO of the Idaho Hispanic Foundation, which helps people learn English and provides other resources. 
Rep. Dale Hawkins, R-Fernwood chats with the House Education Committee’s secretary Amy Bengtzen during a meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
One lawmaker behind the proposed amendment, Rep. Dale Hawkins, R-Fernwood, said the change is meant to encourage people to learn English.
“One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And we see more and more people that are moving to the United States …” he said in an interview. “And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive.”
In Idaho, Hispanics make up about 13% of the state’s population, and the state has welcomed thousands of refugees in recent years. Over the last decade, the state’s Hispanic population grew faster, by 25%, than the state’s overall population, which rose by 10%, according to statistics from the Idaho Commission on Hispanic Affairs. About 11% of Idahoans speak a language other than English at home, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. 
Thirty states have declared English as their official language, according to Ballotpedia. In 2025, President Donald Trump declared English as the nation’s official language in an executive order. Hawkins said lawmakers had worked on the proposed Idaho amendment with the Trump administration.
Amending the state constitution — or undoing an amendment — is a lot harder than passing a state law. 
Amendments to the constitution, which can be proposed in the Legislature, require at least two-thirds support in each chamber of the Legislature. Then they go before the voters for ratification. If a proposed amendment receives more than 50% of the vote, it passes.
State laws, on the other hand, face fewer hurdles. Bills only need at least a majority of support in each chamber of the Legislature and support from the governor. And voters don’t get a direct vote. 
 How will the constitutional amendment work?

Several federal laws require local and state governments to provide materials or services in languages other than English, Seamon said. That includes the Equal Educational Opportunities Act, which requires educational agencies to help students overcome language barriers, such as offering English as a Second Language instruction.
Passing HJR 4 would give Idaho Legislature sole authority to legalize marijuana, other drugs

The Voting Rights Act also requires certain localities to provide voting materials, including ballots, in other languages in certain circumstances. Five Idaho counties are subject to that requirement, according to a list maintained by the U.S. Department of Justice: Clark, the state’s smallest county in eastern Idaho; Clearwater; Idaho; Lewis and Nez Perce counties. Clark is the only county in the state where “Hispanic” is listed as the “language minority group.” In the remaining counties, “All other American Indian tribes” are the listed “language minority group(s).”
Seamon said he could also see a case to apply the U.S. Constitution’s Equal Protection Clause to require languages other than English be available in criminal court cases. 
The amendment itself doesn’t outline enforcement mechanisms, such as penalties. Enforcement, Seamon said, would likely fall to the Idaho Attorney General’s Office, or to the Legislature in the form of oversight, which could include cutting funds for agencies that are suspected to have violated the amendment.
Seamon thinks questions would likely come up as state agencies attempt to implement the amendment. He isn’t sure that the amendment would override the broader exceptions in state law.
“If it said ‘only English,’ then I think it would clearly, pretty clearly, override these exceptions, and eliminate them,” Seamon said. “But it doesn’t say only … So I think that leaves room for discussion about the extent to which these exceptions will still apply.”
Hawkins said the proposed amendment is written to be more restrictive than the state law on purpose, and that it should override the state law.
“The constitution trumps all things, so I would believe that our state laws would have to conform to what our constitution says,” he said. 
Hawkins said whether some of the law’s exceptions would remain, such as the use of other languages by law enforcement soliciting tips to find a missing child or health officials informing the public about an infectious disease outbreak, should be handled on a case-by-case approach.
“Each one of those exceptions would have to be, for lack of a better term, studied and to make sure that we’re not creating loopholes so that we have no effect,” Hawkins said.
 Democratic lawmaker says she’s unsure if the proposed amendment would undo exceptions in state law

Democratic state Sen. Melissa Wintrow, of Boise, opposed the amendment early on. She said she never got a clear answer on her concern that it could wipe out exemptions outlined in state law. 
Idaho Senate Minority Leader Melissa Wintrow, D-Boise, speaks to reporters at a post-State of the State Address press conference on Jan. 12, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“I’m concerned. I have reason to believe we should all be troubled, right?” she said in an interview. “… Could these reasonable carve-outs be eliminated? And then your kid can’t take a foreign language in high school, which I think is deeply troubling to many people.”
She said she didn’t ask the Idaho Attorney General’s Office for a written opinion on HJR 6’s legal impacts, because she said the office had denied her such opinions in recent years. 
In a statement, Attorney General’s Office spokesperson Dan Estes said no lawmaker sponsoring the resolution on the proposed amendment had requested a written legal opinion on it, and he confirmed his office did not issue an opinion on the resolution or proposed amendment. But he said the office still provides such opinions, which are outlined as a duty of the attorney general in state law, including a written opinion that he said that Wintrow received in 2025. 
“We regularly provide legislators of both parties oral and written legal guidance, and publish our opinions and advisory letters in our annual report,” Estes said. “What we no longer do is write opinions at one legislator’s request to attack another’s bill or resolution.”
“Legislative Democrats and their allies have spent three years confusing legal counsel with political ammunition,” he continued. “The Attorney General’s duty is to provide legal advice to legislators. They are upset that they can no longer use our office as a tool to fight their legislative battles.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Out-of-state Dem Govs with 2028 ambitions are working to boost TN U.S. House candidates
description: Two Democratic governors with presidential aspirations are spending money and time in Tennessee to boost the party’s U.S. House candidates ahead of the November midterm election. ​Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s political action committee, PAC, Ready for the Fight, has purchased around $1.6 million in television advertisements in Nashville and Memphis over the[...]
text:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is funding a PAC that is boosting the Democratic candidate in Tennessee’s 9th U.S. Congressional district. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Two Democratic governors with presidential aspirations are spending money and time in Tennessee to boost the party’s U.S. House candidates ahead of the November midterm election.
​Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s political action committee, PAC, Ready for the Fight, has purchased around $1.6 million in television advertisements in Nashville and Memphis over the next four weeks, according to a Lookout analysis of Federal Communications Commission public inspection files.
Ready for the Fight has raised $20 million from Pritzker, a Democrat, according to Politico. The group’s ad attacks Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor in his Tennessee 9th U.S. Congressional race against Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson.
“The new ads are part of Ready for the Fight’s commitment to compete aggressively in places Democrats too often write off,” said PAC officials in a news release.
Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, right, stumped for 5th Congressional District nominee Chaz Molder at a Saturday fundraiser in Nashville. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
While Pritzker is spending in the state, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear visited Tennessee earlier this week to endorse Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder in his campaign for Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District. A Nashville fundraiser Beshear headlined for Molder raised about $130,000.
​Both Pritzker and Beshear are considered potential Democratic Party presidential candidates in 2028. They are trying to boost the party’s chances of winning a congressional seat in Tennessee despite an unfavorable map.
​Tennessee state lawmakers redrew the state’s U.S. House map in May at President Donald Trump’s urging. The goal was to eliminate the last Democratic-held Tennessee congressional seat in Memphis by splitting the majority Black city across three House seats.
​The new map created nine districts that Trump won by 20 percentage points each in the 2024 election, with analysts favoring Republicans to win all nine of the new districts.
​Erin Covey, head of the Cook Political Report’s U.S. House rating, previously told the Lookout that even in an environment where the Democratic Party sees a national blue wave, picking up any of Tennessee’s congressional districts would be difficult.
Democrats face uphill battle in winning any Tennessee U.S. House race

​But Covey added that the party’s best shot in Tennessee would be the 5th, where Molder is running against Republican former Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, and the 9th.
​“Democrats are running serious campaigns that have raised a lot of money and have enthusiasm,” Covey said.
The Ready for the Fight advertisement attacks Taylor for supporting Trump’s war in Iran, while praising Pearson.
Taylor said the advertisement showed he’s the frontrunner in the race.
“Justin Pearson is a far-left Democrat Socialist just like Pritzker,” said Taylor. “Pearson’s specialty is communism. Mine is common sense.”
Pearson didn’t respond to a question about the advertisement.
​The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, DCCC, has put both the 5th and 9th in its 2026 Red to Blue list of seats it plans to dedicate resources to as the party tries to regain control of the U.S. House.
​The DCCC has nearly four dozen House races on its Red to Blue list and would need to flip four seats while holding all its current ones to take the majority.
​Cook rates all nine of Tennessee’s congressional districts as solid Republican, the highest GOP favorability rating it gives when classifying the races.
Sam Stockard contributed to this report.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama public schools expected to see another significant enrollment decrease
description: Alabama public schools may have seen another sharp enrollment decrease in the last school year, Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey told members of the State Board of Education Thursday. Mackey said preliminary numbers for the 2025-26 school year showed there were 702,000 students enrolled in Alabama public schools. That’s down roughly 12,000 st[...]
text:
Alabama State Superintendent Eric Mackey speaks to Alabama State Board of Education members in the Gordon Persons Building after the Alabama State Board of Education meeting on July 8, 2025, in Montgomery, Alabama. Mackey told board members Thursday preliminary enrollment numbers show a 12,000 student decrease. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama public schools may have seen another sharp enrollment decrease in the last school year, Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey told members of the State Board of Education Thursday.
Mackey said preliminary numbers for the 2025-26 school year showed there were 702,000 students enrolled in Alabama public schools. That’s down roughly 12,000 students from the 2024-25 school year.
“We had thought it would probably stabilize this year. We didn’t know for sure, but it turns out this year’s loss is more than double, or essentially double, what last year’s was. So we’ll be digging into those data,” Mackey said after the meeting.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
With a large drop in enrollment, it’s estimated that around 800 teacher units will be lost. A message seeking comment was left with the Alabama Education Association Thursday afternoon.
Rural areas in the state could be the most affected by the decrease.
“The deepest losses appear to be in rural areas, and also in one or two major counties, and so that means that as you get smaller and smaller and smaller, we now have about 10 … districts that have less than 1,000 students. Once you get to less than 1,000 students, it’s really hard to offer all the courses that are required,” Mackey said.
More densely populated areas, such as Jefferson County, could see more losses than other counties, but even rapidly growing counties, Mackey said, aren’t seeing gains in enrollment.
“I  just looked at one of our 10 fastest-growing districts (and they) added six students,” Mackey said after the meeting. “So they’re essentially not growing, and then the losses, you know, are pretty much across the state.”
Mackey did not say which district he viewed enrollment numbers for.
The reasons for the decline are not clear. One possibility could be an aging population and a decline in birthrates. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the median age in Alabama is 39.6 years, compared to 39.2 for the country as a whole.
“The kindergarten enrollment is going to be down about 2,500, which is following national trends. They’re just significantly fewer children being born, so that one is not surprising,” Mackey told board members.
While CHOOSE Act recipients made up some amount of the students no longer in public school, Mackey said those numbers don’t equate to the amount of students lost. A message seeking comment was left with the Alabama Department of Revenue Thursday.
“The CHOOSE Act numbers that the Revenue Department has posted are not anything close to that,” he said to the board. “The number of students, public school students, who have shown that they are going to a non-public school doesn’t seem to add to this number at all, unless there’s something else out there.”
Mackey said “the only elementary gain” was in 5th grade, but he could not give board members a reason for the growth.
“We’ll be looking at these data lots of different ways. For now, the big story is that even when all the errors are cleaned up, there’s no way that we don’t have a significant loss in students, and it will impact the funding, and it will impact the number of teachers units there are,” Mackey said. “And for many local districts, it will be a serious impact on the district because they’ll lose enough students that they have to start cutting staff and those kinds of things.”
District level data for enrollment is expected to be released by the end of the month.
Last year, numbers released by the Alabama Department of Education showed that K-12 enrollment dropped by 5,800 students. Of those students, 3,000 received CHOOSE Act funds and 2,100 students were unaccounted for.
Mackey said tracking enrollment was difficult due to a change in how race and ethnicity is being recorded at schools.
“We know last year some of it was we lost a lot of Hispanic students because we were able to track that,” he said. “But it was hard to track because we were also, last year, in the process of changing the way we collect race category data because the federal government changed the categories, so they weren’t exactly apples to apples from the year before.”

title: Alabama Ethics Commission: Campaign funds can be used for civil lawsuits
description: The Alabama Ethics Commission Wednesday unanimously approved an advisory opinion that said state law from staff that state law allows campaign funds raised by a candidate to pay legal fees for a civil lawsuit if it is related to the job duties while in office. The opinion came at the request of Rep. Matt Simpson, […]
text:
Rep. Matt Simpson, R-Daphne, stands on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on Feb. 8, 2024 in Montgomery, Alabama. The Alabama Ethics Commission said in an opinion issued Wednesday and in response to an inquiry from Simpson that campaign contributions can be used for civil lawsuits related to conduct in office. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Ethics Commission Wednesday unanimously approved an advisory opinion that said state law from staff that state law allows campaign funds raised by a candidate to pay legal fees for a civil lawsuit if it is related to the job duties while in office.
The opinion came at the request of Rep. Matt Simpson, R-Daphne, who has threatened legal action against a political action committee that targeted the state represenative ahead of May’s Republican primary in his House district. Simpson asked if he was permitted to use campaign contributions to help pay for costs associated with litigation under the state’s Fair Campaigns Practice Act .
“Campaign funds can be used for legal fees and costs associated with any civil action, criminal prosecution or investigation related to conduct reasonably related to performing the duties of the office held,” said Brian Paterson, chief counsel of the Alabama Ethics Commission.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Simpson said in an interview Thursday he has not yet filed a lawsuit and is considering his options.
“I feel a lawsuit is warranted because you have these groups that come in and say absolute false statements and lies,” Simpson said. “They put them in mailers and messages out in the community in advertisements and other things saying that I voted for a bill I voted no on, they said I voted no on a bill I voted yes on.”
He also said he “wanted to hold them accountable” for the alleged false statements they made.
In May, Simpson sent a cease-and-desist letter to Alabama Values PAC, a political organization that targeted him with negative advertising prior to the May primary. Simpson demanded the PAC retract a flyer that falsely claimed Simpson voted to prioritize free college for immigrants without legal status.
Simpson in 2024 voted against HB 210, sponsored by Rep. Reed Ingram, R-Pike Road, which would have allowed students without legal status to attend Alabama postsecondary schools if they had applied for legal status or earned a diploma or GED after attending a high school for at least three years. The bill did not become law.
Alabama Values PAC was created in March by former Sen. Dell Hill. It listed Thomas Datwyler, a Wisconsin-based political consultant who claims to have “guided” 400 political action committees, as its chairperson and CEO. Hill said in a statement in March that the PAC would defend “traditional Christian principles that have made Alabama the best place to raise a family, start a business, and build strong communities.”
Hill accused “our so-called conservative leaders” of voting for in-state tuition for immigrants without status; parole for violent offenders; supporting gambling legislation and voting for restrictions on guns or property rights. The statement did not provide specific examples.
Messages seeking comment were sent to Alabama Values PAC and Datwyler on Wednesday.
The PAC told al.com in May that the allegation against Simpson was due to a “printing error” but did not elaborate. Simpson narrowly lost the May primary to Danielle Duggar.
According to its website, Alabama Values PAC also targeted Reps. Phillip Pettus, R-Florence and Frances Holk-Jones, R-Foley, and Sens. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore and Andrew Jones, R-Centre. Pettus and Albritton lost their respective primaries; Holk-Jones was pushed to a runoff but won, and Jones won his primary.
According to the opinion, the law does not limit the use of campaign funds to pay legal fees to defend an elected official from a lawsuit that was filed and does not prevent elected officials from using the money to initiate a civil claim for defamation.
The opinion states that the Ethics Act prohibits people from using campaign contributions to pay legal fees associated with a personal injury claim. That means that if a candidate decides to use campaign funds to pay for legal fees associated with actions of the public office, any compensation from the lawsuit cannot go directly to the official for personal use.
“If campaign funds are used for legal fees and associated costs, then any and all damages that result would need to be paid to the public official’s PCC (principal campaign committee) rather than to the candidate personally,” Paterson said.
That complicates the issue because the FCPA prohibits a candidate from receiving payment of damages from a lawsuit against a political action committee beyond the 12 months prior to an election in which the person intends to be a candidate.

title: Tennessee Trucking Association, fuel providers say clarity is needed on dyed diesel relief
description: The Tennessee Trucking Association and some Tennessee fuel providers are cautioning diesel-powered vehicle drivers to wait for clarity before using dyed diesel meant for off-road vehicles on public roads after recently announced respites from tax enforcement. President Donald Trump issued an executive order Monday instructing the U.S. Treasury Department to[...]
text:
The Tennessee Trucking Association is encouraging members to wait for clarity from the federal and state governments on whether they can use tax-free dyed diesel on roadways. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Tennessee Trucking Association and some Tennessee fuel providers are cautioning diesel-powered vehicle drivers to wait for clarity before using dyed diesel meant for off-road vehicles on public roads after recently announced respites from tax enforcement.
President Donald Trump issued an executive order Monday instructing the U.S. Treasury Department to defer federal taxes on dyed diesel and allow highway use through the end of the year. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee on Tuesday said the state would suspend enforcement of rules limiting the use of the dyed, tax-free diesel to off-road vehicles to provide relief to farmers and loggers from high fuel prices during harvest season.
Red-dyed diesel fuel is chemically the same as regular diesel, but is typically only permitted for use in off-road vehicles because the fuel is exempt from taxes collected by the state and federal government to pay for road maintenance. 
Tennessee governor lets farmers use untaxed diesel on roads after Trump defers federal enforcement

The pause in enforcement is meant to help some diesel fuel users save money at the pump amid record-high diesel prices that economists attribute mostly to the United States’ war in Iran. In Tennessee, untaxed dyed diesel costs around 51 cents less per gallon than regular diesel.
But the details of how this relief will work in practice are hazy, including who is eligible to purchase and use dyed diesel on public roads, whether taxes on the fuel will ultimately be due at a later date, and what reporting requirements will be involved.
Trump’s executive order instructs the Secretary of the Treasury to determine which taxpayers are covered and any conditions on the tax relief and “explore” potential ways to forgive the tax. The Internal Revenue Service has yet to issue implementation guidance.
“The executive order provides for temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral; it does not necessarily eliminate the underlying tax obligations,” Tennessee Trucking Association President and CEO Donna England wrote in an email to the Lookout on Thursday.
“We look forward to reviewing the IRS’s implementing guidance to better understand how the relief will work in practice,” England wrote. “Carriers need clear federal and state guidance on eligibility, reporting requirements and any taxes that remain payable.”



Quotation







There’s no real clarity. I think everybody needs to kind of just pump the brakes and we’ll see how this thing shakes out.


– Caleb Haywood, Espey Oil Co. 


Until that guidance comes, the Tennessee Trucking Association is encouraging its members to “consult with their tax and legal advisors, maintain accurate records, and avoid making assumptions about eligibility,” according to England.
The Energy Marketers of America, a national federation of energy trade associations, has warned truck stops and gas stations to “proceed with caution” until further guidance is issued.
Caleb Haywood — a partner in Espey Oil Co. Inc., based in Huntingdon, Tennessee — said there is a “lot of gray area” and his company has been advised to tell customers not to run dyed diesel in on-road vehicles for the time being.
“There’s no real clarity,” Haywood said. “I think everybody needs to kind of just pump the brakes and we’ll see how this thing shakes out.”
Small & Small Oil Co., a fuel provider based in Fayetteville, Tennessee, posted a statement to its social media Tuesday warning that both Lee’s announcement and Trump’s executive order aren’t clear on “who can take advantage and when they can do it, penalty free.”
Questions also remain regarding what happens when enforcement resumes. 
Tennessee Code states that a civil penalty of $1,000 or $10 per gallon of dyed fuel (whichever is greater) can be assessed against anyone who puts dyed fuel in the tank of a vehicle used on public roadways. This penalty can be waived in whole or in part at the commissioner’s discretion. 
With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes

Lee’s Oct. 2 letter to Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Andy Holt, Transportation Commissioner Will Reid, Department of Revenue Commissioner David Gerregano and Department of Safety & Homeland Security Commissioner Jeff Long directs suspended enforcement of dyed diesel restrictions on the state’s “agricultural economy” through the end of October.
“Specifically, we should not enforce restrictions on persons engaged in agricultural or forestry operations, while that person is using a vehicle on the highways of this State in connection with the harvesting and hauling of crops, livestock, timber and other forest products and the transportation of farm and forestry supplies and equipment,” Lee wrote.
But the dye used to identify the tax-free off-road diesel can remain in fuel tanks and fuel lines even after operators switch back to using clear diesel, according to England.
“Officials need to clarify how these situations will be handled so carriers that complied with the temporary rules aren’t left facing uncertainty,” England wrote.
Haywood agreed. 
“If they do this full-blown, then there’s going to have to be some leniency,” Haywood said, particularly referring to the executive order that lasts through the end of 2026. “January 1st, they can’t start writing tickets again, because there’s going to be some residue left in all these tanks.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Fuel prices, tariffs weigh heavily in east Arkansas’ US House race
description: The spike in fuel prices since the start of the Iran war has hit the farm-heavy 1st Congressional District in east Arkansas especially hard, and Republican U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford doesn’t hold back when talking about the problem. “I’ll be blunt about it. Gas prices suck right now,” Crawford told the Arkansas Advocate. “There’s no […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford, Democrat Terri Yarbrough Green and Libertarian Steve Parsons are running for Arkansas' 1st Congressional District in the 2026 general election. (Courtesy photos) The spike in fuel prices since the start of the Iran war has hit the farm-heavy 1st Congressional District in east Arkansas especially hard, and Republican U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford doesn’t hold back when talking about the problem.
“I’ll be blunt about it. Gas prices suck right now,” Crawford told the Arkansas Advocate. “There’s no other way to put it. Diesel is the lifeblood of our economy.”
As Crawford seeks an eighth term in Congress representing a district spanning 31 counties against Democrat Terri Yarbrough Green and Libertarian Steve Parsons, the effect of the Iran war, fuel prices and President Donald Trump’s tariffs loom large. The three candidates split on how best to address these issues.
Crawford, who chairs the House Intelligence Committee and was first elected in 2010, said he’s focused on more support for infrastructure in the district and pursuing more domestic fertilizer production to help the region’s farmers. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Green is a retired pathologist who said her priorities include finding relief for residents and farmers from prices on fuel and other needs, and working to curb the influence of corporate money in politics. 
Parsons, a retired economist and consultant, is running on a platform that includes cutting federal spending and eliminating international tariffs.
The race is unfolding against the backdrop of a midterm election where Trump’s low approval numbers and the Iran war have raised national Democrats’ hopes of winning back the U.S. House. Political forecasters, including the Cook Political Report and Larry Sabato, have labeled the 1st District seat as safely Republican.
Issue Spotlight: Where Arkansas’ U.S. Senate candidates stand on the Iran war

Iran war, fuel prices
Green and Parsons both oppose the Iran war, which they say has hurt the district due to the rise in fuel and fertilizer prices because of the Strait of Hormuz’s closure.
Green said she would have voted for a war powers resolution that would have halted Trump’s ability to continue military action against Iran without congressional approval. Crawford and the rest of the state’s Republican House delegation have voted against such a resolution. 
“That is a thorny problem that will involve multiple players, but (ending the war) has to be a priority,” Green said. “Ending that war and getting the strait opened up, I think that will help a lot of the price issues.”
Parsons said he wants less military involvement internationally. 
“I want the United States to stop being the puppet of Israel,” Parsons said. “I want to end the war in Iran, and I would take any action that would try and reduce or end the war in Iran.”
Crawford said he understands the frustration surrounding fuel prices, but said there’s more behind the rise in prices than the Iran war and questioned whether they’re artificially inflated. Crawford also said he believes the war has made the world a safer place.
“We’re not going to have an economy left if we roll over and let Iran pursue their nuclear ambitions,” Crawford said. “And I can tell you, based on what I’ve seen and what I know, that’s a real threat for not just the next generation, but the generation after that, and I’m not even sure there’ll be a generation after that if Iran gets their way.”
Trump’s tariffs
Parsons and Green are both critical of Trump’s widespread tariffs. Parsons, who was the Libertarian Party’s nominee, is also critical of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the North American trade pact that Trump signed in his first term that the administration is renegotiating. 
The agreement, which replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement, is set to expire by 2036 and Parsons argued it hurts consumers.
“You took a mediocre trade agreement in NAFTA and you made it worse with more regulations,” Parsons said. “By definition, more regulations mean higher prices for Americans, particularly with USMCA higher prices for automobiles and automobile parts.  
Green called Trump’s tariffs, especially on allies like Canada, erratic and hurtful to the 1st District.
“Tariffs are a tool, and they need to be wielded carefully and thoughtfully, and with surgical precision, not randomly and covering whole countries,” she said. “I think a tariff war with Canada makes absolutely no sense. It’s hurting people here and in Canada, and I don’t see any particular purpose in it.”
Crawford said he believes tariffs are a good beginning for negotiating better trade deals with countries, and pointed to tariffs on steel under Trump and former President Joe Biden. 
Mississippi County, located in the district, is the largest steel-producing county in the country and industry leaders say it has surged after tariffs Trump imposed on China in his first term.
“They’re a good conversation starter, but in real terms, they have actually worked when they have been implemented and sustained over a period of years, like they have on steel,” Crawford said.
However, Crawford has split from Trump on one trade issue. He and other Arkansas Republicans have disagreed with Trump’s plan to allow more beef imports into the U.S. without triggering higher tariffs, a move that has prompted objections from cattle farmers.
Farming challenges
Crawford voted for the $390 billion House Farm Bill that reauthorizes major agriculture programs for five years. The legislation institutes cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax and spending cut legislation Trump signed last year.
The Senate Agriculture Committee recently advanced its version of the legislation, drafted by Republican Sen. John Boozman of Arkansas, who chairs the panel. 
With McConnell back, Senate ag committee advances farm bill on party lines

Crawford said he hasn’t made a comprehensive review of the Senate legislation but said he’s hopeful Congress will approve a final version this year and is encouraged by Boozman’s work on it.
“It doesn’t necessarily mean that we’re going to agree 100% on everything,” Crawford said. “But I would say it’s probably going to come a heck of a lot closer than any Farm Bill we’ve ever had in the time that I’ve been in office.” 
Green said she doesn’t know as much about the Farm Bill as she’d like to, and said farmers need financial assistance as they struggle with higher prices.
“Farmers need immediate help before we would be able to make any lasting changes, or end the war in Iran. That’s not something that’s going to happen overnight,” she said. “So the farmers are going to need immediate relief in the form of just money, just to keep afloat.”
Parsons said he doesn’t support either version of the Farm Bill and the best way to help farmers includes ending the Iran war, stopping Trump trade wars and eliminating bureaucracy surrounding green cards and work visas.
“There is a farm worker shortage right now,” Parsons said. “Whatever the size of that shortage is now, it’s going to be way worse if you continue to make it illegal to bring workers in.”
Healthcare
Green said she supports reviving the Affordable Care Act’s enhanced tax credits for health coverage that expired earlier this year. Arkansas and other states saw a drop in people covered by the federal health overhaul after the subsidies expired.
Green said she supports universal healthcare and mentioned Medicare for all as a possible vehicle for delivering it.
“I believe healthcare should be a right and should be easily accessible,” Green said.
Arkansas’ hybrid Medicaid expansion, created under the health law, faces an uncertain future after the Trump administration rejected a request to renew the program. The state is seeking a temporary two-year extension as it works on a replacement.
Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion

Crawford said the biggest issue that needs to be addressed in Medicaid is fraud, and that changes need to be made in how they’re administered.
“How do we adjust these benefits in a way that encourages personal growth, and people can lift themselves out of the situation so that they don’t need those benefits forever, and they don’t forgo a promotion at work?” he said. “Or they don’t take the extra hours, they don’t take the overtime because they don’t want to lose their benefit package.”
Parsons said to address the rising cost of healthcare there needs to be more efforts aimed at tort reform to address the costs of litigation, an area he says the Affordable Care Act fell short.
“It promised a lot of things that never happened, and for a lot of economists and other people who are in the know, it was predictable that it was going to fall short,” he said.

title: Idaho voters should ask themselves 1 question: Are you better off than you were 18 months ago?
description: The political race was close, with polls showing that the incumbent had a slight advantage and the challenger’s support had flattened out despite voters facing a dire situation. Rising inflation, higher unemployment, soaring interest rates, record high gas prices, family budgets stressed to the breaking point, a frustrating conflict with Iran, and the sense[...]
text:
"I Voted" stickers await Bonneville County voters for the primary election on  May 21, 2024, at the College of Easter Idaho in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The political race was close, with polls showing that the incumbent had a slight advantage and the challenger’s support had flattened out despite voters facing a dire situation. Rising inflation, higher unemployment, soaring interest rates, record high gas prices, family budgets stressed to the breaking point, a frustrating conflict with Iran, and the sense among Americans that the politicians in Washington, D.C., did not care about them.
To turn the momentum in his direction, the challenger asked Americans on the eve of the election: “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” On Election Day, the answer from voters was a resounding “No!”
If this scenario sounds like the state of our nation in the fall of 2026, you are correct. But this was October 1980, and the president was Jimmy Carter and the challenger who asked Americans if they were better off than four years earlier was Ronald Reagan.
Idaho’s general election is less than a month away. Here’s what you need to know.

The dramatic moment came in the last televised debate between Carter and Reagan, which drew the largest TV audience of any presidential debate. Reagan’s question shifted the tide of the campaign to his favor, and he ended up beating Carter in a landslide.
Reagan’s question is as relevant today as it was back in 1980. Do Idaho voters feel better off today than they did 18 months ago when Donald Trump promised to lower inflation, improve the economy, address the kitchen table concerns of American families, keep the country out of foreign wars, and drain the swamp? 
By all objective measurements, the answer to that question should be an overwhelming “No!”— just as it was back in November 1980. And polls show that President Trump’s approval rating is sinking, even in strong GOP states like Idaho. 
Most midterm elections are a referendum on the job performance of the president. But this year’s midterm election is not just a referendum on Donald Trump – it is also a referendum on the acolytes in Congress who have not challenged his policies that have led to the economic carnage we suffer today.
Idaho’s congressional delegation, especially, has supported the president and his policies without question. Instead of remaining faithful to the Constitution and the founders’ system of checks and balances, Idaho’s congressional members have remained silent as the president alienated our closest allies and trading partners, burdened Americans with costly tariffs, and launched an unnecessary and costly war, leading to the runaway gas and food prices we have today.
Not only that, but they also contributed to the damage by voting for the so-called Big Beautiful Bill which provided the greatest tax cut in history to the wealthiest Americans at the cost to our country’s working people and most vulnerable citizens, while adding billions of dollars to the national debt. Debt that our children and grandchildren are now forced to carry. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, who is asking voters to re-elect him this November, and U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo have voted against ending the Iran War 15 times since March. As chairman of the once-powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Risch has not once held a hearing on the war or publicly questioned the president about how he plans to end it.
Meanwhile, last week unleaded gas at Albertsons cost $5.35 and diesel $6.45 cents per gallon. The cost of putting food on the table has risen 3.5 percent since Trump took office, adding hundreds to the average family’s grocery bill.
Elections are about more than voting for someone because they are a Democrat or Republican. Elections are also about holding those in power accountable for their actions – or inactions. In 1980, 27 percent of voters who identified as Democrats voted for Reagan rather than the Democratic president. 
Elections are also about whether those who are asking for another term have fulfilled their responsibilities to help make life better for Americans and their families. 
Unfortunately, the challengers who want to hold our current congressional delegation accountable will not have a chance to debate the incumbents and ask the same question Reagan did: Are voters better off now than they were 18 months ago?
That’s because our congressional representatives have decided that debates are not in their self-interest, forgetting that elections are not about them, but about the people they represent. 
Instead, they have amassed huge campaign budgets which they are using to scrub their lackluster record and convince voters they have their best interest at heart. But they are not willing to defend those records in free town hall meetings or televised debates.
The election is about a month away and many of you are already casting your ballot. This is the hour of upmost importance to our democracy and society.
As you decide, remember this: If you can cut through the paid political propaganda airing on TV or arriving in your mailbox, you can best consider what candidate is working for you. Ask yourself: Does the candidate cling to power for power’s sake and to serve those who are already comfortable? Or does the candidate stand with you and your family?
The best way to judge that is to ask what Ronald Reagan did in 1980: Are you better off now than you were 18 months ago? If the answer is a resounding “No!” what are you going to do about it?

name: Michigan Advance
title: Corrections isn’t a political sideshow. Michigan’s next governor must make it a priority.
description: There is a reason Michigan’s Department of Corrections rarely makes it to the top of the list of political priorities. Jobs, roads, taxes and schools all make for more comfortable campaign-trail conversations. If there’s any campaign talk of prisons, it’s usually along the lines of “How many more should we build?” The conversation rarely goes […]
text:
A protester outside the Michigan Department of Corrections headquarters in Lansing. July 31, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. There is a reason Michigan’s Department of Corrections rarely makes it to the top of the list of political priorities.
Jobs, roads, taxes and schools all make for more comfortable campaign-trail conversations. If there’s any campaign talk of prisons, it’s usually along the lines of “How many more should we build?” The conversation rarely goes much deeper than that, likely because prisons force politicians to confront a much less comfortable question: What does the state owe the people it locks up?
Few politicians want to answer that question with any earnestness. And it’s not a huge mystery why.
The people at the center of the issue are convicted criminals. They have committed crimes, harmed victims and, in many cases, been sentenced to years, maybe even life, behind bars.
That makes corrections an easy problem for politicians to ignore.
Michigan’s next governor will face major challenges at the Department of Corrections

But there is an inconvenient fact that cannot be ignored: inmates are wards of the state. We, collectively, are responsible for their well-being. 
Once Michigan takes someone into custody, the state assumes responsibility for that person’s basic safety, health and welfare. That responsibility does not depend on whether the person is popular, sympathetic or deserving of anyone’s applause.
And it certainly does not excuse the state from doing its job.
That is what makes the latest reporting on the Michigan Department of Corrections so troubling — and so important.
As Michigan Advance’s Katherine Dailey reported Tuesday, the next governor will inherit a department facing severe staffing shortages, violence, concerns about conditions inside its facilities and bipartisan calls for new leadership. 
Nearly every correctional facility has vacancies, with some facilities carrying vacancy rates above 25%. Corrections officers are working mandatory overtime, in some cases 16-hour days on consecutive days. 
This isn’t merely a labor problem. This is a people problem.
And ultimately, it is a gubernatorial problem.
When prisons are chronically understaffed, everyone suffers. Officers become exhausted. Safety deteriorates. Violence becomes harder to control. Basic operations become more difficult. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Incarcerated people can lose access to recreation, meals outside their cells, family communication and programs designed to prepare them for release. 
And whether or not you have any sympathy for prisoners, that last point matters.
Remember — most people in Michigan’s prisons will eventually leave them.
The question is what kind of people Michigan is sending back into its communities.
A prison system that cannot reliably provide basic programming, treatment, education and security is not only failing inmates. 
It is failing you and me.
It is also failing a group whose interests deserve far more attention: the people who work inside these facilities.
Corrections officers aren’t political abstractions. They are public servants going to work every day in an environment where violence is an occupational hazard. They should not have to choose between serving their state and burning themselves out.
Safety concerns in Michigan prisons grow after pension bills are vetoed

The current staffing situation described by corrections union leadership — including mandatory overtime and prolonged 16-hour shifts — should be unacceptable to anyone who believes government has an obligation to protect its own employees. 
This is not a question that can be meaningfully reduced to whether one is “tough on crime” or “soft on crime.”
It should be about whether Michigan’s prison system is competent.
Competence means having enough trained officers to safely operate a prison and providing those officers with competitive pay and benefits.
But just as importantly — perhaps even more so — it means making sure incarcerated people receive the medical care, mental-health services, education, vocational training and other programming the state says they should receive.
And it means recognizing that better conditions for inmates and better working conditions for corrections officers are not mutually exclusive. They are inseparable.
A prison staffed by exhausted employees is not a safer prison. A prison where programming routinely breaks down is not necessarily producing better outcomes. A prison where violence becomes normalized is bad for the person incarcerated, bad for the officer who has to confront it and yes; bad for you and me and the communities we live in to which many of those prisoners will eventually return.
While it is clear that MDOC Director Heidi Washington, who has served in that role for 11 years across two administrations, has outstayed her welcome, simply replacing one bureaucrat with another will not solve the problem.
MDOC reports fourth death at Women’s Huron Valley prison in under two months

The next governor will need to confront this issue with the understanding that there is no magic fix. Even lawmakers quoted by Michigan Advance acknowledge that this will require multiple policies over time. 
But the first step is political.
The next governor has to decide that corrections matter.
Not because prisoners are an especially sympathetic constituency. They aren’t.
And not because corrections are a politically fashionable issue. They aren’t.
But because the state cannot take away someone’s liberty and then shrug when the institution responsible for that person begins to fail.
And because the men and women who work in those institutions deserve better, too.
Michigan’s next governor — Democrat or Republican — will inherit this problem.
The real question is whether that governor will finally have the courage to deal with it by enacting systemic change, and not just deciding to add or subtract dollars from its budget.
