name: WyoFile
title: The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Amanda MacLeod falls for actors as a Hollywood double
description:
Dancing and ski racing her way through high school gave her the skills to make it in Tinseltown.
The post The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Amanda MacLeod falls for actors as a Hollywood double appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Amanda MacLeod has fallen across silver screens throughout the country while working as a Hollywood stunt double, using skills she learned from skiing and dancing while growing up in Wyoming.
Before she could walk, her father carried her in a backpack while he skied in the Teton backcountry. She was in dance classes by age 4, learning skills that would lay the foundation for a career on stage and in front of the lens.
Through school years, her athleticism grew as she played soccer, cycled, climbed, hiked, danced and paddled, much of it among Wyoming’s hills. Her grandmother was a ballroom dancer, her mother a dancer with the local troupe, her father an avid skier.
“I was dancing and skiing side-by-side my whole life,” MacLeod said. But when she saw a performance by the Diavolo: Architecture in Motion dance company, it swayed her to focus her talents and provoked a fateful conversation.
“Sorry, Dad. I’m going to join the Dancers’ Workshop Junior Company.”
That decision sent MacLeod down a coast-to-coast path — dancing in New York, moving to L.A., working odd jobs and finally, landing on a film set. Among other roles, she was the stunt double for Doug Jones in “Hocus Pocus 2.”
“Which is crazy because he’s a 6’-4” guy, and I’m a 5’-4” woman,” she said. Jones played zombie Billy Butcherson, she his headless double.
“A lot of it is just Doug Jones’s talking head, and then me stumbling around the world,” she said. Her skiing and dancing skills gave her a foundation for soundstage antics.
“If you don’t know how to bail and fall on skis or a bike, if you don’t know how to roll out of that, you’re really going to be in a world of hurt,” she said of learning her art. “Being a dancer has allowed me as a stunt performer to jump into most anything. You know where every part of your body is at all times … something that I haven’t found in any other athletic endeavor. That’s what helps me stumble without hurting myself.”
MacLeod said she knows when she’s hit the mark.
“A stunt person’s favorite thing is when the crew or the director goes, ‘Oh my God, are you okay?’”
Kept up with the boys
“Without my dance background, I would not be where I am in my career,” she said, “and without my extreme sports background, I also would not be where I am in my career.”
Now 37, she forged her ethos in the sometimes cruel crucible of high school and “a patriarchal environment of extreme sports.”
“If you were kind of popular, it was because you could hang and keep up with the boys, or because they wanted to sleep with you,” she said of her formative years. “I was the one who kept up with the boys.”
Dancers provided more inspiration than cliff-jumping dudes. “I saw a couple of big companies from New York and London around my freshman year, and it just put me completely on fire for dance.”
She earned a BFA in dance and choreography from Mason Gross School of the Arts at Rutgers University in New Jersey and became a performance artist in Brooklyn.
“I was doing artsy-fartsy stuff in basements and galleries and what have you, while also working for a nonprofit and a restaurant. I was hitting the ground hard in my 20s. I got kind of burnt out, having to work so hard just to survive.”
“I was the one who kept up with the boys.”Amanda MacLeod
She packed two suitcases and moved to Los Angeles, for a Pilates apprenticeship in Laguna Beach, a discipline that cured a back injury. On a whim, she took a job with a tech startup.
“After six months, I kind of came to,” she said of her corporate stint. “It wasn’t for naught,” she said of the alien culture, because it gave her key communication and networking skills.
In L.A. she made good on a promise she’d made to herself in high school: dancing with Diavolo, the company that had inspired 17-year-old MacLeod to focus on dance back in Jackson.
“The amount of athleticism that that company requires and the strength that it requires — we’re literally running, sprinting, jumping, leaping, and flying 25, 30, feet through the air … caught by a few guys — helped [me] get over this really gnarly disorder,” she said. “And it also inspired me to go, ‘I’m going to join that company someday.’ And 10 years later, I did.”
The experience, and the daily discipline required to keep up, cured her of a troubled eating behavior, she said.
Old white dude with an eye patch
As she became more established, MacLeod began working with art departments on film sets and learning about stunt work.
“It’s like adult playtime,” she said of her work on the movie sets. Then someone said “Oh, you should go to this open call.”
It was a dance tryout that drew 300 dancers, actors and stunt workers, everyone from college cheerleaders to martial artists, gymnasts and parkour athletes.
“And there’s this man, this old, like older white dude, sitting in a chair, bald with an eye patch, and I’m just like, OK, who are you and what’s happening? This is great.
“He’s giving everyone one minute to do a pass. He’ll put two people in front of the whole group and say, ‘Okay, go,’ and you just have one minute to show off some shit, and that’s it.”
MacLeod jumped, dove, and bounced off walls. “And he just went ‘perfect’” she said. “I went ‘OK,’ [and] just walked away because people blow smoke up your ass a lot in this town.”
But she was “perfect” and got a callback, then another. Before long she found herself in front of cameras, working on pre-production for “Avatar: The Way of Water.”
Hollywood has its problems. “There’s still a lot of tropes about women sleeping around for work,” she said. She sometimes wonders, “am I getting hired because this guy’s going to hit on me and try to get me to sleep with him, or is he hiring me because of my skills?”
“I went ‘okay,’ [and] just walked away because people blow smoke up your ass a lot in this town.”Amanda MacLeod
Things are changing and new Screen Actors Guild rules that women should double for women and other guidelines are boosting opportunities. Yet, “it’s still very much a man’s game,” she said. “They have way more jobs.”
Her niche is as a double. “If you can double an actress and become tight with them, you can get carried with them for their career.”
MacLeod sees potential for filming in Wyoming. “Think about outside of Lander, or near the Wind Rivers. There’s so much environment that could be used there. There are plenty of talented cinematographers in Wyoming. There’s a bunch of people that know how to rig that just need the right training.
“We have people who could do it, but they don’t because it’s really expensive to live in Jackson, and there’s no film incentives in Wyoming.”
It would be nice to work in her home state, MacLeod said, in part because “I’m kind of over cities.”
“I’m so grateful for everything I’ve been able to accomplish and do. But none of it matters if I don’t have trees and mountains and rivers to go home to.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Summit pushes for utilities commission action on outstanding pipeline dockets
description: The Iowa Utilities Commission has denied a request from Summit Carbon Solutions, the company seeking to build a carbon sequestration pipeline in Iowa, to consolidate outstanding dockets and schedule a hearing.  The IUC issued hearing schedules for two sections of pipeline in the company’s second phase of the project, but denied Summit’s request to combine […[...]
text:
Kathy Carter, a Floyd County landowner, speaks outside of the Iowa Utilities Commission Oct. 8, 2026 in opposition to a carbon sequestration pipeline. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) The Iowa Utilities Commission has denied a request from Summit Carbon Solutions, the company seeking to build a carbon sequestration pipeline in Iowa, to consolidate outstanding dockets and schedule a hearing. 
The IUC issued hearing schedules for two sections of pipeline in the company’s second phase of the project, but denied Summit’s request to combine the dockets. 
The IUC did not rule on the remaining dockets for phase 2, which could still be consolidated in the future, as Summit has requested. Summit’s phase 2 pipeline routes would add laterals to the pipeline, allowing it to connect to more biorefineries than the original route included. 
In the request, Summit said the IUC has scheduled and held hearings and issued orders for “several other energy infrastructure projects” but has been “ignoring Summit.” Summit’s initial filings for the project were made between October 2024 and September 2025, according to the request, but the company said it has not received the “basic procedural path” forward. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Even if this Commission’s answer is ultimately no—though we see no reason why that would be the case, giving the Commission’s prior rulings—further delay on the bare minimum process (setting a hearing) will irreparably harm Iowa’s reputation,” the company wrote in the request for consolidation.
Summit argued that while other states and the federal government are “speeding up the permitting process, recognizing that energy infrastructure is paramount” the IUC is “making the process longer and more cumbersome.” 
Summit said the drawn-out process is harming the ethanol industry and farmers who want access to the low-carbon biofuel markets the carbon sequestration pipeline would open up. The company said delaying a hearing on the docket is also harming landowners who want their objections heard and rural communities with a stake in the investment. 
Colleen Tucker, a landowner from Mitchell County, addressed commissioners during public comments at a meeting Thursday and said it was “incredibly bold and frankly offensive” for Summit to speak on behalf of landowners in its filing. 
Tucker said the IUC is not responsible for Summit’s investments and that the company’s investment in the project “doesn’t give the company a regulatory shortcut or a cut to the front of the line.” 
IUC, in its order denying the consolidation of dockets, noted the lawsuit against Summit’s permit for phase one of the project as “part of the larger picture” impacting the docket.
Summit’s initial permit for more than 600 miles of pipe through Iowa, phase one of the project, was approved by the Iowa Utilities Commission in 2024, giving the company the right of eminent domain for the project. Landowners, the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and several counties challenged the permit, arguing Summit should not be considered a common carrier. 
In fall 2025, Summit filed a request to amend its permit with the IUC to no longer travel through South Dakota and to a sequestration site in North Dakota. The lawsuit over the initial permit was partially remanded to the IUC because of the amendment, and according to the IUC response, comments on how to proceed with the permit included a request to keep the Floyd and Ida County dockets in phase two as “stand-alone dockets.” 
IUC held a hearing in September to determine a hearing schedule on dockets for two sections of pipe planned for Ida and Floyd counties, both of which are less than 5 miles. In its responses denying Summit’s consolidation request, IUC finalized hearing dates for the segments. The docket pertaining to Floyd County will be heard March 23, 2027 and the Ida County hearing will occur Feb. 23, 2027. Both will be held in Des Moines and are later than the middle of December hearing dates requested by Summit.
Summit announced in May that it planned to direct the pipeline west toward Wyoming and that it was considering using the CO2 for enhanced oil recovery, a process where the liquified carbon dioxide in the pipeline can be injected into the ground near existing oil fields to help push the oil to the surface. 
Landowner opposition 
Landowners opposed to the project said some of them were denied requests to intervene in the upcoming hearings because, though they live near the proposed route, they don’t own property in the counties. 
Don Johannsen, a Cherokee County landowner, said the route is on adjoining land to his property and would directly impact him.
“They’re assuming that because I’m not on the line in Ida County, that it doesn’t affect me, but it clearly does,” Johannsen said while speaking to reporters Thursday morning. 
Jon Dunwell was recently appointed to serve on the Iowa Utilities Commission. He joined commissioners Oct. 8, 2026 for a public meeting. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The issue of who can intervene has been brought up throughout the Summit proceedings with the Iowa Utilities Commission. Lawmakers opposed to the project, or its use of eminent domain, have proposed legislation to widen the pool of people who could intervene in proceedings. 
Landowners gathered Thursday ahead of the Iowa Utilities Commission’s first monthly public meeting with its newest commissioner, Jon Dunwell, who was appointed Monday by Gov. Kim Reynolds. Those gathered, in their signature red shirts, said they were opposed to the recent appointment and argued Dunwell’s past as a legislator made him partial in the pipeline issue.
Dunwell resigned his seat in the Iowa House of Representatives to accept the commissioner appointment, which will require Senate approval.
Kathy Carter, a Floyd County landowner, said she was “really concerned” with the newest commissioner. 
“Because of his past on the Legislature and his ability to vote, I believe it’s a conflict of interest,” Carter said Thursday ahead of the IUC public meeting. “Anybody who’s been in that position to affect any legislation should not have the ability to vote on the IUC.”
Dunwell voted in favor of legislation in 2025 that would have imposed certain limitations on carbon sequestration pipelines in the state. This bill passed the Senate in 2025 after a group of senators held up votes on budget bills until the body debated the legislation. The bill was ultimately vetoed by Reynolds. 
Dunwell voted against a House bill earlier this year that would have banned the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines in Iowa, but the bill was not taken up in the Senate. 
During the public meeting, Commissioner Joshua Byrnes, who also previously served as a state legislator, said commissioners are not always able to be “experts” on everything, noting the number of issues the commission handles, in addition to pipeline issues. 
Property rights and the election 
The landowner group said they have sent out surveys to all of the candidates running in state, federal and local races to ask them about property rights. Weston Grow, a Guthrie County landowner, said the group plans to release the responses to the questionnaire next week. 
“Each and every legislator will tell you they are for property rights – they have been for almost six years,” Grow said. “We’re tired of waiting. It’s election time. Just like all the phony political ads we are reading, hearing, and seeing, don’t believe just because a politician says they are for property rights doesn’t mean that they actually are.”

title: Tennessee prepares for heavy rain, strong winds brought by Hurricane Isaias
description: Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee this weekend, according to the National Weather Service. The hurricane is expected to intensify as it nears the Gulf Coast and make landfall Friday night, then move through the Tennessee River Valley over the weekend.  While the storm is projected […]
text:
The remnants of Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee between Oct. 9 and Oct. 11, 2026. (Courtesy of the National Weather Service)Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee this weekend, according to the National Weather Service.
The hurricane is expected to intensify as it nears the Gulf Coast and make landfall Friday night, then move through the Tennessee River Valley over the weekend.  While the storm is projected to weaken before it crosses into Tennessee, the National Weather Service has issued flood watches for most of West Tennessee and Middle Tennessee, in addition to counties along the state’s southern border in East Tennessee from Friday evening through Sunday morning.
A high wind watch is also in place along Tennessee’s eastern border from Saturday morning to Sunday morning.
West Tennessee
Total rainfall is expected to be between one to three inches, though areas near the Tennessee River could see local amounts up to four inches, the National Weather Service reported Thursday.
Rain greater than two inches is most likely along Tennessee’s southern border above Mississippi and Alabama. Memphis has a 49% chance of seeing more than two inches of rain. 
Counties under flood watch include Benton, Carroll, Chester, Crockett, Decatur, Dyer, Fayette, Gibson, Hardeman, Hardin, Haywood, Henderson, Lauderdale, Madison, McNairy, Shelby and Tipton.
Wind gusts could reach 35 miles per hour.
Middle Tennessee
Middle Tennessee is expected to see between one and three inches of rain, mostly on Saturday through Saturday night.

title: Ocean County elections board, GOP chair sued over voter challenges
description: The League of Women Voters asked courts to step in after the Ocean County elections board challenged some Democratic and unaffiliated Bay Head voters.
text:
The League of Women Voters asked courts to step in after the Ocean County elections board challenged some Democratic and unaffiliated Bay Head voters. (Photo by Daniella Heminghaus/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey League of Women Voters and a trio of Bay Head residents sued the Ocean County Board of Elections and its Republican chairman, George Gilmore, alleging they violated a state voting rights law.
The lawsuit comes after the board warned Democrats and unaffiliated voters on a list compiled by Dennis Shaning, who chairs the all-Republican borough council, that they may be deemed ineligible to vote because their tax bills were sent to an address outside Bay Head. The list excluded Republican voters in the same position, the suit argues.
“The Ocean County Board of Elections has intimidated and discriminated against voters in Bay Head and put unconstitutional barriers in the way of the exercise of their fundamental right to vote,” said Liza Weisberg, supervising attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, which is representing the plaintiffs.
Voters on the list were told their suffrage may be challenged unless they filled a lengthy questionnaire and attended an Oct. 13 Board of Elections hearing. The deadline to register to vote in the Nov. 3 elections is Oct. 13.
The suit alleges the board violated a recently enacted state voting rights law by attempting to intimidate voters.
It also says the board violated the equal protection clause of New Jersey’s Constitution by leaving in place the registrations of Republicans whose tax bills were sent to an address outside the borough.
“The Gilmore Letters created a separate class of voters — registered non-Republican voters whose tax bills are mailed to addresses outside Ocean County — and treated them differently than everyone else,” the suit says.
Gilmore, who is also chair of Ocean County’s Republican Party, did not immediately return a text message seeking comment.
Last month, Gilmore told the New Jersey Monitor that the elections board is merely following up on a letter it received, a practice the board has done for more than three decades.
“We don’t go out looking for people. We react to challenges that come into the board,” he said.
The suit asks a judge to enjoin the board from weighing the eligibility of voters on Shaning’s list based on their party affiliation, tax bill mailing address, questionnaire responses, and meeting attendance.
Those voters should not be required to cast their vote using a provisional ballot, the suit said. The plaintiffs asked the court to declare the board’s inquest unlawful and award attorneys’ fees and damages under the New Jersey Voter Empowerment Act.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: USDA says it will be cracking down on dog breeders in Iowa and elsewhere
description: U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins appeared at the Animal Rescue League of Iowa this week to tout the agency’s efforts to shut down puppy mills in Iowa and other states. While at the ARL on Tuesday, Rollins said although the USDA inspectors used to visit a facility, cite violations, and then leave, “those […]
text:
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, left, holds a kitten at the Animal Rescue League of Iowa during a news conference Oct. 6, 2026, with U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, center, and ARL CEO Tom Colvin. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins appeared at the Animal Rescue League of Iowa this week to tout the agency’s efforts to shut down puppy mills in Iowa and other states.
While at the ARL on Tuesday, Rollins said although the USDA inspectors used to visit a facility, cite violations, and then leave, “those days are over. We are now in the active process of shutting down these puppy mills.”
Rollins said the USDA is “increasing our agents by 20 percent” and is focusing enforcement efforts on states such as Iowa and Missouri where there are significant issues with compliance.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Iowa is right at the top of the list,” Rollins said. “Virginia and a couple of other states where we’re really, really focusing — I think you’re going to see even more significant action coming very soon.”
Rollins appeared at the ARL alongside Rep. Zach Nunn, a Republican seeking reelection in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District. Earlier this year, the U.S. House approved a farm bill amendment backed by Nunn that his office says will “reinforce” the USDA’s authority to police breeders who violate the law. Nunn’s amendment deleted text from the bill that would have raised the threshold on the level of suffering necessary before the USDA could consider seizing animals believed to be at risk.
Nunn is also a co-sponsor of Goldie’s Act, or HR 349, which seeks to expand certain enforcement provisions of the Animal Welfare Act. The bill, which has yet to be approved in either the House or Senate, would direct the USDA to share with state and local officials the detailed descriptions of violations uncovered during inspections, and require that the USDA conduct follow-up inspections when violations are cited.
In February, Rollins announced the USDA would be taking “historic actions to hold chronic companion animal welfare violators accountable.” At the time, Rollins said, “if you are breeding dogs and not meeting the Animal Welfare Act’s humane standards of care, your time is up. We will not allow a handful of bad actors to tarnish the reputation of responsible American breeders or compromise the humane treatment of animals.”
Rollins: Action on unlicensed breeders
Citing statistics that suggest breeders’ compliance with the Animal Welfare Act has risen from an average of 67% in 2015 to over 92% in 2025, Rollins has said that change reflects both regulatory improvements and increased industry cooperation across the country.
Still, she said, the USDA intends to “root out bad actors with a history of noncompliance” by initiating enforcement action against repeat violators and deploying “specialist teams” to aggressively investigate unlicensed breeders.
Last month, Rollins held what the USDA called a “strikeforce roundtable” with other federal agencies and announced a series of steps to improve regulatory oversight of breeders.
Among those steps:
— New regulations: The USDA says it intends to propose regulations that will be responsive to the “overwhelming” public support for strengthening Animal Welfare Act standards for dogs. At her Iowa appearance this week, Rollins said the agency will be “strengthening licensing requirements under the AWA, strengthening oversight on who conducts surgeries, dental procedures, and euthanasia – they must be licensed vets, which isn’t happening right now.”
— Communication: The USDA will amplify its communication efforts by distributing 2,000 “regulatory refresher mailings” to dog-breeding facilities. The agency says that move will “make crystal clear what the law requires for humane care.”
— Enforcement: The USDA says it has deployed its Animal Protection Bureau to conduct “targeted compliance reviews” and implement modernized enforcement strategies. In 2026, the agency says, it prioritized this focus on “bad actors” by denying or terminating a total of eight dog breeder licenses, suspending six licenses, and revoking five licenses. That same year, the agency conducted over 2,000 inspections of dog breeders and brokers around the nation.
ASPCA cites ‘policy of non-enforcement’
Although the USDA says it is beefing up animal-welfare regulations and oversight, the agency is facing allegations that it doesn’t enforce regulations already on the books.
The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals is currently suing the USDA, challenging the agency’s decision to license three Iowa dog breeders — Steve Kruse, Brian Lichirie and Wuanita Swedlund — accused in the lawsuit of being involved in a puppy-laundering scheme intended to disguise the origin of dogs sold to retailers.
The ASPCA lawsuit was filed in 2024 but has moved slowly through the courts with no scheduling orders issued and no discovery or depositions having taken place.
The ASPCA is now seeking to amend and expand its lawsuit against the federal agency, claiming the USDA’s “ongoing policy of non-enforcement persists to this day.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota Farmers Union asks governor and lawmakers to approve a state fuel tax holiday
description: As further complications arose Thursday around actions meant to ease the burden of high diesel prices, the South Dakota Farmers Union asked the governor and state lawmakers to call a special legislative session to approve a state fuel tax holiday. “The governor says this all the time, that agriculture is king, and you hear it […]
text:
South Dakota Farmers Union President Doug Sombke participates in a press conference Oct. 12, 2023, at the Denny Sanford Premier Center in Sioux Falls. Sombke and the Farmers Union are calling for a fuel tax holiday in the state. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/100826-Dyed-Diesel-Clarification-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
As further complications arose Thursday around actions meant to ease the burden of high diesel prices, the South Dakota Farmers Union asked the governor and state lawmakers to call a special legislative session to approve a state fuel tax holiday.
“The governor says this all the time, that agriculture is king, and you hear it from legislators as well,” said South Dakota Farmers Union President Doug Sombke. “So, then let’s treat it as such, and let’s make sure that we take care of it as such.”
The organization is asking the governor and lawmakers to approve legislation that would temporarily reduce the state tax on gasoline and diesel from 28 cents to 1 cent per gallon. Requiring at least 1 cent of tax would allow for tracking of the amount of highway funding lost to the tax holiday so lawmakers could replace it later, the Farmers Union said, possibly with reserve funds.
The Farmers Union said legislation should also temporarily allow the use of federally tax-exempt, offroad, red-dyed diesel in highway vehicles, while shielding people from state fuel tax penalties, retroactive audits or enforcement actions, and providing clear direction for law enforcement agencies to suspend enforcement.
The Governor’s Office, in a response to South Dakota Searchlight questions, said in a written statement that “all options are on the table, and we will continue to do what we can to support farmers and taxpayers during this turbulent time.”
Chance of dyed diesel lingering in tanks makes some farmers hesitant to accept Trump’s help

Sombke’s request comes after the state Department of Revenue on Thursday clarified the state’s response to President Donald Trump’s Monday executive order. Trump’s order is intended to allow broader use of dyed diesel, which is only legal for offroad use in machinery such as farm equipment.
Red-dyed diesel is the same as regular diesel apart from the dye added to help with enforcement. Trump’s order suspends penalties for unauthorized uses through the end of the year.
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden responded Tuesday by directing the state Department of Public Safety to “prioritize commercial motor vehicle inspections that present a threat to public safety and not attempt to identify the use of dyed diesel fuel on highways and public roads” while the federal order is in effect.
“By taking this action, we will provide meaningful relief to South Dakota farmers,” Rhoden said in a news release Tuesday, and “allow all taxpayers to realize meaningful savings from using dyed diesel.”
But dyed diesel is delivered in bulk to permitted users such as farmers and is not readily available to the general public. Additionally, some farmers are concerned about being fined for trace amounts of the dye left in their vehicle fuel tanks after Trump’s order expires.
The state’s Department of Revenue said Thursday that although dyed diesel is federally tax exempt, which saves approved users 24.4 cents per gallon, it’s only exempt from state and local taxes when it’s used for approved agricultural purposes. Thus, anybody else who buys dyed diesel should be paying state and local taxes on it, and those taxes could “reduce or eliminate any tax benefits” from federal tax relief.
Based on that legal reality, the department said in a news release, “only agricultural producers with a valid agricultural exemption certificate should fuel with red dyed diesel for on-road use at this time.”
Rhoden cannot suspend state taxes himself, because they’re established in state law. That’s why Sombke’s organization is calling for a special session of the Legislature. A special session can be called by the governor, or lawmakers can petition for it with two-thirds support from both the House and Senate.
In a letter to Rhoden and legislative leaders, the Farmers Union said that because of all the complications surrounding the actions with dyed diesel in South Dakota, “citizens, commercial operators, and agricultural producers are placed in an unfair and precarious situation.”
Gas and diesel prices have risen sharply since the beginning of Trump’s war in Iran, which has disrupted global fuel supply chains. In at least four other states — Georgia, Indiana, Ohio and Utah — leaders have moved to temporarily suspend or reduce the state tax on gasoline.

title: State lawmaker under investigation for misusing office, Oklahoma Ethics Commission says
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A Republican state lawmaker is now being investigated for allegedly misusing his elected position to support a for-profit business and two nonprofits, the Oklahoma Ethics Commission announced Thursday.   The Oklahoma Ethics Commission said it is investigating state Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, for violations of state ethics rules for misu[...]
text:
Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, speaks to the House Rules Committee meeting Sept. 24, 2026 at the state Capitol ahead of a vote to censure him as well as recommend that he resign and end his bid for reelection following allegations of misconduct and sexual harassment. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A Republican state lawmaker is now being investigated for allegedly misusing his elected position to support a for-profit business and two nonprofits, the Oklahoma Ethics Commission announced Thursday.  
The Oklahoma Ethics Commission said it is investigating state Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, for violations of state ethics rules for misusing his office and authority and lacking the impartiality required of a state officer, according to a redacted copy of the allegations made public Thursday. The Ethics Commission’s investigation is unrelated to a separate House inquiry into Williams’ conduct.
The investigation is ongoing, but the Commission has identified “substantial evidence” suggesting that Williams used his office to improperly advance his personal, financial and organizational interests, said Lee Anne Bruce Boone, executive director of the Ethics Commission, in a statement.
Williams has 20 days to respond to the Ethics Commission’s allegations, either in person or in writing, and failure to do so will be considered an admission, according to the Commission’s notice of allegations. The Commission may then take action, potentially in the form of a civil lawsuit, and attempt to collect monetary damages and any other court-ordered penalties. 
His attorney, David Herber, said Thursday that Williams will respond to the allegations by the deadline provided by the Ethics Commission. 
“He has cooperated with the Commission’s investigation and will continue to do so,” Herber said. “It should be noted that Rep. Williams does not receive compensation from any nonprofit corporation and has not benefited financially from any of his service with any nonprofit organization, nor has he benefited financially from any interaction with a state agency.” 
The Ethics Commission’s letter states that it is investigating Williams for using state resources and his elected office to engage in fundraising for a nonprofit and for receiving benefits like transportation and lodging at hotels and casinos. 
Williams is also accused of endorsing a for-profit company’s product at the Department of Corrections earlier this year and using his office and position to help with contracts, legal documents, onboarding of medical providers and sales, among other things, according to the Ethics Commission’s letter. The Ethics Commission’s letter also alleges Williams was involved in selling a product to the Seminole County Jail, according to the notice of allegations. 
The letter also alleges Williams chaired a second nonprofit that received funding from a state mental health grant. 
Bruce Boone said in a statement that Williams has “not been forthright with the Commission,” which has hindered its ability to obtain timely and complete information. 
The Commission decided to publicly release the allegations because the investigation won’t be complete prior to the Nov. 3 general election, she said. 
“… There’s a process here, but we can’t possibly finish that process before the election and it’s in the public interest to get the information out there,” she said after Thursday’s meeting.
Oklahoma House lawmaker faces sexual harassment allegations. Committee recommends he resign.

Williams is seeking reelection to the represent House District 28, which includes parts of Pottawatomie and Seminole counties. He faces Democrat Blake Cummings on Nov. 3.
This marks the second investigation Williams has faced this year. 
The state House conducted an internal and external investigation into accusations that Williams sexually harassed multiple female employees. After holding two days of closed-door hearings, a House committee announced that it had substantiated multiple claims of sexual harassment against multiple employees. That committee last month voted to request the full House publicly reprimand Williams and suggested a series of sanctions. It stopped short of recommending expulsion. 
Williams has denied wrongdoing in that matter, claiming he hasn’t broken any laws or House rules.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘It’s a Beautiful River in the Middle of a Hellscape’
description: The Pecos River headwaters rush untamed through miles of steep canyons and pine-covered slopes. When it exits New Mexico, the Pecos looks more like a tightly managed creek — a conveyance delivering carefully tallied water through the middle of the Permian Basin, the country’s most productive oil and gas region.
text:
A hiker crosses a bridge over the Pecos River, downstream from its source in the Sangre de Christo Mountains in northern New Mexico. (Photo by Jerry Redfern/Capital & Main)
It’s an early May afternoon, and Charlie Barrett has parked his pickup in a pullout along a county road a few hundred feet from the Black River in southern New Mexico, just a mile from where it empties into the Pecos River.

He has stopped to set up a video camera that detects heat and gasses invisible to the eye to check for emissions at a nearby oil and gas operation.
Stepping out of the truck, Barrett finds the pullout muddy and dotted with puddles — an anomaly during an ongoing drought. A gray chunk of salt the size of a medicine ball sits near a mud puddle flecked with shimmering, white crystals.
“Unfortunately this is pretty common,” he said. “It’s also quite dangerous.” It appeared that someone had dumped oilfield wastewater — also known as produced water — at the pullout. The extremely saline and toxic byproduct of oil and gas production carries a mix of petroleum compounds and oilfield chemicals. Produced water can be radioactive, too. Barrett said he worries that people would unwittingly drive through the muck or pull off the road and walk through it.
All day, every day, hundreds of semi trucks haul the toxic produced water from well sites to disposal stations along the highways and backroads of this far corner of New Mexico. That water is an unwanted byproduct of oil and gas development. More than three barrels of wastewater come out of the ground for every barrel of extracted oil, on average in New Mexico. As fossil fuel production has skyrocketed in the Permian Basin, the amount of produced water has followed. In addition, the water-to-oil ratio increases as wells and oilfields age — a process known as “watering out.”
Charlie Barrett, a thermographer with Oilfield Witness, points out a chunk of salt that likely fell off of a truck carrying oilfield wastewater near Malaga, New Mexico. (Jerry Redfern/ Capital & Main)
New Mexico state rules ban produced water use for anything outside the oilfield. This has led to a parallel industry devoted to gathering, transporting and reinjecting produced water deep underground. That, in turn, has led to a rise in seismic activity in the region, as well as dramatic blowouts that spew toxic water when injection wells fail.
Barrett works for industry watchdog Oilfield Witness as a thermographer, using a thermal camera to measure gaseous emissions from oilfield equipment. As he set up to record, produced water trucks rumbled by under a cloudless sky.
Barrett began filming. “Oh, man, that’s f—ing terrible,” he said. On its small screen, in wavy, candy-colored hues, the camera revealed the heat signatures of three active flares near a house. “Got a person’s home here and then this mess … all producing CO2 and methane and other volatile organic compounds, blowing right into their home,” he said, looking through the viewfinder. “Jesus, man. It’s ridiculous.”
When he looked at the footage later on a bigger screen, he found another lit flare in the video, in addition to the first three. One shot — four flares. This despite the fact that New Mexico has banned nearly all flaring since 2022.
Companies burn off — or “flare” — natural gas for a few reasons, including: it doesn’t meet specifications; it is over pressurized in a pipeline; or it’s required for equipment maintenance. Though better for the climate than venting unburned gas into the atmosphere, flaring still produces carbon dioxide and other toxic pollutants.
Later, Barrett sat on a small boulder along a quiet bend in the Pecos River, talking about his work. The river gurgled; dragonflies hovered, and the grasses rustled as more oilfield trucks rumbled over a nearby bridge, a reminder that Barrett was sitting in one of the most prolific fossil fuel basins on the planet.
“It sucks,” he said. “It’s a beautiful river in the middle of a hellscape.”
Charlie Barrett documents emissions coming from nearby oil and wastewater storage tanks on an oil well site near Loving. (Jerry Redfern / Capital & Main)
Several months earlier, the last time Barrett visited this spot, he found salt deposits covering the ground between the bridge and the riverbank. “I mean, the whole road was flooded over,” he said. “We couldn’t confirm one way or another if that was an actual produced water spill,” he added, but there are few other possibilities.
Such a spill would represent another environmental shock for this troubled river. The irony: The river needs more water. U.S. Geological Survey data going back nearly 40 years shows the annual snowpack slowly but steadily declining in the mountains around the Pecos River’s headwaters. River flow measurements in the upriver town of Pecos show the same.
As climate change heats and dries New Mexico, and the Pecos River runs ever lower, one of the biggest drivers of that change sits atop the river’s banks, just feet from where Barrett sits — 75,000 square miles of oil and gas wells across 55 counties in New Mexico and Texas: the vast Permian Basin.
Water and Geology
The Pecos River, favorite of Looney Tunes character Yosemite Sam and the historic demarcation line of the Wild West, starts among some of New Mexico’s highest mountains east of Santa Fe and runs south for more than 500 miles before entering Texas at New Mexico’s lowest point.
Its headwaters rush untamed through miles of steep canyons and pine-covered slopes, garnering it a National Wild and Scenic River designation. Its waters nourish farms and ranches across the center of New Mexico. But where it exits the state, the Pecos looks more like a tightly managed creek — a conveyance delivering carefully tallied water through the middle of the Permian Basin, the country’s most productive oil and gas region.
The environmental group American Rivers has twice named the Pecos one of the country’s most endangered rivers: once in 2024, along with New Mexico’s other waterways, and in 2021 all on its own.
Both the river and the Permian Basin are natural features of a landscape transmogrified by the human desire for energy from fossil fuels.
Over the last century, people have drilled tens of thousands of wells, stitched the basin with pipes and released carbon trapped tens of millions of years ago, all to power cars and jets and buildings. That released carbon changed the chemistry of the atmosphere, trapping heat that warms the planet and dries New Mexico.
Meanwhile, on the Pecos, as on other rivers across the state, there is a greater demand for less and less water year after year. Last winter’s snow bust only added to the pressure.
“It is totally terrifying in a lot of ways,” said Hannah Riseley-White, the director of the New Mexico Interstate Stream Commission. Her job is to make sure that the state meets its obligations to all of the groups that have a stake in river water.
“Everyone this spring got tired of me at the beginning of every meeting screen-sharing the snowpack figures for all of the basins that we manage,” she said. “It fell off the cliff. It wasn’t just record breaking. It was beyond anything that we could have imagined in terms of snowpack.”
The previous winter wasn’t much better. Neither are the long-term forecasts. Riseley-White said she expects a 25% to 30% decrease in river water by 2070.






“So the biggest challenge that the Pecos faces is just aridification due to climate change,” she said.
The percentages come from New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s 50-Year Water Action Plan, which lays out how global warming will shrink New Mexico’s water supplies in coming decades. It also proposes how to conserve existing supplies and create new water sources in a very dry state. That includes treating oilfield wastewater — the stuff Barrett believes he found on the roadside — to make it clean enough that the state will allow it to be used outside the oilfield for industrial and other, broader uses.
“The industry’s actually advocating for repurposing produced water and pumping it into this river,” Barrett said, while sitting beside the Pecos.
To date, the legal maneuvering to make that happen has been unsuccessful. A recent push to change state rules and allow the broad use of treated wastewater ended when Lujan Grisham appeared to have influenced a rulemaking body’s deliberations. Another push to change state rules is underway, but no deadlines have been set. State environmental groups strongly oppose the idea, arguing that it’s not possible to be 100% sure that all toxic chemicals are removed from the water.
Meanwhile, over the border, the Texas branch of the Sierra Club has tallied five proposals to discharge treated produced water into the Texas portion of the Pecos River watershed, though none have yet been approved.
“Do I think [treated] produced water will solve all of our problems in the Pecos? No,” Riseley-White said. “But thinking about it as one of the many sort of tools in the toolbox I think makes sense.”
She added: “Part of coming up with creative solutions is going to necessarily require looking at all of the options, and that’s certainly one of them. And I think technology is there to clean water to various standards. It’s just a question of whether financially the incentives are there.”
Other Dangers
Endangered animals live along the Pecos River, including the dunes sagebrush lizard and the Texas hornshell mussel. The lesser prairie chicken was part of that group until the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service formally removed its protections under the Endangered Species Act in early 2026, despite its declining population.
“There’s going to be just increasing challenges in ensuring that there’s sufficient water for those species, just like for the other users that depend on it,” Riseley-White said. One successful example: While working with the hornshell on a tributary of the Pecos, “landowners recognized that if there was water in the Black [River] for the hornshell, that meant that there was water there for them, too,” she said.
The latest challenges to endangered animals’ survival comes from Washington. In early July, the Department of the Interior rolled back the definition of “harm” to mean only directly injuring or killing endangered species. Noise and habitat destruction would no longer be considered threats to an endangered species’ well-being.
A string of oil wells lines the Pecos River south of Loving. There are 380 oil and gas wells within a half-mile of the river in New Mexico. Aerial photography made possible by LightHawk.
In late July, the department rescinded the so-called “blanket rule” that covered threatened species with many of the same protections afforded endangered species. It also imposed consideration of the economic cost of protecting plants and animals — i.e. the additional costs to oil and gas production.
Taken together, the two changes undo historic protections for plants and animals across the country, including those that call the Pecos River watershed home. Of the thousands of oil and gas wells that pierce the ground in New Mexico’s share of the Permian Basin, 380 are within a half mile of the river. Another 11 injection wells — used to dispose of produced water — lie within that same stretch.
“The sound pollution and light pollution also affect this river ecosystem,” Barrett said. He studied ecology and wildlife management and previously worked for the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and the Texas A&M Forest Service as a staff ecologist. He said the oilfield disturbance “drives a lot of species away from this ecosystem, which can lead to extirpation, which is regional extinction.”
Despite the enormous challenges, Riseley-White said she remains optimistic.
“My hope in the Pecos is that as we face these challenges, we can get all of the different interests at the table and find solutions that make sense to everybody,” she said.
“I think it’s challenging, but I think it’s definitely possible,” she said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Death of Des Moines nursing home resident leads to negligence lawsuit
description: A Des Moines nursing home with a history of violations related to resident injuries is now being sued by the family of a woman who died, allegedly after being dropped to the floor by caregivers. The estate of Lena K. Rocha is suing Des Moines’ Scottish Rite Park Health Care Center in Polk County District […]
text:
Scottish Rite Park Health Care Center in Des Moines. (Photo via Google Earth) A Des Moines nursing home with a history of violations related to resident injuries is now being sued by the family of a woman who died, allegedly after being dropped to the floor by caregivers.
The estate of Lena K. Rocha is suing Des Moines’ Scottish Rite Park Health Care Center in Polk County District Court.
The lawsuit alleges Roch had a documented history of falls at the facility, and that there had been multiple incidents involving the improper transfer of other residents prior to Rocha’s death earlier this year.
According to the lawsuit, “Scottish Rite had dropped and/or failed to properly transfer” Rocha on multiple occasions in December 2022, July 2023, January 2024, May 2024 and August 2024. Rocha’s family allegedly met with Scottish Rite Park leaders on numerous occasions prior to May 2026 to discuss the incidents and how they might be prevented in the future.
The lawsuit claims that on April 29, 2026, Scottish Rite Park employees were transferring Rocha using a mechanical lift when they “negligently dropped” Rocha from the device. According to the lawsuit, Rocha “was dropped on her head and face, striking it first on the hard floor of the Scottish Rite facility.”
The lawsuit alleges A state investigation concluded that a “loop” used to hold Rocha within the lift had detached, and that the Scottish Rite Park staff had admitted they failed to follow the protocol that requires them to check all of the loops to ensure they were securely attached before attempting to transfer a resident.
The lawsuit asserts Rocha sustained serious head injuries from the fall and died on May 8, 2026, with the cause of death listed as “complications of subdural and subarachnoid hematoma” stemming from “blunt head trauma” due to a fall at Scottish Rite Park.
State records show Scottish Rite Park was cited and fined by state inspectors for having caused “severe harm” and “life-threatening injuries” in the incident.
Scottish Rite’s conduct ’caused catastrophic injuries and death,” the lawsuit alleges. It seeks unspecified compensatory damages for negligence, recklessness, wrongful death, dependent adult abuse and breach of contract.
The lawsuit also seeks punitive damages, in part due to what it characterizes as Scottish Rite Park’s “repeated failures, despite actual knowledge of the danger and explicit promises of corrective action” related to the use of mechanical lifts.
Scottish Rite Park has yet to file a response to the lawsuit. Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach the home’s administrator, Daniel Boor, for comment Thursday.
State records indicate Scottish Rite was cited by the state in February 2024 for allegedly dropping a resident – not Rocha — from a mechanical lift, resulting in that resident sustaining a fractured shoulder. Later that year, the home was cited for allegedly failing to properly transfer a different resident, resulting in the individual sustaining a fractured ankle. In January 2025, the state cited Scottish Rite Park for allegedly failing to ensure the certified nursing assistants were competent in performing safe resident transfers.
After the incident involving Rocha, the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing initially assessed a $7,750 fine and then tripled that to $23,250 due to it being the second resident-safety citation in the past 12 months.
However, state records show the facility had last been cited for a resident-safety violation in January 2025, which was 15 months before the April 29, 2026, incident — outside the 12-month window for tripling the fine.
After the Iowa Capital Dispatch asked DIAL whether a separate resident-safety violation had been cited in the past year but not publicly disclosed, the department checked its records and reversed course on the tripling of the penalty, bringing it back down to $7,750.
DIAL’s records show the January 2025 penalty against Scottish Rite Park was itself a tripled fine due to the repeat nature of that violation. Originally, Scottish Rite Park was to be penalized $5,000 for injuries sustained by a resident who fell and fractured an ankle while the staff was transferring her to a recliner. Because the home had been cited in July 2024 for a similar safety violation involving a resident transfer, the January 2025 penalty was then tripled from $5,000 to $15,000.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Barbour, Ezell talk hurricane reflections and lessons as Isaias approaches Coast
description: The sky builds with clouds over a beach near Gulfport as the Coast prepares for Hurricane Isaias, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026
text:
BILOXI – Coast residents and officials filed into the Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College’s hospitality center to talk about disaster preparedness as Hurricane Isaias, an expected Category 2 storm as of Thursday, approached the state’s shores. 
The state’s Public Service Commission put on the timely “From Recovery to Resilience” summit, announced a few weeks ago, just before Isaias’ expected landfall on Friday evening. The hurricane’s path shifted east since initial forecasts earlier this week, but as of Thursday Jackson County was under a hurricane warning and all of Mississippi’s Coast was under a storm surge warning. 
Mississippi Emergency Management Agency Director Stephen McCraney said MEMA will likely send National Guard members to support Alabama and Florida, where Isaias is expected to have the greatest impacts.  

But the summit attempted to shift the public’s attention from the short term to the long term: What can we do now to prepare for storms down the road? The event was the PSC’s second in a series of resilience summits, following one in Tupelo over the summer focused on lessons learned from Winter Storm Fern in January. 
Thursday’s edition, led by Southern District Public Service Commissioner Wayne Carr, homed in on hurricanes, and featured speeches from former Gov. Haley Barbour and U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell. 
Ezell, a Coast native elected to Congress in 2023, discussed efforts to improve federal disaster assistance. One bill he introduced last year, for example, would aim to reduce the reporting burden for survivors applying for federal assistance. 
Former Gov. Haley Barbour speaks at a resilience summit in Biloxi on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Alex Rozier / Mississippi Today
“A mayor, emergency manager or family shouldn’t have to submit the same information over and over again,” he said. 
Another bill Ezell backed would increase the amount of time applicants for assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency would have to appeal denials, from 60 days to 90. That bill passed out of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure in September. 
“ Somebody may have lost their home, they’re dealing with insurance people, they’re replacing documents, they’re talking with contractors,” Ezell said. “All those things compounded, dealing with FEMA can be a nightmare.”
The House has not acted on either bill.
The congressman also said he’s hoping to tackle rising insurance premiums on the Coast, which have skyrocketed since Hurricane Katrina. Ezell criticized FEMA for “relying on outdated hurricane information.”
Barbour, who was in office during Hurricane Katrina in 2005, emphasized a broad approach to preparedness. In the decades before Katrina, the state had prepared for another version of Hurricane Camille in 1969. But the two storms’ impact, it turned out, was completely different, he said. While Camille had stronger winds, Katrina delivered an immense storm surge. 
Prospective linemen listen as U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell speaks at a resilience summit in Biloxi on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.
CLICK HERE: Mississippi Today’s disaster guide
“I thought to myself, ‘Have we prepared for the wrong storm?’” Barbour reflected. 
The former governor also lauded Mississippi’s ability to recover quickly and the confidence it restored in residents. Schools on the Coast, for instance, were able to reopen that November, to his surprise. 
“People had a feeling we would recover,” the ex-governor said.

name: VTDigger
title: A decade of remembering: Good grows from grief
description:
A 2016 crash has the grim distinction of being Vermont’s deadliest mass homicide. The effects of the tragedy rippled through the Harwood high school community foremost, stretching outward to Vermont as a whole.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A decade of remembering: Good grows from grief.
text:
Top from left: Janie Chase Cozzi, Eli Brookens; bottom from left: Cyrus Zschau, Mary Harris, Liam Hale. 

This story by Lee Kahrs was first published in the Waterbury Roundabout on Oct. 7, 2026.
You can see them at night, white stars shining on the side of barns, bridges, businesses and homes in the Mad River Valley all the way to Waterbury. Not just during the holidays, but all year round, lit up in remembrance of five lives cut short.
On Oct. 8, five families, multiple schools, communities spanning six towns and countless Vermonters are feeling the weight of 10 years since the deadly crash that took the lives of five local teens: Eli Brookens, Janie Chase Cozzi, Liam Hale, Mary Harris and Cyrus Zschau. In their place, there are stars and hearts, scholarships and fundraisers, season passes and beauty products, a pavilion, a gazebo, a bench and a lot of love.
Ten years.
Ten years since Steven D. Bourgoin purposely drove the wrong way on Interstate 89 in Williston and crashed his car into a Volkswagen Jetta on French Hill, killing all five teens. Afterward, Bourgoin left his damaged Toyota Tacoma pickup and fled in a Williston police cruiser belonging to the first responding officer, who was trying in vain to rescue the occupants of the burning car. Bourgoin briefly drove south, made a U-turn, and returned to the accident scene, crashing into the wreckage again.
It was a Saturday night. The young friends were coming home from a concert by popular hip-hop artist Mike Stud at Higher Ground in South Burlington. Four were 16 and juniors at Harwood Union High School; Cozzi, from Fayston, was 15 and a sophomore at Kimball Union Academy in New Hampshire.
In 2019, Bourgoin was found guilty of five counts of second-degree murder. The case went to the Vermont Supreme Court, which in 2021 upheld the conviction. Bourgoin, who was 36 at the time of the crash, is currently serving a prison sentence of 30 years to life in Mississippi, according to the Vermont Department of Corrections. 
The 2016 crash has the grim distinction of being Vermont’s deadliest mass homicide, and the effects of the tragedy rippled through the Harwood community foremost, stretching outward to Vermont as a whole.
Flags were flown at half-staff across the state, and over 1,000 people attended a candlelight vigil at Harwood two days later, where Gov. Peter Shumlin was among the speakers. A gubernatorial debate was postponed so the candidates could attend. Then-Lt. Gov. Phil Scott was running; his Democratic opponent, Waterbury resident Sue Minter, had a son at Harwood at the time. The news seemingly affected every Vermonter in its wake in some way.

As dusk falls over a community vigil attended by hundreds at Harwood Union High School, students launch paper lanterns in memory of their classmates and friends on Oct. 10, 2016. Photo by Gordon Miller

Like eons … like yesterday
“There are days when it seems like eons ago, and days when it feels like yesterday,” recalled Lisa Atwood, who was one of Harwood’s co-principals at the time of the tragedy.
“It was such a horrific time back then,” she said in a recent phone interview. “It truly brought our six communities together for a common purpose, and that in itself was amazing. It was truly amazing the way communities came together to support the families and the schools, not just throughout the state but across New England and across the country.”
The task of bringing comfort to the school staff and student body stretched out across the weeks and months that followed. A year after the crash, the class of 2018 dedicated a memorial gazebo to their lost classmates. The structure sits near the school’s main entrance.
“The importance of trying to heal was enormous, and the school… was able to fund and finance all kinds of support for the families, the students, and the staff,” Atwood said. “I look back and I have no idea how we got through it. It literally took a village.”
Atwood knew all five of the students.
“These kids were outstanding athletes, good students, involved in their communities and in activities outside of school,” she recalled. “They each had an impact that went far beyond their relationships to other students and the schools. The ripple effect was enormous.”
Atwood said Janie Chase Cozzi came to see her the day before the crash, just to say hi. She was in town visiting for the weekend from Kimball Union Academy, where she had transferred the year before.
Looking back today, Atwood remarked that as much as the sentiment “Time heals all wounds” is thrown around as fact, it’s not always the case.
“I think we all get better at managing the loss and the heartbreak,” she said. “The things that got me through were the community and the availability of resources, because it changed who we were, and we had to learn what a new normal was going to be, and I couldn’t be more proud of the faculty and the students and the families.”
For the families and close friends of the students, getting past loss and heartbreak has come to involve unique projects that honor the lives of each of the five students and keep their memories anchored to the community.
Eli Brookens Memorial Fund
Alive
Why is life worth living / because we make it so. / You, and only you / can dictate the path
you travel down. / There will be others / but none like you. — Eli Brookens
The poem titled “Alive” was inscribed on the handmade wooden bench placed in 2019 in memory of Eli Brookens overlooking Waterbury’s Dac Rowe Park, where he spent hours of his childhood playing sports.
Recently, a new granite bench has replaced the wooden one, which was not holding up in the Vermont weather and had to be brought indoors each winter. Eli’s mother, Colleen Ovelman, contacted Vermont Granite Works and had the new bench made so it could stay in place year-round.
“I wanted a physical marker of Eli to be in the community,” she said. “We decided on that spot because it overlooks the fields where he spent so much time, and Camels Hump and Bolton.”
In 2019, the family also started the Eli Brookens Memorial Fund, which has supported the winter sports program at Crossett Brook Middle School, where Eli was a student through eighth grade.
“He just loved to ski,” Ovelman said. “He found a lot of joy and peace being in the woods.”
The goal of the fund was to make skiing more affordable and possible for kids who might not have the resources to pursue the sport. “That’s what we wanted to do, make skiing accessible to other kids,” Ovelman said.
The fund also provides a Sugarbush season pass to a Harwood student each year.
Ovelman said the family is now sunsetting the memorial fund but will keep funding the season pass as long as money is available.
To donate to the program in Eli’s memory, send directly to the CBMS Winter Sports Program by mail to: Crossett Brook Middle School, 5672 Vermont Rt. 100, Duxbury, VT 05676.
Liam Kenneth Hale Adventure Scholarship
Sue Hale said establishing the Liam Kenneth Hale Adventure Scholarship in 2017 helps keep her son Liam’s memory alive.
An avid skier and mountain biker, Liam spent most of his time at Sugarbush, which he grew up looking at every day from the family’s home in Waitsfield, along with his younger brother, Joe.
“Since they were out of diapers, they were up there skiing,” she said, adding that Liam had just started getting into golf when he died. He had also worked in the mountain bike shop.
“So just every year, he was there,” she said. “Every season.”
She admits that she once assumed that most kids at Harwood were taking advantage of the mountain in their backyard, but she learned otherwise. Her son Joe had the idea for the Adventure Scholarship, now given annually to a Harwood sophomore about to enter their junior year.
The recipient receives a Sugarbush Four Season Pass, good for unlimited skiing/riding, golf, mountain biking, scenic lift rides and yearlong Sugarbush Health & Recreation Center access. Valued at more than $3,000, it also offers benefits such as half-off day tickets at affiliated resorts, lessons, lodging, tuning and rental discounts, and golf discounts. The scholarship also includes an equipment allowance.
A registered nurse at the University of Vermont surgical and intensive care unit for 30 years, Hale says it is definitely a unique experience when it’s your own child.
“I’ve seen horrible things and tragic loss, and it’s interesting to be on both sides,” she said. “People at work look at you like, ‘Are you OK?’ Yeah, I’m OK.”
Some of her co-workers were on their way home that fateful night and came upon the horrific scene. Hale recalls how one of those nurses, Allie Harris, held a yoga event that raised thousands of dollars in the aftermath of the crash.
Hale also stays in touch with two police officers who responded to the crash scene: former Williston Police Chief Todd Sheppard and former Williston Police Sgt. Brian Claffy, both retired. Hale said they will always carry that tragic night with them.
“I see them every year,” she said. “I want to give a shout-out to the police, and how remarkable and caring they were. They were instrumental in the healing process for the Hales. It was horrible for them too; we can’t forget that.”
Perhaps the most enduring relationship Hale and her husband have maintained is with their son’s surviving friends from Harwood, which was also key for their younger son, who was 13 at the time of the crash.
“One of the most healing relationships I have, still, is with a good half-dozen of Liam’s friends,” she said. “They’re like big brothers and sisters (to Joe). We love the fact that we have such an integral relationship with these young people. We’re involved in their lives. It’s been the most beneficial for Joe. You have to cultivate those relationships.”
The 2026 Liam Kenneth Hale Adventure Scholarship went to Harwood junior William Clark, an avid skier who hasn’t skied much since the middle school program ended. He said in his essay that he’s looking forward to rejoining friends on the slopes, as well as exploring golf and mountain biking, through the scholarship.
The scholarship is awarded each year on Liam’s birthday, May 9.
“For us, it’s better to think about his birthday than the day he died,” Hale said. “Sometimes it feels like yesterday, sometimes it feels like 10 years. It’s sad, but I like the idea of appreciating the time we had with him.”
Contributions to the Liam Kenneth Hale Adventure Scholarship may be made directly to Harwood Unified Union School District, P.O. Box 1059, Waitsfield, VT 05673.
Mary Harris Youth Soccer Day
Mary’s mother, Liz Harris, and Janie’s mother, Erin Chase, both grew up in the Mad River Valley and have been friends since middle school. Their daughters met as babies and were forever friends before they died together in the crash.
“It comes on in different ways,” Chase said of her grief. “But I still lose my breath and I think, ‘Oh, my God, she’s dead.’ When you carry someone so strongly in your life, it just happens. Her friends are getting married and buying houses.”
Chase said staying in touch with Janie’s friends over the last decade has helped her cope.
“I’m so lucky to have her friends in my life,” she said. “It’s such a gift. There are a lot of people, and you get to know your kid in a different light. You’re learning more about them, even though they’re not here anymore.”
Harris agreed, adding that the mental health of their daughters’ peers and fellow students became her focus in the years following the crash. She said she posted on Facebook every day for two years after Mary died, and quickly realized that her daughter’s friends and classmates needed support as well.
“I would look at the likes and count the number of kids that were friends with my kid, and there were 200 likes from those kids,” she said. “They would come to me and say, ‘It should’ve been me,’ and I would say, ‘No. You are valuable.’ They would comment and say, ‘I miss …’ So, many suffer from mental health issues.”
That’s why, she said, she became a paraeducator in the school district, and why she and Chase have always been accessible and vocal about their daughters since the crash.
“We were very concerned about the kids because we had kids that age,” she said. “We were very vocal. We talked about Mary and Janie all the time. We’re pretty much an open book talking about them. The task is to help people see the greatest in life, even when you’re handed a raw deal.”
Mary was known for her warm smile, friendly disposition and team spirit. After the crash, Harwood girls soccer coach Mike Vasseur and Mary’s teammates decided to dedicate the annual Youth Soccer Day in Mary’s honor to celebrate the younger girls playing soccer in the district. The Mary Harris Girls’ Youth Soccer Day has been held every year since the crash.
The event would include special T-shirts each year for all of the players with the motto “Love Like Mary,” which has become a mantra of the soccer program. Stickers handed out would carry a quote from an essay that Mary wrote about kindness: “So I ask you to be kind. Be compassionate. Be respectful. Be selfless. Because without kindness, what’s the point?”
The youth soccer day has been suspended this year as Harris and Chase prepare for a special event marking 10 years since the tragedy. Called “Still We Rise,” a special immersive art, light and multimedia exhibition is planned at The Big Picture Theater in Waitsfield for the weekend of Oct. 16-18. The event will commemorate the anniversary of losing the five teens while celebrating the community resilience, support and joy that surrounded the families through the tragedy.
The Janie Chase Cozzi Foundation
The Janie Chase Cozzi Foundation was created after the crash in memory of Janie.
The foundation offers three different scholarships for middle school and high school girls in the areas of education, leadership, global awareness, arts and athletics. There is also a peer-to-peer mentoring program for girls in middle and high school, as well as collaborations with organizations to create woman-to-girl mentoring.
Since its inception, the foundation has given out scholarship money to eight girls, and there are plans to expand the foundation to focus on funding for group projects.
“We’re really hoping to do smaller projects that reach more girls,” said Erin Chase, Janie’s mother. “We love the individual aspect of the scholarships, but we think the goal is to bring more girls into the program.”
In addition to the foundation, Chase also started No. 19, a beauty products company named for Janie’s soccer jersey number.
The products range from lip balm to moisturizer and deodorant, all gender-neutral and all made with phytonutrients, biologically active compounds derived from plants. All proceeds go to the foundation, and Chase said the company also donates No. 19 products to fundraisers and other worthy causes. 
Information and a foundation donation form are at playforjanie.com.
LIFT Scholarship & Cyrus Zschau Memorial Fund
“Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things cannot be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.” — Mark Twain
That famous quote by Mark Twain graces the home page for the LIFT (Launch Into Foreign Travel) Scholarship and the Cyrus Zschau Memorial Fund. Sarah and Chris Zschau started the scholarship fund in 2019 to honor their son’s love of travel.
“The community was incredibly generous when we lost our kids, and we wanted to give something back,” said Sarah Zschau.
Cyrus loved to travel, Zschau said, and was looking forward to a spring school trip to Greece and Italy when the crash happened. His parents decided to pass on the trip to one of their son’s friends.
“Instead of giving money back, we wanted to send someone in Cyrus’ place, so we took some money from what the community gave us and that’s what we did,” she said.
They started fundraising in 2018 and started the LIFT nonprofit. To date, the Zschaus have given LIFT scholarships to 34 Harwood students, for a total of $37,125. The family’s annual fundraiser was just held on Aug. 29 at Lawson’s Finest and featured live music from local bands. It raised $16,216. 
The LIFT Scholarship goes to two Harwood students in 10th grade and older to be used toward educational travel for school-sponsored trips. The Zschaus work with Harwood’s already well-established travel abroad program, and students have gone to Rwanda, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy and India with help from LIFT.
“Harwood has an amazing program with travel connections that they’ve cultivated over the last 20 years,” Sarah Zschau said. “Travel takes students out of their comfort zone and gives them a broader view of the world.”
Closer to home, the family beach shack on Martha’s Vineyard was Cyrus’ favorite place in the world, the Zschaus said, and he looked forward to the family’s annual summer trip. This year, the Zschaus postponed their usual visit in July and were headed to the island this week instead. “We’ll be there for the anniversary,” she said. “That seems like the right place to be.”
Donations to the scholarship fund can be made at czlift.org or by check to LIFT The Cyrus Zschau Memorial Fund, mailed to: Zschau, 961 Route 100 B, Moretown, VT 05660.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Peggy Flanagan boosts affordability message with pledge to back labor’s populist economic agenda
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan promoted her affordability message on Thursday, pledging to support a union-backed package aimed at raising wages, reducing healthcare costs and weakening corporate power in Washington. At a campaign stop at the headquarters of the Minnesota AFL-CIO, the federation of unions representing more than 300,000 worke[...]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan pledges her support of a labor-led economic agenda that includes raising the minimum wage and lowering healthcare costs at a campaign event at the Minnesota AFL-CIO headquarters in St. Paul on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan promoted her affordability message on Thursday, pledging to support a union-backed package aimed at raising wages, reducing healthcare costs and weakening corporate power in Washington.
At a campaign stop at the headquarters of the Minnesota AFL-CIO, the federation of unions representing more than 300,000 workers, the lieutenant governor said unions built the middle class and are essential to a strong, fair economy.
“The rich keep getting richer, while the rest of us are told to settle for less, to stay quiet, and to accept scraps. That’s Donald Trump’s America,” Flanagan said.
Flanagan is the third U.S. Senate candidate to sign on to the working-class commitments, following Democrats Troy Jackson in Maine and James Talarico in Texas. The commitments were developed locally through surveys with workers and vary from state to state.
The 12 “Commitments to working Minnesotans” span a broad swath of populist economic proposals, including raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 an hour, eliminating the income cap on Social Security contributions that winds up lowering taxes on the wealthy, creating a public option for health insurance, banning elected officials from trading individual stocks and making it easier to unionize.
“When this election is over, we are going to make sure these commitments become policy,” said Minnesota AFL-CIO President Bernie Burnham.
While union membership has suffered a decadeslong decline, unions continue to be a potent political force with widespread popularity. Americans’ approval of labor unions is the highest it’s been in six decades, with 71% in favor, according to Gallup.
Democrats have hammered Republicans on affordability, blaming President Donald Trump’s trade war and Iran war for driving up the cost of goods and gas, while the expiration of healthcare subsidies has resulted in double-digit insurance cost increases on the individual marketplace.
The median Minnesota family saw their purchasing power reduced by $1,410 in 2025 as inflation rose faster than wages, according to a study by North Star Policy Action, a left-leaning think tank.
After riding a wave of progressive enthusiasm to a Democratic primary landslide, Flanagan is now running a close race against Republican Michele Tafoya. Polls show Flanagan is essentially tied with the former sportscaster and conservative podcaster.
Tafoya has sought to tie Flanagan to Minnesota’s fraud crisis and Gov. Tim Walz, who dropped his bid for a third term amid intense scrutiny of the state’s management of safety-net programs. She’s also positioned Flanagan as a radical whose progressive policy ideas are out of step with the average voter.
“People are tired of crazy,” Tafoya recently told Fox News’ Sean Hannity. “This is a clear contrast in common sense versus crazy.”
But like Republicans across the country, Tafoya faces her own challenge: distancing herself from a deeply unpopular and erratic president — he suggested this week that Iran could “take out” southern California — without upsetting his loyal base. Tafoya’s campaign ads describe her as an independent voice, but in fundraising messages she’s asked donors for their support to protect the “President’s Senate majority.”
“These MAGA folks are either afraid of Donald Trump or proud to stand with him. The result is the same: that they do whatever he wants them to do,” Flanagan said.
Flanagan has deep ties to the labor movement in Minnesota, having campaigned to raise the minimum wage when she led the Children’s Defense Fund of Minnesota.
While she was lieutenant governor, Democrats took control of the Legislature and passed the most significant package of pro-labor laws in generations: paid family leave, paid sick time, increased enforcement against wage theft, a ban on captive audience meetings, a nation-leading labor standards board for nursing home workers and greater safety oversight of meatpacking plants and large warehouses.
“Everything that I have done that has been of real value, I have done in partnership with the people in this room,” Flanagan said.

description: Lindsay Rankin, a special education teacher in the Springdale School District, was named the 2027 Arkansas Teacher of the Year Thursday.  Gov.
