title: Another South Dakota Republican lawmaker is facing a criminal charge
description: A South Dakota state senator was cited for driving under the influence this week, marking the third time criminal charges for a state lawmaker have come to light in the space of four months.  Leola Republican Mark Lapka, 45, was cited for driving under the influence between Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning, McPherson County […]
text:
Sen. Mark Lapka, R-Leola, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on March 4, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota state senator was cited for driving under the influence this week, marking the third time criminal charges for a state lawmaker have come to light in the space of four months. 
Leola Republican Mark Lapka, 45, was cited for driving under the influence between Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning, McPherson County State’s Attorney Austin Hoffman confirmed to South Dakota Searchlight. Lapka was cited, not arrested, Hoffman said, “due to the circumstances of the situation.”
He declined to offer further details, citing the ongoing investigation. No charges have been filed yet, Hoffman said, because the clerk of courts for McPherson County was not immediately available to file them.
Sheriff David Ackerman said the incident occurred near the edge of town in Leola, but also declined to elaborate due to the ongoing investigation.
A first offense of driving under the influence is punishable by up to a year in jail and a $2,000 fine. Lapka has no criminal record in South Dakota beyond the pending charge and a speeding ticket, according to a search of the state’s court record database.
Lapka is running uncontested for reelection to his seat in District 23, where he represents all of McPherson and Edmunds counties and parts of Brown, Campbell, Faulk, Hand, Potter and Walworth counties. He did not return a call or text from Searchlight.
December trial date set for South Dakota lawmaker facing election-related felony charges

Sioux Falls Republican Sen. Chris Karr, one of the chamber’s top leaders as president pro tempore, did not immediately respond to a call and a text seeking comment. 
Two other Republican lawmakers were charged criminally in June. Newell Rep. Travis Ismay was charged with felony damage to a road, but the charge was reduced when he agreed to plead no contest to a misdemeanor version of the same crime. Ismay agreed to pay back the county for the cost of re-grading the gravel road he’d graded himself.
Ismay is running unopposed for reelection to his seat in District 28B. That district includes Butte and Harding counties and parts of Perkins County.
Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, awaits trial on two felony counts of attempting to file a false or forged instrument. That case accuses Pischke of signing and submitting nominating petitions for county party precinct positions without those candidates’ knowledge. The Minnehaha County Republican Party chairman has alleged that Pischke was motivated by a dispute within the party, and wanted to add committee members to make it more difficult for county party meetings to achieve a quorum.
A December trial date has been set for Pischke, who dropped out of his reelection race in July after saying he’d be unable to be “transparent” during the campaign while his criminal case is pending.
Pischke serves in District 25, which includes northern Minnehaha and all of Moody County. 
Former Republican lawmaker Bryan Breitling is running for Pischke’s seat as an independent. The Minnehaha County Republican Party chose Bart Sample, of Flandreau, to replace Pischke on the Republican ticket. Sample finished third in a three-way primary race on June 2 for two Republican nominations for the district’s state House seats.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis revels in ‘the biggest judicial smackdown that I have ever seen’
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis claimed vindication Thursday in light of a state appellate ruling handed down the day before expunging the Hope Florida grand jury report that harshly criticized much of the state’s Republican leadership. He called for prosecution of whoever leaked the report to CBS News Miami. The document alleges “misappropriation” by his administration o[...]
text:
The Florida First District Court of Appeal courthouse in Tallahassee. (Credit: Michael Moline)Gov. Ron DeSantis claimed vindication Thursday in light of a state appellate ruling handed down the day before expunging the Hope Florida grand jury report that harshly criticized much of the state’s Republican leadership.
He called for prosecution of whoever leaked the report to CBS News Miami. The document alleges “misappropriation” by his administration of $10 million from a $67 million Medicaid overbilling settlement to advance the governor’s political goals.
“This process has now culminated in what I think is probably the biggest judicial smackdown that I have ever seen in my entire career as an elected official. All the narratives crashed and burned with this opinion by the 1st District Court of Appeal,” Desantis said during a Miami news conference.
“Whoever leaked this report needs to be prosecuted,” he continued.
“If you leak the report, you violated the law knowingly, willingly, or at least recklessly. And there are people in that report who are private citizens, there are people in that report who are midlevel government employees who should never have been subjected to this,” the governor said.
Attorney General James Uthmeier, who’d been the governor’s chief of staff at the time and central to funneling the money into the campaign against a citizens’ initiative to legalize recreational pot, joined the news conference and seconded the motion.
“Yeah, I think this is something law enforcement’s looking at. I don’t have an update from them at this point, nothing to share,” he said.
“But, upon a finding of a violation of law, that’s something that state attorneys could prosecute. If it crosses over circuit lines — you know, which is very possible, given CBS Miami engaging in perpetrating the fraud — then it could involve the statewide prosecutor,” he continued.
“If somebody shows a violation alone, no matter where it is, I pursue it. I enforce the law. Everywhere, from retail theft to election crimes, child predators, you name it. Somebody broke the law, they should be prosecuted.
 The ruling
Judge Lance E. Neff of the 1st DCA in Tallahassee wrote the opinion. He cited a Florida law that requires any grand jury report, or “presentment,” that doesn’t include an indictment to remain confidential until named parties have a chance to block release.
“A grand jury may investigate and report, but it may not declare conduct unlawful and then decline to charge it, and it may not condemn people by name without indicting them,” the 19-page opinion reads.
“Nor may the State release a confidential presentment before those it impugns have had the opportunity Florida law guarantees to seek its repression or expungement.”
The Florida Democratic Party, which has been using the grand jury report and its findings on the campaign trail, blasted the DCA ruling , noting in a written statement sent to the news media Thursday that it “doesn’t change what happened.”
“The grand jury heard testimony, reviewed evidence and concluded that the $10 million was misappropriated as part of a scheme to fund political activity. Erasing the report does not erase those findings,” Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said.
“The questions remain: Why was $10 million carved out of a Medicaid settlement and sent to Hope Florida? Why was it moved into political organizations? And why have the people involved fought so hard to keep Floridians from seeing what happened?
The probe into the Hope Florida Foundation originated when the Republican-controlled Florida House held hearings in the spring of 2025 amid speculation that First Lady Casey DeSantis — who started the Hope Florida initiative — might run for governor. The program is intended to divert welfare recipients into community-based assistance through churches and other providers.
Rep. Alex Andrade, a Pensacola Republican, turned over information to the Tallahassee prosecutor that became the catalyst for the grand jury investigation.
The grand jury said the foundation “quickly funneled” the money to two nonprofits that directed some of it to the campaign to defeat the pot amendment.
The panel blasted several top state officials, including Uthmeier and Jason Weida, a former Agency for Health Care Administration secretary, now chief of staff to DeSantis, but the report did not result in anyone getting charged.
The report was written in January 2026 but remained confidential until it was leaked to CBS Miami, which posted it on its website.
The report says U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, state attorney general at the time, knew about the money transfer.
 Money not ‘misappropriated’
In opining that the grand jury erred in its findings, Neff relied on two laws, one of which bars expenditure of negotiated court-settlement funds absent a legislative appropriation and requires settlement money to be placed in the general revenue fund or another trust fund. The second law the grand jury relied on also governs court actions but applies only to money paid to the state.
Neff said the agreement between ACHA, the Attorney General’s Office, and Medicaid managed care plan Centene, was “settled before any civil action was filed. Because no ‘civil action’ had been filed in court,” he continued, the “$10 million was paid to Hope Florida, not the State.”
“While some may question the propriety of settlements with payments to third parties, the Florida Legislature has not made such action illegal, as the grand jury’s recommendations implicitly acknowledge,” Neff wrote.
“Indeed, Florida’s attorneys general from 1996 to 2020 executed 107 settlements in which third-party payments were directed to entities other than the State. The federal government has also engaged in this practice.”
Judges Ross L. Bilbrey and Ross L. Bilbrey, both appointed to the appeals court by former Gov. Rick Scott, concurred with Neff’s conclusions. DeSantis had appointed Neff.
In a separate, opinion, Bilbrey cited a different law, one stating, “Grand jury proceedings are secret,” and that a grand jury or interpreter “shall not disclose the nature or substance of the deliberations or vote of the grand jury.”
He noted that copies of the presentment had been shared with two people involved in the grand jury who were not accused of any wrongdoing — a forensic accountant who assisted the grand jury in sorting through bank records and a Bank of America representative.
“Here, various people, companies, and organizations who were not ‘the individual concerned’ were given the Presentment that was not related to them before actual related and concerned individuals had a chance to challenge the Presentment,” Bilbrey wrote.
 Unlike Neff,  Bilbrey agreed thqt the report should be expunged but he reached that conclusion without “reaching the substance of the Presentment.”
 ‘Hostile’ venue
DeSantis focused largely on the harm he believes was done to witnesses identified by the grand jury report. Circuit Judge James Lee Marsh had ordered their descriptions expunged, as well as additional information that totaled 112 of the original 116 pages, according to the written opinion.
Those witnesses,  “went in front of a judge who’s hostile to our administration and the judge agreed none of those people should have had that derogatory information published. It was unlawful to have a report with that in it,” he said.
He criticized Leon County’s role as the venue, too, noting that the county preferred Democrat Charlie Crist, his 2022 reelection challenger, by 20%  points while DeSantis himself won the state by that same margin.
“They’re not representative of the state of Florida. The idea that you’re going to go into these areas that have political hostility and you’re going to conduct oversight?”
The governor singled out an employee from CBS attending his news conference.
“CBS, are you here? Anyone from CBS?” he asked.
“Oh, they didn’t send a reporter? Do you want us to send you a copy of this opinion so they will read it and see the results and how that conflicts with some of the narratives they’ve been spewing?
“I think you have a responsibility to correct the record. I think you have a responsibility to show that there has been some adult supervision that has been rendered with the 1st DCA and that the kangaroo court is over, and that this is the law, these are the facts, and it’s the same that we said a year and a half ago.”
 ‘Nothing changes’
The governor brushed off the whole controversy as politics, even though it was state House Republicans who launched the probe into the transfer.
“There was a cabal in the Legislature,” said DeSantis, who has butted heads with House leaders over the past two years.
“There was an attempt to weaponize this using the legal system,” he said.
Angie Nixon, the Democrat running against Moody for U.S. Senate, has attempted to use the grand jury report against her opponent. Casey DeSantis is also being smeared, DeSantis alleged.
“Nothing changes the fact that on thieving Moody’s watch, sick children were robbed of the $10 million dollars they desperately need for their care. Nothing changes the fact that we all have to wonder how many kids will die because of her corruption and insatiable desire for power and control,” Nixon insisted in a written statement.
“Stealing from kids to fund political ads in order to silence the voices of Floridians voting for policies to improve their own lives is disgusting. And absolutely nothing changes the fact that Moody refuses to answer for these shameful actions in a debate with me because she’s scared to be held to account in the court of public opinion.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Former President Barack Obama endorses David Crowley in Wisconsin race for governor
description: Former President Barack Obama endorsed Democratic candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the race for Wisconsin governor in a video posted to social media Thursday. Crowley faces Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in November in what is anticipated to be a close race in one of the most purple states in the country. […]
text:
Obama, who was elected the first Black president in 2008, said in the video that he hasn’t known many leaders like Crowley. (Screenshot via Crowley campaign YouTube)Former President Barack Obama endorsed Democratic candidate and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the race for Wisconsin governor in a video posted to social media Thursday.
Crowley faces Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in November in what is anticipated to be a close race in one of the most purple states in the country. If Crowley wins, he’ll be the first Black governor of Wisconsin and only the fourth Black governor elected in U.S. history.
Obama, who was elected the first Black president in 2008, said in the video that he hasn’t known many leaders like Crowley. 
“David’s life story is about overcoming adversity, and his life’s work is about bringing people together,” Obama said. Crowley, a father of three daughters, grew up in Milwaukee, the son of an electrician and a service industry worker. Both of his parents struggled with addiction and mental health issues. While growing up on Milwaukee’s North Side, Crowley and his mother were in unstable housing conditions and faced eviction three times. 
Crowley’s childhood has shaped his career in politics. He started out working as a community organizer and aide to former U.S. Sen. Russ Feingold before running and winning a state Assembly seat. In 2020, he ran for Milwaukee County executive, becoming the first Black person to hold the position.
“Like me, David started out as a community organizer, and he happens to be a girl dad, too,” Obama said, noting that Crowley’s daughters have gone to public school. 
Obama added that Crowley has helped create jobs and balanced budgets as county executive.  
“As governor, David will fight to make Wisconsin more affordable, so that you’re paying less at the pump, at the doctor’s office and less at the end of the month. There is nobody better to lead Wisconsin forward, so vote David Crowley for governor,” Obama said.
Obama carried Wisconsin twice, when he was elected president in 2008 and again in 2012 when he was reelected, by margins considered large for the swing state. 
Crowley said he was “deeply honored” to have Obama’s endorsement and that the former president is “someone who defines what leadership is — fighting for everything possible to make life better for everyday Americans.” 
“Thanks to President Obama, millions of Americans were able to get healthcare, millions found jobs, and now he’s passed the baton to a new generation of leaders like myself who want to make Wisconsin and our country the best place to call home,” Crowley said. “I know with President Obama’s support, we can win this election and move Wisconsin forward.” 
President Donald Trump endorsed  Tiffany early during the Republican primary, helping to clear the primary field for the 7th CD congressman. 
In his January endorsement, Trump praised Tiffany for having “always been at my side.” 
Tiffany said then that he was honored to earn Trump’s endorsement. “Just one year into his second term, wages are rising, gas prices are down, our economy is growing and our border is secure,” he  said at the time. 
Since then, gas prices have risen due to Trump’s war in Iran, with diesel prices hitting a record high, averaging $6.22 a gallon in Wisconsin, according to AAA.
Trump’s popularity has also fallen, with 60% of registered voters disapproving of him in the most recent Marquette Law School Poll.
Trump highlighted his endorsement of Tiffany on Wednesday in an announcement that he’d be giving the state nearly $18 million in disaster aid. He said that he had recently spoken to TIffany and reiterated his “Complete and Total Endorsement” for the Republican candidate.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: New filing shows how Collins’ and Jackson’s wealth compare
description: Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson made most of his recent income as a consultant to two international unions based in Maryland, according to a financial disclosure filed on Monday.  The disclosure is the first look into Jackson’s personal finances. Senate candidates are typically supposed to file personal financial disclosure reports within 30 days[...]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson answers questions at a campaign event in Brunswick on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson made most of his recent income as a consultant to two international unions based in Maryland, according to a financial disclosure filed on Monday. 
The disclosure is the first look into Jackson’s personal finances. Senate candidates are typically supposed to file personal financial disclosure reports within 30 days of becoming a candidate, but Jackson requested a 55-day extension. He became the nominee in late July, replacing Graham Platner, who dropped out after an accusation of sexual assault, which he denies. 
Jackson, former Maine Senate president and logger, reported making the most from the International Association of Machinists: $90,000 over the past two years, $50,000 in 2025 and $40,000 in 2026. 
The next-highest portion of his income in that period was $48,000 from the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades, $30,000 in 2025 and $18,000 in 2026. 
Jackson is no longer consulting for either union, according to his campaign. 
In 2025, he also made $5,100 from the Eastern Maine Labor Council and $4,800 from the nonprofit Food and Medicine, both based in Brewer.
“Troy’s financial disclosure reflects a lifetime of working for a paycheck,” an unnamed campaign spokesperson said in a statement. “He’s a logger and union member who understands what it means to worry about making ends meet — and he would bring that experience to a Senate dominated by millionaires.”
Federal disclosures do not provide a comprehensive picture of net worth since assets, such as stock holdings, are disclosed as a range. But the forms do show that Jackson’s opponent, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, has far more assets. 
Jackson disclosed between $147,000 and $430,000 in assets, with the largest share, between $100,001 and $250,000, coming from his spouse’s retirement plan. 
Collins’ latest financial disclosure report filed in May, which covers the 2025 calendar year, showed assets between roughly $4 million and $10 million, mostly from her spouse’s investments. Collins also earns at least $174,000 a year for being a U.S. senator. Congressstock.com puts the senator’s net worth at $7.1 million.
Collins’ spokesperson Blake Kernen criticized Jackson for pushing back his financial disclosure date, and for taking money from unions and the 501(c)(4). Kernen also said Collins has never bought, sold, or owned individual shares of stock during her service, and that her husband’s investment decisions are made by a third-party advisor.

title: Obama featured in videos boosting Bottoms, Ossoff in Georgia
description: Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign for governor got a boost Thursday with a heavyweight endorsement from former President Barack Obama. In a video released Thursday, Obama praised Bottoms’ record as the former mayor of Atlanta and touted some of the Democrat’s campaign promises, saying that “there is a lot at stake in this election.”  “Keisha believes […]
text:
Former President Barack Obama campaigned in Atlanta the day before Election Day 2020 and returned a few times since then. On Thursday, ahead of the November 2026 elections, the former president released videos supporting Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection. Stanley Dunlap/Georgia RecorderKeisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign for governor got a boost Thursday with a heavyweight endorsement from former President Barack Obama.
In a video released Thursday, Obama praised Bottoms’ record as the former mayor of Atlanta and touted some of the Democrat’s campaign promises, saying that “there is a lot at stake in this election.” 
“Keisha believes that public service is about putting you first. She’s invested in young people. Delivered historic pay raises for police officers and firefighters and balanced the budget without raising taxes,” Obama said. “Now, Keisha has a plan to lower costs, expand Medicaid, strengthen rural hospitals and give communities the option to eliminate grocery taxes. And as a mom of four, Keisha understands the importance of giving every child a strong start. And that’s why she’ll work to guarantee pre-K for every 4-year-old.”
An ad featuring Obama making the case for Sen. Jon Ossoff’s reelection was also released Thursday. Ossoff, who is the only Democratic senator on the ballot this year in a state President Donald Trump won in 2024, faces U.S. Rep. Mike Collins in November.
The video plugs are part of an uptick in the former Democratic president’s political activity ahead of the November midterms. On the same day, Obama endorsed Democrat Troy Jackson’s bid to unseat Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in Maine.

Bottoms will face Republican Rick Jackson, a healthcare executive and billionaire, to become Georgia’s next governor in November. Early voting starts Tuesday, Oct. 13. 
Gov. Brian Kemp, who is a Republican, is term-limited and can’t seek reelection. The race is virtually tied according to recent polling, with Jackson slightly ahead but still within the margin of error.
Rick Jackson was endorsed by President Trump in July after Trump’s preferred candidate, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, lost the Republican primary. The GOP nominee for governor also appeared alongside Trump at an event in July. Jackson often invoked Trump’s name at campaign events earlier in his campaign, saying he would be Trump’s “favorite governor” and that he would be like Trump but with a “Southern tone.” 
But Jackson has since distanced himself from the president while moderating his stances and aligning himself more with Kemp. At a recent hourlong debate, Jackson did not mention Trump and instead tied himself to Kemp. 
“I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said. 
At the same debate, Bottoms frequently tried to tie Jackson to Trump, who is currently facing record low approval ratings.
“My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on … I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor. I’m running to work on behalf of people like you,” Bottoms said at the debate.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Celebrating Congaree: 50 years in the life of a forest
description: Some trees in Congaree National Park were already centuries old when the United States was founded, so five decades might seem like only a brief moment in the life of the forest. As the park marks its 50th anniversary, that span tells a larger story, one that is not just about forests and floodplains but […]
text:
Congaree National Park covers more than 26,000 acres in Richland County. It was initially preserved in 1976 as Congaree Swamp National Monument. It was redesignated as a national park in 2003. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)Some trees in Congaree National Park were already centuries old when the United States was founded, so five decades might seem like only a brief moment in the life of the forest.
As the park marks its 50th anniversary, that span tells a larger story, one that is not just about forests and floodplains but about what we choose to value and protect.
Congaree exists today because a group of South Carolinians in the 1970s refused to let it disappear. At the time, timber prices were climbing, and the old-growth giants of the Congaree floodplain were at risk of being logged.
Inspired by journalist and conservationist Harry Hampton, a local grassroots coalition formed to publicize the significance of these endangered ecosystems and rally for their protection.
With backing from national environmental groups and bipartisan political support, their efforts culminated in the establishment of Congaree Swamp National Monument in 1976 and its redesignation as Congaree National Park in 2003.
For more than 20 years, my research at Congaree has exposed me to a complex living system that continues to yield new scientific insights. I’ve introduced groups of students, teachers, and community members to the park and organized workshops and symposia around it.
‘Just wonderful’: USC musicians perform at Congaree National Park for country’s 250th birthday

Like many who spend time there, I’ve come to see Congaree not just as a place of study but as a source of perspective.
Congaree protects one of the largest remaining expanses of old-growth bottomland hardwood forest in the country. Its loblolly pines rise 170 feet above the forest floor, making them some of the tallest trees east of the Mississippi River.
The park is home to thousands of other species, from iconic bald cypress and alligators to lesser-known Rafinesque’s big-eared bats and golden orb-weaver spiders.
And each spring, synchronous fireflies transform the forest into a weekslong light show that draws visitors from across the country.
But Congaree’s value extends beyond its ecology. It’s also a place where people can experience an old-growth forest firsthand by hiking its trails, paddling its waterways or simply spending time in a landscape that feels increasingly rare.
In a world where many natural systems have been fragmented or lost, Congaree preserves a sense of continuity that is difficult to find elsewhere.
As part of the National Park System, Congaree shares a mission to protect natural and cultural resources while making them accessible to the public. Maintaining that balance between access and long-term protection remains just as important today as it was a half-century ago.
The park’s rare landscape invites visitors to learn about the natural world or simply spend time outdoors. Its value is not tied to any single use but rather to the collective benefits it provides, including economic.
Roughly 250,000 people visit Congaree each year. In 2024, visitor spending on lodging, dining and other goods and services supported 134 jobs and contributed $17.6 million to the local economy.
Congaree’s anniversary provides an opportunity to reflect on its past, but it should also remind us that national parks and other protected places require our continued support as visitors, benefactors, volunteers, conservationists and advocates.
In a forest where many trees are centuries old, the effects of today’s decisions may not be fully visible for decades.
Congaree stands as a reminder that some places are worth protecting not only for what they offer today but for what they can continue to offer in the decades ahead.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrats see opening in NC as Whatley campaign pauses ads
description: North Carolina has some of the country’s most expensive media markets in Charlotte and the Raleigh-Durham area.
text:
Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley speaks with reporters in Rocky Mount ahead of a Trump rally on Dec. 19, 2025. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)National Democrats are rethinking their campaign strategy in North Carolina as Republican groups — and even the GOP candidate — pause spending in the state’s open U.S. Senate race.
The campaign for Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party, has temporarily pulled its ads from television while reevaluating its target audience, according to The News and Observer. 
The Whatley campaign, North Carolina Republican Party, and National Republican Senatorial Committee did not respond to requests for comment. 
Last week, multiple outlets reported the Senate Leadership Fund, a leading GOP super PAC, is pulling millions of advertising dollars away from the North Carolina U.S. Senate contest, directing the money to races in other states instead. 
Whatley has consistently trailed Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper in polls and fundraising. He’s also closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, a decision that may hurt his electability given the president’s dwindling approval ratings in North Carolina. 
Trump and Vice President JD Vance separately visited the Tar Heel State last month, holding rallies to stump for Whatley and downballot Republicans. 
On the Democratic side, Senate Majority PAC press secretary Christyna Thompson said Republicans have run out of reasons to keep supporting Whatley.
Republican super PAC pauses spending in North Carolina’s key US Senate race

“They’ve spent over $30 million trying to sell voters on him, but a few false ads and bringing in the president doesn’t change the reality on the ground,” Thompson told NC Newsline. “Whatley has a record of putting North Carolina last, and voters know it, no matter how much the GOP try to distract.”
WinSenate, a group that’s connected to Senate Majority PAC, pulled $1.1M in ad support for Cooper, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The group is still scheduled to spend $18.8M in the Tar Heel State by Election Day. 
North Carolina has some of the country’s most expensive media markets in Charlotte and the Raleigh-Durham area, leading to costly campaigns for both parties. 
At the moment, Republicans hold 53 seats in the U.S. Senate, while Democrats have 45. Two independent senators caucus with the Democrats. 
That means Democrats need a net gain of three seats for a 50-50 split of the upper chamber, and four to gain a majority. On the national level, Republicans have a massive cash advantage. 
Other viable pick-up opportunities for Democrats — some with cheaper media markets — include Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Texas, and Iowa. They’re also defending seats in Michigan, Georgia, and New Hampshire. 
Cooper is the best-known U.S. Senate candidate Democrats have fielded in decades. He’s won statewide elections six times — twice as governor, and four times as attorney general. His 16-year tenure in that office was the longest in North Carolina history. 
North Carolina last elected a Democratic U.S. senator in 2008, when Barack Obama became the first Democratic presidential candidate to win the Tar Heel State in 32 years. No Democratic presidential or senatorial candidates have won in North Carolina since. 
While Democrats view the spending pause as a good sign, they aren’t celebrating just yet. There’s still four and a half weeks until Election Day, and North Carolina is a battleground state.
“We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense,” Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen told NC Newsline.

name: Delaware
title: Ramone, Lauzen Clash Over Independence, Financial Expertise in Treasurer Debate
description: Republican says Delaware needs an independent watchdog in Dover; Democrat argues investment experience and fiduciary responsibility are essential to safeguarding taxpayer money. WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware’s candidates for state treasurer offered competing arguments Thursday over what voters should value most in the office: an independent voice willing to ch[...]
text:
Republican says Delaware needs an independent watchdog in Dover; Democrat argues investment experience and fiduciary responsibility are essential to safeguarding taxpayer money.

WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware’s candidates for state treasurer offered competing arguments Thursday over what voters should value most in the office: an independent voice willing to challenge state government or an experienced financial professional qualified to manage billions of dollars in public funds.
Republican Mike Ramone and Democrat Ted Lauzen faced questions during an Oct. 8 luncheon hosted by the Wilmington Rotary Club at the Hotel du Pont.
The forum was moderated by Jake Owens, editor of Spotlight Delaware. Questions were submitted by Rotary Club members and were not provided to the candidates in advance.
  Although both candidates pledged transparency, independence and responsible financial management, they differed over the experience and leadership needed to serve as Delaware’s next treasurer.
Ramone, a longtime business owner and former House minority leader, argued that Delaware needs an independently elected official willing to challenge financial decisions in a state where Democrats control the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly.
Lauzen, an investment adviser and wealth management professional, argued that the treasurer’s primary responsibility is to safeguard public money through professional investment management and a fiduciary obligation to taxpayers.
Editor’s Note:   The quotes from both candidates were provided from the transcript of the event on October 8th and are unedited.
Ramone: Independence provides accountability
Ramone repeatedly emphasized the importance of political independence, arguing that the treasurer should provide additional oversight of financial decisions made in Dover.
“The most important reason to have a treasurer who’s maybe not from the party in power of the state of Delaware would be transparency,” Ramone said.
He argued that the treasurer’s participation on state financial boards and committees provides an opportunity to question spending decisions, financial policies and the use of taxpayer money.
“We’re the people, and it’s our money, and we have the opportunity to participate in knowing what is being done with it and where it’s going,” Ramone said.
Ramone pointed to his 16 years in the General Assembly, legislative leadership experience and decades of operating businesses as qualifications that would allow him to work across party lines while challenging decisions when necessary.
“I have the independence to be able to say no, and I have the experience to know when to say yes,” he said.
Ramone argued that Delaware would benefit from a treasurer who is not politically dependent on the governor or legislative leadership and who can raise difficult questions without fearing political consequences.
Lauzen: Financial skills protect public money
Lauzen presented a different case, emphasizing his professional investment management experience and his responsibilities as a fiduciary.
A former Marine helicopter pilot who earned graduate degrees from the University of Pennsylvania, Lauzen is a co-founder of Great Fox Wealth Advisors.
He said the treasurer’s responsibilities require technical financial knowledge and experience managing investments.
“The state treasurer also has that responsibility of acting as your elected fiduciary in the management of our cash reserves and our long-term investments,” Lauzen said.
He explained that a fiduciary has a responsibility to act in the financial interests of those whose money is being managed.
“That mandate prioritizes stability, liquidity, and then long-term growth,” Lauzen said.
He identified investment allocation and management fees as two important factors the treasurer can influence when protecting public funds and generating returns.
Lauzen also pledged independence and transparency, supporting public disclosure of the criteria used to select financial institutions and evaluate investment partners.
For Lauzen, independence means exercising professional judgment based on the state’s financial interests, even when that judgment differs from the preferences of other government officials.
Two approaches to managing the Treasury
The differences became particularly clear when the candidates discussed the state’s investment portfolio.
Lauzen emphasized that investment management is already his profession.
“I don’t sing very well, I don’t dance very well, but I do invest money really well,” he said in his opening statement.
Ramone acknowledged that he does not have Lauzen’s investment management background but argued that the office requires leadership, judgment and the ability to assemble qualified financial professionals.
“I’m not the guy who’s going to have all the answers,” Ramone said. “I’m the person who’s going to build the team around me.”
He said he would rely on experienced financial advisers and professionals while providing leadership, independent oversight and accountability.
Ramone argued that the treasurer should know when to question recommendations, challenge assumptions and bring together people with different expertise.
Lauzen countered that professional investment experience provides an important foundation for making those decisions and evaluating the performance of the state’s financial managers.
State finances and AAA rating raise concerns
Both candidates addressed Delaware’s AAA bond rating, the state’s reliance on corporate franchise revenue and the growing cost of employee benefits.
Ramone warned that Delaware depends heavily on corporate revenue and must protect the state’s competitive position while examining opportunities to control government spending.
He questioned the practice of routinely seeking additional revenue to offset rising annual expenses rather than looking for ways to reduce costs and improve efficiency.
Lauzen identified three major risks to the state’s financial position: concentrated revenue sources, outdated debt policies and growing unfunded retiree health care obligations.
He suggested modernizing debt management practices and considering opportunities to reduce long-term liabilities.
Both candidates agreed that protecting Delaware’s corporate franchise business is important to maintaining state revenue and financial stability.
Retirement programs offer common ground
The candidates found agreement on Delaware Earns, the state-facilitated retirement savings program intended to help workers whose employers do not offer qualifying retirement plans.
Lauzen called the program an important first step but suggested reducing administrative responsibilities for small businesses and expanding retirement savings options.
Ramone said lawmakers had worked on the program through a bipartisan process and emphasized the importance of employer input, stability and transparency as it develops.
Both supported financial literacy programs and efforts to help Delaware residents prepare for retirement.
Independence becomes a defining issue
In one of the final questions, the candidates were asked how they would exercise independence while serving alongside a governor and legislature responsible for most state fiscal policy.
Ramone described his opposition to a proposed gasoline tax increase during Gov. Jack Markell’s administration.
He said he challenged the proposal because he believed Delaware could benefit economically by maintaining lower fuel taxes than neighboring states, encouraging motorists and commercial vehicles to purchase fuel in Delaware.
Lauzen pointed to his work in investment management and nonprofit financial oversight, where he said independent judgment sometimes requires disagreeing with organizational leadership.
He argued that independence should be exercised constructively while working with other officials to protect the state’s financial interests.
The exchange reinforced the central difference between the candidates.
Ramone portrayed the independently elected treasurer as an additional check on decisions made by state government, particularly under one-party control.
Lauzen emphasized the treasurer’s independent fiduciary responsibility to make sound financial decisions and protect taxpayer investments.
A respectful exchange before Election Day
Despite their differences, the candidates avoided personal attacks and acknowledged areas of agreement.
Ramone praised Lauzen’s financial expertise and said knowledgeable investment professionals would play an important role in his administration.
Lauzen recognized the importance of independence and emphasized cooperation among state leaders.
In his closing statement, Ramone returned to the themes of independence, transparency and leadership.
“There’s no one that’s going to be enabled to enhance transparency more than me because I have nothing to lose,” Ramone said.
Lauzen closed by encouraging Delawareans to participate in the election and emphasizing the importance of public service.
The debate offered voters two different approaches to the office: one emphasizing independent government oversight and experienced leadership, the other emphasizing professional financial expertise and fiduciary responsibility.
Voters will choose Delaware’s next state treasurer in the Nov. 3 general election. Early voting begins Oct. 22.

title: NU regents to consider increasing Project Health budget by $557M, extending president’s contract
description: OMAHA — The University of Nebraska Board of Regents this week will consider extending NU President Jeff Gold’s contract by three years, to mid-2032, and increasing the $2.19 billion budget for NU’s “Project Health” by 25%. The amended agenda for Friday’s meeting proposes extending Gold’s contract from June 30, 2029, until June 30, 2032. His base […]
text:
Dr. Jeffrey Gold, president of the University of Nebraska system, gives his first "State of the University" address in the Nebraska State Capitol. Sept. 4, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — The University of Nebraska Board of Regents this week will consider extending NU President Jeff Gold’s contract by three years, to mid-2032, and increasing the $2.19 billion budget for NU’s “Project Health” by 25%.
The amended agenda for Friday’s meeting proposes extending Gold’s contract from June 30, 2029, until June 30, 2032. His base salary has remained at $1.06 million since he became president on July 1, 2024.
Gold’s base salary is about $31,000 more than his final salary when he was chancellor of the University of Nebraska Medical Center, which he led for 10 years. Gold previously served as chancellor of the University of Nebraska at Omaha between May 2017 and June 2021. He then became NU’s chief academic officer in July 2021 until he became president.
University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold holds a model of how the University of Nebraska Medical Center’s footprint would grow in Omaha with the $2 billion “Project Health” endeavor. Oct. 3, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former NU President Ted Carter’s base salary when he started Jan. 1, 2020, was $962,000.
Friday’s vote could also eliminate eligible performance-based merit pay for Gold, up to 15% of Gold’s base salary ($159,386). Instead, Gold could be eligible for merit-based salary increases only if NU is offering a merit-based salary pool systemwide.
For example, if NU can pay employees a 2.5% increase, Gold would receive the same increase unless the regents offer him a different percentage.
Regents will also consider increasing Gold’s deferred compensation from 11.5% of his base salary to 21.5%. Each year, NU places those additional funds, plus possible interest, in a separate pot for Gold that he can access if he stays as president for multiple years.
Should Gold leave his position before June 30, 2031, what would be the final year of the amended contract, he would need to pay NU at the following rates:

Before June 30, 2027 — $250,000.
Between July 1, 2027, and June 30, 2028 — $250,000.
Between July 1, 2028, and June 30, 2029 — $125,000.
Between July 1, 2029, and June 30, 2030 — $75,000.
Between July 1, 2030, and June 30, 2031 — $50,000.
After July 1, 2031 — $0.

Gold has continued to help lead NU through major changes at UNMC. This includes Project Health, the multibillion-dollar endeavor to set up the next generation of healthcare training, and the transaction this year to transfer NU’s partner with the Nebraska Medicine nonprofit from Clarkson Regional Health Services to the Omaha Community Foundation.
Rendering of the future Project Health facility — the glass structure connected by pedestrian skywalks to a future parking garage and the CORE building that’s under construction on the west side of Saddle Creek Road in what is dubbed The Edge District. (Courtesy of University of Nebraska Medical Center)
The other major item for Friday’s meeting is a proposed $557 million increase to Project Health. That’s an increase of about 25% over the projected $2.191 billion cost, up to $2.748 billion.
The increase is partially to construct an additional level for the 1.54-million-square-foot building. The meeting agenda states this is “essential to deliver the full strategic solution, providing the capacity and critical adjacencies needed to expand surgical and intervention services, modernize and consolidate clinical laboratory services, strengthen education and research, and support future growth.” 
Project Health’s increase would also account for increased costs since 2024. The building is anticipated to open in 2033.
Friday’s meeting is set for 9 a.m. Friday at the University of Nebraska at Kearney.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Unable to rid blight on its own, Jackson officials want property owners to foot the bill
description: The Grand Chateau Apartments, dilapated and abandoned, located at 1576 W Capitol Street, Monday, July 27, 2026, in Jackson
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Bright yellow signs papered windows two months ago at a west Jackson apartment complex, condemning the Grand Chateau as uninhabitable and warning trespassers they could be fined. 
Despite the city’s efforts, several squatters remain in the dilapidated building. Furniture still sits abandoned in walkways, and clothes hang from railings. 
Prompted by the city’s request, a city judge last month put the property’s owner, Ramesh Ramchandran, on notice: Fix the property or go to jail.
The Grand Chateau has become an early test of Jackson’s more aggressive approach to landlords accused of neglecting properties and contributing to blight across the city. In recent months, city attorneys have filed lawsuits against the owners of three apartment complexes in Jackson’s environmental court, including the Grand Chateau. 
A look at some of the units at the Grand Chateau Apartments, located at 1576 W Capitol Street, Monday, July 27, 2026, in Jackson Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Without the money to eliminate Jackson’s blight issue, the city is turning to more aggressive means to reduce stress on the city’s resources.
Jackson has more than 3,200 identified blighted properties, the majority of which are single family homes but also includes large apartment complexes and commercial properties. 
“It would cost something like $80 million to locate and clean up and or demolish all of the blighted properties in the city,” City Attorney Drew Martin said.
“That’s almost the entire city budget,” he said. “We don’t have the kind of money to do that.”
The city can only afford to demolish a few large-scale properties a year, with larger developments like apartment complexes costing hundreds of thousands of dollars to demolish, Martin said. 
Jackson usually relies on liens to recoup costs on cleaning, maintaining and demolishing blighted properties. Ward 7 councilmember Kevin Parkinson said at a recent council meeting that the city netted $12,000 out of the nearly $900,000 spent on work this past year.
The recent environmental court filings are meant to shift costs to property owners — focusing on those the city deems to have the resources to rehabilitate or demolish properties on their own. 
The Grand Chateau is not the only property the city is targeting.
Environmental Court Judge Jeffery Reynolds found the owner and senior asset manager of Chapel Ridge apartments, another development in west Jackson, guilty of four code violations because of debris and burned structures. 
Khristina Miracle, left, chats with former neighbor Joe Jackson near the unit where they once lived at the Chapel Ridge Apartments located at 1636 Raymond Road in south Jackson, Monday, Jan. 26, 2026. The apartment unit was destroyed by a fire Saturday night. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Owners of another property, Addison Place Apartments  — which shut water off to residents in July — appeared in environmental court Tuesday over various code violations. In addition to the lack of running water, the property had broken windows, mold, roof damage and unmowed grass.
While litigation has become the face of the fight against blight, Martin said the city is working to enforce more administrative action early on by better enforcing existing codes, including Mississippi’s nuisance laws.
Martin said the city will be filing similar suits with Hinds County Chancery Court to rehabilitate dilapidated properties.
The city can do more to prevent properties from falling into disrepair, Martin said, so blighted properties don’t become city responsibilities.
He pointed to House Bill 1404, which was passed during the last legislative session and signed into law, that makes it a criminal offense for landlords to receive payment for utilities from a tenant but fail to pay them to the provider — resulting in interruptions to the tenant’s utility service.
Chapel Ridge faced a $100,000 unpaid water bill with JXN Water — an issue that led to the complex rapidly becoming a blighted property. 
While the city is turning to the courts to hold property owners accountable, it can only do so when owners can be located and are willing to cooperate.
Ramchandran was served with a trial notice at his 6,000-square-foot Georgia home on Aug. 22 — just short of a month after Entergy shut power to the Jackson complex. 
Ramchandran serves as the manager of Kayram Atlanta LLC, according to the Mississippi Secretary of State’s Office. The Georgia-based company has owned the West Capitol Street property since 2021.
Criminal charges can help hold property owners accountable. In the event they flee, they can be arrested. Martin said there’s not much the city can do against a property owner who disappears prior to action being taken.
City Attorney Drew Martin speaks on the city’s water issues during a town hall meeting held at City Hall, Monday, Feb. 16, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“We’ve got to do more to make sure people don’t feel like they can get away with that,” Martin said. 
Last month, Reynolds found Ramchandran guilty of seven environmental charges stemming from unsafe structures, illegal dumping and lack of upkeep. He called the Grand Chateau a “dangerous menace.”
He ordered Ramchandran to pay $1,750 in fees and face 630 days in jail unless he applied within 30 days – now about two weeks left – for a permit to fix or demolish the property. 
Ramchandran was also required to post a $1.25 million secured appearance bond in case he fails to comply with the court’s order. The amount would cover the cost of razing the Grand Chateau.
Ramchandran did not respond to numerous requests for comment.
The Grand Chateau became part of the city’s fight against blight when Entergy cut power to the complex in July after signs of meter tampering. The complex was supposed to be vacant.
Ramchandran testified during his court hearing that eviction notices were sent to tenants in May 2025 to prepare the complex for renovations, which the property owner asserts were ultimately stopped because of what he described as gun violence. 
One former contractor, Kendrick Holmes, disputed that claim and asserted that renovations stopped in 2024 because of payment issues. He recounted being sent to Lowe’s weekly for renovation supplies using Ramchandran’s company card, only for it to be declined.
A previous property manager, Pierce Wiburn, corroborated Holmes’ claims about the lack of gun violence and payment issues. 
The property incurred several violations from code enforcement officers after Holmes left the project. 
Outside of legal action, city officials are exploring other avenues to lessen the city’s blight problems.
Jackson City Council member Vernon Hartley listens during a council meeting at City Hall in Jackson on Tuesday, April 21, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Councilmembers Vernon Hartley and Ashby Foote want to establish a blight and neighborhood recovery plan, now in the works for more than a year.
In collaboration with Jackson State University, which helped collect data for the city, Hartley said the plan creates a step-by-step guide to clear roadways, remove trash from illegal dumping sites and demolish properties.Hartley said the city hopes to present the plan during the state’s next legislative session to get financial backing for the city’s fight, although he could not specify an amount Jackson would seek from lawmakers.“We’re gonna have to show something first,” Hartley said. “It’s gonna require us going in and showing folks, ‘Hey we’re serious about it.’”
Hartley said there are discussions to hire an investigator to help the city identify and build cases against owners of blighted properties.
Parkinson also wants to enlist volunteers to help already strained code enforcement officers identify blighted properties. In September, the City Council approved a proposal from Ward 4 Councilmember Brian Grizzell’s that would partner the city with a debt collection firm to recoup costs from owners who owe the city money. 
It’s not clear if these efforts will make long-term changes to Jackson’s blight issues. There’s no tangible evidence that any of these efforts are working outside of current pending litigation, and there won’t be for several months, Martin said.
However, he said he’s confident Jacksonians will begin to see results from the continued efforts within the coming months.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel files federal antitrust lawsuit against Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan
description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel filed an antitrust lawsuit against Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan Mutual Insurance Company Thursday, alleging that the company has violated both state and federal law through agreements with other Blue Cross Blue Shield entities to “eliminate competition for health insurance services to large employers like the State[...]
text:
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan building in Lansing on March 12, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel filed an antitrust lawsuit against Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan Mutual Insurance Company Thursday, alleging that the company has violated both state and federal law through agreements with other Blue Cross Blue Shield entities to “eliminate competition for health insurance services to large employers like the State.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal district court in the Eastern District of Michigan, alleges that the actions of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan have caused two types of harm in Michigan. 
First, the suit alleges a conspiracy among Blue Cross Blue Shield entities to “allocate customers and territories, to restrict output, and to eliminate competition for health insurance services,” which the lawsuit says prevents competition for the contract for state employee medical insurance plans, which the lawsuit says “has allowed Blue Cross to overcharge the State for administering the State employee plans for years.”
Insurance prices for non-state employees insured by Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan have also increased — in 2026, Blue Cross filed 23.3% to 24% annual increases for individual plan members, and 11.2% increases for small group markets, according to the Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services.
Attorney General Dana Nessel speaks about food security and SNAP at a roundtable in Lansing. Nov. 18, 2025. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Second, the lawsuit claims that due to the company’s dominant market position in the state, it pays healthcare providers lower rates compared to national rates, at times “well below the providers’ cost to provide necessary care,” at which point, the suit says, “Unable to obtain appropriate, market payments from Blue Cross, Michigan providers have been forced to reduce services, cut staff, close facilities, or exit the Michigan market entirely.”
Blue Cross controls 65% of all health insurance products and 79% of the PPO market, according to an American Medical Association report cited by the state’s lawyers, making it one of the least competitive markets in the nation. 
Nessel said in a press release that the lawsuit seeks to rein in “Blue Cross’s unchecked market power.”
“Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan has implemented substantial premium increases and deep reimbursement cuts, unchecked by meaningful competition, to drive up our costs of care, drive down our quality of care, and turn our worsening medical outcomes into their increasing profits,” Nessel said. “Today we’re taking a significant step toward ending the Blue Conspiracy and their illegal monopoly.”
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan said in a statement that it was “blindsided” by the announcement from Nessel, and that as it has not yet been served with the lawsuit, it could not comment on the specifics of the case. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We fundamentally disagree with the Attorney General’s characterization of an uncompetitive insurance market in Michigan. Competition exists everywhere in our state’s insurance markets, with strong local and national insurers competing with us every day,” Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan’s statement continued. “For nearly 90 years, Blue Cross has provided coverage for citizens across Michigan, in every county, without exception.  This heritage, and the quality of products and services we provide, is foundational to our success in Michigan.”
The lawsuit requests a jury trial in the case, and asks the court to “permanently enjoin BCBSM from continuing their anticompetitive conduct in Michigan’s healthcare markets, and award the State all available damages, disgorgement, and civil monetary penalties.”
Representatives from the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot measure campaign celebrated Nessel for the lawsuit. 
“No corporation should be too powerful to evade accountability. We applaud Attorney General Nessel for making Blue Cross Blue Shield answer for their illegal monopoly that has taken money out of Michiganders’ wallets time and again, while reducing their access to quality affordable healthcare at the same time,” Christy McGillivray, a member of the group’s steering committee, said in a statement.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Shapiro, Garrity debate skill games as zero hour for the industry closes in
description: The televised debate Wednesday in Harrisburg happened as state lawmakers and skill game industry members petitioned the state Supreme Court to extend a stay.
text:
A sign in a convenience store window advertises skill games, slot machine-like devices. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)With less than a week before the court decision that skill games are illegal takes effect, Gov. Josh Shapiro and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity shared their positions on the future of the industry during their gubernatorial debate. 
The televised debate Wednesday in Harrisburg happened as state lawmakers and skill game industry members petitioned the state Supreme Court to extend a stay. The move aims to delay the effect of the decision until Feb 10 to give lawmakers more time to pass a regulatory scheme.
Garrity, the Republican nominee for governor, told moderators she supports a flat monthly fee of $500 per machine. With 50,000 machines statewide, it would generate about $300 million in new revenue to the state, she said, without specifying where in the state budget she would spend it. 
She was also critical of Shapiro’s plan to tax skill games at 52%, claiming he aimed to kill the industry to benefit a political supporter with interests in the casino industry. Casino slot machines and video gaming terminals are taxed between 34% and 54% depending on the category of casino.
“He knows that they can’t survive at 52% and it’s because one of his biggest benefactors is Michael Rubin, who is the CEO of Fanatics and also owns a casino,” Garrity said.
Diamond urges House leaders not to allow skill games deadline to pass without a solution

The sportswear mogul made $78,200 in in-kind contributions to Shapiro’s campaign committee listed as travel, which The Philadelphia Inquirer reported reflect trips on Rubin’s private helicopter. Rubin co-owns the Fanatics sportsbook at Ocean Casino Resort in Atlantic City with rapper Jay-Z. 
“I would urge the governor to think about the jobs and all the money that these groups give back to the community, because American Legions, VFWs, fire halls, small businesses-they are the backbone of Pennsylvania,” Garrity said.
Shapiro did not address Garrity’s claim, but said he has been unwavering in his plan to regulate and tax the games at the same rate as casinos. 
“I would drive those dollars into the general fund and then use a core chunk of that to fund mass transit across Pennsylvania,” he said, adding that the state House of Representatives has passed legislation to enact his plan. “The Senate of Pennsylvania, led by Republicans, has refused to bring it up.”
State Sens. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) and Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) and Rep. Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne) filed, withdrew and refiled a petition this week asking the Supreme Court to use its emergency powers to extend the Oct. 13 deadline to pass legislation legalizing skill games. The refiled petition 
On Thursday morning, a group described as the Skill Games Business Consortium also filed a petition to intervene in the case in support of an extension. The filing doesn’t identify members of the consortium and lawyers for the group did not return calls Thursday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At the same time, a group of seven district attorneys signed a letter to the General Assembly urging lawmakers to act on skill game legislation in the interest of public safety, noting law enforcement sought clarity on regulations for the devices even before the Supreme Court’s decision.
“The public safety concerns associated with certain machine locations — including theft and other criminal activity — also warrant consideration as the Commonwealth establishes its legal framework,” the letter says. It was signed by Bedford County District Attorney Ashlan Clark, Butler County District Attorney Richard Goldinger, Clearfield County District Attorney Ryan Sayers, Elk County District Attorney Beau Grove, Franklin County District Attorney Ian Brink, Juniata County District Attorney Cory Snook and McKean County District Attorney Stephanie Vettenburg-Shaffer. 
The high court ruled June 15 that skill games are subject to the commonwealth’s Gaming Act and the Crimes Code. As a result, anyone operating a skill game machine is required to be licensed by the state Gaming Control Board.
Recognizing the impact on skill game hosts and operators, the Supreme Court instructed that no law enforcement agency was to act on the decision for 120 days.
In their filing, the three lawmakers say they are co-sponsors of compromise legislation to establish a licensing, taxation, and regulatory framework for skill games. 
As the deadline approaches, Pennsylvania State Police and the state Attorney General’s Office have warned that all skill game machines need to be removed from establishments before the ruling takes effect.
The lawmakers’ petition said that in addition to being a burden on businesses and organizations that host the machines, their removal would delay any tax revenue from the machines when the General Assembly passes skill game legislation.
“The Commonwealth would begin its new regulatory program by first recovering the very devices that program is designed to license,” the filing said. “A defined extension of the existing safe harbor avoids that remove-and-return cycle and preserves an identifiable device base for qualification under the new law if the legislation is enacted.”
