title: Louisiana borrowers to face biggest ‘tax bomb’ from student loan forgiveness
description: Some Louisianians could see their tax bills triple — the biggest increase in the country — following the expiration of a law that kept forgiven student loan debt from being treated as income, according to a new report.  Student loan debtholders in Louisiana and the rest of the South are expected to be the hardest […]
text:
Graduates stand during the May 16, 2025, commencement ceremony at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, held at the Cajundome. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Some Louisianians could see their tax bills triple — the biggest increase in the country — following the expiration of a law that kept forgiven student loan debt from being treated as income, according to a new report. 
Student loan debtholders in Louisiana and the rest of the South are expected to be the hardest hit because they tend to have larger balances and lower incomes, according to the analysis from Protect Borrowers, an advocacy group that studies the impact of various types of debt. Mississippi, Arkansas, Alabama, Kentucky and South Carolina also rank in the top 10 for states that will see the largest income tax increases.  
In 2021, Congress exempted cancelled debt from federal student loans from being treated as taxable income, but lawmakers allowed that exemption to expire Dec. 31, 2025. 
Roughly 2 million to 3 million borrowers who will have their debt cancelled in the next decade can expect a “tax bomb,” according to the analysis. The additional taxes impact federal student loan borrowers who are on an income-driven repayment plan, which bases monthly payments on their take-home pay and the size of their families.
For Louisiana, the average student loan borrower can expect an additional tax cost of $7,668 from cancelled debt for tax year 2026. That’s roughly $300 more than the rate in Mississippi and nearly $800 than Arkansas.
“This tax bomb will force millions of working-class families, who have been diligently making payments for two decades or more, to trade their student loan debt for debt to the IRS,” said Jennifer Zhang, author of the Protect Borrowers report.
The report recommends that Congress and state legislatures pass laws to end taxation of cancelled student loan debt.

name: Daily Montanan
title: A prison sentence shouldn’t take away a citizen’s vote
description: It was Election Day, 1964. My mother took me to the polling site –  Meadowlark Elementary in Great Falls. She held my hand. We stood in line.  A voting booth opened, and we entered.  My mother pulled a lever. A curtain closed. She explained that Democratic candidates were on one side. Republicans on the other. People […]
text:
An election worker hands out “I Voted” stickers at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)It was Election Day, 1964.
My mother took me to the polling site –  Meadowlark Elementary in Great Falls.
She held my hand. We stood in line.  A voting booth opened, and we entered.  My mother pulled a lever. A curtain closed. She explained that Democratic candidates were on one side. Republicans on the other.
People could tell whether you were a Republican or Democrat by which side of the voting booth you stood. My mother, the daughter of a former Republican Governor, stood on the Republican side.  Then, she reached over to vote for all Democrats, except for my father, a Republican candidate. He ran for lieutenant governor as a Republican, but was a proud union member.
In my family, voting was a responsibility.  A sacred duty.
Growing up, I assumed every adult voted; universal suffrage, a cornerstone of democracy.
As a lawyer, I learned that Montana denies thousands of citizens the opportunity to vote.
Yes, citizens – people in prison.
We take away people’s freedom. We also take away their right to vote. It’s called disenfranchisement.
What is the public policy behind disenfranchisement?  Good question.
Is losing the right to vote part of the punishment?  What does that accomplish?  Why should a person be prohibited from exercising their responsibility of citizenship? There is no connection.
It is bad public policy.
In Montana, our prison population has exploded. With mass incarceration comes mass disenfranchisement.
In 2024, an estimated 5,330 citizens were barred from voting in Montana. Most in our prisons, but also more than 600 in our jails.  Put this in perspective.  In Montana during the 2024 election, five legislative house races were decided by fewer than 300 votes, one by only 17 votes.
When elections are so close, we should scrutinize any law that limits who can vote.
The Montana Constitution, Article IV, Section 2, and Montana Code Annotated Section 13-1-111(2) curtail some voting rights.  A person “serving a sentence for a felony in a penal institution” cannot vote.  Fortunately, under Montana law, a person becomes eligible to vote again after their release.  They do not have to complete parole or probation.
It isn’t that way everywhere.  Maine and Vermont, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico allow people in prison to vote.
It’s worse in other states.  It’s illegal for some citizens to vote. I’m not talking about making it “harder” for someone to vote. Against the law.
In some other states, many citizens still can’t vote after they are released from prison. They have been released, but not all of their rights have been restored. Some may be precluded from voting while they are on probation or parole.
The Sentencing Project’s Report, “Locked Out 2024” estimated 4,049,978 American citizens could not vote because of a felony conviction. Around 2.9 million weren’t even in prison.  They were in the community, working, and raising families. However, they were still legally barred from voting.
It isn’t this way in other countries. In Canada, the convicted still vote. In South Africa, prisoners have a constitutional right to vote. In Europe, many prisoners vote. Voting restrictions apply only to certain crimes or sentences.
Think about this: What justifies depriving more than 4 million American citizens of their right to vote while also eliminating a cornerstone of our democracy?
There is a difference between loss of freedom and citizenship. A person in prison is still a citizen. Most will return to our communities. Voting allows them to participate in our communities.  We want them to be good citizens when they return. Why forbid them from practicing good citizenship now?
We can punish a crime without taking away a person’s right to vote. Disenfranchising them denies them a voice and representation and undermines our democracy.
I remember my mother holding my hand as we entered the voting booth.  She taught me that with citizenship came responsibility.
Our fellow citizens in prison are still citizens. We want them to be better citizens when they return to our communities. Forbidding them from voting is contrary to our interests and intentions. A prison sentence should not erase their responsibilities as citizens.
Montana should change its constitution and laws to allow people in prison to vote.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota urban/rural divide: We have more in common than we presume
description: I grew up in Twin Valley, a town of 723 in the northwestern part of our state. I was born in St. Paul, and I live in Minneapolis today. In my life I have had a rare first-hand experience in seeing the differences between Greater Minnesota and the Twin Cities.  And what I have learned […]
text:
Vermillion, Minnesota, left, and downtown Minneapolis, right. (Photos by Nicole Neri and Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)I grew up in Twin Valley, a town of 723 in the northwestern part of our state. I was born in St. Paul, and I live in Minneapolis today. In my life I have had a rare first-hand experience in seeing the differences between Greater Minnesota and the Twin Cities. 
And what I have learned first and foremost is that we have a lot more in common than we think.
There are differences. For the most, for instance, Greater Minnesota has a lower cost of living. In the Twin Cities, we’re all aware of the big-time sports, entertainment and large-scale events. 
But many of my neighbors in both places hold numerous inaccurate ideas about the other. The Twin Cities were often so revered by young people where I grew up that if I had even received a pen from Minneapolis, I would consider it a treasure. I would also hear among others the significance of making a trip four hours southeast to the Twin Cities. A highlight of grade school was our sixth-grade class trip (a tradition still continuing today) in which we spent a night in the Twin Cities and went sightseeing.
But at the same time, people in Greater Minnesota often considered the Twin Cities to be out of touch. People were worried that metro progressivism was dismissive of small-town Minnesota issues. 
I was also warned that people in the big city were not welcoming, and that hospitality belonged in the country alone.
But though they may be geographically distant, I have seen that people in Minneapolis typically have lots of interest in the state outside the metro. At the University of Minnesota, people regularly discuss life, upbringings and issues in Mankato, Duluth, Fergus Falls, Moorhead, International Falls and everywhere in between. In my experience, people from the cities, the suburbs and exburbs are as warm and welcoming as those in my hometown. 
As an active political canvasser, having knocked well over 1,000 doors across the Twin Cities, I’ve been offered beverages, welcomed to barbeques, introduced to family members, and so much more by neighbors who truly care about others. 
Simply put, Minnesota nice is statewide.
Living in the Twin Cities and being active in my community, I have also been made aware of local perceptions held both for and against those in Greater Minnesota. Many people in the Twin Cities admire Greater Minnesota for its natural landmarks, small-town nice, local culture, affordability and simple quiet. People in the cities view Greater Minnesota as a place of retreat. It’s the destination for trips to the Boundary Waters, annual visits to the family cabin or a hunting trip.
But people in the cities also fall into the trap of viewing their Greater Minnesota neighbors as all close-minded and conservative. Many also believe Greater Minnesota is economically stagnant, and economic opportunity limited. 
These perceptions are distorted. Sure, Greater Minnesota favored President Donald Trump heavily in 2024, but political identity is not uniform. In my hometown, for example, Trump won 54% of the vote, with Kamala Harris taking 42%. Take 10 people, and at least four were Harris voters. When I mention this to people, they are surprised at the result in a small town in the most conservative congressional district in our state. The majority of our city also voted for Sen. Amy Klobuchar for reelection.
Greater Minnesota is anything but economically stagnant and lacking in opportunities. Agriculture, mining, manufacturing and tourism are all significant avenues of economic growth. There are also numerous well-renowned colleges driving economic growth, including Minnesota State in Moorhead, where I graduated in 2025, MSU Mankato, Rochester Community and Technical College, and more. To be sure, many small towns are struggling with tariff-fueled inflation, increasing gas prices and working-age immigrant families leaving our communities due to Operation Metro Surge.
When I first moved to Minneapolis, these misconceptions were on my mind. But what I found in the end was that we have more commonalities than differences. Simply put, I know that my friends in the cities would get along great with my friends in the country.
We can overcome these misconceptions. 
That starts with thinking twice before jumping to conclusions about our fellow Minnesotans. 
With all that is happening in our country right now, we have a choice to make in our state: We can be productive and build for a better tomorrow, or we get nothing done. 
I say we work together and build up for the future of Minnesota.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky Senate budget chair questions whether politics are influencing budget forecast
description: A Republican leader has raised concerns about whether political games are being played with budget forecasts that show new revenue amid a very uncertain economic forecast. At a legislative meeting Wednesday, Senate Appropriations and Revenue Committee chair Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, said he was worried about a revised state revenue forecast last mont[...]
text:
Sen. Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, speaks on the Senate floor, Feb, 4, 2025. (LRC Public Information)A Republican leader has raised concerns about whether political games are being played with budget forecasts that show new revenue amid a very uncertain economic forecast.
At a legislative meeting Wednesday, Senate Appropriations and Revenue Committee chair Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, said he was worried about a revised state revenue forecast last month that Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear touted as being an extra $1.7 billion that could be spent on Kentuckians.
Beshear cited “strong fiscal management by my administration” and a “surging economy” as reasoning for the extra funding. But the group of economists who revised the state revenue forecast had a more gloomy future outlook on the economy because of “much uncertainty” about artificial intelligence investment and the ongoing war with Iran. 
During the Wednesday meeting, McDaniel said that the “the words don’t seem to match the numbers.” Greg Harkenrider, a deputy director within the state budget office, was giving a presentation on the new outlook for state tax revenues. 
“I have a concern when the underlying conditions are a continuation of a war, tighter energy markets, higher energy prices, greater uncertainty, erosion of consumer and business confidence, declining consumer demand,” McDaniel said. “And oh, by the way, with all of those — now we’re going to bring in a billion dollars more in taxes.” 
Meanwhile, during a Wednesday press conference, Beshear called on state lawmakers to spend the new funding on Medicaid, universal preschool and senior meals. 
When asked by a reporter about if he’s spoken with legislative leadership, Beshear said meetings were coming up.
“There is real opportunity to help our people with recurring revenue, because our economy is still surging, even if our families aren’t feeling it. So the General Assembly is going to have a basic question to answer: With additional recurring revenue, are they willing to help people or not?” Beshear said to reporters.
Wednesday’s dueling commentary could be a preview of future debates when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets next year on whether to reopen the state budget during the shorter non-budget session. Lawmakers could reopen the state budget but would need to meet a higher vote threshold on any bill to do so. It would also be the last legislative session where Beshear would be governor because he is term-limited. 
GOP-controlled state legislature had already crafted and passed a two-year state budget when they met in early 2026, a budget the minority Democrats and Beshear argued significantly underfunded needs including Medicaid and education. Republican lawmakers have pushed back on those characterizations, seeking to control what they see as unsustainable executive branch spending. 
The debate whether to spend new tax revenue is happening as Republicans in the legislature try to eventually eliminate the state’s income tax, traditionally a major source of tax revenue for the state. In a letter last month, Hicks wrote to state lawmakers that the state missed a fiscal trigger by more than $1 billion to further cut the state’s income tax rate.
A group of economists being ‘co-opted’? 
 The Consensus Forecasting Group is the nonpartisan group of economists from around the state who had made the “pessimistic” projection of how much future funding the state will bring in. 
State Budget Director John Hicks had requested the group meet again to revise the tax revenue forecast after the state had received hundreds of millions of dollars of “unexpected” corporate income tax payments this summer, according to the governor’s office. At one point, McDaniel asked if those corporate payments were “goosed” by AI investment and whether there was a “bubble.” 
McDaniel also questioned the timing of Hicks calling in the Consensus Forecasting Group.
“A lot of us have a worry that what we’re beginning to see is the utilization of CFG in a manner that it’s not intended for,” McDaniel said, mentioning concerns that “important institutions appear to be co-opted for political purposes.” 
“If CFG happens to be wrong with this revised forecast and we spend this money, the very governor who’s proposing the spending will not have to stand to account for it because he will be out of office, the budgetary shortfall will fall on the next guy, and it becomes very problematic,” McDaniel said. 
In an emailed statement, Beshear spokesperson Scottie Ellis said statements by McDaniels “are baseless and politically motivated.” She pointed to state law that requires the state budget director to “monitor the financial situation” of Kentucky. 
“The Consensus Forecasting Group has been called on two other times during the Beshear administration — the only difference is that in this instance, there is a surplus from which dollars can be used to help Kentuckians through Medicaid, senior meals and more,” Ellis said. “While these are the very programs the Republican supermajority cut in the last session, claiming lack of funds, they have no excuse in the upcoming session.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC law guaranteed teachers 2 days of planning time. Some schools still aren’t complying.
description: Roughly one in five teachers reported not receiving their legally required planning days, the state's largest association of educators found.
text:
Some teachers said they didn't get their legally required two days of planning time ahead of this school year, the state's largest association of educators found. (File/Photo by Richard Ross/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — When teachers went back to school this summer, a state law guaranteed them two days free of meetings to plan for the year ahead.
Nearly 1 in 5 teachers didn’t get those planning days, according to a survey done by the Palmetto State Teachers Association, the state’s largest educator advocacy group.
The guaranteed planning time was part of last year’s sweeping education law titled the Educator Assistance Act, which both chambers passed unanimously. Meant to help keep qualified teachers in classrooms, the law required a spate of changes for schools.
Under the law, schools must give teachers an estimated salary before renewing contracts, give a heads-up before moving teachers to a different school or subject, and count professional development meetings toward teachers’ required training credits.
Teachers’ advocates called the law a huge win for teachers and pointed to the required planning time as one of the biggest victories included. Before that, state law allowed districts to give teachers up to two days of planning time but didn’t require it, letting schools eat up that time with meetings and other assignments.
SC Senate advances bill on teacher contracts called a ‘huge win’ for K-12 educators

Although teachers told the association they didn’t get their full work days, just one official complaint was made to the state Department of Education, spokeswoman Christy Cox said in an email.
“At this time, we are not aware of widespread compliance issues,” Cox said.
Setting aside two days each year before school starts should have been an easy way to improve teachers’ lives, said Patrick Kelly, a teachers’ advocate for the Palmetto State Teachers Association. The law gave schools some flexibility in setting schedules, allowing them to dole out the time in half days if needed.
But teachers say their schools aren’t following the rule, Kelly said.
That didn’t surprise him, he added.
Roughly a quarter of teachers who responded to the survey also reported not receiving their 30-minutes’ worth of breaks throughout the day as required under a 2022 law, he said.
That was meant to ensure teachers have time to go to the bathroom and eat lunch. Legislators put that into law after hearing from teachers that they had to wear diapers because they didn’t have any break time during the school day.
“There needs to be a greater commitment to implementation of state law,” said Kelly, who teaches advanced government classes at Blythewood High School.
Uninterrupted planning
Kelly expected some schools to fail to follow the law last year.
Gov. Henry McMaster signed the bill into law May, 7, 2025, and it took effect July 1, just weeks before the school year started. Most districts already had their back-to-school schedules set, making it harder to carve out teacher planning time not already included, Kelly said.
So, when about 22% of teachers surveyed last year said they didn’t get two full days of uninterrupted planning time, Kelly wasn’t surprised. He was more surprised when this year’s survey results showed 18% of teachers still didn’t get their two days.

“This is not a terribly difficult piece of legislation to implement if you have the will and desire to implement it,” he said.
The responses came from teachers across the state and across grade levels, Kelly said. No single district or school accounted for a large number of the responses, suggesting a wider-reaching issue of implementation, he said.
There was no single reason teachers gave for their school not giving the allotted time, Kelly said.
Very few cases seemed to involve a teacher asking for their planning days and being told “no,” Kelly said. More often, teachers said they technically had the days scheduled as planning time but got pulled into meetings or told how to spend that time, which the law was supposed to prevent.
Dena Crews, president of the South Carolina Education Association, heard similar complaints from teachers this school year, she said. The association is in the process of conducting its own survey to figure out how widespread the concerns are from its members.
Like Kelly, Crews heard complaints from teachers who had planning days on the schedule but got pulled away from their work into meetings.
“That time is being taken away from them and isn’t being protected the way it’s supposed to be,” said Crews, a former elementary school teacher and reading coach.
Planning time before the start of the school year is essential, Kelly and Crews said.
New teachers need time to get familiar with their lesson plans and set up their classrooms. Veteran teachers need time to refresh and update what they’re teaching. And all teachers need to learn about their students for the coming school year, said Senate Education Chairman Greg Hembree.
With meetings and other tasks still eating into teachers’ planning time, Hembree questioned how teachers are supposed to get everything done.
“Should they do it in their free time?” the Little River Republican said. “That doesn’t seem fair. It’s part of work.”
More than anything else, great teaching is built on strong relationships with students so teachers can support them in the ways they need, Kelly said. Teachers can’t do that part of the work if they spend every spare minute in meetings or doing administrative work, he said.
“Who ultimately is going to suffer is students,” Kelly said.
Potential penalties
When the Department of Education gets complaints, the agency first tells the district and offers help to resolve the issue, with state “involvement as needed,” Cox said.
The agency sent out a memo to superintendents last year explaining the law and setting guidelines for how districts can comply, to include splitting the time into half days.
“The Department strongly supports protecting teachers’ valuable planning and preparation time and ensuring educators have the tools and flexibility they need to begin the school year successfully,” Cox said in a statement.
SC House advances bill crediting teachers for prior work experience

With that in mind, there’s no reason teachers shouldn’t get their allotted time, Crews said.
“It’s not a choice of, ‘I’ll give it if I can and I won’t if I can’t,’” Crews said. “This is law.”
She supports the agency’s approach of helping districts schedule the time instead of punishing them for not following the law.
Generally, teachers are reluctant to make official complaints that get their district in trouble. If the state takes away funding because of administrative problems, students lose out on resources, Kelly said.
But there is no financial penalty in the law for failing to give teachers unencumbered planning time.
And in the survey, no teacher reported violations of the law that would be costly, he said. Schools that fail to give teachers a proposed contract, including an estimated salary, for the upcoming year by May 1 stand to lose $10,000 per late contract.
Hembree said legislators might need to consider some sort of penalty for schools not providing two meeting-free days. Without a consequence for enforcement, districts have little incentive to do what legislators say, he said.
“I’ve been worn out with schools ignoring state policy,” Hembree said. “They act like they’re the boss, and they’re not.”
Otherwise, the only way to force a school to follow the law is through the courts, which is unlikely since filing a lawsuit is time-consuming and expensive, Hembree said.
“If there’s no penalty, there’s no rule,” Hembree said.

name: National
title: Feds unlikely to change abortion pill policy before next year
description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said late Wednesday that it expects to complete its  long-awaited safety review of abortion pills by mid-December and issue a report evaluating the results by March 2027. The agency disclosed the information in a court-mandated status report it submitted in the federal lawsuit Louisiana v. FDA. The timeline aligns […]
text:
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a safety review of abortion medication last spring, following an anti-abortion pressure campaign urging the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to overturn a Biden-era rule allowing abortion pills to be prescribed via telemedicine. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said late Wednesday that it expects to complete its  long-awaited safety review of abortion pills by mid-December and issue a report evaluating the results by March 2027.
The agency disclosed the information in a court-mandated status report it submitted in the federal lawsuit Louisiana v. FDA. The timeline aligns with recent reporting that the Trump administration intends to delay controversial decisions around abortion until after the midterm elections.
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the review last spring, following an anti-abortion pressure campaign urging the FDA to overturn a Biden-era rule allowing abortion pills to be prescribed via telemedicine. More than a year later, national anti-abortion leaders are criticizing the administration for delaying action, and have signaled they would reject a review that finds medication abortion safe if they don’t find it to be thorough enough.
“The FDA’s court-ordered update on its abortion-drug study is alarming,” said Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser in a written statement released late Wednesday night. “Instead of the promised gold-standard study, the FDA is trying to peddle fool’s gold.”
The Trump administration has used the ongoing study to delay several federal lawsuits related to medication abortion regulation. Louisiana, as well as Missouri and Texas, sued the federal government, arguing that federal policies allowing mifepristone to be prescribed via telehealth and distributed by mail undermine state abortion bans. Six months ago, a federal district court in Louisiana granted the FDA’s motion to stay proceedings in the case until the government completed its review of the current mifepristone-misoprostol regimen.
Abortion foes plan to push pill restrictions in the states

The FDA says it is comparing the safety profile of medication abortion to the safety profile of surgical abortion and analyzing a variety of data sources within, and outside of, the FDA’s Sentinel system, a distributed database related to medical product safety.
The agency says it is also reviewing mifepristone’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS), a drug-safety program the FDA uses for certain drugs. That includes reconsidering the agency’s 2023 decision allowing for telehealth abortion.
“Following completion of its study and review, FDA will decide whether changes to the Mifepristone REMS Program are necessary and, if applicable, initiate any such changes in accordance with established processes,” reads the status report submitted by the U.S. Department of Justice.
Mary Ziegler, a law professor at the University of California, Davis, expects the FDA’s review to be guided by politics rather than science.
“I think the fact that the Trump administration has not yet issued new restrictions on mifepristone is primarily because Republicans think it’s dangerous to do that politically,” Ziegler said. “I think if they do impose new restrictions, it’ll be to cater to the base.”
Anti-abortion groups urge attorney general to halt mailing of abortion pills

Anti-abortion groups have urged the administration not to wait until the study is complete to take action on abortion drugs, and warned they would not accept inaction even after the study is complete. They’ve also said they will continue to pursue abortion-pill restrictions in the states.
“The Pro-Life Movement is prepared to reject a methodologically flawed review where the agency has simply gone through the motions to rubber stamp the current REMS, or lack thereof,” said John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life, in a written statement.
His group was involved in a movement-wide effort to produce and promote research on medication abortion, analyzing commercially available Medicaid insurance claims data. White papers produced by the Ethics and Public Policy Center and the Foundation for the Restoration of America found that about 11% of patients who took mifepristone experienced serious adverse events, which is 22 times higher than what’s on the current drug label for mifepristone. The papers, which were not published in peer-reviewed scientific journals, used a broader definition of serious adverse event than what the FDA uses.
Anti-abortion leaders told Stateline they have been expecting the FDA to conduct its own analysis of Medicaid insurance claims data as part of its review. They say the agency should not only use its internal systems, calling them insufficient.
“I’m certainly hopeful that the FDA is using more robust data sources like an insurance claims database,” said Dr. Christina Francis, CEO of the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which was a plaintiff group in a previous lawsuit challenging the FDA’s regulation of abortion pills, which the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed over standing issues.
The Indiana OB-GYN said the FDA’s review is “long overdue” and said her practice has seen complications from abortion pills “at least on a monthly basis.”
Ushma Upadhyay, a professor at the University of California, San Francisco, who has co-authored several studies showing low rates of serious adverse health risks for medication and telehealth abortion, said it would be difficult to draw conclusions about telehealth abortion just from insurance claims data.
“Insurance claims are an excellent way to understand safety of many medications, and I also think it is useful in understanding the safety of medication abortion, but not specifically telehealth, because most of the telehealth abortion providers do not accept insurance,” Upadhyay said.
Ziegler said the results of the safety review are unlikely to change the debate over abortion pills.
“Mifepristone is one of the most studied, most politicized drugs in the country,” she said. “Obviously it’s not being studied because it hasn’t been studied.”
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas GOP candidate for secretary of state fined $93,000 for breaking federal labor law
description: Republican Pat Proctor explains why a bureaucrat concluded he owed $93,000 in overtime and minimum wage compensation to restaurant employees.
text:
State Rep. Pat Proctor, a Leavenworth Republican running for secretary of state, says a federal agency claimed in 2016 that he owed $93,000 to his restaurant employees for violations of minimum wage and overtime statutes. In this April 9, 2026, photo, Proctor speaks chats at the Kansas Capitol (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas secretary of state candidate Pat Proctor blamed zealous bureaucrats for assessing his restaurant businesses $93,000 in penalties after failing to comply with federal wage and overtime laws.
Proctor, a Leavenworth member of the Kansas House, a retired U.S. Army colonel and recipient of a doctorate from Kansas State University, said he ran into trouble with the U.S. Department of Labor because he didn’t understand fundamentals of labor law. He had been in the restaurant business for approximately 10 years when the department raised the issue with him in 2016.
“One day, here comes the labor department in, saying, ‘Hey, you owe all these people money because you didn’t record their hours,'” Proctor said during an interview with KMAN radio host Mike Matson. “Here comes this bureaucrat into the restaurant with some regulations that we didn’t know about, and it cost us.”
In Kansas, the secretary of state is responsible for oversight of elections and manages business records filed by companies throughout the state.
Proctor said the original complaint alleged Baan Thai Restaurant Inc., which he co-owned with his wife, should have paid 31 salaried employees $93,008 for work performed from 2014 to 2016. The labor department said Proctor’s obligations included $79,133 for unpaid overtime and $13,875 for failure to comply with the $7.25 federal minimum wage. In total, he was cited for 41 violations.
In the KMAN interview, Proctor said he couldn’t recall whether compensation paid his staff was negotiated down to $68,000 or $78,000.
Proctor is the Republican Party nominee to replace Secretary of State Scott Schwab, who unsuccessfully sought the GOP nomination for governor rather than seek reelection in 2026. Proctor’s Democraticic Party opponent in the general election is Jennifer Day of Lawrence. The Nov. 3 ballot also will include Scott Morgan, the Lawrence nominee of the United Kansas Party.
“If Pat Proctor can’t pay his own employees, how can we trust him to run our elections?” Day said. “The fact that Proctor withheld tens of thousands of dollars from dozens of his employees — depriving workers of fair wages — shows he has no regard for the people of Kansas and that he thinks the rules don’t apply to him.”
Day, who owns a real estate investment business, said the candidate elected secretary of state should be a standard bearer in terms of elections and business filings. Those duties start with being accountable for personal mistakes, she said.
“As a small business owner myself, I know how important it is that these offices be run with integrity,” Day said. “My opponent has proven that he won’t put Kansans before his own interests, and it’s a record Kansas voters deserve to know about.”
Proctor co-owns Baan Thai restaurants in Leavenworth and Manhattan and recently opened Noodles of Asia in Leavenworth.
In the KMAN interview, Proctor said kitchen staff in his restaurants from 2014 to 2016 were paid salaries above the minimum wage. He said the federal government claimed he should have kept records of his employees’ time on the job because anything above 40 hours per week was overtime requiring bonus pay. Proctor said he didn’t track the hours worked by those restaurant employees, which deprived them of income.
Proctor said if elected secretary of state he would reconfigure the office’s website and deploy artificial intelligence to provide information to business owners about federal, state or local requirements for operating companies of all types. He said the Kansas Legislature should pass a law exempting Kansas companies from regulatory fines if the website proved inadequate to prepare company owners.
“If the government is going to make me do something, in my mind, it’s the government’s responsibility to make sure I know I have to do it,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PURA OKs changes to how utilities purchase electricity
description: CT regulators approved a framework for 'dynamic' procurement, which was required as part of a bipartisan energy-savings bill passed in 2025.
text:
Connecticut regulators on Wednesday approved several changes to the process through which utility companies purchase electricity, with hopes of saving customers money by giving them access to better deals on the day-to-day energy markets.
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority voted 5-0 to approve a framework for its new “dynamic” procurement model, which it is required to implement as part of a bipartisan energy-savings bill passed by lawmakers in 2025.
“This decision is a positive step forward in improving our procedures to procure energy at the best price for Connecticut ratepayers, while preserving important safeguards from market volatility,” PURA Chairman Thomas Wiehl said in his public remarks Wednesday.
How much customers can expect to save from the changes remains to be seen. PURA has until February to draft a more detailed plan to implement the new procurement model, and officials said it will likely be mid-2027 or early 2028 before any impacts are seen in customers’ bills. 
Under the current system, Eversource and United Illuminating both purchase nearly all of the power used by their standard service customers through fixed-price, six-month contracts with wholesale suppliers. Wholesalers can include power plant operators that generate their own electricity, or other firms that buy and sell electricity on markets run by ISO New England, the regional grid operator.
The price of electricity on those wholesale markets can change as often as every five minutes based on factors such as the weather, consumer demand and the availability of natural gas, which is the primary fuel source used by most of the region’s power plants.
Therefore, wholesalers assume all of the risk — and any potential savings — from day-to-day fluctuations in the cost of electricity. Customers, in turn, benefit from more stable prices. 
The changes approved by PURA on Wednesday will allow utility companies to bypass this system and procure some of their electric load — starting with a target of around 20% — directly from the wholesale markets, also known as “dynamic market purchasing.” 
The hope is that by allowing utilities to access better deals on the wholesale markets, they will be able to pass those savings on to customers. Under Connecticut’s de-regulated energy structure, utilities do not own or profit from the generation of electricity at power plants. Those costs are passed along to customers, without markup, through supply charges on electricity bills.
“This decision takes a thoughtful and measured approach to improving Connecticut’s procurement process for standard service electric customers,” Consumer Counsel Claire Coleman said in a statement. “The goal of both the enabling legislation and throughout this proceeding was to build enough flexibility into the framework to benefit from lower-cost opportunities as they become available while maintaining protections that help shield customers from sudden changes and volatile swings in energy markets.”
Even supporters, however, note that changes to the procurement process also carry risks for customers. 
“If you do it more dynamically, maybe you will save money maybe you won’t,” said state Sen. Norm Needleman, D-Essex. “It depends as much on external factors such as wars and pandemics.”
Needleman, who serves as co-chair of the legislature’s Energy and Technology Committee, was one of the drafters of the 2025 law that required changes to the procurement process. He said that by limiting dynamic purchasing to a portion of the utilities’ total load, and allowing PURA to oversee the process, the risk to customers can be mitigated.
Representatives from both Eversource and UI released statements on Wednesday saying it was too early to tell what impact the changes to the procurement process would have on customers’ bills. Both companies requested changes be made to the final framework approved by PURA on Wednesday.
“It’s unquestionable that high, and oftentimes unpredictable, energy supply costs are the leading cause of the energy affordability challenges facing customers across New England, and those challenges can’t be meaningfully addressed without bringing more energy supply into the region,” Eversource spokesperson Tricia Taskey Modifica said in a statement.
“We’re closely reviewing the order to determine if we can effectively implement it to ensure customers have access to safe, reliable service at the lowest possible cost,” she added.
Angela Baccaro, a spokesperson for UI, said in a statement that the company supports the framework adopted by PURA on Wednesday.
“The specific customer, operational, and resource impacts of the approved framework will become clearer as implementation planning progresses and additional details are developed,” Baccaro said. “We look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to implement the framework.”
Because utility companies do not profit off of energy procurements, Wiehl, the PURA chairman, said that reforming that process was an area where regulators and utilities could work together to find savings for customers. However, he lamented in his comments before Wednesday’s vote, the companies seemed more focused on their own self-interest, including assurances that they will be reimbursed for any costs to implement the new procurement system.
“In my opinion, the exceptions and arguments from the utility companies in this case did not fully reflect that cooperative spirit,” Wiehl said. 
He added, “Here, where meaningful cooperation seems so attainable, what I read and heard was a focus on minimizing financial risk and public accountability.”
The changes will not impact customers who have switched off standard service, onto one of the third-party supply rates offered through Connecticut’s retail electric marketplace.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI gubernatorial candidates talk housing, energy and education in first general election debate
description: The first gubernatorial debate of the 2026 general election cycle began cordially enough. Moderator Gene Valicenti asked the three candidates if their opponents had the temperament and experience to serve as governor. Republican Aaron Guckian readily acknowledged that each of them was “a smart individual,” while independent Ken Block conceded that Democratic[...]
text:
Left to right, Rhode Island gubernatorial candidates Ken Block, Helena Buonanno Foulkes and Aaron Guckian face moderator Gene Valicenti during the live debate hosted by NBC 10 WJAR in the lobby of the Providence Performing Arts Center on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. (WJAR)
The first gubernatorial debate of the 2026 general election cycle began cordially enough.
Moderator Gene Valicenti asked the three candidates if their opponents had the temperament and experience to serve as governor. Republican Aaron Guckian readily acknowledged that each of them was “a smart individual,” while independent Ken Block conceded that Democratic opponent Helena Buonanno Foulkes at least had the temperament. Foulkes deferred to her opponents to speak for themselves.
But niceties were soon replaced with accusations and interruptions as the candidates bickered over policy and politics. 
One of the most divisive topics of the hourlong debate, hosted by NBC 10 and Coastal ABC in the Providence Performing Arts Center lobby, was whether candidates could work with Providence’s Democratic mayoral nominee, David Morales. The 28-year-old democratic socialist ousted incumbent Mayor Brett Smiley in a high-turnout primary shaped by opinions over rent control and the Israeli-Palestine conflict.
Foulkes, 62, of Providence, who also defeated incumbent Gov. Dan McKee in the  Democratic primary has already said she would endorse Morales in the general election, noting their shared focus on housing affordability, though she made clear she does not agree with the proposed rent stabilization policy Morales has pledged to enact.
“I am a capitalist, not a socialist, but we share a lot of things in common,” said Foulkes, who leads the race in public polling and fundraising. “The people of Providence have spoken. They picked him. The governor of this state has to have a good relationship with the mayor of the largest town.”
Guckian, in contrast, called Morales “one of the most dangerous politicians in the country,” denouncing Morales for previous statements to defund the police, which he has since walked back.
Foulkes fired back, indignant at Guckian’s proclamation minutes after the candidates were asked about their ability to work with the Trump administration. Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, repeatedly emphasized his ability to foster relations and secure funding from federal officials, despite his campaign fundraising woes. Guckian had just $7,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5, less than 4% of either of his opponents.
Foulkes denounced Trump, who she blamed for jeopardizing Rhode Island’s renewable energy projects, while creating fear around reproductive rights and immigrant safety in jeopardy.
“I can’t believe you’re calling David Morales one of the most dangerous people,” she said to Guckian. “I would say Trump is one of the most dangerous people.”
Another heated exchange over ideology emerged between the party nominees on the question of whether “biological males who identify as females” should be allowed to play women’s sports. Guckian replied “no,” while Foulkes deferred to local teams to decide while emphasizing the importance of protections for the transgender community.
“You are a wildly left Democrat,” Guckian said of Foulkes. “I am absolutely shocked. I thought you were a down the middle Democrat.”
Foulkes jumped in, “Thank you so much for calling me a proud Democrat, that’s what I am.”



Quotation







You are a wildly left Democrat. 


– Aaron Guckian to Foulkes.


Block and Foulkes went toe-to-toe on energy, education and housing. Foulkes’ housing plan centers on using the newly enacted state millionaire’s tax to create a public revolving fund, with loans to developers to spur affordable housing development. The estimated $1 billion in revenue over the next eight years will create 20,000 new units, she said.
Block, 60, of Barrington, proclaimed the math behind Foulkes’ plan “fantastical,” countering that subsidies cannot be replenished to a revolving fund, and that her proposal would in fact create no more than 375 units.
Block instead suggested working with municipalities to tailor housing creation to their individual circumstances, and using state bonds to acquire vacant or underused land for redevelopment.
Foulkes responded that her plan was the “most ambitious,” noting the absence of details in Block’s alternative proposal.
“You have no plan, Ken,” she said. “You can criticize mine all day long.”



Quotation







You have no plan, Ken. You can criticize mine all day long. 


– Helena Buonanno Foulkes to Block


Plans — or no plans — again emerged as a critique during discussion of education proposals. All three candidates agreed on the importance of improving lackluster test scores among public school students while addressing longstanding teacher and resource shortages. But details differed.
Foulkes pitched a $100 million bond to expand career and technical education opportunities, while Guckian, who taught music in North Kingstown public schools for two years, proposed a reading and math-focused curriculum modeled after a turnaround plan in Mississippi.
Block again noted the differences among the state’s 36 local education districts, calling for individual solutions for each.
“They both missed the point,” Block said of his opponents. “There isn’t one magic bullet to fix our educational problems. We haven’t broken the cycle of poverty.”
He continued. “I will drive everybody to come to the table with solutions.”
Guckian characterized Block’s response as “word salad,” while Foulkes noted a lack of concrete details.



Quotation







They both missed the point. 


– Ken Block 


None of the three have held elected office before, with each casting themselves as the change-agent needed to bring transparency and efficiency to government.
None wanted to restart the truck toll program.
There was unanimous agreement to vote no on the Providence ballot question limiting city investments in foreign countries with human rights abuses — though only Foulkes lives in Providence and could actually vote on the referendum.
Guckian and Block both supported a temporary suspension of the state gas tax — mirroring proposals under consideration by states including Massachusetts as well as federal lawmakers — while Foulkes said she was “open to it.”
On reproductive health, both Block and Foulkes identified as pro-choice, though Foulkes insisted she was the only candidate to champion reproductive health. Block said existing state laws enshrine abortion rights, leaving little room for the federal government to threaten such protections. Guckian, who is pro-life, sidestepped questions about his commitment to abortion rights by answering that social issues have already been settled.
The debate ended with another tense back-and-forth, led by Valicenti.
In asking candidates for their proposals to address homelessness, Valicenti said the state has “shoveled tens of millions of dollars” to Crossroads Rhode Island, alleging the nonprofit service agency spent $700,000 on colored outdoor lighting.
Foulkes, who serves on the board of directors for Crossroads, said the lighting improvements outside the agency’s Broad Street shelter were a safety feature.
Block responded that the normally blue lights were pink when he drove by recently.
“That’s very condescending of both of you,” Foulkes said, rebuking Block and Valicenti. 
Mike Raia, a spokesperson from Crossroads, said in an interview Thursday that the project was funded through grants and philanthropy, not public money, and that the lighting was a small part of a broader exterior renovation and repairs of the 100-year-old Providence building. 
The three candidates will meet on Oct. 13 for pre-recorded radio debate on WPRO — airing at noon the same day — and again for a live, televised debate hosted by WPRI-TV 12 on Oct. 20.
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Most candidates for Alaska governor pledge to live in Juneau if elected
description: Three of the four Alaska candidates for governor told a Juneau crowd they would live and maintain the seat of government in the state’s Southeast Alaska capital city at a forum in Juneau on Wednesday.  The candidates’ commitment signals the potential for a significant shift. Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who has served for eight years and […]
text:
The Alaska governor's mansion in Juneau is seen on Aug 14, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Three of the four Alaska candidates for governor told a Juneau crowd they would live and maintain the seat of government in the state’s Southeast Alaska capital city at a forum in Juneau on Wednesday. 
The candidates’ commitment signals the potential for a significant shift. Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who has served for eight years and cannot run again because of term limits, has maintained his primary residence in Wasilla and conducted state business primarily from Southcentral, with periodic trips to Juneau.
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republicans Bernadette Wilson and Dave Bronson expressed their commitment to Juneau while answering questions from the Juneau Chamber of Commerce about their views on the economy, business and state government relationships with private industry. 
Republican Treg Taylor did not attend the forum due to scheduling conflicts, according to organizers. Taylor’s campaign did not respond to questions Wednesday about whether he would live and maintain his administration from Juneau, if elected. 
The location of Alaska’s capital has long been debated and there have been  many attempts over the years to relocate the capital to the state’s population center of Anchorage. Juneau is landlocked and only accessible by plane or boat. Some say the state’s government would be more accessible to the rest of Alaska if it were located on the road system. Others say Juneau should remain the capital because it has been so since statehood, with state offices, workers and administrative functions established in Southeast. Many also say the cost of relocating the capital to Anchorage is impractical.     

Democratic gubernatorial candidate  Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce in Juneau on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Moderators asked candidates what executive leadership, state agencies and investments would be maintained or expanded in Juneau, and whether their cabinet and commissioners would be expected to be based in the capital. 
Kreiss-Tomkins alluded to Dunleavy’s lack of presence in Juneau, saying he would govern from Southeast. “I want to restore Juneau’s position as the seat of government, and have as many commissioners as possible living here,” he said. 
“(In) Governor (Frank) Murkowski’s administration, and Governor (Tony) Knowles’s administration, that was a reality in Juneau, and people felt it. There was a degree of camaraderie and a degree of connectivity that I think have been lost in the years and administration since, and I want to restore that,” he said. 
Bronson said he would require his commissioners to live in Juneau if their department is based in the capital. But he noted that he would be flexible for commissioners who may live elsewhere if they are well qualified: “If the talent says, ‘I live in Anchorage, I live in Fairbanks’ — our commissioner right now of DOT, Ryan Anderson, who was my former boss, he lives in Fairbanks. Are you going to lose talent to compel them to live here and change, uproot their lives that much? I don’t think so.”     

Republican gubernatorial candidates Bernadette Wilson speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce in Juneau on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Wilson joked that the left-leaning capital city would get a new registered Republican voter if her campaign prevails, and she noted the “gravitas” of hosting at the governor’s mansion. “There is a lot of influence within the four walls of that building that I think have very much been underutilized across the state of Alaska, and quite frankly, for the benefit of all of Alaska,” she said.     

Republican gubernatorial candidate Dave Bronson speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce in Juneau on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Wilson and Kreiss-Tomkins said they would plan to live in the governor’s mansion and host public events, guests and state business there. Bronson said he would commit to living there during the regular legislative session. 
“I will live here, but I won’t be here all year,” Bronson said. “Because a lot of government is spread out throughout the state. And I’ve learned as a young lieutenant in the military — it’s called leadership by walking around — and walking around for government means getting in the car and driving around and visiting people throughout the state.”
Bronson’s views of Juneau have changed from his position several years ago. In 2019, Bronson co-sponsored a ballot initiative to move the regular legislative session to Anchorage, which state analysts estimated could cost up to $42 million. But the petition was not filed in time and failed to advance.  
Bronson agreed Wednesday that the capital should be maintained in Juneau. 
“So is Juneau the seat of government? Should it stay here? Yes, it is, and yes, it should.”

title: Journalism ‘exposes the corruption of the system,’ John Grisham says
description: Best-selling author John Grisham speaks at the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Best-selling author John Grisham said Wednesday that journalism plays a critical role in Mississippi and the nation.
Grisham, the keynote speaker at Mississippi Today’s 10th Anniversary Celebration, told an audience of more than 200 people that the work of journalists “is important, not only to tell the truth, but to expose the corruption of the system, to make known what has happened, to try to pressure the authorities and legislators to make changes in the law.
Former state Rep. Bobby Moak, left, Jackson Mayor John Horhn and author John Grisham speak during the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct.7, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“And as a sideline, to give people like me something to fictionalize about.”
Grisham, who grew up in Southaven and once practiced law there, has authored more than 50 consecutive No. 1 bestsellers. He has received the Library of Congress Creative Achievement Award for Fiction and twice won the Harper Lee Prize for Legal Fiction. All but two of his books have been novels.
He doesn’t think of himself as a journalist, but he did the work of a journalist in writing his first nonfiction book, “The Innocent Man: Murder and Injustice in a Small Town,” about a former baseball player wrongly convicted of rape and murder. That man, Ron Williamson, spent 11 years on death row in Oklahoma before DNA and other evidence helped exonerate him in 1999.
Grisham knew nothing about the case until he read Williamson’s obituary in The New York Times. He telephoned his publisher, told him about the obit and said he was writing a book about it. The next day, Grisham took off for Oklahoma to talk with his family.
 ”I had never thought about nonfiction,” he said. “I was having way too much fun with the novels. I knew it’d be a lot of work, but I didn’t care.”
That case, he said Wednesday, “took me into the world of wrongful convictions.”
A novel usually takes Grisham about six months to write. That nonfiction book took him 18 months. 
That grind made him swear he would never write another nonfiction book. With a novel, he said he’s never worried about accuracy. He just makes things up.
“The Innocent Man” led him to meet Jim McCloskey, founder of Centurion Ministries, the first organization in the world dedicated to freeing the wrongfully convicted. While working as a prison chaplain, McCloskey learned that one man, Jorge de los Santos, was wrongfully convicted. He started Centurion, helping to free him and 70 others.
Best-selling author John Grisham speaks at the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Grisham joined the board of directors of Centurion and the Innocence Project. Through that work, the author has heard many exonerees share their stories.
He now opposes the death penalty because he has concluded the way it’s applied is unfair and can result in the execution of innocent people.
In 2024, he released his second nonfiction book, “Framed: Astonishing True Stories of Wrongful Convictions,” which features stories of 23 people caught up in the criminal justice system. He co-wrote the book with McCloskey.
Under pressure to solve crimes, authorities often pick a suspect and ignore all the evidence that contradicts it, Grisham said. Since 1989, there have been more than 3,700 exonerations in the U.S.
After the release of “Framed,” Grisham swore he would never again write another nonfiction book. Now he’s working on another one. 
The subject matter of his new book? Another wrongful conviction case, this one in Texas.
“My last,” he said. “I swear.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A Connecticut report shows uptick in AI campaign ads nationally
description: More politicians are using Artificial Intelligence in campaign ads leading up to this year's midterm elections.
text:
More politicians are using Artificial Intelligence in campaign ads leading up to this year’s midterm elections.
The Wesleyan Media Project is a Connecticut-based nonpartisan research project that has tracked and analyzed political ads for 16 years. But researchers said since the start of the year, they have seen an uptick in the use of artificial intelligence.
Erika Franklin Fowler, Ph. D. is the co-director of the project and a government professor at Wesleyan University. Fowerler said the team was able to identify a range of AI use in ads from both parties in races across the country.
“We’ve identified almost 170 AI generated political ads this year and that’s just through early September. That has had at least $80 million dollars of spending behind it,” Fowler said.
Some ads include satirical depictions of candidates that are meant to poke fun, Fowler said. While other examples include hyperrealistic deepfakes that feature an AI generated depiction of candidates both as an attack ad or using AI to make them look more favorable.
According to the report, that exact number is164 political ads. But Fowler expects that number will accelerate in the weeks leading up to the election. The initial report in May identified just 33 ads, totaling about $20 million in spending. The real time tracking has allowed the team to compare findings.
“It’s a multipronged system but it’s also really important to say that this is absolutely an undercount of AI used in campaigns because in a lot of ways there’s little disclosure,” Fowler said.
Almost 70% of the ads and 78% of the spending did not have a disclaimer that disclosed the use of AI tools. Fowler said that’s because there are no federal laws that require disclosure. Some states have passed laws that require a disclaimer for political advertisements that contain AI generated content. While some laws ban the use of deepfakes directly.
In 2025, both Connecticut and New York introduced bills that sought to ban the creation of election related deepfakes within a certain window of time before an election. In New York the legislation became law. Despite the passage of several AI related bills in Connecticut, none were restrictions on election related deepfakes.
“There are a lot of barriers to putting regulations in place but I do think, what we’re seeing already at the state level do see already at the state level and in the national conversation, along with public opinion ,” Fowler said. “I would imagine that there would be at least some policy conversations about potential for AI regulation in advertising.”
This story was first published Oct. 8, 2026 by WSHU.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Chelsea considering eliminating parking minimums to promote housing production
description: Across the country, cities are abandoning their parking minimums and hoping to end up with fewer parking lots and walkable, transit-oriented neighborhoods. The local rules have been used to ensure new developments can accommodate residents with cars and do not overwhelm on-street public parking. But urbanists have argued that the requirements gobble up land[...]
text:
CHELSEA IS JOINING a growing list of Massachusetts cities to consider whether the road to more housing runs through fewer parking spaces.
The city announced last week that it will hold two community meetings this month to discuss making mandatory parking minimums for new developments a thing of the past and allowing developers to build the number of parking spaces they see fit.
The city of 40,000 currently enforces rules that require builders to create a certain number of off-street parking spaces whenever they construct new housing. For larger residential buildings with three or more units, developers must build at least 1.5 parking spaces per unit. For every unit in a building of this size with more than two bedrooms, the builder must add an extra 0.5 parking space for each additional bedroom.
For smaller projects, like a single-family home or a two-family duplex, builders in Chelsea are required to provide two parking spaces per home.
Across the country, cities are abandoning their parking minimums and hoping to end up with fewer parking lots, more housing, and walkable, transit-oriented neighborhoods.
The local rules have historically been used to ensure new developments can accommodate residents with cars and do not overwhelm local on-street public parking spaces. However, urbanists have argued that the requirements gobble up land that could be used for more housing and drive up construction costs. Developers who can’t build enough parking will often downsize their housing developments, meaning fewer units are constructed.
Chelsea, which is connected to Boston via multiple bus lines as well as the MBTA commuter rail, has a total land area of approximately 2.2 square miles. It’s the smallest city in Massachusetts by area and the third most densely populated after Somerville and Cambridge — which, in 2022 and 2024, became the first two cities in the state to do away with baseline parking requirements for new construction. Approximately one third of Chelsea residents do not own a car, and 24 percent of employed residents use public transportation to get to work.
If a zoning change is passed, Chelsea would join Salem, a fellow Gateway City that discarded its parking minimums for new multifamily housing in 2025 after a year and a half-long effort.
“Chelsea needs, and our residents want, more homes and fewer empty parking spaces at our new developments,” said City Manager Fidel Maltez. “By eliminating our parking minimums, we would free up space for more housing units, open space, and other community-desired uses, which are essential to making sure Chelsea is a vibrant and affordable place to live.”
Collectively, the state’s 26 Gateway Cities need to add 83,000 housing units over the next 10 years to catch up to demand, according to the MassINC Policy Center. (The policy center is part of the same organization that publishes CommonWealth Beacon.) Chelsea needs to build more than 1,600 homes in the next decade to address its current shortage, keep up with modest household growth, and replace the older housing stock that is lost each year after either being condemned or demolished.
A commission created by Gov. Maura Healey — officially dubbed the state’s Commission on Unlocking Housing Production — released a 106-page report in 2025 with more than 50 policy recommendations to increase the state’s housing supply. Getting rid of parking minimums made the list.
Parking structures often create sprawl and make neighborhoods less walkable. In a dense city like Chelsea, which has already been dubbed a heat island in part because it lacks open green space and shaded areas, asphalt from parking lots can also trap heat and create runoff. Parking minimums also add major costs to new housing construction — upwards of $50,000 per unit, according to the state’s Commission on Unlocking Housing Production. Those costs can translate directly to higher rents.
“Not only would this policy make housing easier and more affordable to build, it would also reduce the cost of housing in Chelsea, encourage sustainable transportation choices, help alleviate traffic congestion, and reduce pollution in our city,” said Ben Cares, director of the city’s housing and community development department.
By examining overnight residential parking data, the Metropolitan Area Planning Council (MAPC) has consistently found that parking is overbuilt and underutilized at multifamily housing sites throughout the Greater Boston area. Actual demand for parking averages just 0.78 space per housing unit in Chelsea, according to MAPC data, which is far less than what the city requires. The average utilization rate of parking spots in Chelsea is roughly 80 percent, meaning some 20 percent of off-street residential parking spaces in multifamily developments sit vacant overnight.
Throwing out the parking rules will require a formal permitting and land-use zoning amendment to be approved by both the planning board and city council. City Council president Roberto Jiménez-Rivera said forcing developers to build private parking spots doesn’t do anything to solve the city’s street parking or housing crisis. He added that when new housing projects are built next to public transit, the need for a car and a parking spot is reduced.
“We need our requirements to be flexible to the realities of each project,” Jiménez-Rivera  said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. health officials face multiple fronts as measles outbreak overlaps with respiratory virus season
description: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak crossed a historic threshold this week: at 1,078 cases in 41 counties, the state has recorded the nation’s largest measles outbreak in the last three decades. Five people have died with infections and nearly 200 people have been hospitalized.
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley, California, in a 2015 file photo. (Photo illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)This story was originally published by WESA. It is not available for republishing.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak crossed a historic threshold this week: at 1,078 cases in 41 counties, the state has recorded the nation’s largest measles outbreak in the last three decades. Five people have died with infections and nearly 200 people have been hospitalized.
As the outbreak overlaps with the start of the respiratory virus season, state health officials are facing several fronts. And despite a recent rift with the Trump administration, it appears that federal help is still on the table.
“It’s all hands on deck,” Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen said Monday. “We have a very robust response from our own Department of Health as well as many of our partners across the state.”
Local officials confirmed the first case among Allegheny County residents Monday, though people were exposed in August at Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh when infected patients from out of town visited the emergency room.
Health providers across Pennsylvania have administered nearly double the number of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in a typical month since the outbreak began. Pennsylvania medical providers typically administer around 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine per month. In August, that number jumped to 49,000 doses. In September, providers administered 53,000 doses of the vaccine.
UPMC Presbyterian Hospital in the Oakland neighborhood of Pittsburgh on October 13, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The MMR vaccine is extremely effective in preventing measles infections, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. One dose is about 93% effective against infections. The recommended second dose brings that immunity up to 97%, and it’s lifelong.
Bogen stressed the importance of the MMR vaccine at an event at the Hilltop Pharmacy in Pittsburgh’s Allentown neighborhood Monday.
“The MMR vaccine has proven to be effective for decades, and we didn’t have cases for decades because of the effectiveness of the vaccine,” Bogen said.
Still, measles infections continue to climb in Pennsylvania. More than half of the state’s 67 counties have tallied cases. Nearly 30 new infections were reported just over the weekend.
It’s not yet clear if the state’s effort to ramp up vaccinations have improved waning immunity in Pennsylvania classrooms. One in three kindergarteners in Allegheny Countyattend class at a school with immunization rates below the recommended threshold.
Bogen said the state is coordinating its measles response with federal health agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But the outbreak has placed Pennsylvania at odds with U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Under his leadership, the CDC website reflects just two of the five measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
In a letter to the CDC last month, Bogen requested support from the federal government, but on the condition that the CDC acknowledge the additional deaths.
“The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “If CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the Department will respectfully rescind our request,” for aid, she wrote.



Quotation







It’s all hands on deck. We have a very robust response from our own Department of Health as well as many of our partners across the state. 


– Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen


On Monday, Bogen doubled down on her comments, contending that “not recognizing the deaths minimizes… the loss of life that we’ve had to vaccine-preventable illness.”
“I just want people to understand how serious this infection can be,” she said.
Bogen said the state is determining the need for additional support from the federal government to manage the measles outbreak. She downplayed the impact of such help, noting that it would add one or two people to the department’s staff of 300 already responding to the outbreak.
“[We] would welcome any support that comes our way, but again, we do have a very robust response already with very good technical assistance,” she said.


Bogen joined Allegheny County Health Department officials to highlight the availability of the COVID-19 vaccine ahead of the respiratory virus season. Bogen and Department of Human Services Secretary Val Arkoosh each got updated COVID-19 boosters at the Hilltop Pharmacy.
Medical experts broadly recommend the COVID-19 vaccine for everyone aged 6 months and older in consultation with a healthcare provider. Vaccination is especially important for older adults, the immunocompromised and others at higher risk of severe illness, according to the American Medical Association.
Pennsylvanians with private insurance can get their COVID-19 and flu vaccines covered with zero out-of-pocket costs, Bogen said. Those without can still get a free shot at federally qualified health centers, state health centers or through the Allegheny County Health Department.
Bogen also stressed the importance of the flu vaccine, which she said she planned to get in the coming weeks. Most patients can get the flu and COVID-19 vaccine in the same visit.
Forecasting the severity of the upcoming respiratory virus season — when influenza, RSV and COVID-19 are more likely to circulate — is challenging. Health experts often can’t determine the dominant flu strain until the season develops.
Last year, more than 13,000 adults and 1,200 children were hospitalized with COVID-19 infections in Pennsylvania, according to the health department. Nearly 600 people died.
The flu, COVID-19 and measles can all exhibit similar symptoms such as fever, cough and a runny nose. Bogen encouraged people to take a test to determine what kind of infection they have before coming into contact with others, especially the immunocompromised.
“For 30 years I didn’t ask families who came to my clinic during [the] respiratory [virus] season, ‘Have you been exposed to measles?’ But nowadays I think that’s an additional question people should be asking,” Bogen said.
