title: Can Tom Tiffany survive ties to toxic Donald Trump?
description: It is still weeks until the Nov. 3 midterm, but the early returns are in for Donald Trump, who wants voters to pretend he is on the ballot.   Trump is at his lowest point ever in Wisconsin, with 60% of registered voters disapproving of him, 53% strongly, Marquette University polling says.  Yet Tom Tiffany, Trump’s […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, Republican candidate for Wisconsin governor, and President Donald Trump (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner and Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)It is still weeks until the Nov. 3 midterm, but the early returns are in for Donald Trump, who wants voters to pretend he is on the ballot.  
Trump is at his lowest point ever in Wisconsin, with 60% of registered voters disapproving of him, 53% strongly, Marquette University polling says. 
Yet Tom Tiffany, Trump’s endorsed candidate for governor and a 100% supporter of his policies — which almost all poll even worse than Trump himself — is virtually tied with Dem David Crowley.  A good chunk of the electorate has not yet made the Tiffany-Trump connection. That may be the deciding factor over the home stretch.
Trump’s Iran war and its impact on skyrocketing gasoline and diesel prices are widely unpopular, and Tiffany has repeatedly voted to support the war and to leave  Trump unchecked.  One new Crowley TV spot takes Tiffany’s voting record  head-on, calling Tiffany “loyal to Trump, not Wisconsin.”  Trump is toxic.  Crowley is not just  running against “three billionaires” who have bought Tiffany with over $45 million — the majority of the money raised by the Republican gubernatorial  campaign.  Diane Hendricks, along with Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, are Trump’s billionaires. 
When Trump lost the 2020 election, the Uihleins provided millions of dollars to political groups that helped organize and promote the events of Jan. 6, 2021. And prior to the violent insurrection that day, Trump accomplice Tiffany  signed on to a brief to overturn the outcome of the 2020 election, voted against certifying the election results in Arizona and Pennsylvania, and said he would have opposed the will of Wisconsin voters and invalidated our state’s electoral votes, too.
This week, in an interview with WLUK in the Fox Valley, Tiffany was asked if he’d be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump. Tiffany’s response: “They should check Tom Tiffany’s record.” 
Tiffany’s record in Washington is one of rubber stamping everything Trump has done to make things worse for Wisconsin. One hundred per cent of the time. Tiffany has supported Trump’s chaotic trade wars and reckless tariffs that have devastated farmers and raised the cost of groceries. He voted for healthcare cuts and rising insurance premiums for working families to pay for…you guessed it — tax breaks for Trump’s billionaires. 
Craig Gilbert, longtime Journal Sentinel political reporter who analyzes, interprets and explains polls, put it this way in his piece based on the latest MU poll: “Trump disapprovers” — those who disapprove of Trump — are a key voting bloc.
Tiffany now gets 11% of those voters.  Gilbert says he needs 15 to 20% to get to a majority on Nov. 3.  Crowley has a big lead among independent voters, but Tiffany is chipping away at that with his negative TV onslaught funded by the Trump billionaires. 
The MU poll shows 81% of independents disapprove of Trump, and even 62% of non-MAGA Republicans disapprove.  Those voters will be the target audience as Election Day approaches. 
As I was writing this, as if to underscore my point,  the Crowley campaign just launched a hard-hitting TV spot that makes the connection between Tiffany and Trump.  The subject line on a Crowley fund-raising email today is “100 percent of the time.” You can expect to hear a lot more about Tiffany and Trump between now and Nov. 3.
Voters don’t need to pretend Trump is on the ballot. For Wisconsin voters who will decide the outcome of the governor’s race, he is.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Woof! Animal welfare advocates want Georgians to know their state lawmaker’s record on pet issues
description: The dogs and cats in your life don’t get a vote on Nov. 3, so they’re counting on you to get it right. That’s the message from the Georgia Pet Coalition, a nonpartisan group of Georgia humans who advocate state and local governments on behalf of the state’s companion animals. “We do not endorse candidates, […]
text:
State Rep. Sharon Cooper models a shirt featuring her corgi, Maggie, named for former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. Cooper has sponsored pet-related legislation including a bill to protect pets in family violence proceedings. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThe dogs and cats in your life don’t get a vote on Nov. 3, so they’re counting on you to get it right.
That’s the message from the Georgia Pet Coalition, a nonpartisan group of Georgia humans who advocate state and local governments on behalf of the state’s companion animals.
“We do not endorse candidates, and we remain nonpartisan,” said Peggy McCarthey of the coalition’s board of directors. “But we do want to educate our voters about what the pertinent issues are.”
Dogs and animal advocates gathered at the GeorgiaCapitol in 2025. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
The coalition recently sent supporters legislative scorecards for the state House and Senate as well as a list of animal welfare-related questions to ask candidates at town halls and community events ahead of next month’s big midterm election.
McCarthey said speaking out on behalf of pets doesn’t have to mean lobbying lawmakers under the Gold Dome.
“It’s not even going to the Capitol,” McCarthey said. “It’s meeting with your local lawmakers, your city councils, your county commissions, making appointments, meeting them in person, and being polite and respectful and providing education and resources. And the same thing for state lawmakers.”
This year, McCarthey said six of the nine bills they supported passed with broad bipartisan support, and in 2025, that number was seven out of 10.
Pet coalition-supported bills that have passed in recent years have dealt with some weighty issues like adding protections for household pets in cases of family violence and establishing a database of animal cruelty offenders to prevent animals from being placed in dangerous situations.
McCarthey said it’s not hard to find animal lovers among Georgia lawmakers, and when she walks into committee rooms at the Capitol, it’s not uncommon for lawmakers to pull out their phones and proudly show off photos of their own pets.
But she said Georgia still has plenty of room for progress, especially when it comes to the number of homeless cats and dogs. Coalition data shows the number of dogs that died in Georgia public shelters grew to over 20,000 between 2021 and 2025, increasing by nearly 10,000 dogs during that timeframe.
“Even if you don’t care about animals and their well-being, lawmakers need to care about public health, and that does involve pet population management,” she said.
McCarthey said high numbers of stray animals in communities can mean diseases transmitted to humans, bite incidents, traffic accidents and higher cost for taxpayer-funded shelters.
“So by investing upstream in something like pet population management, which means access to affordable spay and neuter, now you prevent a large amount of these downstream consequences,” she said.
State Rep. Marvin Lim. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Norcross Democratic state Rep. Marvin Lim, who has sponsored animal welfare legislation and hosted pet vaccination, microchipping and spaying and neutering events in his district, said lawmakers largely agree about protecting animals, but a sticking point often comes during appropriations as lawmakers are looking to make the budget leaner.
The governor vetoed more than $300 million in new spending, including funding for domestic violence and sexual assault programs, this year to help pay for an income tax package that created a $1.3 billion deficit.
“When you have to balance the budget, as is constitutionally required here in Georgia, there wasn’t enough money for things like sexual assault centers, domestic violence centers,” he said. “So without even saying, ‘Oh, we would prioritize that over animal welfare or animal-related legislation,’ we are just seeing all sorts of things that are important being cut.”
Other issues, like proposed statewide bans on tethering dogs or cockfighting, have seen opposition on cultural grounds, he said. Georgia is the only state where cockfighting is not a felony.
“The closer you get to maybe farming practices or practices that have been generally accepted, particularly in non-urban areas, the more, I suppose, pointed or controversial it can be,” he said.
State Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republican state Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick of Marietta has sponsored animal welfare bills including one creating partial student loan repayments for veterinarians who work in shelters or sterilization clinics. She said there are several bills that have failed in the past that she hopes to see action on, including the cockfighting bill and one she sponsored to provide legal protections for people who damage property to rescue animals from hot cars.
“We’ve still got work to do,” she said. “We’ve still got puppy mills all over the place, and those create a huge burden on the rescue organizations and the counties who have to clean up the mess.”
“Everybody cares about animals, and they are a big part of many of our lives,” she said. “And people don’t like seeing animals being treated poorly, just the public doesn’t like it, and the legislators are people too, so they don’t like it either.”

title: Bayer will build a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in central Ohio
description: Bayer is building a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in New Albany, Ohio, the company has announced. This will create 1,500 construction jobs and 600 highly-skilled permanent jobs “focused on developing the compounds that make Bayer’s medicines work,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said.  “This is an historic win for Ohio,” DeWine said. “It is by […]
text:
Republican U.S. Senator Bernie Moreno (right), Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and leaders from Bayer speak to the media. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Bayer is building a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in New Albany, Ohio, the company has announced.
This will create 1,500 construction jobs and 600 highly-skilled permanent jobs “focused on developing the compounds that make Bayer’s medicines work,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said. 
“This is an historic win for Ohio,” DeWine said. “It is by far Ohio’s largest international healthcare project and the largest German direct investment in Ohio history.”

Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said this will “impact multiple generations.”
“The new site will be home to manufacturing expertise and a skilled workforce that will strengthen our ability to deliver innovative, high-quality medicines to patients both in the United States and abroad,” Anderson said. 
Anderson wouldn’t say what other cities were finalists for the plant. 
“We saw some really great sites, but the combination of the workforce, the proximity to important healthcare institutions, and research institutions, and frankly the attitude of everyone we worked with from JobsOhio, the state leaders, the federal leaders, it made a difference.” 
Anderson said he expects the new plant will mostly hire people from Ohio. 
“If we wanted people from someplace else, we would have gone there,” he said. 
The Ohio Life Science Training Center in New Albany, a $30 million building expected to open next year, will be used to prepare people for careers in pharmaceutical biomanufacturing and Bayer will build a production facility five miles away in New Albany. 
“In just a year, newly certified Ohioans will walk out of this training center, drive a few miles down the road, and go to work making the ingredients for medicines that will improve lives all over the world,” DeWine said. 
Bayer’s new plant will be close to Ohio’s seven major research universities. 
“We’re excited for Ohio State researchers to work alongside Bayer teams toward our shared goals, and we’re especially proud of the integral role that our university and Ohio higher education partners play in securing economic wins like this for our state, Ohio State University President Ravi Bellamkonda said in a statement.
The plant’s groundbreaking is expected next year and manufacturing is expected to start in 2031. A second module for drug product manufacturing is scheduled to follow in 2034.
Bayer, a German pharmaceutical company, has treated 4.5 million people in the United States with their prescription medicines in the last three years, Anderson said. 
“After a competitive global review, we’re happy to expand our production footprint here,” Anderson said. “We see a tremendous chance to build the biopharma ecosystem here and partner with your research institutions. What’s next in medicine will go through you, New Albany, Ohio.” 
Bayer’s U.S. pharmaceuticals headquarters is in Whippany, New Jersey and has other U.S. sites in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Berkeley, California; Cambridge, Massachusetts; Research Triangle Park, North Carolina; and San Diego, California. 
New Albany is home to other new biotech companies including drug manufacturer Amgen, telehealth company Hims & Hers and vitamin maker Pharmavite. 
“We’ve created an environment where businesses grow, where people can find meaningful careers, and where economic development strengthens the community and the region for generations to come,” said New Albany Mayor Sloan Spalding. 
The massive Intel chip plant near New Albany is years behind schedule. Factories were supposed to start production last year, but production has been pushed back to at least 2030.

title: Trump claims Ohio’s economy is ‘booming.’ The November election might show if Ohio voters agree.
description: In these surreal times that try men’s souls, Ohio has come to a moment of reckoning. Early in-person voting and absentee voting by mail has begun. The midterm elections are a month away. The Nov. 3 referendum, in the middle of a presidential term, is essentially a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on the status quo. You […]
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)In these surreal times that try men’s souls, Ohio has come to a moment of reckoning. Early in-person voting and absentee voting by mail has begun. The midterm elections are a month away. 
The Nov. 3 referendum, in the middle of a presidential term, is essentially a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on the status quo. You either like the way things are going or you don’t. 
The outcome of this off-year election will show as much about Ohio voters as it does the candidates on the ballot. What will it say about us in 2026?
In 2024, over 3-million Ohioans voted for Donald Trump giving him, as he boasted at a weekend rally in the state, “the highest vote total in the history of Ohio.” 
He returned to Vandalia, for first time since his 2024 campaign stop at the Dayton airport, to galvanize support for Ohio Republicans in tight races for the U.S. Senate and governor. 
His profanity-laced, hour-and-a-half speech at Butler High School was pointedly crude. So much for presidential decorum. 
His sales pitch (?) for electing appointed U.S. Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy “even if you hate” them was lousy. 
He promoted data centers with Husted and Ramaswamy under fire for them. Trump, who’s approval rating on the economy has dropped to an all-time low, told rallygoers Ohio’s economy is “booming” just days before a nearby truck factory laid off 1,400 workers. 
He derided Haitian immigrants down the road in Springfield, the same day the community buried one of its own, a 20-year-old college student who reportedly took his own life over the shame of wearing a conspicuous ICE ankle monitor. 
He singled out a female reporter again for personal attacks — as the approving crowd in the high school gym erupted in loud boos.
Rally attendees chanted “Deport!” when Trump made several false statements about Springfield’s Haitians, inferred that they ruined a “beautiful, idyllic” town, and promised that it will soon be better because “they’re all being brought back to their country.”  
(Most of the immigrants living and working in the metro Springfield area arrived legally through Temporary Protected Status, a humanitarian relief program for people fleeing countries unsafe from violence and disasters). 
The Trump administration abruptly ended TPS for Haiti — considered too dangerous for American travel due to extreme risks of violent “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care” — but apparently fine for terrified Ohio Haitians sentenced to a life-threatening fate. “Deport! Deport! Deport!”
While massive chants swept the Trump rally in a Dayton suburb, hundreds of Ohioans, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and his wife, grieved in Springfield and agonized over the inhumanity that had killed a promising young man. 
“This country needs people like Pierre Damas Bel,” said DeWine after Bel’s heartbreaking funeral. “We need people who are smart, hard-working, who seek their own version of the American dream. We need these people. We needed him.”  
But even after the 20-year-old died, as the news paralyzed his family and friends with fresh, unbearable pain, the anti-immigrant hostility expressed at the Trump rally appeared online. 
“One less plane ticket that we have to pay for” said one callous post on X. 
Yet as ICE activity has escalated dramatically across Ohio, following federal termination of TPS nationals from countries such as Haiti, Syria, and Yemen, recent polling in the state showed a majority of voters disapprove of brutal Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics (that brought down Bel) despite strong support for border security. 
Thumbs down to masked, armed thugs in unmarked vehicles indiscriminately targeting people with no criminal background (including American citizens) who have the wrong skin color but thumbs up to secure borders done right. 
A majority of Ohio voter also think their state is on the wrong track economically, regardless of Trump’s bluster. They give the state a fair/poor rating with Trump’s job approval at 35%. 
Affordability tops Ohioans concerns weeks away from the election as inflation outpaces income and costs climb on everything from childcare, utilities, housing, groceries, health care, and gasoline. 
A temporary gas tax pause, enacted in a day by state lawmakers as a pre-election gimmick, hardly puts anyone on easy street. 
Trump’s endless war of choice in Iran continues to drive up gas and diesel prices along with products you buy that now cost more to move and his reckless tariffs have hit families and businesses hard. 
He may draw cheers from his diehard fans about the “golden age” he has supposedly brought to Ohio, but many Ohioans aren’t feeling it. 
Polls also show most do not buy Trump’s upbeat spiel on Ohio’s rapid data center expansion — greenlit by state and local governments with zero transparency or community input.
Ohioans are sharing space with over 200 gigantic data centers that consume vast amounts of energy and millions of gallons of water daily while generating continuous noise pollution and air emissions from backup generators. 
They are subsidizing tech companies worth trillions with higher utility bills and insane tax breaks while AI giants strain grids and deplete local resources with no public guardrails or value benefit to the community in permanent jobs. 
But Trump dismissed data center concerns as he praised Husted, who once touted them, for a futile attempt to pass a “toothless” Senate bill with optional ratepayer protections that states would only be required to consider without any actual safeguards around paying for data center energy use. 
Ohioans have come to a reckoning. On all of the above. We know where the candidates land from rallies to funerals. But what will this election say about us?

description: The Milwaukee Police Department intends to renew its contract with Flock Safety, the multi-billion dollar producer of controversial AI-powered license plate reader cameras. In a statement, an MPD spokesperson said that the contract will be renewed “to maintain the investigative and public safety benefits the system provides.” Flock cameras store images of tr[...]
text:
A Milwaukee police squad in front of the Municipal Court downtown. (Photo | Isiah Holmes)The Milwaukee Police Department intends to renew its contract with Flock Safety, the multi-billion dollar producer of controversial AI-powered license plate reader cameras. In a statement, an MPD spokesperson said that the contract will be renewed “to maintain the investigative and public safety benefits the system provides.”
Flock cameras store images of traveling vehicles and their license plates in a database which can be searched by law enforcement. While police say that the cameras are valuable tools used to investigate serious crimes like gun violence, theft and kidnapping, Flock surveillance has been criticized as an invasion of privacy. Numerous cases of officers misusing the cameras for personal reasons to surveil people have emerged around the country, including in Wisconsin. 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Two of those cases played out in Milwaukee over the last year. Former Milwaukee police detective Tehrangi Chapman pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to felony misconduct in public office and misdemeanor misuse of a GPS device. Chapman is accused of  using Flock to track the movements of two people 20 times for personal reasons, and also of placing a GPS device on one of their vehicles. He’d kept tabs on these individuals even before Milwaukee adopted Flock in 2022. 
As an internal affairs detective, Chapman was involved in the investigation of Josue Ayala, a former Milwaukee officer who used Flock to track an ex-girlfriend and her new partner over 170 times. Ayala was given probation and avoided prison time. 
Both Chapman and Ayala were reported by the people victimized by their use of surveillance technology. Websites like haveibeenflocked.com helped them determine that they had been tracked. Two other cases of officers or sheriff’s deputies being charged for Flock misuse have also appeared in Kenosha County and the city of Menasha. 
As opposition to Flock grew in the community, Milwaukee PD has gone through a couple of phases of tightening and restricting the cameras. The department restricted access to the system to supervisors only, and limited the kinds of crimes that can trigger Flock use. Following a trend among some other agencies, MPD created a transparency portal describing how Flock is used, and restricted its network to use by outside agencies including  other local jurisdictions. One of the main appeals of Flock is the ability to conduct searches across a network composed of thousands of law enforcement agencies. 
MPD has also increased auditing of the system to flag suspicious uses. The Milwaukee County Board of Supervisors voted last week to remove Flock cameras from county property. In arguing to keep the cameras, the sheriff’s office attributed a 43% decline in certain crimes around county parks between 2023 and 2026 to the cameras. 
Their removal from county property follows a cascade of cities and towns across Wisconsin canceling their Flock contracts. Stevens Point, Fond du Lac County, Winnebago County, Sheboygan, Verona, Stoughton, Dane County, Sturgeon Bay, Appleton, Manitowoc, and  other  local governments have worked to cancel contracts and disable their cameras.

name: Washington State Standard
title: 4 takeaways from the Gluesenkamp-Perez debate
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and John Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate who is challenging her in a critical congressional duel, faced off on Wednesday in a televised debate, exchanging digs on the Iran war, policies of President Donald Trump, gas prices, and at each other. This match-up in the […]
text:
State Senate Republican Leader John Braun and Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez are dueling in southwest Washington's 3rd Congressional District. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and John Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate who is challenging her in a critical congressional duel, faced off on Wednesday in a televised debate, exchanging digs on the Iran war, policies of President Donald Trump, gas prices, and at each other.
This match-up in the 3rd Congressional District seat in southwest Washington is among a handful of competitive races nationwide that could decide which party is in charge in January.
Gluesenkamp Perez, 38, of Skamania County, is in her second term. She entered Congress after beating Republican Joe Kent in 2022, flipping the seat for Democrats in one of the year’s biggest electoral surprises. She beat Kent in a rematch in 2024.
Braun, 59, of Chehalis, is in his fourth term as a state senator. He has served as the Senate minority leader since 2020.
As of mid-August, Gluesenkamp Perez had reported raising three times as much as Braun, $6.3 million to $2.2 million. But that is only part of the story as political committees for the Democratic and Republican caucus in the House, and independent committees are spending big too.
Here are four takeaways from their hourlong debate conducted in a studio at KOIN6 in Portland.
They oppose the Iran war differently
Braun sought to thread the needle on wanting the conflict to end without directly blaming the president for keeping the U.S. engaged.
“I would not support an open-ended war with no clear objectives to end it,” he said. “We don’t have that right now.”
Gluesenkamp Perez pounced. “This war has been a disaster for our families at home, for our military families, for our geopolitical security,” she said. “We’ve got to get out of this war and I’ve voted six times to do that already.”
The two did agree the war is driving up fuel and energy prices and both said they would support freezing state and federal gas taxes to bring short-term relief to high fuel prices.
Trump got a lot of mentions
Gluesenkamp Perez made certain early and often that viewers knew Braun had the full-fledged backing of President Donald Trump and would back his policies.
“He’s got President Trump’s endorsement and the millions of dollars that comes with that in political spending,” Gluesenkamp Perez said. “I’ve proven I’m loyal to our community, not party bosses.”
Braun’s retort was to tag the incumbent as a “D.C. politician” who had passed only one bill in four years, to name a post office. “A good name, good post office, but not something that’s making a difference in your lives,” he said. 
Braun is clear on income tax, MGP is not
An initiative to repeal the state’s new high-earners income tax is one of the election’s hottest topics. Gluesenkamp Perez detoured around an answer when asked “Do you support the tax?”
“Okay, so there are basically two problems with politicians in Olympia. They spend money like a Connecticut horse girl, and working people are paying too much in taxes,” she said. “Adding another revenue stream isn’t fundamentally going to fix the problem.”
She said if it drifted down to middle and lower incomes, she wouldn’t support it. “I don’t work in state government,” she said, implying it’s not her issue.
Braun, who voted against the tax in the state Senate this year, seized on her non answer. “It’s wrong-headed. It’s clearly unconstitutional,” he said. “I didn’t hear the congresswoman take a position on that one way or another, but she should.”
Given a chance to respond, a somewhat flummoxed Gluesenkamp Perez said “I don’t work in Olympia. I don’t work for a caucus. I work to represent working people and families in southwest Washington.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It happened again with light rail and the I-5 bridge
Gluesenkamp Perez stepped around another local controversy, the proposal to build a new I-5 bridge over the Columbia River between Washington and Oregon. The estimated cost of the entire project has nearly doubled to $15 billion and the candidates were quizzed on whether to proceed.
Braun said a bridge is needed and should be built with the $6 billion in state and federal funds scraped together so far. Everything else, including light rail, should be set aside until there is money. “We need a bridge, but we need a bridge we can afford and one we can build on time and on budget,” he said.
Gluesenkamp Perez cited the $2.1 billion in federal funds she’s helped secure for the project. “That’s a big number, but this is fundamentally a state project, and you know we haven’t seen that commitment from people in Olympia to make sure that we’re getting the resources we need,” she said. 
When asked if she would be willing to take light rail out of the mix if it would help secure more federal funds, Gluesenkamp Perez said it is, “Zero percent the federal government’s role.” 
They’ll meet again next week
Gluesenkamp Perez and Braun will face off on Oct. 13 on KATU.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Laurene Powell Jobs and Darren Walker speak about community solutions and local journalism
description: Bill Bynum, Deep South Today board member and CEO of Hope, from left, Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, and Darren Walker, president and CEO of Anonymous Content, speak during the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Philanthropists Laurene Powell Jobs and Darren Walker said Wednesday night at Mississippi Today’s 10th Anniversary Celebration that they believe it’s important to invest in the people who are building sustainable community solutions, and that’s why they decided to put resources into journalism in Mississippi. 
“It’s really easy for me to be bullish on Mississippi and its future,” said Walker, the president and CEO of Anonymous Content. “And so, I hope that people here understand that this country is watching you. This country is watching this state in this moment because it is a harbinger for the future of America.” 
Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, speaks during the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The conversation between Walker and Jobs, who is the founder and president of Emerson Collective, was moderated by Bill Bynum, the founding CEO of HOPE Credit Union and a board member for Deep South Today, Mississippi Today’s parent company.
It was part of an evening that also included a performance by the Tougaloo College Choir, a speech by best-selling author John Grisham and remarks by Mississippi Today founders Donna Barksdale and Andrew Lack, Jackson Mayor John Horhn, Deep South Today Executive Editor and Chief Content Officer Adam Ganucheau,  Mississippi Today Editor-in-Chief Emily Wagster Pettus and Deep South Today board member Tray Hairston.
Emerson Collective, an investment and philanthropic company, is a financial supporter of Mississippi Today and Deep South Today and an investor in Anonymous Content, a global media company whose films include “The Revenant” and “Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.” 
Darren Walker, president and CEO of Anonymous Content, speaks during the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“It’s really the exquisite entrepreneurs that I ended up meeting who are building community, solutions, durable, smart public private partnerships,” Jobs said. “And what I found the first time that I came, when I toured around with (Bill Bynum) over a decade ago, was all the work that’s happening at the community level already well underway.”
Walker is a former president of the Ford Foundation, another funder of Mississippi Today. He and Jobs said they choose to invest in local institutions instead of coming in assuming they can bring the solution. 
“We come to learn and meet people who are actually problem solving at the community level,” said Jobs, whose late husband, Steve Jobs, was the co-founder of Apple. 
Bill Bynum, Deep South Today board member and CEO of Hope, from left, moderates during the Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
One of those solutions is local journalism. The Emerson Collective has helped fund almost 100 newsrooms that have formed in the last decade, including Mississippi Today.
“Over the last 15 years, we’ve seen about 3,500 local newsrooms shut down,” Jobs said. “And the business model just no longer works, mainly because of local advertising dollars. And so the nonprofit newsroom for local journalism is actually a truly elegant solution.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida county wants motocross course on land bought for conservation
description: One of the great things about hiking around Florida’s precious conservation lands is how quiet they can be. You can get away from all the noise and — I SAID, YOU CAN GET AWAY! FROM ALL THE NOISE! WHAT? YOU CAN’T HEAR ME? IT MUST BE BECAUSE OF ALL THESE DIRT BIKES ROARING AROUND! Well, […]
text:
Dirt bike riders line up for a race at the Pax Trax MX motocross track in Bunnell. Volusia County officials want to build their own motocross track on land that was bought for conservation. The new Volusia track would put Pax Trax out of business, the owner says. (Photo via Pax Trax Facebook page)One of the great things about hiking around Florida’s precious conservation lands is how quiet they can be. You can get away from all the noise and — I SAID, YOU CAN GET AWAY! FROM ALL THE NOISE!
WHAT? YOU CAN’T HEAR ME? IT MUST BE BECAUSE OF ALL THESE DIRT BIKES ROARING AROUND!
Well, that’s a problem, isn’t it?
Volusia County, where Florida’s practice of preserving land for environmental purposes has a rich history, has gotten itself tied into knots over the proper use of some recently purchased conservation property
The county spent $4.6 million in taxpayer-approved preservation funding to purchase 365 acres. Then, after the deal went through, county officials decided to preserve only 279 of those acres.
The other 77, they said, would be used for a county-sponsored motocross course.
They voted for motocross even though that land is smack in the middle of the Florida Wildlife Corridor. It’s supposed to be for bears, bobcats, and panthers, not dirt bikes.
“None of this makes any sense,” said DeLand resident Lourdes “LuLu” Gonzalez. She’s a court interpreter and outdoor enthusiast who has sued to stop the motocross course.
Don Dempsey via his campaign website
Lourdes Gonzalez via subject
The county official pushing hardest for motocross is a DeLand lawyer named Don Dempsey. He’s a Volusia County Council member whose son just happens to be — surprise! — a motocross racer.
Dempsey denied he’s pursuing this for personal reasons.
“I’m not doing this for me or my son,” he said, according to the Daytona Beach News Journal. “I’m doing this for the community,”
He insisted motocross can get kids off the couch and into the great outdoors, explaining, “I don’t want video game vegetables on my watch.”
Of course, hiking, camping, fishing, kayaking, canoeing, and horseback riding have the same effect, but with a lot less noise, gas consumption, and exhaust fumes.
Far less chance of scaring away wildlife, too.
 Bait and switch
Volusia County has long been known for what Tom Cruise once called “a need — a need for speed.”
In 1906, a steam-powered car called the Rocket Racer blazed across Ormond Beach’s hard-packed sand to set a world record of 127 mph, a speed you now occasionally witness on I-95.
In 1935, a British driver, Malcolm Campbell, set a new world record on Daytona Beach of 276 mph. When he got home, he was knighted, which perhaps inspired the TV show “Knight Rider.”
In 1947, racing promoter Bill France Sr. gathered some friends in Daytona Beach’s Streamline Hotel to form the National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing aka NASCAR, created to promote the practice of turning left a lot.
Volusia County also holds a different historic record. It’s where voter-approved land-buying programs began — not just in Florida, but nationwide.
Clay Henderson via subject
Forty years ago, an environmental activist named Clay Henderson helped spearhead the nation’s first voter-approved land-buying project. Volusia County’s 1986 Endangered Lands program used a $20 million bond issue to buy 34 properties.
Voters liked it so much, in 2000 they approved a new version called Volusia Forever. They approved it a third time in 2020, this time by a 75% margin. It was far more popular than any politician. So far, the program has saved 63,000 acres of forests, swamps, and beaches.
Henderson is well aware of the controversy over using Volusia Forever land to build a motocross course, calling it “a classic bait-and-switch.”
He worries that turning it into a racing venue will erode the public’s support for the preservation program. The track will hurt the county’s track record.
“Clearly, the optics are bad,” Henderson said, then pretended to be the county officials pushing the idea: “Hey, let’s put something there that makes a lot of noise and attracts a lot of people!”
He’s not kidding about the “a lot of people.”
In 2024, the council hired a consultant, Hunden Strategic Partners, to analyze what it would take to build a motocross facility. County officials said Hunden could skip the usual study of whether such a thing was needed. They’d already decided on that part.
The 40-page Hunden report said that to make the motocross work would require two tracks — one for practice, one for competition — plus 50 to 100 R/V slips, bathrooms, concession stands, electrical hookups, a pro shop, and parking for 250.
Although the plan doesn’t mention bleachers, I think they miiiiiight need some. The plan says, “The total attendance in Year 1 is projected at roughly 9,400 and is estimated to grow to nearly 35,600 by … Year 5.”
The cost: a mere $10 million.
Jeff Brower via his campaign website
To the critics pointing out that motocross isn’t synonymous with environmental preservation, Volusia County Council Chair Jeff Brower had a simple response: There’s no asphalt! It’s all made in the mud!
“There’s no paving going on,” Brower told WESH-TV in May. “It’s dirt.”
I don’t think “it’s dirt” is what all those conservation-minded voters had in mind.
 Risky business
I’m no Paul Krugman but, as I understand economics, the two key factors in making a business work are called “supply” and “demand.”
When it comes to supply, there’s no shortage of motocross courses in Florida. But the demand is questionable.
The MX Parks website lists 32 tracks in Florida. They include the Orlando MX Park, which has been around since 1969.
Although it’s an expensive sport — dirt bikes cost at least $6,000, plus protective gear, gas, and maintenance — nobody’s making a ton of moolah. In other words, what Volusia County wants to get into is (to shout-out a different Tom Cruise film) risky business.
At least one member of the county council has acknowledged this. Brower told his colleagues that “local track owners … expressed concern about the financial viability of the project.”
C.J. Harris via subject
The closest track to Volusia is one in Bunnell called Pax Trax. Its owner, C.H. Harris, showed up at a January meeting to warn the council not to do this.
Harris is so passionate about the sport that he named his son “Moto.” But if he saw sufficient demand for a new track in Volusia County, he said, “I would buy the land myself and build a track.”
A county-sponsored track would hurt the privately owned tracks like his before it sputters to a stop, he said.
“I know you want this, but it will shut me down,” Harris told them.
Dempsey refused to believe him.
“To say that this sport … is just a niche sport for just a small percentage of people is not true,” he insisted. “There’s a ton of kids that do this stuff. I did it as a kid.”
I talked to Harris this week. He hasn’t changed his mind. He told me Dempsey had invited him to bid on building the Volusia track. He decided against it.
“That land they purchased is absolute garbage to build a motocross track on,” he told me. To make it work, he said, you’d need to destroy even more of the wetlands that were supposed to be preserved.
Whoever Volusia hires, he said, “It’s probably going to bankrupt somebody.”

 Like a bad dream
The people opposing this motocross move include the leaders of Volusia County’s chapter of the Sierra Club.
The county’s original location for the track was too close to a neighborhood that didn’t want it, they told me. That’s how the county wound up putting it on conservation land not close to any homes. Instead, it’s adjacent to the county’s Longleaf Pine Preserve.
Say goodbye to the peace and quiet of the preserve. Dirt bikes can generate more than 100 decibels of noise. That’s actually worse than a data center.
The Sierra Club leaders see the council’s actions as a perversion of the popular conservation program.
Melissa Lammers via subject
Steve Wonderly via subject
“It’s like a bad dream you can’t really wake up from,” said Melissa Lammers of Ormond Beach.
This particular Volusia Forever purchase was handled differently from previous ones, she and another Sierra Club leader, Steve Wonderly, explained.
Normally, the land purchase doesn’t go through unless Volusia Forever gets matching funds from another agency, such as the state government. Then, any infrastructure needed — bike paths, picnic tables, etc. — is paid for by the county’s ECHO fund, which stands for Environmental, Cultural, Historic, and Outdoors.
But for this purchase, the county council “matched” the Volusia Forever funding by pulling money from its ECHO fund, they said. The county matched ITSELF, using money that’s never before been used for buying land.
The county didn’t disclose that some of the wetlands on the property had been illegally damaged by a previous owner, they said. Instead of restoring the wetlands, that became the site for the proposed motocross site.
But what particularly infuriated opponents was when Dempsey began waving around a paper that he said justified building the course on conservation property.
 A bigger debate
The contract to build the motocross track is now steaming toward approval like the Rocket Racer rolling over Ormond Beach.
In her lawsuit, Gonzalez accuses Dempsey of arranging for the contract to go to a business associate of one of his family members, a potential conflict of interest she alleges he never disclosed.
Her suit names the contractor as Tyla Rattray, a former South African motocross racer who trains other racers and who in 2022 got into a noise dispute with neighbors of his motocross track in Sumter County. My efforts to reach Rattray for comment were unsuccessful.
The need for speed in signing the contract seems to be driven by the fact that there’s an election coming up. The motocross has become an issue in Dempsey’s reelection campaign.
His opponent, a Ph.D. biologist named Wendy Anderson, says the idea of building a motocross course on conservation land is cuckoo.
“If Amendment 3 passes and we have to cut expenses,” Anderson told me, “the first thing to go on the chopping block in Volusia is that motocross course.”
Dempsey, meanwhile, has been trying to change the focus of the debate from the motocross course to something bigger: the whole land-buying program.
Despite the Volusa Forever program’s incredible popularity, he sees problems with it. He delved into those problems in a series of five, count ’em, FIVE YouTube videos that he posted to his campaign website.
He doesn’t like that the land is supposed to be set aside forever. He thinks there should be a time limit on keeping it undeveloped. Nobody knows what Volusia County is going to need in the year 3000, he said.
In his fifth YouTube video, he makes the argument that Lammler and Wonderly found so infuriating. He says the rules governing Volusia Forever not only allow but actually encourage building a motocross course.
As proof, he proffers a list from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Among the approved “resource-based recreation” uses are motorized off-road vehicles.
“So, all this talk that you’re hearing that we shouldn’t allow motorcycles and dirt bikes in conservation lands is not what we voted for,” Dempsey says. “I think it’s high time that we started giving people what they voted for.”
Henderson — also a lawyer — told me he thinks Dempsey’s argument is a stretch at best. He pointed out that the county comprehensive plan says Volusia Forever land “should receive the greatest degree of protection and suffer the least impacts from development.”
That doesn’t allow for repeatedly reenacting Steve McQueen’s motorcycle jump from “The Great Escape.”
Dempsey’s argument is similar to what we’ve been hearing a lot in Florida lately. Our state parks with breathtaking natural views need golf courses too! We should add pickleball courts to our pristine state-owned beach! Our quiet state forest should be bisected by a busy connector highway!
Nature is never enough for some people. Even though we see less and less of it, these people think a quiet natural area is a waste of space. They want some big, noisy manmade distraction.
I did a quick search of Volusia County Property Appraiser records and Dempsy owns a lot of land. I bet he’s got room to build his own commercial motocross course without using any taxpayer dollars. Then the conservation land the county bought could be used for what the voters intended.
I tried calling Dempsey several times to make this suggestion, but I could never reach him. Maybe he couldn’t hear the phone ringing over all the motorcycles. I SAID, MAYBE HE COULDN’T HEAR THE PHONE!

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll: Majority of voters oppose data center construction anywhere in Maryland
description: A majority of Maryland voters are opposed to building data centers in the state and they have a dim view of artificial intelligence, which they believe will have a negative impact on society, a new poll shows.
text:
A data center opponent in Arkansas. In Maryland, a new poll shows an overwhelming majority of voters oppose building data centers anywhere in the state. Most are skeptical of any possible benefits, and said they believe more harm than good will come from the facilities and technology. (File photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)A majority of Maryland voters are opposed to building data centers in the state and have a dim view of artificial intelligence, which they believe will have a negative impact on society, a new poll shows.
Half of those surveyed in the poll released Thursday by the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County were asked about support for data centers being built anywhere in Maryland and the other half were asked about a data center near their community. In both cases, nearly 8 in 10 were opposed.
“What I think is really striking is that people don’t like it across the board, whether it’s next to them or some other place in the state,” said Mileah Kromer, director of the poll. “It doesn’t matter where it’s at, they don’t want it here in the state.”
The survey is based on interviews with 776 Marylanders who said they were likely to vote. The survey, conducted from Sept. 22-27, has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5%.
Overwhelmingly, voters said data centers would negatively impact the costs of household utilities, quality of life, as well as water and air quality.
While supporters argue that data centers would have positive impacts on the economy, state tax revenue and jobs, voters in the UMBC poll were skeptical.
Nearly half said they believed the impact of data centers on the state economy and tax revenue would be mostly negative, while 37% said data centers would have a mostly negative impact on employment compared to 26% who said it would be mostly positive.
Just 23% of those surveyed said they believed AI would have a positive impact on society.
Moore job approval remains flat
Gov. Wes Moore (D) speaks to reporters after his debate with Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox on Tuesday. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
The poll also showed that Maryland Gov. Wes Moore may be on track to win a second term, even as voters expressed mixed opinions on his job performance.
Forty-nine percent of likely voters in the poll said they approve of the job done by Moore. Those same voters are also unhappy with the direction of the state and overall economic conditions, but so far are not pointing a finger at Annapolis.
“I think it’s really difficult to have a higher approval rating than that with these types of economic attitudes,” Kromer said of Moore. “That is, to me, what was probably holding down his numbers. People get upset with leadership when the economic conditions are not what you’d hope they’d be. I think that’s probably what’s what’s happening here with with Gov. Moore.”
Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, agreed.
“Everything is nationalized these days, and we do have a national economy,” he said. “When gas prices are high, they’re high everywhere. When energy prices are high, they’re high everywhere. The problem with 3% inflation is it’s hitting people everywhere, not just in the state of Maryland.”
The poll Thursday found 49% of Marylanders approved of Moore’s performance, while 42% said they disapproved and 8% said they did not know. Those numbers are essentially flat compared to a poll in April, when 48% of voters approved of Moore’s performance and 42% disapproved.
Eberly said Moore’s approval numbers likely remained unchanged because so much of what is driving the economic pain is the result of decisions affecting the entire country.
“There is a lot of general dissatisfaction,” Eberly said. “It’s being expressed in this poll as dissatisfied with Maryland, but I think it speaks to the fact that people in general are uncomfortable with the direction of things in the country right now.”
In Maryland, registered Democratic voters account for just over half of the state’s more than 4 million registered voters, while Republican and unaffiliated voters account for about a quarter each. And Moore’s approval numbers are bolstered by Democrats, 70% of whom said they approved of his work. Disapproval stood at 88% among Republicans and 49% among unaffiliated voters.
A UMBC poll released earlier in the week showed Moore, the first Black governor in the state’s history, who is seeking a second term, with a 27-point lead over Republican challenger Dan Cox roughly one month before the election.
Poll: Voters oppose redistricting ballot question when presented ‘meat of the political outcome’

“This is sort of where [former Gov.] Martin O’Malley’s approval rating was when he was seeking a second term in his rematch against Bob Ehrlich, and O’Malley won by like 13 points,” Eberly said.
Moore entered office in 2023 with a job approval hovering at 64%, which was 35 points higher than those who said they disapproved. Today, that gap is seven points.
‘Maryland does not exist in a separate universe’
A plurality of Marylanders said they are unhappy with the direction of the state: Roughly 49% said the state is on the wrong track compared to 37% who believe it is headed in the right direction.
In March, the UMBC poll found 59% said the state was on the wrong track and 30% said it was moving in the right direction.
Again, Republicans and unaffiliated voters are the most unhappy with 90% and 55% respectively saying the state is on the wrong track. Half of Democrats said the state is moving in the right direction.
Economic conditions are top of mind for those voters, with 81% saying the economy has been poor or fair. Just 17% described it as excellent or good.
“Marylanders are angry and upset, but so are voters across the nation,” Eberly said. “Maryland does not exist in a separate universe from the rest of the country, despite what some people think sometimes.”
Kromer’s poll offered a look into factors shaping the views on the economy, asking voters what they think of when assessing the economy:

94% complained about the prices of everyday goods and services;
90% said their personal finances;
86% said the increased cost of housing;
84% said state taxes and fees;
74% said interest rates;
67% said state unemployment rates and job reports;
and 41% said the stock market.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The federal SNAP cliff and CT’s human infrastructure
description: Across Connecticut, frontline food security organizations are witnessing an unprecedented surge in demand.
text:
When structural shifts happen in Washington, the shockwaves are rarely felt in boardroom suites first. They land squarely on the phone lines of local non-profits.
Following sweeping federal eligibility rollbacks to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), more than five million Americans have been abruptly cut from food assistance rolls nationwide. While the public debate focuses on the fiscal prudence of these rollbacks in committee rooms, the human fallout has arrived faster and heavier than state officials originally projected.

Nailah Ricco-Brown

What reads on paper as a minor fiscal adjustment translates directly to an immediate crisis in our communities. Across Connecticut, frontline food security organizations are witnessing an unprecedented surge in demand. Every day, helpline operators speak with panicked parents, low-income workers, and older adults whose grocery budgets have been slashed by hundreds of dollars. For these families, losing SNAP means forcing a brutal math onto basic survival: choosing between filling a life-saving prescription, buying enough gas to get to a shift, or skipping meals entirely so their children can eat.
For over a decade, End Hunger CT! has operated the state’s premier frontline defense against food insecurity. During the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, we ran the state’s only independent SNAP hotline operating approximately 70 hours per week.  Today, that same infrastructure faces a different kind of breaking point. Over the past year, federal rollbacks stripped nutrition benefits from nearly 63,000 Connecticut residents, and nearly 29% of them were children. By July 2026, the state’s total SNAP enrollment plunged below 300,000 for the first time in modern history, marking a 10-year historic low. This collapse forced an unprecedented crisis onto our privately funded call center, bringing more than 5,000 panic calls onto our helpline in less than ten months.
We are answering this crushing surge seven days a week with just one single, full-time employee on the line. We are meeting a massive public emergency despite compounding budget cuts and an overall reduction in operational support.
We are doing more with less, but “less” has officially become the least.
Yet, as the public demand for food security infrastructure breaks records, the underlying funding model that keeps this infrastructure alive is quietly fracturing. Institutional philanthropy is pulling back. Across the country, major foundations, corporate giving circles, and traditional grant-making institutions are reeling back operational support. Development pipelines that once stabilized statewide advocacy groups for decades are drying up, creating a dangerous paradox where non-profits are asked to handle an unprecedented public crisis precisely while the private resources needed to keep their doors open are being restricted.
We can no longer approach food justice through the lens of transactional charity. We treat non-profits as safety valves that can indefinitely absorb the collateral damage of federal policy shifts, but we must fundamentally change the way we view this infrastructure. When a bridge or a highway faces a structural threat, the nation does not expect a single department to fix it alone. We pull together public, private, and community resources to reinforce it. Our human safety net requires that exact same structural commitment.
To solve this crisis, Connecticut’s corporate responsibility sector, healthcare executives, utility providers, and the philanthropic sector must join us at the table. On October 29, 2026, End Hunger CT! is convening the OneCT! Equity & Action Symposium. We have intentionally made this statewide gathering completely free to ensure that frontline advocates, neighborhood organizers, and local agency staff can access critical data and strategy spaces without financial barriers.
But spaces like this, and the vital helplines backing them, require dedicated underwriting to remain sustainable. This is an invitation for Connecticut’s commercial leaders, private philanthropists, and human services foundations to view community stability not as a charitable line item, but as a critical infrastructure investment. 
The OneCT! Symposium will not only address food insecurity, but explore other intersectional topics like housing stability, mental health, K-12 education, and the criminal justice system, because we know that addressing one directly relieves pressure on the other. Funding this frontline safety net directly braces our entire ecosystem; it protects patients from diet-related emergency room visits, shields utility consumers from financial default, and keeps our local economic channels moving.
The federal funding environment has fundamentally changed, and the old philanthropic playbook is obsolete. If corporate titans, philanthropic leaders, and institutional funders continue to watch from the sidelines as non-profit infrastructure collapses under the weight of federal cuts, they will find that reacting to a broken safety net is far more costly than investing in its preservation.
Our phone lines are ringing, and the safety net is fraying.
The people with the power to fund this baseline survival infrastructure must decide who will help us answer the call.
Nailah Ricco-Brown is Development Director at End Hunger CT!

description: The two candidates running to represent Colorado’s most competitive congressional district met Wednesday for their only debate ahead of the November election, sparring over federal immigration policy, affordability and the economy, and healthcare.  U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican finishing his first term in Congress, and Manny Rutinel, a Comme[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, left, a Fort Lupton Republican finishing his first term in Congress, and Manny Rutinel, a Commerce City Democrat and former state legislator, debated Wednesday in Berthoud ahead of their race to represent Colorado's 8th Congressional District. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)The two candidates running to represent Colorado’s most competitive congressional district met Wednesday for their only debate ahead of the November election, sparring over federal immigration policy, affordability and the economy, and healthcare. 

U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican finishing his first term in Congress, and Manny Rutinel, a Commerce City Democrat and former state legislator, faced off at a debate in Berthoud organized by the Berthoud Weekly Surveyor and the American Cancer Society’s Cancer Action Network. 
Evans called Rutinel “the most radical person to ever be nominated to run for Congress in the state of Colorado” while Rutinel said Evans “only responds to one man, and that is Donald Trump.”
Both candidates throughout their campaigns have talked about affordability as a key priority for constituents of the 8th District, but they disagree on the best way to address it: Evans says his votes in Congress have improved affordability, while Rutinel says cost of living has skyrocketed because of those votes.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Evans defended his votes in favor of legislation backed by Trump that will result in cuts for public assistance programs many 8th District constituents rely on. He said those bills cut “fraud, waste and abuse” and further fund healthcare. He voted in favor of a Republican plan to reduce Medicaid spending by an estimated $625 billion over the next 10 years. The plan became law with Trump’s signature on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or H.R. 1., the Republican tax cut and spending bill.
Evans voted in support of H.R. 1., which made changes to eligibility requirements in programs like Medicaid and the Supplement Nutrition Assistance Program. Dollars diverted from Medicaid will go toward tax cuts prioritized by Trump, along with new spending on immigration control and defense projects. Evans touted his support of measures in Congress that cut taxes on tips, overtime and small businesses.
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans speaks at a debate against Manny Rutinel, a Commerce City Democrat and former state legislator, on Wednesday. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)
Rutinel said he wants to restore Affordable Care Act tax credits and expand Medicaid so health insurance will be more affordable. He also blamed the war in Iran and Trump’s tariffs for increasing the cost of living. Evans, who voted against a war powers resolution to direct Trump to remove U.S. troops from Iran, did not mention the conflict in Iran. He flagged past comments Rutinel has made against the oil and gas industry as well as anti-factory farming stances. 
Immigration
The two Latino candidates will face off in November to determine which party will represent the district that has the largest Latino population in Colorado. Both candidates said they want secure borders and immigration reform. 
Evans said violent crime in the country is low because the border is secure and because “we are going after the bad guys” under Trump, blaming the Biden administration for high crime rates. He claimed Rutinel supports open borders and defunding the police, but Rutinel said law enforcement should have the resources it needs to “prevent trafficking of drugs and people through our border.”
The economy would be “in a much better spot” if Trump and Evans focused on the economy instead of targeting immigrants, Rutinel said.  
“Right now, Donald Trump and Gabe Evans are trying to find new ways to torment our immigrant neighbors,” Rutinel said. “They’re using masked ICE agents without judicial warrants.  They are raiding schools and hospitals to rip families apart.”
Manny Rutinel speaks at a debate against U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans on Wednesday in Berthoud. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)
The Trump administration has increased immigration raids across U.S. cities since he returned to office, and research has found that a minority of those arrested by ICE have had criminal records.  
Since initiating a run for Congress, Rutinel has backtracked on past positions that leaned progressive. Evans called him “a flip flopper” and said Rutinel voted in the Colorado Legislature to increase taxes, legalize hard drugs and cut jobs. Rutinel voted in favor of a measure that would have allowed cities to open overdose prevention centers.
“We don’t have to ask how he would legislate in Washington, D.C., we can see it now,” Evans said. “We’re living it now in Colorado as an extreme outlier when compared to the rest of the country.”
Rutinel previously worked for public interest environmental law group Earthjustice, which Evans claimed argued a case before the U.S. Supreme Court to allow Colorado local governments to sue fossil fuel companies over climate change. Earthjustice filed a brief in support of the two local governments that want to sue, but it was not directly involved in arguments before the court this week. 
Evans said his loyalty is to his district, not Trump. He emphasized his support for overriding Trump’s veto of a bill that would have supported a water pipeline project in Southern Colorado and his vote to block a Trump executive order related to federal worker bargaining rights.
The 8th District, which includes the northern Denver suburbs and extends into parts of southern Weld and Larimer counties, is one of a handful of toss-ups in the country. The race could help decide which party has control of the House. It is also the state’s newest congressional district, drawn by an independent redistricting commission after the 2020 census.  
Evans was elected to represent the 8th District in 2024 when he defeated then-U.S. Rep. Yadira Caraveo by fewer than 2,500 votes — less than 1 percentage point. Evans has aligned himself closely with House Speaker Mike Johnson and Trump and has ranked as one of the country’s most vulnerable Republican House incumbents.
The race to represent the 8th District has drawn large amounts of campaign funding in support of both Evans and Rutinel. CPR reported Wednesday that the race has seen about $11 million in outside spending since Rutinel won the Democrat primary election at the end of June.
Election Day is Nov. 3. County clerks in Colorado began to mail ballots to registered voters this week.
