description: A judge has upheld a North Dakota environmental agency’s permit issued for what is planned to be the state’s largest dairy farm. The Dakota Resource Council challenged the Department of Environmental Quality’s permit for the Herberg Dairy in Traill County. The animal feeding operation permit covered areas such as manure management and water water discharge [[...]
text:
People walk into the Traill County Courthouse in Hillsboro, North Dakota, on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A judge has upheld a North Dakota environmental agency’s permit issued for what is planned to be the state’s largest dairy farm.
The Dakota Resource Council challenged the Department of Environmental Quality’s permit for the Herberg Dairy in Traill County. The animal feeding operation permit covered areas such as manure management and water water discharge for the planned 25,000-cow Herberg Dairy southeast of Hillsboro, near the Red River.
Landowner group sues over Wahpeton water sale for large dairy

It is one of two large dairies being built in North Dakota’s Red River Valley by Riverview, based in Morris, Minnesota. 
East Central District Court Judge Susan Bailey issued the ruling affirming the permit Oct. 1. Bailey heard arguments on the permit challenge in July in Hillsboro. 
Dani Replogle is the attorney for the environmental group Food and Water Watch that represented the Dakota Resource Council.
“My main takeaway from the opinion is that this is just another instance of courts deferring to agencies despite evidence showing that they (the agencies) are not doing their job,” Replogle said Wednesday. “North Dakotans deserve better.”
The lawsuit named Riverview as well as the Department of Environmental Quality.
“We appreciate the court’s review and decision,” the agency said in a statement. “We remain committed to a thorough, transparent permitting process grounded in sound science and consistent application of the law to protect human health and the environment.” 
Riverview officials did not return voicemail or email messages sent Wednesday. 
Jim Murphy, economic development director for Traill County, said Riverview has started construction in earnest on the Herberg Dairy, after initial work on housing for dairy workers. 
The Dakota Resource Council and a group of Wahpeton-area landowners also have filed suit against the North Dakota Department of Water Resources. They are challenging a water sale for Riverview’s other Red River Valley milking operation, the Abercrombie Dairy in Richland County. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Coordinated lawsuits against in-state tuition for immigrants a ‘threat to rule of law,’ groups say
description: TOPEKA — A nationwide campaign to dismantle access to in-state college tuition for children of immigrants is “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets,” said an attorney for a Latino civil rights organization. A coalition of advocacy groups released a report Wednesday detailing the coordinated nature of the […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on Oct. 2, 2026, as he campaigns in GOP-leaning states ahead of the midterms. (Photo by Dan Anderson/Alabama Reflector)TOPEKA — A nationwide campaign to dismantle access to in-state college tuition for children of immigrants is “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets,” said an attorney for a Latino civil rights organization.
A coalition of advocacy groups released a report Wednesday detailing the coordinated nature of the Trump administration’s efforts to eliminate in-state tuition for students who are brought into the U.S. as children and attend public universities and colleges.
Kansas is one of 24 states and Washington, D.C., in active litigation with the United States government over its tuition policies. In September, a federal judge appointed by President Donald Trump struck down Kansas’ law, leaving immigrant students without the access to the in-state higher education they qualified for since 2004.
“The students in these lawsuits are not outsiders,” said Gabby Pacheco, president and CEO of The Dream.US, one of the report’s authors. “They’re students who grew up right here in our backyards, in our country, in our communities, and they are embedded in our states.”
The median age of arrival for students in the U.S. is 4 years old, Pacheco said during a virtual press conference Wednesday. There are 8,800 students, about 4,500 of whom have graduated college, represented in the 26 total lawsuits across 24 states and D.C. Immigrant students and graduates are asking to be treated the same as the classmates they’ve grown up with, Pacheco said. 
Their families have been contributing to states across the country not just with their labor but their taxes, she said. She called the lawsuits “self defeating.”
“Not only are they threatening and harming the dreamers and their opportunities for their future, but the future for the broader states and the communities that they live in,” Pacheco said.
Kansas is uniquely positioned among the coordinated series of lawsuits, said Thomas Saenz, president and general counsel for the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, or MALDEF, during a virtual press conference. The federal case against Kansas has been appealed to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals, where a panel of judges will review whether the decision to overturn the law will stand and whether a group, Kansas Students for Affordable Tuition, can intervene in the case.
The appeal, however, is preceded by one in a case against Oklahoma. That case is “well ahead” of Kansas’, and Kansas’ case doesn’t yet have a briefing scheduled, while Oklahoma’s has been fully briefed, Saenz said. It’s unlikely Kansas’ will make it to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Judges across the country are split on whether these state tuition laws are in conflict with federal law, as the Trump administration argues. In Minnesota, a decision went in favor of students. In Illinois, a judge ruled in favor of the U.S.
Saenz said the Trump administration has used “very sharp tactics” to prevent outside parties from becoming involved in the cases. Saenz said the cases are just as much a part of the Trump administration’s immigration policies as immigration enforcement raids and “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets.” 
In Kansas, that has included Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, who tried to intervene in the case and defend the state law. 
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, sided with federal prosecutors, culminating his years-long push to rid the state of its tuition equity law.
Kobach said in a non-binding legal opinion published in February that the law ran afoul of federal statutes, classifying in-state tuition for immigrant children as “tuition at greatly reduced rates” and “therefore a public benefit forbidden to illegal aliens.”
The Republican-controlled state Legislature attempted to overturn the law earlier this year, but Kelly vetoed the legislation, allowing immigrant students to receive in-state tuition until the court blocked the law in September.
Saenz pointed out Kelly is term-limited and could be replaced by a Republican governor in January, eliminating a barrier to passing legislation.
But, at this point, Saenz said, “there’s no reason currently for the state Legislature to do anything.”
The cases are “fundamentally about the nation’s talent pipeline,” said Miriam Feldblum, president, CEO of President’s Alliance, an organization involved in releasing Wednesday’s report.
It is “about the immigrant domestic talent pipeline that goes through our nation’s colleges and universities, and that spurs innovation, that fuels our workforce, that enables states and communities to prosper,” Feldblum said. “This is about both individual lives, and this is about the communities that they support, and the institutions and states that they enable to prosper.”
If there isn’t an attempt to defend in-state tuition for immigrant students, Feldblum predicted the ripple effects will be visible for decades.

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Advocates blast Trump campaign against in-state tuition for immigrants
text: WASHINGTON — Leading immigration advocates and experts sounded the alarm Wednesday on the Trump administration’s sweeping efforts to undo state laws allowing some immigrants to pay in-state college tuition in the states where they reside. The U.S. Department of Justice has sued 24 states, Washington, D.C., and the University of Delaware since President Donald Trump retook office over laws or policies that allow noncitizen students who meet certain requirements access to in-state tuition, regardless of their immigration status.  The lawsuits are part of a larger push from the administration to curb any benefits that could extend to immigrants more broadly.Leaders of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and TheDream.US defended the state laws during a virtual press conference, while warning of the setbacks noncitizen students face to accessing affordable higher education when these policies are struck down. The groups also released a joint report Wednesday charting the landscape of such laws and the DOJ’s legal challenges against the policies. The administration’s challenges “limit opportunities for thousands of students and undermine the social and economic well-being of communities across the country,” said Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a nonprofit and nonpartisan organization. “When access to in-state tuition is taken away, many undocumented students cannot bridge the gap between in-state and out-of-state rates,” Feldblum added. Gaby Pacheco, president and CEO of TheDream.US, called the Trump administration’s efforts “coordinated assaults on tuition equity.”They are “just one part of a larger pattern of legal and policy barriers and restrictions being put in place that threatens Dreamers and immigrants’ educational opportunities, their stability, their safety and their futures,” she said. TheDream.US grants scholarships to immigrant youth, including individuals under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA, who are also known as Dreamers. DACA is intended to help people brought into the country without legal documentation as children. The program, created in 2012, protects participants from deportation and allows them to receive work permits and obtain driver’s licenses.Six state laws blockedIn six of the lawsuits the DOJ filed — targeting Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas — courts have already struck down the laws. But in a blow to the administration’s efforts against Virginia’s in-state tuition policies, a federal judge earlier this week scrapped the DOJ’s challenge, upholding the Virginia law.Lawsuits are also pending in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Utah, Vermont and Washington state.Debate over 1996 lawThe DOJ’s challenges center on the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which bars a state from offering in-state tuition benefits to people not lawfully present in the country if that same benefit is not granted to U.S. citizens from another state. Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the DOJ’s Civil Division has noted that “colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens” and that the agency “will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”Thomas A. Saenz, president and general counsel of MALDEF, which has sought to intervene on behalf of affected students in cases targeting the laws, described “extraordinary” aspects of the DOJ’s “litigation campaign,” including that “the administration uses very sharp tactics to attempt to prevent anyone from coming in to defend the state tuition-equity laws.” Saenz also pointed out that all of the state tuition-equity policies across the country were enacted after the 1996 law was enacted. “What that means is that they are using a provision that was on the books when all of these legislators acted to create laws like the Texas Dream Act,” Saenz said, pointing to the Lone Star State’s 2001 law — the first of its kind in the country — that has since been blocked.He added that “no administration prior to this one has ever gone to court contending that that 1996 law somehow renders these tuition-equity laws passed beginning in 2001 unconstitutional or preempted.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Health Connector expects another ‘unique’ sign-up period amid federal cuts
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: Nearly 350,000 Bay Staters are currently enrolled in individual Connector coverage. People will need to navigate double-digit premium hikes and some discontinued plans, particularly among Tufts Direct and Fallon Health enrollees.
text:
THE OPEN ENROLLMENT PERIOD at the state’s health insurance marketplace is about two weeks away, and officials are anticipating another wave of coverage losses tied to federal eligibility changes.
Last year’s open enrollment window was particularly bumpy, as state leaders unsuccessfully pleaded with Congress to extend federal subsidies under the Affordable Care Act. Gov. Maura Healey ultimately pumped an additional $250 million into heavily subsidized plans to prevent premium spikes.
This cycle will be “another unique open enrollment period,” predicted Massachusetts Health Connector Executive Director Audrey Morse Gasteier, as the state absorbs the ongoing effects of the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
People can sign up for coverage through the Connector, including heavily subsidized ConnectorCare plans for eligible Bay Staters, starting October 23, with open enrollment stretching through January 23, 2027. Residents must select a plan by December 23 to ensure their coverage starts Jan. 1, while coverage selected after that deadline will take effect February 1, said Erin Ryan, the Connector’s deputy chief for external affairs.
Nearly 350,000 Bay Staters are currently enrolled in individual Connector coverage. People will need to navigate double-digit premium hikes and some discontinued plans, particularly among Tufts Direct and Fallon Health enrollees.
“We are working with all of our members in our communications and our outreach to make sure people understand their options, be they the availability of ConnectorCare and other supports to help people absorb cost challenges and make sure that they’re in the right plan for them that fits their budget,” Morse Gasteier said during a media briefing Wednesday afternoon.
“There’s a lot of cost challenges and pressures that families across the commonwealth and the country are facing right now, so we understand how tough some of the decisions facing people around health coverage and plan choices can be, particularly when it comes to cost,” she added.
Under the state’s individual mandate, residents must have health insurance that meets certain standards or face a tax penalty.
Insurance regulators approved an average premium jump of 10.4 percent in the merged market where many individuals and small businesses get coverage, and residents enrolling in the Connector’s unsubsidized non-group plans will see an average premium increase of 12.4 percent.
About 30,000 to 35,000 lawfully present noncitizens are expected to lose their eligibility for federal subsidies on January 1, though they’ll be allowed to purchase Connector plans at full cost. Morse Gasteier said the Connector is “most worried” about those individuals, as she stressed other categories of immigrants like green card holders will remain eligible for federal subsidies.
Nearly 23,000 people terminated their Connector coverage for 2026, with about half of those enrollees affected by the expired federal tax credits. Meanwhile, more than 46,560 people newly enrolled in coverage for 2026. Morse Gasteier said she expects a similar dynamic this open enrollment cycle, with new enrollees offsetting coverage losses.
“There will be another tranche of individuals losing their subsidy eligibility because of federal policy, and we are going to be doing everything we can, working with those populations to help support them and deciding if they could afford to or want to remain in coverage,” Morse Gasteier said.  She added, “But if many of them do end up leaving coverage, we are also going to be very hard at work trying to sign up other individuals and hopefully balance out any enrollment losses, so that we are keeping pace with our goals and keeping as many people in Massachusetts as possible covered.”
The Connector’s call center and more than 50 in-person “navigator” locations around the state are available for residents who need help selecting insurance plans, Ryan said. There are also 24 navigator organizations that provide personalized assistance in nearly 30 languages.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: You shouldn’t need a law degree to hunt moose in Alaska
description: The last thing a hunter needs to pack before a moose hunt is a crash course in federal regulations and bureaucracy. We shouldn’t need to spend the days before a hunt refreshing federal websites, comparing land-status maps, deciphering emergency action, and trying to determine whether our regular hunting spot is suddenly subject to a different […]
text:
A few moose are seen in from the air in a forested area of Interior Alaska in this undated photo. (Photo by Mark Nelson/Alaska Department of Fish and Game)The last thing a hunter needs to pack before a moose hunt is a crash course in federal regulations and bureaucracy. We shouldn’t need to spend the days before a hunt refreshing federal websites, comparing land-status maps, deciphering emergency action, and trying to determine whether our regular hunting spot is suddenly subject to a different set of rules. But apparently, thanks to the feds, that’s where we are now. 
On Sept. 3, actively in moose hunting season, the Federal Subsistence Board approved Emergency Wildlife Special Action Request WSA26-09 by email, closing specified federal public lands in Unit 25D, a more than 17,000 mile swath of the upper Yukon River region, to moose hunting by non-federally qualified hunters from Sept. 10-20. 
That’s right. A federal board made a consequential decision about who could hunt public land, and did so via an email string completely out of public view. There was no Zoom meeting to tune into. No teleconference where hunters could listen to Board members deliberate. No public meeting where Alaskans could hear, in real time, how each member justified their decision. Instead, the vote happened in their inboxes. 
The Board’s rules may allow that. But “allowed” and “ideal” are two very different things. When a decision about who can hunt public land is made by email just days before the closure takes effect, Alaskans deserve to see how that decision was made and hear the reasoning behind it. Decisions that shut hunters out of public lands should be made in public. 
In fact, the Board’s own meeting guidelines call an open public meeting the “preferred forum” for emergency special actions. So why wasn’t there one? Why couldn’t the Board get on a public Zoom or teleconference and let Alaskans watch their government make the decision? How were the votes collected and verified? What safeguards surrounded the vote? Was there discussion among Board members before or while they voted? 
If the answer is simply, “The rules allow us to do it by email,” that’s not good enough. Transparency isn’t a technicality. It matters most when the government is exercising its power to tell people that public land they expected to hunt is suddenly off-limits. 
Here’s what makes this even more infuriating: this wasn’t some unforeseen wildlife emergency that suddenly appeared in September. The underlying decision was made in April through Wildlife Proposal WP26-75. The feds had months to address this. But because the federal regulatory process wasn’t completed in time, hunters received an emergency action just as moose season was arriving. Their delay became a hunter’s emergency. Moose season didn’t sneak up on anyone. September is on the calendar every year, last time we checked. 
And after the last-minute decision came the next problem: figuring out what it actually meant in real life. In Unit 25D, WSA26-09 applies to specified federal public lands along major river corridors. But navigable waters present an entirely different jurisdictional question. Depending
on land status and navigability, state-managed hunting opportunities may remain below the Ordinary High Water Mark while the federal uplands immediately beside it are closed. 
Got all that? You’d better. Because while the government makes the rules confusing, the government doesn’t pay the price when you misunderstand them. You do. 
On Sept. 16, the Board considered Emergency Wildlife Special Action Request WSA26-12, seeking to implement yet another April decision, Wildlife Proposal WP26-31, changing moose hunting on our public lands in Unit 13, which is south of Fairbanks. Again, the vote happened by email. 
This time, however, the Board rejected the request because it arrived too late. Hunters were already in the field, and implementing the closure at that point could create “confusion and conflict.” You think? 
That’s exactly the problem. Hunters shouldn’t find out that the rules are shifting while we’re packing camp, driving to the trailhead, running upriver, or already sitting in hunting camp. Government decisions about who gets to hunt federal public lands shouldn’t disappear into an email inbox where the people affected can’t watch the deliberation happen. 
Hunters have responsibilities. We must know the regulations and whose land we’re on. We must, and should, respect private property, understand boundaries and follow the law. The feds have responsibilities, too. Finish the regulatory process on time and give hunters adequate notice. Make the rules understandable to a normal person and show us exactly what’s open and what’s closed. And if you’re going to vote to remove hunting access, do it in the open where the people losing that access can watch it happen. 
It’s not an unreasonable ask. It’s the bare minimum. Alaska hunters shouldn’t need a law degree, or a sneak peek into a federal official’s inbox, to know where they can hunt moose.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA officials consider steep cut to developmental disability services
description: A Washington state agency has floated cutting services for more than 2,600 residents with developmental disabilities with the goal of saving money to close a looming budget gap. As part of its requests for the state’s next two-year spending plan, the Department of Social and Health Services suggested restricting eligibility for services could save $13.3 […]
text:
The Washington state Capitol in Olympia on March 7, 2026. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)A Washington state agency has floated cutting services for more than 2,600 residents with developmental disabilities with the goal of saving money to close a looming budget gap.
As part of its requests for the state’s next two-year spending plan, the Department of Social and Health Services suggested restricting eligibility for services could save $13.3 million, about $6 million of which would come from the state’s general fund.
The proposal would raise the bar by requiring people with developmental disabilities to show they need support with more activities of daily living to be eligible for state-paid services than they do now. These include bathing, dressing, eating and taking medication.
This suggested change would end Medicaid eligibility for an estimated 2,655 residents, according to the Department of Social and Health Services. It would mean some people receiving care in residential facilities would lose their housing since it’s contingent upon qualifying, potentially pushing them into homelessness.
Advocates decried the idea. The Arc of Washington State Executive Director Stacy Dym said “changes to eligibility like this proposal call into question Washington state’s commitment to serving our most vulnerable residents in the most integrated setting appropriate to their individual needs.”
“Individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities rely on essential services from a network of state and federal agencies in order to live in their community free from isolation and institutional care,” Dym said in a statement. “Unfortunately, cutting community services will end up costing the state and taxpayers more.”
She believes this will push people into hospitals and other more expensive settings that will provide worse care. 
Agency spokesperson Jessica Nelson described the proposal as a “first step in the budgeting process.”
“The budget options are designed to both help the agency continue to provide core services and ensure that Washington has a sustainable approach for their future funding,” Nelson said in an email. “Given the current budget climate and the ongoing increases in service costs and qualifying applicants, making changes in service eligibility is one way to sustain critical services within the available resources.”
Nelson noted the changes would “affect clients currently receiving services with the lowest support needs” to help prioritize resources on those who require more complex assistance.
This would save $13 million starting in fiscal year 2029 and increase in future years, according to agency documents. Lawmakers anticipate a multibillion-dollar budget shortfall to deal with when they return to Olympia in January.
The idea now goes to Gov. Bob Ferguson, who will release his proposed two-year spending plan in December for legislators to consider next year. Ferguson has said his proposal will lean on spending cuts to bridge the projected budget gap. The budget will run from July 1, 2027, to June 30, 2029. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Ferguson, a Democrat, included a similar idea in his budget proposal for the current fiscal year, but lawmakers decided against the cuts. 
The proposal comes after the state agency considered suddenly axing a longstanding program aiding families of people with autism and other developmental disabilities. Amid an outcry over the potential cut, officials instead decided to keep the program running while trimming its funding by 10%.
The proposal also comes as the state has ferociously condemned federal cuts to Medicaid pushed by Republicans and President Donald Trump.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s ‘slopaganda’ problem
description:
After a successful challenge of Vermont's AI political media law, computer-generated election satire continues to make waves.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s ‘slopaganda’ problem.
text:
Hank Poitras, better known as “Planet Hank,” speaks during a social media livestream in May 2026. Screenshot

Curtis Hier uses “Planet Hank” as a verb. 
He used the controversial Brattleboro content creator’s moniker to describe the inspiration behind Flip Vermont Red, the political action committee dedicated to electing more Republicans to the State House that he founded last month.
“Somebody just sort of said to me … ‘Oh, I wish we could “Planet Hank” Dave Wolk,’” Hier said in an interview, referring to the independent State Senate candidate. “I started thinking I could ‘Planet Hank’ Dave Wolk.”
AI-generated political content, sometimes referred to as “slopaganda,” has gained traction on social media following a successful challenge of a state law regulating synthetic material during election season. Containing renderings of candidates and legislators, some experts and politicians are concerned that, despite the ridiculous and satirical nature of the content, slopaganda is changing the political atmosphere.
University of Vermont philosophy professor Randall Harp said he is concerned about the volume of AI-generated political content online. It can harm social and information systems, he explained. In an interview, he compared AI content to fashion magazines. 
“If we get flooded with manipulated images in certain spaces, like fashion magazines, … even though we all know or understand that these are manipulated images, it still has a cumulative effect on the way that we think about ourselves,” Harp said.
In the same way, he said, sometimes the human brain can’t process content as satire when it “looks like reality.”
Most political deepfakes — generally AI-generated images or videos that misrepresent a real person — don’t intend to mislead, but distinguishing satire from deception has proved legally intractable, researchers at Purdue University found.
Thirty one states have enacted laws regulating the use of AI in political media. When Montana enacted its law requiring disclaimers on election deepfakes, Federal Judge Susan Watters struck it down, arguing that satire exemptions force government officials to make subjective judgments about protected speech. Vermont’s Act 75 contains the same exemption.
Flip Vermont Red’s first Facebook post was not AI-generated. It contained a real image of Sen. Ruth Hardy, D-Addison, overlaid with text criticizing her role in overriding Gov. Phil Scott’s 2024 veto on controversial land use bill Act 181.  
The PAC’s second Facebook video was AI-generated. It depicts a realistic rendering of Hardy nailing a “REGULATED BY THE STATE OF VERMONT” sign into a farm property. A farmer removes the sign from the dirt. Hardy then installs more signs, and hands the farmer a property tax bill. The farmer then packs boxes, farm animals and equipment into a moving truck. “AI made me do it,” small, white text in the video’s top left corner reads.
Hardy has been named or depicted in at least 11 posts by Flip Vermont Red.
Hank Poitras, known online as Planet Hank, has posted AI-generated political videos as recently as Sept. 22. 
A June 11 video Poitras posted depicted then-Republican U.S. House candidate Mark Coester criticizing U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., before using an excavator to lift her into a trash bin. 
Attorney General Charity Clark investigated that video for violation of Act 75, which requires that “realistic” AI-generated content contain a specific disclaimer. Poitras’ video did not contain such a disclaimer, but a federal judge ruled that the video fell into the law’s satire exemption.
Political satire and parody have deep roots in American discourse. First Amendment scholars note that exaggeration, irony, and invented scenarios are traditional tools of political critique. Hany Farid at UC Berkeley said deepfakes are becoming “more sophisticated and compelling,” but the research offers no clear path to regulation that survives constitutional scrutiny.
When asked for comment on the videos he had posted, Poitras wrote, “Planet Hank believes in and fully supports the First Amendment.”
Flip Vermont Red doesn’t include disclaimers in its posts, either. Hier said he is not concerned whether the PAC’s posts violate Act 75. 
“Our synthetic media are neither deceptive nor fraudulent,” Hier wrote in an email statement. “We use cartoons or outlandish imagery.”
Hier is a college application coach and a former high school teacher, according to his LinkedIn profile. He is also an administrator on the Facebook page Fair Haven, VT GOP where he reshares Flip Vermont Red posts, uploads news articles and advertises events with the Rutland County Republican Office. 
He added in an interview that he aims for a 100% AI rating if his content were pasted into an AI-checker.
Hier said that “tossing Becca Balint into a dumpster is not something we would do,” because Flip Vermont Red’s message “is not ridiculous.” 
“There’s a point to it,” he said. “It’s not just, you know, take out the trash. It’s somebody is doing something wrong or that we believe is wrong, and we want to tell people about it.”
Hardy said that, while she has avoided most of Flip Vermont Red’s posts, she doesn’t believe they will impact her reelection campaign. 
“The people that I’ve heard from are upset by the videos,” she said. “They don’t feel like they’re appropriate. They don’t feel like they’re accurate. They don’t reflect me as a human, as a senator, as a policymaker, as their representative in the legislature.”
Wolk also wrote in an email that he believes in voters’ judgments when viewing this kind of content.
“They know the difference between my track record of public service in Vermont for over 50 years and an AI-generated portrayal from an anonymous account,” he wrote. “Too often the loudest voices on the left and the right consume all of the attention, while the important work facing Vermonters gets ignored.”
Hier provided VTDigger with an early cut of an AI-generated video which depicts a realistic Wolk in an office at Castleton State College. A cartoon Wolk then walks around the campus as buildings pop up behind him. He then sings a song, seemingly mocking Wolk’s spending during his 16-year tenure as president. Hier said Flip Vermont Red plans to use it in a Facebook ad campaign paid for by donors to the PAC. 
The video of Hardy will also be boosted as a part of the advertisement campaign, he said. 
Hier uses a $9.99 monthly Adobe Firefly subscription to produce AI images. He said he outsources production of the videos that Flip Vermont Red posts, declining to comment by whom he outsources from. 
The lead sponsor of Act 75, Hardy believes it’s “no accident” that she is being targeted by AI-generated political content. She, now and in writing the bill, said she wants to protect the First Amendment and protect voters’ access to “accurate information.”
Hardy declined to comment on whether a court could find Flip Vermont Red in violation of Act 75, but said that the bipartisan-supported bill may need to be edited in the next session. 
“I think it sort of speaks to this moment that we’re in,” Hardy said. “The technology and the use of that technology is spreading, advancing and spreading so quickly that legislators can’t keep up with it.”

title: Gov. Kay Ivey declares state of emergency as Isaias approaches Gulf Coast
description: Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday declared a state of emergency in 40 of Alabama’s 67 counties as Tropical Storm Isaias headed toward the Gulf Coast and continued to strengthen. The National Hurricane Center said Wednesday afternoon the storm had reached winds of 65 mph. Isaias is expected to become a hurricane on Thursday and strengthen further […]
text:
Tropical Storm Isaias's forecasted track is seen as of Oct. 7, 2026. Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday declared a state of emergency ahead of the storm, which is expected to strengthen into a hurricane on Thursday. (National Hurricane Center)Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday declared a state of emergency in 40 of Alabama’s 67 counties as Tropical Storm Isaias headed toward the Gulf Coast and continued to strengthen.
The National Hurricane Center said Wednesday afternoon the storm had reached winds of 65 mph. Isaias is expected to become a hurricane on Thursday and strengthen further on Friday. The storm could produce 3 to 7 inches of rain from southeast Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, and the NHC said some areas could see up to 10 inches of rain.
“As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop,” Ivey said in a statement. “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”
The state of emergency applies to Autauga, Baldwin, Barbour, Bibb, Bullock, Butler, Chambers, Chilton, Clarke, Choctaw, Coffee, Conecuh, Coosa, Covington, Crenshaw, Dale, Dallas, Elmore, Escambia, Geneva, Greene, Hale, Henry, Houston, Lee, Lowndes, Macon, Marengo, Mobile, Monroe, Montgomery, Perry, Pickens, Pike, Russell, Sumter, Tallapoosa, Tuscaloosa, Washington and Wilcox counties. It will be in effect until Oct. 14.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC legislators can’t say how much of the gas tax cut will trickle down to drivers
description: North Carolina lawmakers voted nearly unanimously Wednesday to pass legislation suspending the gas tax until the end of November. But it’s unclear when prices at the pump will actually drop, or by how much. The House approved the bill 111-1 Wednesday afternoon, sending it over to the Senate. Rep. Pricey Harrison, D-Guilford, was the sole […]
text:
NC Senate Leader Phil Berger (R-Rockingham) talks to reporters on Oct. 7, 2026, after the Senate voted unanimously to suspend the state gas tax. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)North Carolina lawmakers voted nearly unanimously Wednesday to pass legislation suspending the gas tax until the end of November. But it’s unclear when prices at the pump will actually drop, or by how much.
The House approved the bill 111-1 Wednesday afternoon, sending it over to the Senate. Rep. Pricey Harrison, D-Guilford, was the sole vote against it. Senators voted 41-0 in favor and sent it on to Gov. Josh Stein.
House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said this is the first time North Carolina has suspended the entire gas tax, which currently totals 41 cents per gallon. He conceded consumers aren’t likely to see prices drop by that amount, based on what’s happened in other states.
“I would expect 30 cents, maybe 35 cents in reduction from this bill,” Hall told reporters. Timing of the price reductions may vary based on location, he said. “We’ll see what the global market does as well.” 
It’s also unclear when those savings will appear. The measure says retailers don’t have to cut prices on wholesale gas they bought and paid taxes on before the tax holiday took effect.
House Majority Leader Brenden Jones, R-Columbus, claimed the bill would offer consumers “immediate relief” at the pump, and also said it “requires that the cost of the fuel actually reflect the savings” from the tax holiday.  
Senate Republicans contradicted him. 
Sen. Buck Newton, R-Wilson, said he could not say when or whether gas stations will drop prices by 41 cents a gallon.
“I don’t know because I won’t know what they’re buying it for from the wholesaler or what the wholesaler is getting it for at the terminal, and on up the line,” Newton said.
The legislature can control the state gas tax, so that’s what it’s doing, Newton said. 
Sen. Val Applewhite, D-Cumberland, said consumers will want to know how much they’ll save at the pump. That Republicans in the Senate Finance Committee couldn’t say seems “disingenuous and a little bit weird to me,” she said.
Senate Democrats said there’s no guarantee that retailers will pass the tax savings on to drivers.  
An amendment proposed by Sen. Jay Chaudhuri, D-Wake, that would have allowed the Attorney General to go after retailers for price gouging if they didn’t apply the tax cut to gas prices was ruled out of order and did not receive a vote. 
“Nothing in this bill makes sure gas stations actually pass these savings along to you,” said Senate Democratic Leader Sydney Batch, D-Wake.
Democrats said the bill was a political move ahead of the general election in response to Republicans’ low poll numbers. 
House Democratic Leader Robert Reives, D-Chatham, said his caucus was voting yes, because members will “take any relief we can get” for North Carolinians. But he said gas prices have been high for a long time already.
NC Republicans tout a gas tax cut that Democrats call an election-season desperation move

“If we’re that serious about helping people, we could have done this in the normal session, could have done it two weeks ago,” Reives said. “I would just ask all of us to keep that in mind.”
Sen. Lisa Grafstein, D-Wake, said consumers will save a little money, which will be welcome, though no one can say how much. 
“Let’s not pretend that this is not about politics first and foremost,” Grafstein said. 
“There will also be a whole lot spent on new ads going out by some of our colleagues claiming to have taken steps to address the cost of living crisis,” she said. “I’m sure the identical social media posts are already teed up and ready to go.”
The bill also requires farmers and loggers as well as retailers to be notified about the suspension of taxes as well as the extension until Dec. 31 of the current waiver for on-road use of dyed diesel. Special notice to these key voting constituencies contributes to her cynicism, Grafstein said. 
Hall said lawmakers didn’t approve a gas tax holiday earlier this year because gas prices were declining in July when the legislature adjourned.
The prices have risen again in recent weeks, so lawmakers wanted to provide relief ahead of holiday travel, according to Hall. The current suspension runs through Nov. 30. Hall said it’s possible the legislature could extend it. 
However, Senate Leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, told reporters there have been no discussions between his chamber and the House about extending the gas tax holiday beyond November. “This is something that we’ve looked at as a temporary measure,” he said.
 When asked why Republican leaders didn’t also consider tax relief on groceries, Hall said the gas tax suspension helps farmers lower their costs in harvest season. With lower costs for agriculture, he said, there should be a downstream effect for buyers at the grocery store. He also predicted it could help lower retail prices by reducing transportation costs.
“From an economic standpoint, and in terms of bang for the buck, trying to get the most help to taxpayers using their money, we felt like this time of year really makes sense for a lot of reasons,” Hall told reporters.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Help Montana’s hungry bears stay safe
description: I’ve started counting tipped-over garbage cans this month as I make my early morning gym commute. Some mornings there’s trash strewn along the road, block after block. A few weeks ago, our doorbell camera caught a bear hanging out on our front porch.  Even as a lifelong Montanan, it’s a startling number of bear sightings. […]
text:
Bears rummage in human garbage. (Photo courtesy of MT FWP) I’ve started counting tipped-over garbage cans this month as I make my early morning gym commute. Some mornings there’s trash strewn along the road, block after block. A few weeks ago, our doorbell camera caught a bear hanging out on our front porch. 
Even as a lifelong Montanan, it’s a startling number of bear sightings. 
It can be tempting to look at this phenomenon and wonder if there are just too many bears. But what we’re actually seeing are hungry black and grizzly bears moving down into communities because the food they normally depend on has failed. 
The best course of action is to make smart decisions to head off conflict between people and these awe-inspiring animals.  
The main cause of these bear sightings is sad and simple. It has been a brutal year for bears across the northern Rockies. Spring green-up arrived early and late frosts hit chokecherries, serviceberries and other foods that bears rely on, making this year one of the worst natural food failures on record. 
When berries fail in the mountains, bears look elsewhere. Unfortunately, people have built a remarkably good buffet — garbage cans, fruit trees, chicken coops, pet food, livestock feed and on ranches, dead or vulnerable cattle. That’s bad news for bears, especially for females with cubs, who are more likely to wander into human spaces searching for food as they try to pack on the pounds to survive a Montana winter.
We saw the consequences of this in Bozeman, where 14 black bears were recently euthanized after wildlife officials determined they had become dangerously comfortable with people and were apparently eating human food. This was an avoidable tragedy. Keeping food and garbage away from bears is one of the simplest and most effective things we can do to prevent them from being killed. 
Those of us lucky to live in Montana’s beautiful bear country have an important role to play, which mostly comes down to basic property maintenance. We can use bear-resistant garbage cans, take down bird feeders, bring pet and livestock feed inside, glean fruit trees and secure chickens and goats behind electric fencing. 
Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks should be called early if there’s a risk of conflict, before a bear learns that wandering into a yard earns them an easy meal.
The state should fully fund compensation programs so ranchers aren’t left carrying the cost when they lose livestock to grizzlies. We also need to invest more in preventing those losses in the first place by removing carcasses that attract bears, using electric fencing around calving areas and beehives, and supporting range riders who can keep cattle and bears apart. The Blackfoot Challenge in Montana has shown us how successful this can be. 
These are practical tools that are far cheaper than an endless cycle of dead cattle and dead bears, and they’re poised to become even more important.
That’s because the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Services is currently considering changes to how grizzly bears are managed across the lower 48 states. Its current proposal would maintain grizzly bears as “threatened” under the Endangered Species Act but would give states far more flexibility to kill grizzlies in response to conflict. 
The Center for Biological Diversity, where I work, opposes that proposal because it wouldn’t solve or avoid conflicts that put bears and people at risk. It would just make it easier for states to kill grizzlies. We already have the tools to reduce conflict. We just have to use them. 
Many Montanans chose to live in areas where bears have lived for thousands of years. With this choice comes the duty to recognize that living in bear country requires some responsibility on our part. As climate change disrupts our wild ecosystems, hungry bears will return and they may even visit more frequently. 
But we shouldn’t confuse seeing more bears with having too many bears. 
The bear on my porch didn’t show up because bears are taking over. They showed up because this has been a hard year and they were looking for an easy meal. The best thing we can do, for Montana’s bears and for ourselves, is to make sure they don’t find one. 
Kristine Akland is a Montana-based attorney and the Northern Rockies director at the Center for Biological Diversity.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: ‘Wanton abuse of power’: Kelly, union leader criticize southwest Kansas ICE raids, seek reform
description: TOPEKA — Federal immigration officials subjected southwest Kansas to a “wanton abuse of power,” Gov. Laura Kelly said, and she pledged to union members that she would work to restore immigrants’ sense of belonging and security.  Kelly spoke at a United Food and Commercial Workers member meeting Monday in Dodge City, highlighting the importance of […]
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly spoke to members of the United Food and Commercial Workers Union in Dodge City Oct. 5, 2026, about federal immigration raids in the area. Martin Rosas,  right, president of the union's Local 2, also spoke at the event. (Photo from Kansas Governor's office.)TOPEKA — Federal immigration officials subjected southwest Kansas to a “wanton abuse of power,” Gov. Laura Kelly said, and she pledged to union members that she would work to restore immigrants’ sense of belonging and security. 
Kelly spoke at a United Food and Commercial Workers member meeting Monday in Dodge City, highlighting the importance of immigrants in Kansas. The union’s local chapter is based in Bel Aire and represents 14,852 members in meatpacking, grocery, food processing, healthcare,  retail, and other industries. 
On Sept. 22, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in Garden City, Liberal and Dodge City, as well as smaller surrounding towns, to detain immigrants who didn’t have proper documentation, ultimately arresting about 110 people. No comprehensive list of those arrested has been released.  
“Under no circumstances should you have been subjected to the wanton abuse of power you experienced two weeks ago,” Kelly said. “I wanted to come that week to assure you that your governor and your state law enforcement officials were with you. I didn’t come then because after several calls with Martin (Rosas) and others, I believe my presence would have put all of you in more jeopardy.
“But I’m here now to listen and to do whatever I can, whatever my administration can, to restore your sense of belonging, your sense of security, and your pride in being a candidate,” she added. 
Martin Rosas, president of the union’s Local 2, encouraged union members to make their voices heard by voting. 
After the meeting, Rosas said the majority of industries in the area rely on an immigrant workforce, and often workers come from “mixed status” families, meaning one person will have legal papers to work but the rest of the family won’t. 
The meatpacking industry uses E-Verify, the government system that confirms work status, he said. But the people who didn’t go to work in southwest Kansas were afraid to leave their families because they may not be here legally.
“They don’t show up for work, not because they can’t attend to work. It’s because they’re afraid to leave their house when we got these goons knocking on people’s doors, kicking doors open, shooting people, killing people. We have seen that,” Rosas said.  
Immigrants have seen delays since 2016 in government action to provide a legal pathway to residency or citizenship, and then the “aggressive position that this administration has taken against immigrants as a whole or people of color” has generated fear, he said. 
Politicians can no longer delay or “kick the can down the road,” Rosas said. 
“The demand for labor workforce is growing in the United States,” he said. “However, the current immigration system doesn’t recognize that need. While we evolve with more and more need for workers in America, the politician has not done anything, other than like this current administration attacking the immigrants.”
Immigrant labor is crucial for the U.S. workforce, he said. Positive responses to ICE and deporting immigrants online make Rosas realize how people think about the immigrant workforce. 
“When you see those reactions, everything is a result of years of dehumanizing the immigrant workforce that is very significant to the production and the economy of the United States,” Rosas said. 
Rosas, who is an immigrant and became a U.S. citizen in 1996, said that when he sits down and talks with people one-on-one, they have a different view of the immigration system and understand the need for reform. 
He pointed to recent news that Oklahoma’s Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt recognized that if undocumented people left the state, it would put a “huge dent” in the economy, Rosas said. 
He referred to comments Stitt made to NewsNation offering full support to Trump for closing borders but saying that people who aren’t criminals shouldn’t be deported because beef prices will go up. Stitt gave an example of an Oklahoma immigrant who had a marijuana violation 20 years ago. Although the man’s employer was willing to vouch for him, ICE deported him. 
“People have to analyze, really, what is the cost of us not doing anything with immigration?” Rosas said. “No one, including myself, no one is loving to have open borders. If you’ve been in the country for a period of time, you’ve been doing everything according with the law, good civic human being, good human person, you should be allowed to regularize your status. The system itself has created this problem, and by not taking action, it’s aggravating the problem to the point where it is today.”
Kelly called for immigration overhaul in her remarks, asking the nation to “return to being a beacon of civility, humanity and opportunity.”
She noted how the makeup of southwest Kansas has shifted since she first moved to the state in 1986. As executive director of the Kansas Recreation and Park Association, she visited recreation centers, parks, ball fields and other areas, which offered opportunities for area families. 
“But I was also struck by how segregated programs were,” she said. “The children of the white families played in the city-sanctioned leagues. The children of the Hispanic families played in their own separate leagues. Fast forward over those 40 years, the entire culture in Southwest Kansas has radically changed. 
“Hispanic and Latino citizens and immigrants from other parts of the world now make up the majority of many of our communities,” she said. “The schools, the businesses, the arts, the very economy of Southwest Kansas thrive because of the influx, the integration, and the influence of the multinational makeup of this region.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Board approves hiring powerhouse law firm to defend Moore in defamation case
description: The Maryland Board of Public Works Wednesday approved a $50,000 contract to hire a powerhouse outside law firm to defend Gov. Wes Moore (D) against a defamation lawsuit filed by the owner of the Baltimore Sun.
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) will be represented by a DC law firm in a defamation lawsuit filed against him by David Smith, owner of the Baltimore Sun and executive chairman of Sinclair Broadcast Group. Moore is seeking a dismissal citing immunity protections. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)The Maryland Board of Public Works Wednesday approved a $50,000 contract to hire a powerhouse outside law firm to defend Gov. Wes Moore (D) against a defamation lawsuit filed by the owner of the Baltimore Sun.
David Smith, who is also executive chairman of the Sinclair Broadcast Group, filed the lawsuit in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court in July. Smith, in a court filing, alleges defamation and false light invasion of privacy for comments made by Moore during a June interview on MSNOW.
The Office of the Attorney General asked for approval of the contract, saying outside counsel was needed “because representation by the Attorney General or an assistant is impracticable.” The office retained Foley Hoag, a Washington, D.C., firm with experience in First Amendment and defamation claims.
“I just want to be clear that the state is covering this representation because the law says that when a public employee is sued in the course of performing their official duties, the state will defend them,” said Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D), one of the three members of the Board of Public Works. “That holds for a state trooper, park ranger, professor, and for a governor.
“Courts across the nation have agreed that speaking to the press about matters of public interest is well within a public official’s job,” Lierman said. “So when Gov. Moore goes on the TV networks, he is speaking to the people of Maryland, and he is speaking as our governor, elected by 1.3 million voters.”
Smith filed the lawsuit this summer, a month after Moore made comments about Smith on the MSNOW show “The Weeknight.”
In the interview, Moore linked Smith to Jeffery Epstein saying the owner of Sinclair “had been invested in” by the New York financier who was charged with sexual abuse and trafficking underage girls.
Moore, in that same interview with Michael Steele, the former Maryland lieutenant governor, said Smith was using the Baltimore Sun “to do Donald Trump’s work and to spread his message.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
According to Smith’s lawsuit, investment firms controlled by Epstein did purchase shares in Sinclair, a publicly traded company. But Smith’s filing said he was unaware of the connection — his suit said the “allegedly Epstein-related entities” held, at most, 0.063% of Sinclair’s Class A stock — and that such purchases do not establish a personal relationship with any stockholder.
Moore’s comments about Smith promoting Trump’s agenda tie back to a 2018 article in The Guardian detailing a meeting between Trump and Smith. The Guardian quotes Smith as saying that during a 2016 meeting with Trump, who was running for president, he told Trump that Sinclair was “here to deliver your message.”
In his lawsuit, Smith notes that those comments were made years before he purchased The Baltimore Sun.
Smith is seeking unspecified damages.
Attorneys representing Moore last week asked for a dismissal of the lawsuit, saying the governor’s statements “are absolutely privileged” and that Moore has legal immunity.
The contract approved by the board Wednesday caps fees for the firm representing Moore at $50,000.
“If that motion [to dismiss] succeeds, which I think it probably will, that’s where the cost ends,” Lierman said during the meeting.
Lierman went on to defend the hiring of outside attorneys and, to some degree, Moore’s comments saying it was “important that we vociferously defend the governor in this case because we believe in protecting free speech and the free speech of our public officials.”
“We don’t want a country, I certainly don’t want a country where anyone with a big legal budget can sue a public servant into silence, or can even chill public servants’ speech,” she said. “I don’t want a country where you cannot speak your mind, even when powerful people and corporations disagree. In this country, the answer to speech that you don’t like has always been more speech, not enforced silence.”
Moore himself did not attend the meeting. Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller chaired the panel in his absence.
Lierman and Treasurer Dereck Davis voted to approve the contract. Miller recused herself from voting on the contract, but did not give a reason. A senior member of Miller’s staff who attended the meeting was not immediately able to provide an explanation.
The two Foley Hoag attorneys who filed the motion to dismiss for Moore have extensive experience in media and defamation law.
Michael J. Grygiel is chair of the firm’s First Amendment and Media Practice Group. His practice has focused on First Amendment law including defending news organizations from newsgathering and publication claims as well as defamation and invasion of privacy lawsuits, according to the firm’s website.
Kelly L. McNamee is a partner in the firm’s First Amendment and Media Practice Group.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Curtis Flowers, wrongly imprisoned, enduring six trials, dead at 56
description: Curtis Flowers flanked by sister Priscilla Ward, right, exits the Winston Choctaw Regional Correctional Facility in Louisville, Miss., Monday, Dec. 16, 2019. Flowers' murder conviction was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court for racial bias, and he was granted bond by a circuit judge and is free, with some conditions, for the first time in 22 years. (AP Pho[...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Curtis Flowers, a Black man whose six trials for murder in Mississippi became a landmark case for racial bias in jury selection, has died, according to the Montgomery County coroner. 
Flowers was 56.
His cause of death was not immediately released. Montgomery County Coroner Allan Pratt told Mississippi Today in a statement that Flowers’ body was found on Wednesday and that his death is an “ongoing investigation.” 
On July 16, 1996, four people were shot and killed at Tardy Furniture in Winona, located about 92 miles north of the capital city of Jackson. The victims were store owner Bertha Tardy and employees Robert Golden, Carmen Rigby and Derrick Stewart. 
Then-Montgomery County District Attorney Doug Evans prosecuted Flowers six times for the murders, as Flowers maintained his innocence throughout the prosecutions. Each time Flowers was prosecuted, it either resulted in a hung jury or a guilty verdict that was later overturned by a higher court. 
Evans secured a conviction in the sixth trial, and Flowers was sentenced to death. In June 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court voted 7-2 to overturn Flowers’ conviction and said Evans intentionally struck black people from serving on the jury that convicted Flowers.
Flowers was released on bail in December 2019 to await a seventh trial. Evans recused himself, and the state attorney general’s office took over the case. Circuit Judge Joey Loper, in September 2020, dismissed the capital murder charges with prejudice after a motion by the AG’s office. 
After the case was dismissed, a judge ordered Mississippi to pay Flowers $500,000 in wrongful-imprisonment compensation.
The American Public Media podcast “In the Dark” investigated the case. It presented an analysis showing a long history of racial bias in jury selection by Evans, and evidence suggesting another person may have committed the crimes.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama screentime commission makes 1st recommendations on best classroom practices
description: An Alabama state commission plans to recommended the state further define screen time and work toward “fostering digital literacy” as it develops best practices for screen use in public school classrooms.  The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, is scheduled to send a final report to the governor within two months.  “(We […]
text:
A woman scrolling on a cell phone.  The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction Wednesday made its first recommendations on best practices for screen-based instruction in classrooms. (Getty Images)An Alabama state commission plans to recommended the state further define screen time and work toward “fostering digital literacy” as it develops best practices for screen use in public school classrooms. 
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, formed by Gov. Kay Ivey, is scheduled to send a final report to the governor within two months. 
“(We should be) considering digital citizenship and digital literacy curriculums, parent training materials, professional development for teachers, all those types of things, and that is because digital literacy has been shown to kind of mitigate some of the negative impacts of the increased screen use,” said Nashedra Barry, a child psychologist with Children’s Hospital of Alabama in Birmingham and a member of the commission.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ivey earlier this year signed HB 78, sponsored by Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, into law. The bill set screen time limits for children up to five years old in licensed child-care facilities. Ross also filed HB 584 which would have expanded the limits for all public school students, but the bill failed to pass before the Legislature adjourned in April.
Ivey established the commission in July to study the risks, usage and benefits of screen-based instruction in K-12 classrooms across the state.
Commission member Laren Hammonds, a middle school teacher in Tuscaloosa,, said in addition to further defining screen time, the commission should consider “the learning activity that screen use enables, replaces, or interrupts.”
Ross, who chairs the commission, said after the meeting the committee’s recommendations were reasonable, and that she would wait on the final recommendations before considering further legislation. 
“They’re going to be something that teachers and school officials are going to easily be able to implement and consider because right now what we’re most concerned with is making sure people are aware that screen time should be quality, and there’s certain types of screen time that should be limited or not (done) at all,” she said.
Commissioners Wednesday also discussed how screen time legislation looked in other states. Tennessee’s legislation on screen time for children, signed into law in April, states that local boards and public charter schools must have a policy for kindergarten through 5th grade on appropriate screen usage. 
The policy must prioritize teacher-led instruction that does not use screens; prohibit students from accessing social media through school internet servers; require that digital tests and tools used by students are developmentally appropriate; limit the usage of school-issued devices in classrooms, and provide parents with transparency on the types of devices being used in classrooms.
“I think Tennessee’s model, what’s good about it was it’s very concise, and it made sense,” said Houston County Superintendent Brandy White. “It still allowed for some local control, but it identified some things that we needed to focus on using technology.”
Ross said she believes that the findings from the commission will build on what Tennessee has. 
“We have more evidence, we have more research, and it may be that we build upon this, but I see it as being a little more comprehensive,” she said.
The committee will deliver its final report to Ivey on Dec. 1.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former SC legislator pleads guilty to money laundering, wire fraud
description: Ex-Rep. Marvin Pendarvis admitted to swindling legal clients out of roughly half a million dollars in legal settlements.
text:
Former Rep. Marvin Pendarvis, pictured at a Statehouse news conference in January 2024, pleaded guilty Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, to charges of wire fraud, money laundering and identity theft. (File photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)A former state representative pleaded guilty in federal court Wednesday to taking settlement money from his legal clients, sometimes by pretending to be them.
Ex-Rep. Marvin Pendarvis, a personal injury attorney, pleaded guilty to nine counts of wire fraud, money laundering and aggravated identity theft. He faces up to 20 years in prison for the wire fraud and money laundering charges, along with two years for the charges of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors agreed to drop one of the 10 charges Pendarvis faced, which accused him of illegally conducting interstate commerce.
A federal judge in Charleston County will decide his sentence at a later date.
According to an indictment filed against him last year, Pendarvis lied to his clients about how much money he had negotiated for them to receive, claiming insurance companies settled for less than they actually did. He then wired the rest of the money into the law firm’s bank account, then into other accounts from there, according to the indictment.
In some cases, he forged clients’ names and filed settlement documents without their knowledge or approval, according to the indictment.
Pendarvis pocketed at least $532,000 between January 2022 and April 2024, when the State Law Enforcement Division began investigating claims in a former client’s civil malpractice lawsuit, according to the indictment.
That lawsuit is ongoing.
Along with prison time, each charge could carry fines of up to $250,000. A judge will also be able to order Pendarvis to pay back the money he stole from the people who should have received it, according to the guilty plea.
The North Charleston Democrat, first elected in a 2017 special election, resigned from the House in September 2024, four months after the state Supreme Court suspended his law license. Running unopposed, he still won re-election, then declined the win, triggering a special election.
Pendarvis’ attorney, public defender Brendan Daniels, declined to comment Wednesday. Pendarvis did not respond to a call requesting comment.
A spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, which prosecuted the case, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Doña Ana County seeks state disaster declaration as officials begin flood recovery
description: Officials overseeing New Mexico’s second largest county are urging Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham to declare an emergency due to recent floods they estimate have caused at least $15 million in damages to public infrastructure.
text:
Officials in Doña Ana County have estimated that recent flooding has caused at least $15 million in damages to public dams, roads or bridges. Above: A washed-out road in the county pictured Sept. 23, 2026. (Courtesy Doña Ana County) Officials overseeing New Mexico’s second largest county are urging Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham to declare an emergency due to recent floods they estimate have caused at least $15 million in damages to public infrastructure.
Such a declaration would unlock additional state money to help with recovery.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Two large rain events in late September — from late-season monsoons and the remnants of Hurricane Polo  — dumped more than 5 inches of rain in Las Cruces and surrounding Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico
The Doña Ana County Commission, in a resolution it passed Tuesday, listed Las Cruces and 11 other towns as suffering damage to homes, businesses, roads, utilities and flood-control infrastructure. 
In total, Amanda Bowen, the county’s emergency manager, has calculated at least $15 million in damage, according to data that county officials provided Source NM on Wednesday. That includes at least $9 million in damages reported by the Elephant Butte Irrigation District, which oversees the network of dams, drains and other infrastructure along the southern stretch of the Rio Grande. 
Bowen told commissioners Tuesday that $15 million is almost certainly a low estimate of damages, as she continues to reach out to other public entities to collect more information. 
“We’ll continue, as water subsides and they’re able to better assess all of their infrastructure,” Bowen said. 
Bowen’s office also calculated at least $2.2 in damages within the City of Las Cruces, as well as at least $1.8 million in costs to the county, ranging from more than $1 million to infrastructure the county’s Flood Commission oversees and $561,000 in road damages to $2,000 in overtime for the county animal control officers, according to data county officials provided Source NM on Wednesday.
The governor’s office did not respond to Source NM’s inquiry Wednesday about whether it was considering a disaster declaration for the county. 
The governor’s office last week approved up to $3.75 million in emergency funding statewide for flooding-related costs. It’s not clear from the orders how much of that funding went to Doña Ana County. 
The flooding last month marks the second year in a row of damaging floods in the county. Last July, flash floods in Vado and Del Cerro flooded at least 110 homes and caused additional damage. 
In that case, the Doña Ana County Commission approved $500,000 in an emergency housing fund for indigent families who lost homes they rent or own. County officials described the fund as the first of its kind in New Mexico. 
Commissioners said Tuesday that roughly $166,000 remained from that funding. The disaster declaration they signed enables the remaining balance to go toward families whose homes suffered damage in the flooding last month.

name: VTDigger
title: Don’t tax Vermont expats out of coming home
description:
A huge tax increase on second homes could push out owners with deep Vermont roots and let wealthier buyers with fewer ties take their place.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Don’t tax Vermont expats out of coming home.
text:
Dear Editor,
I oppose proposals to impose a substantially higher property tax rate on second homes in Vermont. I was born and raised in Shaftsbury, graduated from Mount Anthony Union High School and Saint Michael’s College, and was married in Manchester. Vermont is not simply a place where my family vacations; it is home.
After college, I moved to Massachusetts to find a stable, well-paying job with benefits because my skills and training did not align with many of the opportunities then available in Vermont. Today, I own a second home in Waterbury and regularly return to Shaftsbury to visit my widowed mother. My family consistently supports locally owned businesses in Waterbury, the Shires and communities across the state, from bookstores and restaurants to other small businesses. We make a deliberate choice to spend locally rather than at national chains.
Census data shows that only about half of Vermont’s residents were born in the state. By any reasonable measure, I am a Vermonter, and maple runs through my veins. My goal is to move back to Vermont full time when it becomes financially viable for my family. Our careers and family circumstances simply do not make that possible today.
When we purchased our Waterbury home, we paid the higher property transfer tax required for a second home, significantly more than the standard rate. We could have tried to qualify for the lower rate by designating the property as a long-term rental through a short arrangement with a friend or relative, as others reportedly do. Instead, we followed the spirit of the law and paid our fair share.
A proposal that could effectively double the base property tax rate for some nonhomestead residences would materially affect our family. Vermont should create pathways for people with deep roots here to return, invest and participate in their communities, not adopt a one-size-fits-all policy that may push them away.
We are fortunate, and we recognize that. But we are not wealthy. We worked hard and saved for years to own a home in Vermont again. We are not property developers, short-term-rental operators or seasonal visitors who appear only for foliage and ski season. We are a Vermont family maintaining our connection to the state we love and working toward a permanent return.

READ MORE

I understand the urgency of Vermont’s housing and affordability crisis. Too many people are struggling to buy or remain in their homes, and policymakers should act. But a broad tax increase on second homes will not produce the intended result. Families like mine could be forced to sell, while buyers with greater wealth and fewer ties to Vermont take our place. That would do little to expand attainable housing or strengthen year-round communities.
If lawmakers move forward with a higher tax on second homes, I urge them to include a carefully designed exemption or credit for owners who were born in Vermont or lived here for at least 20 years, particularly those who do not use the property as a short-term rental. A targeted policy can distinguish commercial or luxury ownership from people seeking to preserve longstanding ties to their home state. Without that distinction, Vermont risks driving away the very people it should be welcoming back, without meaningfully addressing the housing crisis.
Bryan Burke
Westford, Mass., and Waterbury, Vt.
