name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge dismisses Tameshia Shelton’s murder indictment
description: Tameshia Shelton's daughter Trinity, left, and niece Danyell Randle, right, embrace Shelton outside the Clay County Detention Center after her release on June 29, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WEST POINT — A Mississippi judge Wednesday threw out the murder indictment against Tameshia Shelton, putting an end to the case that has haunted the mother of four for nearly two decades.
Shelton, now 48, was slated to face a new murder trial in Clay County on Monday, but Circuit Judge James T. Kitchens canceled the trial and agreed with Columbus-area District Attorney Scott Colom that the murder indictment should be dismissed.
Shelton, who has maintained her innocence, served 11 years in prison after a jury convicted her of murder in the 2009 shooting death of her sister’s 21-year-old boyfriend, Danelle Young. Shelton was freed on bond in June, after the state Supreme Court upheld an appellate-court ruling overturning her murder conviction and ordering her a new trial. Young’s family could not be immediately reached for comment.
Tameshia Shelton beams at a crowd of family members after her release from the Clay County Detention Center on June 29, 2026. She walked out in a shirt from her niece, featuring a photo of her taken before she was sentenced to life in prison 11 years before.  Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
When Shelton heard Wednesday that the judge had dismissed her murder indictment, she said she felt ecstatic. “Now I can breathe,” she said. “God, thank you.”
The dismissal marks the end of the nightmare that began 17 years ago when authorities first accused her of murder, she told Mississippi Today. “It’s been a long time coming. It feels like a whole lot of weight has been lifted off my shoulders.”
She said her sister, Shenikia, told her, “Now, we can celebrate.”
The dismissal means this judicial district that covers Clay, Lowndes, Noxubeeand Oktibbeha counties has seen seven people freed from prison after courts overturned their murder convictions — the most of any judicial district in the state. All were prosecuted under the previous district attorney, Forrest Allgood.
Allgood has told Mississippi Today that just because people have their convictions tossed doesn’t mean they’re innocent. “Only God knows if a man is innocent,” he said. “That’s why we have no verdict of ‘Innocent’ in our law — just ‘Guilty’ or ‘Not Guilty,’ or, in Scotland, ‘Not Proven.’”
Last December, the Mississippi Court of Appeals ordered a new trial for Shelton, saying prosecutors failed to prove “beyond a reasonable doubt” she killed Young. 
Jurors never heard the apparent suicide note that Young wrote after Shelton’s sister decided against living with him.
“I have no life without her,” he wrote. “These are my last words. Bye, bye.”
Three jurors shown the note this year told Mississippi Today that Shelton deserved a new trial.
On June 1, Mississippi Today published its four-year investigation into Shelton’s case, showing how much of the evidence suggested that Young died from suicide. The pathologist who originally ruled the death a homicide reversed himself.
Days later, the state Supreme Court let stand the appeals court’s decision, clearing the way for Shelton to receive a new trial. The judge has now canceled the trial and dismissed the murder indictment.
“At last, this case that should have never been brought is over,” said Shelton’s lawyer, Sandra Levick. “Ms. Shelton was convicted of a murder that never happened at a trial that was not fair by a jury that never heard all the facts.”
She thanked Colom, who had directed Shelton’s family to the Innocence Project in 2018. “If he had not agreed to look into this case,” Levick wrote, “this day would never have come.”
She also said, “We are grateful as well to generations of law students at Ole Miss, to our many experts including Dr. (Liam) Funte who did the hard thing and admitted that he had been wrong.”
She also thanked her co-counsel Jake Howard from the MacArthur Justice Center, Tucker Carrington, director of the Mississippi Innocence Project, and “everyone else who helped claw back this injustice.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan set to open new $383 million psychiatric hospital in Northville
description: Dozens of state officials, healthcare providers and community members celebrated the completion of the new 406,000-square-foot, 264-bed Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville Wednesday.  The state-run hospital, which has been three years in the making, cost $383 million and was built on the former site of the Hawthorn Center, a children’s psyc[...]
text:
Grounds of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Dozens of state officials, healthcare providers and community members celebrated the completion of the new 406,000-square-foot, 264-bed Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville Wednesday. 
The state-run hospital, which has been three years in the making, cost $383 million and was built on the former site of the Hawthorn Center, a children’s psychiatric hospital. Patients at the Walter P. Reuther Hospital in Westland, which currently houses adult patients, will be transferred to the new facility starting later this month.
The new hospital, which has 192 adult beds and 72 youth beds, increases the state’s capacity to serve children and adults by 54 beds, bringing the total capacity to 730 beds statewide.
“It has been thrilling to watch this dream become reality,” Mary Clare Solky, the hospital’s director, said. “Providing compassionate, high-quality psychiatric care for adults, children and adolescents is not just our mission. It is our responsibility.”
The hospital will be the state’s only psychiatric hospital providing inpatient services to children, and according to acting Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Director Amy Epkey, it was completed on schedule and under budget. 
The department’s fiscal year 2027 budget allocates $33.8 million to begin operating the new hospital. To help lower costs, the facility is heated and cooled by 352 geothermal wells drilled 550 feet underground. Andrew Miller, a project executive at Christman Construction, said using this renewable energy will save at least $10,000 a month.
Mary Clare Solky, director of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville, at the facility’s opening on Oct. 7, 2026. Solky said she feels “incredibly supported that mental health care is being prioritized in Michigan.” (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
A connection to nature
Solky said on average, adolescents stay in these long-term care facilities for three to six months. She said adults can stay for up to a year or longer. The two age groups share common spaces, like courtyards, but remain separated. 
The hospital has 12 courtyards, a nondenominational chapel, a music room, art room, movement room, hair salon, group therapy rooms, dining rooms, a gymnasium and patient clinic. The patient clinic includes exam and minor procedure rooms, dental suites and optometry and dietitian offices. 
Adolescent patients will attend a school within the hospital during the day. The school includes classrooms, a media center, a computer center and workrooms. A library and adult education classrooms serve older patients. 
A dental suite at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
Adult patients who are getting ready to leave the hospital can stay in a studio apartment equipped with a kitchen and washer and dryer. 
Safety is a priority, with special door handles, hinges, ceilings and drinking fountains designed to reduce the risk of harm. 
Throughout the hospital, designers wanted to create a connection between indoor and outdoor spaces. David Giroux, senior vice president of Integrated Design Solutions, said the outdoor landscaping, windows and lights were all chosen to bring the outdoors in.
“There’s a lot of evidence to suggest having patients be outdoors or connected with the outdoors aids in their healing,” Giroux said.
This emphasis on the outdoors is evident on the building’s interior walls, which feature blue, orange, pink and purple indigenous flower designs. 
Patients also have the opportunity to interact with the outdoors through the hospital’s horticulture program. They can water, propagate and harvest plants, which include fruits and vegetables. They can also use the vegetables to make meals, such as fried green tomatoes. 
Courtyard at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)
Mental health care challenges
While connection to the outdoors is a focus of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital, an employee at the Reuther facility claimed in 2023 that children weren’t allowed outside for months.
An audit published in 2025 by the Office of the Auditor General found that Michigan’s Office of Recipient Rights was not sufficiently protecting the rights of recipients of mental health services. 
“Almost 30% of sampled complaints alleging abuse, neglect, serious injury or death were not retrieved or actions initiated until between 2 and 12 days after the complainant-provided date,” stated the audit.
State psychiatric hospitals were also found to lack consistent video surveillance and audio recording.
While Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has increased funding for mental health services, as of 2025, Michigan ranked 47 in the nation for access to inpatient psychiatric beds. Federal cuts to Medicaid continue to threaten inpatient psychiatric services.
“We know that in our communities, mental health beds have been reduced,” Solky said. “So this is a step forward for Michigan.”
She said there is a need for more adult facilities like this one across the state. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she said, mental health providers became more aware of their patients’ needs. 
“Looking at how people maybe spoke up more about mental illness, maybe it kind of came out of the closet a little bit, and I believe it allowed our officials to help us prioritize that,” she said. 
The Walter P. Reuther Psychiatric Hospital opened in 1979, and the Hawthorn Center opened in 1965. Solky did not know what the state plans to do with the Reuther building once all the patients are transferred.
Playground at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)An independent living area at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)An inpatient bed at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)A mural photo at the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Acting Michigan Department of Health and Human Services Director Amy Epkey speaks at the opening of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Mary Clare Solky, director of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville, speaks at the facility's opening on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)Dr. George Mellos, senior deputy director for the State Hospitals Administration at the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, at the opening of the Southeast Michigan Psychiatric Hospital in Northville on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Bella Waters/Michigan Advance)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas education board allows local election to consider creating Sherwood School District
description: The Arkansas State Board of Education on Wednesday authorized an election allowing some Pulaski County voters to decide whether to establish a new Sherwood School District.  The measure, which will be decided during the annual school elections on March 2, 2027, would detach the new district from the existing Pulaski County Special School District.  The […]
text:
State Education Board member Randy Henderson (left) and Education Secretary Jacob Oliva (right) listen to public testimony during a state board meeting on Mar. 9, 2023.

(Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas State Board of Education on Wednesday authorized an election allowing some Pulaski County voters to decide whether to establish a new Sherwood School District. 
The measure, which will be decided during the annual school elections on March 2, 2027, would detach the new district from the existing Pulaski County Special School District. 
The election on the new district was proposed in a resolution by the Sherwood Public Education Foundation that the Pulaski County Special School District board adopted last month. The new district would be created by detaching territory based on the Sylvan Hills High School attendance zone. 
Devin Bates, a lawyer for the Pulaski County Special School District, said the detachment has been discussed for more than a decade, but officials couldn’t move forward because of a desegregation order.
A federal judge ended a 43-year desegregation case in February, ruling that the Pulaski County Special School District was now providing equitable facilities to students after years of court supervision. 
Federal judge ends decades-old Little Rock-area school desegregation case

Linda George, Sherwood Public Education Foundation board member, said was “thrilled” by the board’s decision. 
“After 100 years, the community of Sherwood will have the opportunity to make their voices heard and vote on what best represents the goals and vision of their community for their students,” George said in a statement.
The Pulaski County district, one of the largest in the state, has around 11,000 students and its boundaries wrap around the Little Rock and North Little Rock school districts. Under the proposal, about 4,600 students from the current district’s northeast quadrant would join the new Sherwood district. 
Scott Richardson, an attorney for the Sherwood Public Education Foundation, told the state education board Wednesday that he previously helped with the Jacksonville School District’s detachment from the Pulaski County School District. 
Supporters of Jacksonville and Sherwood detachments have cited concern that the Pulaski County Special School District is a large district with many different communities of interest, Richardson said. 
“And those communities of interest feel like their schools would be addressed if those communities could address the conditions they find there,” he said. “I would submit to you that has worked out well in Jacksonville. It’s all new facilities over there…and the schools are functioning well.”
State education board member David Peacock questioned how the split would affect student demographics.
“I spent a lot of time in the military, and you bring a lot of diverse communities together and as a result, the military’s a better organization because of it,” Peacock said. “I understand the desire to do this, but I think there’s also a loss associated with not being the melting pot that we once talked about pretty regularly.”
Jerrod Williams, a consultant for the Pulaski County Special School District, highlighted a feasibility study commissioned by the Sherwood Public Education Foundation that found racial demographics would be similar, with white students making up about a third of the population in both districts. The Black student population would increase from about 46% in Pulaski County to 49% in the new district, according to the report.
Peacock also asked for a breakdown of socioeconomic status.
“I just think it’s important that we look at all the different factors that impact the education, we shouldn’t just focus on race,” he said.
About 75% of students receive free meals at the Pulaski County Special School District, and that would increase to about 85% of students in the Sherwood district, according to the study. 
The March election will be open to voters who reside in the proposed district. If voters approve the detachment, the law allows a two-year transition period to stand up the new district, Williams said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ agency will conduct daily audits to prevent more voter registration errors, governor says
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill says new daily audits at the Motor Vehicle Commission will prevent any more ineligible people from being registered to vote.
text:
Thousands of people who identified themselves as noncitizens were registered to vote after visits to the Motor Vehicle Commission. Gov. Mikie Sherrill says new daily audits will prevent future mistakes. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission will automatically check new voter registrations against customers’ responses before transmitting them to election officials in a bid to prevent erroneous registrations, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Wednesday.
The new procedures come more than two months after Sherrill announced roughly 6,600 people who marked themselves as noncitizens were registered to vote during visits to the Motor Vehicle Commission as a result of what the administration said was a technical glitch.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
“Our investigation is ongoing, we will follow the facts wherever they lead, fix the problems we inherited, do it the right way, and hold those responsible accountable,” Sherrill, a Democrat, said in a statement Wednesday.
The voter registration gaffe elicited criticism from Republican officials here in New Jersey and nationwide who said it verified their claims of widespread voter fraud. Sherrill said about 340 noncitizens ended up casting ballots, and has noted that the problem arose before she became governor in January.
The new daily audit system Sherrill announced Wednesday will compare customers’ responses to newly created voter registration records to ensure the information is accurate and the voter is eligible.
The automated system, which is in the process of implementation, will flag incomplete or contradictory records for manual review. Under the plan, corrected records can only be released once commission staff confirms they match customers’ responses.
The governor said the ongoing review uncovered other registrations affected by a software error caused by Idemia, the vendor that oversaw the commission’s licensing systems, that registered some voters who marked themselves as too young to be eligible. Idemia has said it was not responsible for the erroneous registrations.
About 750 residents were registered after saying they were not eligible to vote because of their age, though all of them entered birth dates that would have made each of them at least 18 years old at the time, Sherrill said.
“No underage person voted as a result of this error,” Sherrill said. “They appear to have pressed the wrong button on the PIN pad by mistake.”
Still, many of those registrations may not be valid. The administration deleted about 380 registrations of voters who cast no ballots and were entered as a result of the age error. It sent another roughly 320 nonvoting registrants for county review.
About 50 people who registered after marking themselves age-ineligible subsequently cast ballots. Those registrations were deleted and forwarded to counties for review.
The review separately found about 340 individuals who were improperly registered at Motor Vehicle Commission prisoner reentry events dating as far back as 2016. Another 60 falsely attested to eligibility while imprisoned for a felony conviction. Their registrations were sent to counties for remediation.
“I said we were going to run a secure and fair election here in New Jersey and I meant it.  In just two and a half months, we conducted this review and are taking sweeping action to secure our voter registration processes and the integrity of our voter rolls, so that New Jerseyans can feel confident about their election system,” Sherrill said.
Sen. Anthony Bucco, the state Senate’s GOP leader, said Sherrill’s updates on the voter registration debacle create more questions than answers. The public should see a full report about the thousands of people improperly registered and the analysis that supports Sherrill’s conclusions, Bucco said.
“We now have even more evidence that there were serious weaknesses in New Jersey’s voter registration system but still do not understand the full story. It is past time to release that report and give the public the facts. We need to stop learning about new problems through piecemeal press releases and start getting real answers, with a legislative review that leaves no stone unturned and ensures New Jersey voters can have confidence in the integrity of their elections,” he said.

name: WyoFile
title: Sublette County deals surprise blow to billionaire developer Joe Ricketts’ resort plans
description:
Commissioners abruptly reverse resort zoning for luxury resort that TD Ameritrade founder has argued is akin to conservation. 
The post Sublette County deals surprise blow to billionaire developer Joe Ricketts’ resort plans appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Sublette County elected officials unexpectedly delivered a major blow Tuesday to billionaire TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts’ yearslong ambitions to transform the Upper Hoback River area into a destination upscale resort.
In a 3-2 vote, commissioners eliminated a 2021 zoning change that carved out 56 acres of Ricketts’ Jackson Fork Ranch in northwest Wyoming for the resort. 

TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts welcomes guests at the August 2026 Saving Yellowstone conference hosted at his ranch. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Last week, the public learned that the Nebraskan financier had renewed his efforts to bring spas and fine dining to Bondurant — the source of considerable consternation for the small community about halfway between Pinedale and Jackson. In 2024, Ricketts halted construction on the resort, citing high costs, after county commissioners declined to waive seasonal protections for elk and moose that prevented construction during the coldest 5.5 months of the year. 
The undoing of Rickett’s renewed plans came suddenly. The five-person Sublette County Board of Commissioners did not include an agenda item in its Tuesday meeting about the billionaire’s plans for an all-inclusive luxury resort. During an earlier iteration of the project, his agents likened the planned facilities to Saratoga’s Brush Creek Ranch, which charges over four figures per night.
The decision came after commissioners went into executive session, when they can discuss matters in private. They emerged toward the end of the daylong meeting, and Commissioner Doug Vickrey made a motion to “initiate the process of terminating” Ricketts’ zoning, and in turn notify the planning and zoning commission and the landowner. 
There was no discussion on the matter before Sublette County Commission Chairman Lynn Bernard and Dave Stephens submitted aye votes. With Commissioners Sam White and Mack Bradley opposed, the resort zoning was rescinded. 
It’s a decision that boiled down to Sublette County’s zoning and development regulations, according to Bernard. Those rules stipulate that property rezoned to accommodate resorts must undergo “substantial development” within two years or the zoning change “shall” revert.
“Because of that, it was revoked,” Bernard told WyoFile. 
Sublette County commissioners referenced language in Section 2 of the county’s zoning and development regulations in their decision to rescind the resort zoning for Rickett’s property that had been approved in 2021. (Sublette County)
In revoking the zoning change, Bernard said, commissioners de facto invalidated a building permit for a lodge, restaurant and bar, a wellness/spa center, 20 guest suites, and a nearly  50,000-square-foot underground parking garage.
That permit application had been submitted in July and was approved administratively in September, the Jackson Hole News&Guide reported.
A spokesperson for Ricketts, whose family owns the Chicago Cubs, provided WyoFile with a statement on Wednesday.
“Private property rights are a cornerstone of our state, and property owners deserve clear rules, a consistent process, and confidence that their rights will be upheld,” Ricketts’ spokesperson Jessica Jaubert said. 
A detail of the main 20-room guest lodge from a landscape plan submitted July 20, 2026, to Sublette County Planning and Zoning for a new development on Joe Ricketts’ property along the Upper Hoback River Road in Bondurant. (Courtesy)
Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich explained to commissioners earlier in the Tuesday meeting why the zoning change hadn’t already been rescinded. 
“Termination is not something that happens automatically,” he said. “It has to go through a public hearing process and everything else.” 
Around the time of their vote, commissioners did not discuss any hearing or public process. 
But Bernard told WyoFile on Wednesday that he “absolutely” believes the commission’s change was legally sound. 
“The time period on that zoning had expired,” he said. 
The setback for Ricketts comes after he received some positive publicity for his conservation-oriented work under a venture called Saving Yellowstone. The billionaire, who was also in the news recently after filing a federal lawsuit alleging he was bilked out of $34 million, has repeatedly argued that developing resorts and getting wealthy tourists to understand conservation are needed to protect the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. 
Bondurant residents who worry the businessman’s plans will run roughshod over their rural, wildlife-rich corner of Wyoming have criticized Rickett’s rationale. 
“The only people who seem to be buying it are some conservationists,” Upper Hoback resident Dan Bailey said, “and that’s just bewildering that those people would drink that Kool-Aid.” 
Bailey’s girding his loins for another prolonged fight over the 85-year-old Ricketts’ development ambitions. Two years ago, when construction was halted, he told WyoFile he was unconvinced that the fight was truly over, and he reiterated those views on Wednesday. 
“They’ll be back,” Bailey said. “We’re not done. That’s for sure.”
Ed’s note: This story has an updated description about the resort plans.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV lawmakers give Flock until Friday to answer questions
description: As West Virginia lawmakers consider how to reign in artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance technology with legislation during their upcoming session, they’ve given Flock Safety a deadline of this week to answer a series of questions to their satisfaction — or else they may use subpoenas or compel witnesses to answer them.
text:
A Flock camera is seen in a parking lot in Morgantown, West Virginia on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)As West Virginia lawmakers consider how to reign in artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance technology with legislation during their upcoming session, they’ve given Flock Safety a deadline of this week to answer a series of questions to their satisfaction — or else they may use subpoenas or compel witnesses to answer them. 
In a letter Monday, members of the House Committee on Government Organization gave Flock Safety until Friday to provide written answers to questions they sent in a letter dated Aug. 14. 
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, and a member of the committee, said Tuesday lawmakers will introduce legislation regarding the technology in 2027, but the committee is trying to gather as much information as it can before crafting “responsible safeguards.”
“The reality is that the technology continues to evolve, and so it creates all sorts of questions ranging from the technological, to, again, just what protocols they have in place to, again just the efficacy of the product altogether,” Leavitt said. 
Lawmakers’ original request included 19 questions from five categories: security incidents and unauthorized access, surveillance scope and data sharing, accuracy and false positive rates, internal oversight and employee access controls, and data governance and infrastructure. 
Delegates asked Flock, for instance, to provide the number of times when raw video footage has been accessed by unauthorized users for each year the company has existed, and what caused the security breach in each instance. 
In a 10-page response from Flock Safety on Sept. 1, Dan Haley, chief legal officer for Flock, wrote a broad response to each of the five categories of questions, but did not include specific answers to many of the questions lawmakers posed.  
“Flock Safety takes the security of customer data, including video and license plate data, extremely seriously,” Haley wrote, in part, under the heading regarding security incidents. “Because Flock operates technology used by thousands of public safety agencies and handles information associated with active criminal investigations, our security program is designed around continuous prevention, detection, testing, investigation and remediation rather than the unrealistic assumption that a system will never experience a security event.
State lawmakers wrote in a response that many of the answers were not sufficient. 
“A general description of your security program is not a substitute for the information we  requested about raw video footage from Flock devices being accessed,” lawmakers wrote in a response Sept. 3. 
Flock said that they would “welcome the chance to provide a briefing to the committee,” but Lawmakers said in a response that a briefing is not acceptable.
“Meeting behind closed doors is no substitute for providing written responses to questions of such clear  public concern — questions all the more relevant since new Flock camera hacking incidents have come to light,” the letter from Monday reads. “Six weeks after our initial August 14, 2026 request, you have failed to produce these answers. As our last letter clearly stated, we do not intend to sit for a briefing with you until Flock Safety has responded in full to our requests. “
The Oct. 5 letter is signed by Leavitt, Ryan Browning, R-Wayne; Patrick Lucas, R-Cabell;  and Committee Chair Chris Phillips, R-Barbour. 
Several West Virginia municipalities across West Virginia have either considered or contracted with Flock Safety to install surveillance systems, including automatic license plate readers and gunshot detection equipment. The American Civil Liberties Union says the technology is “tracking, logging and sharing your movements without a warrant.” 
Flock Safety has been the subject of privacy and constitutional concerns nationally. The Institute for Justice has reportedly identified more than 100 incidents of Flock abuse, including law enforcement stalking romantic partners, wrongfully pulling people over and other misconduct. 
The ACLU of West Virginia is suing the city of Huntington over its five-year contract with the company to provide the surveillance equipment for more than $2.1 million. A Huntington organization opposed to Flock is pursuing a ballot initiative that would require the city to void its contract with the company. 
Leavitt declined to mention what specific safeguards lawmakers are considering, but said he expects a “very robust discussion” during the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January.
“What has kind of united everybody from all different perspectives on these questions is that Flock needs to answer the requests that we’ve made so that we are best informed to make those decisions,” Leavitt said. 
The request comes about two months after Kevin Kane, director of government affairs for Flock, gave a presentation to the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization during the August legislative interim meetings. 
“You had, really, two different categories of challenges there,” Leavitt said of Kane’s testimony. “One is that a number of detailed questions they simply said ‘we’ll get back to you on that,’ and they clearly intimated they’d like to have a private meeting instead.”
Leavitt said lawmakers believe the information should be provided publicly because the issue has so much public interest, and public interest plays a role in how lawmakers legislate.
“The second real challenge is that there were several different areas where Flock’s representative provided certain information that then, on later questioning, really broke down, and rather gave the impression that he was trying to mislead the Legislature.”
Leavitt said many West Virginians have questions about Flock. Some people are adamantly opposed to the technology, while others are learning about it for the first time, he said. It’s important that lawmakers understand it before regulating it, he said. 
“We want to make sure that we don’t craft the law in such a way that it doesn’t really actually get at what all of the vulnerabilities and issues are,” he said. “So that requires us really honing the depths of this as much as we can, so that we make sure that we do as good a job as possible in the legislation that we pass.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Nashville court rules state must preserve all records from botched Tennessee execution
description: ​A Davidson County Chancery judge ordered Tennessee officials on Wednesday to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution of Christa Pike. ​Chancellor I’Ashea Myles ruled that the Tennessee Department of Correction must “preserve all evidence” related to the failed execution of Pike by two rounds of lethal injection last week. ​Myles’ ruling comes[...]
text:
Randy Spivey, an attorney for Christa Pike, gives an update on her condition following Tennessee’s botched execution on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)​A Davidson County Chancery judge ordered Tennessee officials on Wednesday to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution of Christa Pike.
​Chancellor I’Ashea Myles ruled that the Tennessee Department of Correction must “preserve all evidence” related to the failed execution of Pike by two rounds of lethal injection last week.
​Myles’ ruling comes one day after Pike woke up, with her lawyers confirming she was “confused, “angry” and talking at a local hospital.
​Randy Spivey, an attorney for Pike, said she is battling a blood clot, pneumonia and severe swelling in her arms and hands, and she has a long way to go before recovering.
​“On Monday night, it was our understanding [Pike] was brain dead and life support would be removed the next day,” said Spivey at a news conference. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone… [she] woke up and was talking.”
​Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of her classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 years old when she and her then-17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in a wooded area in Knoxville. Shipp, ineligible for the death penalty because of his age, got a life sentence.
​May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, recently described her daughter to WIBR Knoxville as compassionate and playful, and said she is saddened that the execution often overshadows her identity.
​Pike, now 50, was set to be executed on Sept. 30. She would have been the first woman to be put to death by Tennessee in more than two centuries. But on the night of her scheduled execution, the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed on two separate attempts.
​By protocol, after the second failed attempt, she was transported from Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville,where the execution was taking place, to the hospital where she remains.
​Tennessee changed its lethal injection protocol in 2022, following a review of its effectiveness by Gov. Bill Lee. The state resumed lethal injections in 2025, executing four people over the span of the next 15 months.
Luke Ihnen, an attorney for Christa Pike, argued in court on Oct. 7,  2026, that the state should preserve all records of her failed execution the previous week. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The state also failed in its execution of Tony Carruthers in May. ​Lee stepped in to stop Carruthers’ execution when physicians tried and failed for more than an hour to insert intravenous lines to begin the process in what was later described as “bloody torture.”
​Carruthers was granted a one-year reprieve by Lee, who has so far made no announcement about Pike’s status on death row.
Lee tapped former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton to lead an independent review of the state Department of Correction’s process in Pike’s botched execution, and has paused all executions through the end of the year.
​In January, the term-limited Lee will leave office. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee for governor, and other Republican legislative leaders discussed bringing back the electric chair for executions.
​State lawmakers are expected to take up the issue during next year’s legislative session, which starts in January.
​In the months leading up to Pike’s execution, her lawyer warned state officials that past difficulty with finding her veins to draw blood could lead to a more painful, potentially unsuccessful attempt to kill her.
​Luke Ihnen, a second Pike attorney, argued in court Wednesday that records about her attempted execution needed to be preserved, because the public could “not take the state’s word.”
​“Their word is shrouded in secrecy and legal jargon in attempts to obfuscate what really happened,” Ihnen said.
Will Ayers, a lawyer with the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office, said in court the state was already planning to preserve the evidence from the execution and was willing to work with Pike’s attorneys.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Superintendent candidate Foss supports teacher bonuses as temporary fix, not long-term solution
description: Superintendent of Public Instruction candidate Tracy Foss supports annual bonuses for teachers, but sees the proposal as a temporary fix that does not address underlying education and teacher retention issues. Foss, who received support from the Democratic-NPL Party, responded Wednesday to a proposal announced this week by Superintendent Levi Bachmeier and R[...]
text:
Superintendent of Public Instruction candidate Tracy Foss speaks about a proposed annual teacher bonus program during a press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, in Fargo. (Photo courtesy of the Dem-NPL Party)Superintendent of Public Instruction candidate Tracy Foss supports annual bonuses for teachers, but sees the proposal as a temporary fix that does not address underlying education and teacher retention issues.
Foss, who received support from the Democratic-NPL Party, responded Wednesday to a proposal announced this week by Superintendent Levi Bachmeier and Republican lawmakers to establish an annual teacher bonus.
The proposal, which the lawmakers said they plan to introduce in the 2027 session, would award annual bonuses to public and private school teachers from a portion of the earnings of the Common Schools Trust Fund.
Annual bonuses proposed for North Dakota teachers to improve recruitment, retention

Foss said she does not believe the bonus program will solve the state’s teacher retention problem on its own.
“Not having enough teachers is a symptom of underlying issues within our education system that are causing teachers to leave and individuals to choose other professions,” Foss said during a press conference.
One of those issues, she said, is teacher pay, but burnout and extra duties imposed on teachers also play a large role in educators leaving the profession.
The bonuses do not address the larger issue of fully funding the state’s public school system, she said. 
“We need to fully fund public schools, and I do not want anything getting in the way of that responsibility,” Foss said. 
She added first-year teachers, teachers who took time off the previous year and teachers who took an alternative route to teaching would not be eligible under the bonus program. According to the proposal, teachers must be licensed and have completed a full teaching contract during the previous school year to qualify for the bonus awarded in the fall.
“Unfortunately, the current bill is just a Band-Aid to the teacher retention and recruitment problem and not a solution,” she said. If elected, Foss said she would work with lawmakers to tweak the bill to address some of her concerns before January.
Foss said she does not believe private school teachers should qualify for the state-funded bonus program.
The superintendent position is on the Nov. 3 ballot. While the race is nonpartisan, Foss received a letter of support from the Democratic-NPL Party and Bachmeier has said he identifies as a Republican.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Judge dismisses YouTuber’s defamation lawsuit against Iowa photographer
description: An NCAA wrestling official who runs a YouTube channel dedicated to youth wrestling has failed in his bid to sue an Iowa photographer he claimed had defamed him. The lawsuit was filed late last year in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa by Nima Gharavi, a YouTuber and self-described “registered wrestling official” […]
text:
(Photo by David Talukdar/Getty Images)An NCAA wrestling official who runs a YouTube channel dedicated to youth wrestling has failed in his bid to sue an Iowa photographer he claimed had defamed him.
The lawsuit was filed late last year in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa by Nima Gharavi, a YouTuber and self-described “registered wrestling official” with the National Collegiate Athletic Association, Illinois High School Athletic Association, Illinois Elementary School Association and other entities.
Gharavi sued Allyson Schwab of the Cedar Falls area, a photographer who allegedly has a substantial social media following for the youth wrestling content she produces. A federal judge recently dismissed the case, in part because it dealt with statements of opinion, rather than factual assertions, that were made by Schwab.
In his lawsuit, Gharavi alleged that for many years he has created videos of youth wrestling matches, initially for the exclusive use of wrestling officials. Gharavi says he subsequently created a public YouTube channel to share his passion for the sport and called it Midwest Wrestle, which has more than 175,000 followers on YouTube.
At some point, Gharavi claimed, he realized that websites with which he has no connection had copied, without his knowledge or permission, video content from Midwest Wrestle and posted it to third-party websites that contained pornography or other objectionable content.
In December 2023 and January 2024, the lawsuit alleged, Schwab published multiple posts to her X (formerly Twitter) account, encouraging parents to watch out for “suggestive” online videos of youth wrestling matches that were generating hundreds of thousands of views.
“This makes me sick and why I got this convo going,” Schwab allegedly wrote in one post. “So many parents don’t know their kids are on someone’s YouTube… No reason a 46kg youth girls match should have 2.6 million views … The kids think it’s normal to have 400k views on their video from a local youth or hs tournament…”
The lawsuit stated that while Schwab’s posts did not explicitly name Gharavi or Midwest Wrestle, details in her posts corresponded to Midwest Wrestle’s viewership. For example, the lawsuit claimed, Midwest Wrestle was the only YouTube channel to have garnered 2.6 million views of a 46kg youth girls wrestling match.
The lawsuit goes on to allege that several athletic organizations then canceled or declined to renew their contracts with Gharavi, a third party published Gharavi’s home address on social media alongside the false allegations, and Gharavi was the target of threats and an attempted home break-in.
The lawsuit sought unspecified damages for defamation and invasion of privacy by painting Gharavi in a false light.
Federal judge dismisses lawsuit
Recently, U.S. District Judge Leonard Strand dismissed the lawsuit for failing to state a legal claim against Schwab.
In his ruling, Strand noted that to make a claim for defamation, Gharavi must allege sufficient facts to show that Schwab made a false and damaging public statement about him.
“For starters,” Strand ruled, “there is a significant issue whether Schwab sufficiently identified Gharavi (in her statements). Although she need not explicitly mention Gharavi by name for him to maintain a per se claim, there must be sufficient identifiable details in the statement that a third-party could reasonably understand it to concern him.”
Strand ruled that the fact that other parties had linked Gharavi to Schwab’s statements “might count for something,” but added that “nothing about the posts themselves clearly identify that they are about Gharavi.”
Even if Schwab had identified Gharavi as the target of her posts, Strand found, Gharavi’s defamation claim still would fail. “Pornography is not mentioned nor naturally insinuated from any of Schwab’s posts,” Strand ruled, “much less allegations of creating or peddling child pornography… Nor do the posts contain any clear language besmirching Gharavi’s professional reputation.”
Strand also noted one “difficulty for Gharavi comes down to whether Schwab’s posts are fact or opinion. Expressions of opinion relating to matters of public concern receive full constitutional protection and cannot sustain a defamation claim… On their face, Schwab’s posts appear to offer her opinions on what visual media is being published by others.”
Strand ruled that while he agreed with Gharavi that public accusations that he had engaged in the production of child pornography could amount to extreme and outrageous conduct, “Schwab’s public posts make no such assertions.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former SC governor’s childhood home, Pawleys Island beachfront up for preservation
description: The final resting place of former Gov. Robert McNair and beach front property in Pawleys Island are among SC lands slated for protection.
text:
South Carolina is seeking to purchase 3,400 acres of the former Arcadia rice plantation in Georgetown County for a wildlife preserve and beach access. (Photo courtesy of Ducks Unlimited and Holstein Appraisals)COLUMBIA — The family farm of former Gov. Robert McNair and beachfront property in Pawleys Island are among the latest lands slated for protection under South Carolina conservation programs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A state spending oversight panel gave the initial nod this week to protecting from development the 2,640-acre Ballsdam Plantation along the Santee River in Berkley County and 3,400 acres of the former Arcadia rice plantation along the Waccamaw Neck.
Proposals calls for a conservation easement to safeguard the Berkeley County property, which includes the gravesite of McNair, governor from April 1965 to January 1971. And in Georgetown County, the public would gain beach access to the narrow peninsula between the Atlantic Ocean and the Waccamaw River.
The projects were among 18 forest, wetland and farmland conservation efforts, totaling nearly 21,400 acres statewide, considered for various stages of approval Tuesday by the legislators who sit on the review panel.
Of all the projects, the Pawleys Island property drew the greatest scrutiny from legislators.
A state agency focused on flood reduction received permission to spend $118 million — alongside an additional $3.5 million from the state’s Conservation Bank — to purchase the property in an effort to prevent increased flooding of the coastal retirement destination located south of Myrtle Beach.
The state also plans to apply for a federal grant to recover an estimated $8 million to $10 million of the cost.
SC put $274M into flood response and prevention. Here’s where the money is going.

Formed in the wake of catastrophic flooding in 2015, the state Office of Resilience has taken on 13 such projects statewide, using $200 million in state funds set aside specifically for conserving land, the agency’s chief, Ben Duncan, told legislators. After this purchase, the agency will have just $4.5 million left in the fund.
The Arcadia property marks the largest purchase to date.
Preventing development
“This is a pretty sizable undertaking,” said Senate Finance Chairman Harvey Peeler.
Developers had sought to build on the property, filing a plan in 2002 that promised single-family homes and condos, a retirement village and a golf resort, as well as a hotel, 400,000 square feet of commercial space and a 1.26 million-square-foot office park. The developers renewed those efforts last year.
But with no movement on the development to date, the family that owns the property has decided to sell it to the state instead, turning it into a wildlife preserve run by the state Department of Natural Resources, similar to Botany Bay on Edisto Island.
Georgetown County Council and the Georgetown County School District Board of Trustees are supportive, Duncan said.
In addition to the property’s half mile of beachfront with high, protective sand dunes, there are also nearly 2,500 acres of wetlands that can store and hold back floodwaters in the case of a hurricane, more than 1,000 forested acres and 100-acre fishing lake, Duncan said.
“It’s a big protector of the inland,” he said.
Historic plantation among 1,700 acres in conservation projects SC considers buying

If the property were developed instead, the sponge-like qualities of the land would be replaced by rooftops and asphalt.
“Think about the traffic, all the infrastructure that needs to be put in,” Duncan said.
There’s also a possibility of research work on the property, similar to the Baruch Institute of Coastal Ecology and Forestry Science operated by Clemson University at nearby Hobcaw Barony.
“The brief time I was there, I saw wild pigs running around, two foxes and a turtle nesting area on the beach. So, it is a strong ecosystem,” Duncan said.
Legislators’ biggest concern was ensuring all South Carolinians, whether from Peeler’s Upstate hometown of Gaffney or Democratic Rep. Gilda Cobb-Hunter’s hometown of Orangeburg, could access and enjoy the property once it’s under state control.
A governor’s childhood home
As for Ballsdam Plantation, conservation of the property is expected to protect both its wildlife and historic value.
Located on the “French Santee,” the property is in an area initially settled by French Huguenots during Colonial times. They were the largest group of Huguenots, outside of Charles Town. By 1690, 80 families of French origin had settled there.
The Rev. Pierre Robert, believed to be the first Calvanistic minister in South Carolina, was an early owner. Then, Elias Ball, the property’s namesake, settled there sometime in the 1700s. After him came Dr. John Saunders Palmer, one of the signers in December 1860 of the Ordinance of Succession, which declared South Carolina’s separation from the Union.
McNair’s father purchased the property in 1933 and passed it on to his son, a World War II veteran first elected in 1950 to the state House representing Allendale County. Voters elected him lieutenant governor in 1962, and he ascended to governor in 1965 when Donald Russell resigned to become a U.S. senator. McNair was then elected governor in 1966 and re-elected in 1968, giving him six years in office at a time when gubernatorial terms lasted only two years.
The Democrat, who died in 2007, was at the state’s helm amid the Civil Rights Movement and desegregation.
SC considers protecting nearly 6,000 acres ‘of critical importance’ near Grand Strand river

In legal circles, McNair’s name is perhaps more widely known for the law firm he founded.
After leaving the Governor’s Mansion, he established the law firm of McNair, Konduros & Courley in 1971, which became the massive McNair Law Firm with more than 130 attorneys spanning the Carolinas. Birmingham, Alabama-based Burr & Forman purchased the firm in 2018.
He and his wife are buried in a family cemetery on the property. Pineland Cottage, which still stands today on the property, was McNair’s birthplace and childhood home.
The McNair family now uses Pineland Cottage as a family retreat and hunting cabin. The property has 15 food plots for the deer, turkey and wild boar that live there.
The state will pay the family $1.2 million for a conservation easement keeping the land as is.



Other projects on the list included:

Conservation easements on a pair of tracts in the Gulllah Geechee community of St. Helena Island, including 158 acres of farmland and 121 acres of waterfront and tidal marsh
A working farmland easement for 2,858-acre Tomlinson Farms near Lynchburg, which operates a farm stand and produces row crops, as well as raising turkeys and cattle
A working farmland easement for 1,463 acres of Windham Family Farms near Lamar. The farm produces corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton and peanuts.
A working farmland easement for a 727-acre beef cattle and poultry farm in Oconee County
Preliminary plans to expand the Turtle Island Wildlife Management Area in Jasper County, adding 2,593 acres
A new, 52-acre wildlife perserve near Pickens
A 316-acre expansion of the Little Pee Dee Heritage Preserve- Wildlife Management Area in Horry County
A new, 435-acre wildlife preserve to protect the second tallest peak overlooking the North Saluda River Valley
32 acres in Greenville County allowing trout fishing on the Saluda River
A 38-acre expansion of Jones Gap State Park
Preservation of 595 acres along the Little Pee Dee River in Horry County
Preservation of five properties, totaling 9,338 acres, along the Waccamaw River in Horry County

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear relaxes rules on red-dyed diesel to help farmers
description: Gov. Andy Beshear has declared a state of emergency for Thursday, Oct. 8, that will allow Kentucky farmers and truckers to use untaxed or red-dyed diesel fuel on public roadways to help with high prices during the fall harvest. The move follows a request to Beshear by Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell, asking for that action […]
text:
Gas prices have risen during the U.S. war with Iran and are averaging around $4.06 per gallon across Kentucky, up from $2.9 a year ago.  In October, diesel prices are closer to 6.19.
(Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Gov. Andy Beshear has declared a state of emergency for Thursday, Oct. 8, that will allow Kentucky farmers and truckers to use untaxed or red-dyed diesel fuel on public roadways to help with high prices during the fall harvest.
The move follows a request to Beshear by Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell, asking for that action after President Trump issued an executive order to defer federal taxes on the fuel and allowed the fuel to be used on public roadways.
“The President’s war of choice and unlawful tariffs have caused prices to skyrocket for hardworking Americans – including here in Kentucky – and I have taken urgent action to help families across the commonwealth, including farmers, by lowering gas and diesel prices, suspending the gas tax increase and more,” Beshear said in a statement. “This has been a priority for me, and I am glad to see other leaders recognize that steps need to be taken to help hardworking families across our commonwealth and country.”
The price of diesel and gas have gone up in recent months because of global political conflicts, like Trump’s war in Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supplies are transported.
On Tuesday, Shell told the Kentucky Lantern that a lot of Kentucky farmers already have tanks on their farm for red-dyed diesel, so Shell expects many of them to go into “immediate use.” He added that some issues after the executive order expires, like some of the dye still being in tanks once the prohibition goes back into effect, still needs to be worked out.
Beshear’s order will continue until the end of the war in Iran or the expiration of the President’s executive order on Dec. 31, 2026, whichever is earliest, his office said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: If Democrats win, Himes says Trump won’t ‘accept’ election results
description: Trump wrote Sunday that “Voting in America is CORRUPT” Jim Himes said Trump is trying to cast doubt on the integrity of the midterm elections.
text:
Congressman Jim Himes, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, warned Wednesday of efforts to undermine faith in U.S. elections by foreign powers and one domestic one: President Donald J. Trump.
“We don’t know what the results will be. But if Polymarket is to be believed, it’s not going to be a good Election Day for the president,” Himes said, referring to the prediction markets. “And the president has never accepted the results of an election that he didn’t like.”
Himes pointed to efforts by Trump to sow doubt about the integrity of the midterm elections, beginning with a speech in July claiming evidence of foreign interference.
“Why is he doing these things? Maybe he’s just being Trump, but one assumes that he’s doing these things because he wants to lay the foundation to make the case that an election in which he gets his clock cleaned is not a fair election,” Himes said.
On social media Sunday, Trump contrasted results in Brazil’s centrally-run presidential election with counting in U.S. cities that can stretch past midnight on election days. He ignored that U.S. elections are run by local officials, with paper ballots used in every state but Louisiana.
“In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other U.S. Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate,” Trump wrote in his post. “Voting in America is CORRUPT!!!”
The president’s press office had no immediate comment on Himes’ briefing, but the White House has a standing reply on its elections integrity page: “Ensuring the integrity of our elections is fundamental to preserving trust in American democracy.”
The Himes’ briefing was scheduled days ago, but it largely reflected the same sentiments expressed by Republican political operatives in a Newsweek story posted Monday.
“If Republicans lose both Houses of Congress, expect Donald Trump to make several harsh statements,” Matt Klink, a GOP political consultant, told Newsweek. “He’s already begun writing the excuse before a single ballot is cast.”
Himes, who represents the 4th Congressional District, briefed reporters at his district office in Stamford. As the ranking Democrat, Himes is in line to become chair of the House Intelligence Committee if Democrats regain the majority.
Foreign powers have a long history of trying to influence U.S. elections, but there is no credible evidence they have tried to interfere through efforts to change vote counts or disrupt the casting of ballots, Himes said.
“In my world, we draw a distinction between interference, which is actually trying to get in to mess with the results or the mechanics of the election, and influence, which foreign powers do and have done,” Himes said.
Himes said a classified report by the director of national intelligence confirms the continued efforts to influence, not interfere. He said he could not offer details, given it was classified.
“But that report indicated that it’s kind of same old, same old. Meaning the Russians are sort of thinking about how they could influence — not interfere — but influence the elections there,” Himes said. “It won’t surprise you to know they’re very focused on maybe individual politicians who are very pro-Ukraine.”
In a prime time speech in July, Trump said cheating and interference in elections should be virtually impossible. 
“Unfortunately, the system we have today falls catastrophically short of that standard,” Trump said. “Tonight, I’m announcing the immediate declassification and release of critical intelligence, revealing shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure.”
One of the declassified reports reflected China’s “illicit” acquisition of 220 million voter files, material that is generally available in the U.S. There was no suggestion of China trying to delete or otherwise taint voting rolls.
Himes and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., his Democratic counterpart on the Select Committee on Intelligence in the Senate, wrote last week to Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, pressing him to meet statutory duties to keep Congress and the public abreast of election threats.
“This process should include the declassification and public issuance of the Intelligence Community Assessment (ICA) about foreign threats to the 2024 presidential election. The lack of a public ICA contravenes the law and undercuts needed transparency about IC efforts to keep our elections secure from outside interference,” Himes and Warner wrote.
Without saying so explicitly, they suggested that includes any assessment that might contradict the president.
“A statement noting the absence of indications of significant foreign interference efforts is just as important as a statement exposing any such activities,” Himes and Warner wrote. “Regardless, the American people should receive as much information as we can responsibly provide prior to the election.”
Famously, Trump fired Christopher Krebs, the Department of Homeland Security official who had pronounced the 2020 election as secure, immediately after Trump’s contested loss to Joe Biden. Himes suggested it was a prelude to Trump’s efforts to deny the election results, climaxing in the riot at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 that briefly delayed certification of Biden’s victory.
More recently, the Trump administration laid off nearly one-third of the staff at Krebs’ former agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA.
Himes said he hears from Democrats concerned that Trump somehow will work to block Democrats from taking their seats in Congress. Himes said he fears potential disruptions at the polls, but not a repeat of Jan. 6.
“What’s radically different now is that the president no longer has any meaningful public sentiment on his side, right? His numbers are in the toilet. That was not true on January 6, 2021,” Himes said. 
“A president who is despised by two-thirds of the American population is a much less scary force than one who has the support of 60% of the population,” Himes said. “So public sentiment really matters, and it is not on his side.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Southaven Police Department took millions from Musk-backed companies for drones and Flock cameras
description: A sign banning drones and droids outside a construction site leading to SpaceXAI’s gas power plant on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SOUTHAVEN — Organizations linked to Elon Musk donated more than $3 million to the Southaven Police Department between December and February, as Musk’s SpaceXAI sought approval for a data center in the city amid increasing public hostility toward the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. 
The donations, which came in two transactions, are part of a wider pattern in which companies and nonprofits affiliated with Musk have donated to public agencies and community organizations in locations important to SpaceXAI’s business deals. 
Southaven residents expressed concern on social media that the donations, made in the same period that SpaceXAI and the city negotiated key aspects of a data center deal, presented a possible conflict of interest. Mayor Darren Musselwhite called this perception “simply just not true.” He said that companies commonly donate to support communities where they operate and that Southaven has accepted only money that helps the community at large.


Since August 2025, Southaven has been home to a gas plant that powers SpaceXAI’s largest data center, Colossus II, just across the state line in Memphis. Southaven residents started complaining about noise and pollution soon after turbines were installed, a concern that has led to at least two lawsuits.
Against this backdrop, Gov. Tate Reeves announced in January that SpaceXAI, then called xAI, would invest $20 billion to build a data center in Southaven, the third for the company and the first in Mississippi. Reeves called it the “largest economic development project in Mississippi’s history.”
In the weeks leading to the governor’s announcement, two organizations linked to Musk donated a combined $3.23 million to the Southaven Police Department.
Trucks and cars line up to enter a construction site on Tulane Rd on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026, where SpaceXAI has a power plant and is building another data center. Residents say traffic in the area has increased recently.  Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceXAI, sent the city $1.38 million, earmarked for the police department. A donation agreement, signed in February by Musselwhite, contained a “no quid pro quo” clause, acknowledging that “no goods or services were provided in exchange.” 
A city clerk signed a receipt for the gift on Dec. 17, the day after the Board of Aldermen approved a memorandum of understanding between the city and SpaceXAI relating to the Southaven data center. The memorandum shows MZX Tech will separately contribute $3.46 million to the city to widen and resurface roads near the power plant and the developing data center, “due to the use and strain that MZX’s operations will cause and require of the City’s infrastructure.” The city sent MZX Tech an invoice for that amount on Dec. 17. 
In an email, Musselwhite confirmed that MZX Tech made contributions to improve traffic flow. He called the $1.38 million donation an “unrelated transaction.”
Signs by the side of the road direct cars to Macrohard and Macroharder, SpaceXAI’s second and third data center on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Residents say traffic in the area has increased. Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
A second donation to the police department, for $1.85 million, came from the Musk Foundation, a nonprofit started by Musk and his brother in 2001. A representative from the foundation reached out to the police department late last year offering the grant opportunity, according to Musselwhite. 
“We were made aware that this organization likes to use grant funding to enhance public safety in communities where their ‘for-profit’ companies operate,” Musselwhite said in an email to Mississippi Today. “Public safety grants are not unusual and the City has taken advantage of these for many years.”  
A grant agreement signed by the city finance director on Dec. 29 specified the money would be used to purchase “critical equipment for the Southaven Police Department,” including Flock cameras and an autonomous drone system.
Mississippi Today emailed representatives from the Musk Foundation, MZX Tech and SpaceXAI to seek comment.
Seals for the Southaven Police Department on the doors to their headquarters in Southaven, Miss. on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026.  Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
The combined $3.23 million in donations are a significant windfall for the Southaven Police Department, which had a $21 million budget in 2024, according to the city’s most recent annual audit. 
The department has since used grant money to buy 13 Dodge Durango SUVs for about $540,000 and a Flock drone system for $250,000, among other expenses. The Board of Aldermen also approved the purchase of five Dodge Ram trucks for about $195,000. 
Across the country, Flock has faced widespread criticism for its automated license plate readers, which use high-speed cameras to capture and store billions of license plates a month. 
MZX Tech also approached the city with another opportunity. It wanted a 51-acre lot next to the existing SpaceXAI power plant, a site owned by the city that once housed a police and fire training center. In exchange, MZX Tech agreed to give the city a different plot of land and $40 million for a new training facility, Musselwhite said in an Aug. 18 Board of Aldermen meeting. 
“It was an easy decision to accept this deal,” Musselwhite said in that meeting. “It’s going to be a win-win for the city.”
A truck approaches a closed construction site on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026, where SpaceXAI has had a power plant since August 2025. In response to resident noise complaints, SpaceXAI has accelerated plans to convert temporary gas turbines into permanent ones, the mayor said in a meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
Residents sued SpaceXAI in June. A few weeks after the class action was filed, Musk announced on X that SpaceXAI would offer half-price Starlink internet to residents of Memphis and the Southaven area. 
These donations and deals differ from fee-in-lieu agreements, where companies looking to establish data centers have signed agreements with local governments to pay lower property taxes as an incentive to invest in their communities. The city of Southaven signed a fee-in-lieu agreement with SpaceXAI for the data center on Jan. 9, the day after the governor’s public announcement. 
The Musk Foundation’s donations to the Southaven Police Department are unusual, given the causes the foundation publicly promotes. 
On its website — which contains just 32 words in plain text — the foundation states that it supports renewable energy, space exploration, pediatric research, science and the development of safe artificial intelligence. 
The exterior of the Southaven Police Department headquarters in Southaven, Miss. on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026.  Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
More than three-quarters of the foundation’s donations went to Musk’s own companies in 2024, according to an analysis last year by The New York Times. That year, the Musk Foundation’s largest beneficiary was The Foundation, also known as X Foundation, another nonprofit associated with Musk. 
The remaining donations, such as gifts to MIT and a nonprofit organization promoting girls in robotics, often align with Musk’s scientific interests. Others seem to coincide with his business interests. 
In March 2021, Musk announced on Twitter: “Am donating $20M to Cameron County schools & $10M to City of Brownsville for downtown revitalization.” An hour and a half earlier, a Starship rocket had exploded in Cameron County, Texas, where Brownsville is the county seat. The donations were made through the Musk Foundation. 
Tax filings from 2002 to 2024 show the foundation donated directly to a police department once in that period: $15,000 to the Travis County Sheriff’s Office in Texas in 2024. 
Signs for SpaceXAI’s second and third data centers, Macrohard and Macroharder, near the Southaven power plant on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
The foundation sometimes donated five-figure sums indirectly to police departments through affiliated groups such as the Los Angeles Police Foundation, a private nonprofit. The Los Angeles Police Department has used police foundation money, although not necessarily from the Musk Foundation, to purchase surveillance technology, including from Palantir and Flock. 
Donations made by the foundation from 2025 onward, such as the $1.85 million grant to the Southaven Police Department and any other police department, are not yet public. Southaven Police Chief Seth Kern said several other police departments around the country had also received a grant from the foundation.
In January, the Musk Foundation sent $50,000 to the Memphis Police Association, the union for Memphis police officers, according to the vice president, John Covington, who posted about the donation on Facebook. “Out of the blue, one of Elon Musk’s assistants reached out to the Memphis Police Association,” Covington wrote. “There were no strings attached.”
A Southaven Police Department car is parked outside their headquarters in Southaven, Miss. on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026. Credit: Julie Lee/Mississippi Today
