title: Documents show DHS probed nonprofits, obtained millions of records in hunt for noncitizen voters
text: The Department of Homeland Security obtained tens of millions of unspecified records as part of a sweeping nationwide effort to find voter fraud, according to internal DHS reports, and weighed using undercover agents to investigate voter registration efforts by nonprofit groups.The reports from May and June by Homeland Security Investigations, a sub-agency of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, provide updates on its “election integrity” investigations. They are included in a trove of documents obtained by the pro-democracy group Democracy Forward through a records request and released Wednesday.The HSI reports detail an expansive review of nonprofit organizations involved in voter registration. A June 1 report says 82 “NGOs” — nongovernmental organizations — had been reviewed in Pennsylvania alone. Groups in Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey and Ohio also came under scrutiny.The June 1 report describes the potential for undercover operations, and refers to efforts across Homeland Security to identify organizations that “may be predatory in nature, particularly those suspected of illegal alien registration and voter encouragement." Organizations in New Jersey and Pennsylvania remained areas of focus, the report says.“The objective is to determine potential opportunities to leverage UC (undercover) resources, including the possible deployment of undercover agents (UCAs), to support investigative efforts in the field,” the report says.Overall, the records offer a window into the Trump administration’s push to root out voter fraud, and especially noncitizen voting, ahead of the midterm elections. While a few months old, they suggest that finding noncitizen voters was an active focus within Homeland Security Investigations, along with identifying any organizations suspected of registering noncitizens to vote.Noncitizen votingNoncitizen voting is a rare occurrence, studies have consistently found. The Justice Department has brought a few dozen cases this year, and U.S Attorney General Todd Blanche in late September announced indictments against 10 noncitizens over allegations of unlawfully voting. But the census reports 154 million people voted in the 2024 election.With early voting beginning across many states, Trump’s bid to assert authority over voting has largely failed. The U.S. Supreme Court blocked his plans to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail ballots and the SAVE America Act, which would require voters to show proof of citizenship, stalled in Congress.But Democrats, voting rights groups and some election officials are concerned Trump may take more extreme action in the coming weeks. They have braced for possible federal interference, including the prospect of ICE or other federal agents deploying to the polls (Homeland Security denies any plans to target polling places).“This trove of ICE documents provides chilling new insights into the breadth and depth of the Trump-Vance administration’s efforts to pursue baseless claims of widespread election fraud and assert greater federal control over elections ahead of the 2026 midterms,” Hart Wood, senior oversight counsel at Democracy Forward, said in a statement.Homeland Security and ICE didn’t respond to questions on Wednesday.At a news conference last week to announce indictments against alleged noncitizen voters in Minnesota, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Trump administration would never allow the votes of noncitizens to cancel out the votes of American citizens. He said that only citizens should be electing the country’s leaders.“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: We will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” Mullin said.Nonprofits reviewed, researched The reports in the records obtained by Democracy Forward describe efforts by HSI to research and review an array of nonprofit groups. In some instances, HSI appeared satisfied after its examination. The June 1 report notes that research was completed on approximately 41 non-governmental organizations in New Jersey, with “no derogatory information” found. Research on 20 nonprofit funds linked to a Washington, D.C.-based charitable foundation also turned up nothing, the report notes.But the report also says the Pennsylvania chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations was “flagged for further investigation.” CAIR is one of the country’s leading Muslim civil rights groups.Ahmet Selim Tekelioglu, CAIR Pennsylvania executive director, in a statement said the organization’s civic engagement programs have expanded over the years and include voter registration efforts that seek to ensure Muslim Americans are empowered to vote and fully engaged in the civic process."Our voter registration program follows all applicable voter registration rules and requirements,” Tekelioglu said.Education Minnesota, an educators union, is named in the June 1 report as one of 22 organizations that HSI was beginning to research at the time. Monica Byron, Education Minnesota’s president, said the organization learned of the investigation on Tuesday because of Democracy Forward.Byron said the group shares Democracy Forward’s concerns about potential government surveillance of lawful voter registration activities. “We do not know the details of any investigation into our union, but we will not be deterred in encouraging all eligible members to exercise their right to vote in the upcoming election,” Byron said in a statement.Tens of millions of recordsThe HSI reports show that Heather Honey, a DHS official who came to prominence denying President Donald Trump’s 2020 election loss, obtained 48.4 million records through “independent sources of information.” Additionally, HSI drew upon some 50.6 million records from the Department of Justice.The exact nature of the records isn’t described, but the DOJ has sued dozens of states for voter records, including sensitive personal information such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The department hasn’t won any of the lawsuits, but at least 16 states have voluntarily provided the data.The Supreme Court ruled in September that states can use a powerful Homeland Security program called SAVE to help identify possible noncitizen voters after voting rights groups sued to block its use, alleging that it often relies on inaccurate data and has a track record of wrongly flagging U.S. citizens. The decision’s impact on the midterms is expected to be minimal because most states are already too close to a federal election to conduct mass purges of voters.But the HSI reports suggest that while the legal fight over SAVE was playing out in the courts, Homeland Security was nevertheless analyzing a vast collection of records for signs of voter fraud.HSI’s June 1 report says 26,563 records derived from ICE had been prioritized for “downstream vetting,” with a focus on Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Ohio and Pennsylvania. Priority states for HSI’s review of Justice Department records included those states, as well as Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia and Texas.The report notes that records were sent to iLab — an apparent reference to HSI’s Innovation Lab — for “secondary enrichment and identification of high-value targets.”Jacob Fischler contributed to this report.

description: Staff for the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission are asking commissioners to authorize a formal investigation into the state’s largest electric provider after widespread customer complaints of exceedingly expensive bills. In a Tuesday filing, they wrote that electric provider PNM in July began estimating residential customer bills, rather than obtaining[...]
text:
Staff for the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission are seeking an investigation into the state’s largest electric provider following resident complaints of expensive bills that sometimes exceeded $1,000. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Staff for the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission are asking commissioners to authorize a formal investigation into the state’s largest electric provider after widespread customer complaints of exceedingly expensive bills.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a five-page filing to the commission Tuesday, staffers on the entity’s Public Interest Advocacy team wrote that electric provider PNM in July began estimating residential customer bills, rather than obtaining readings from meters, in the Alamogordo and Ruidoso areas because of a meter reader shortage. The practice quickly spread statewide, they wrote.
The commission subsequently held a September town hall meeting in Alamogordo, where some residents complained that their monthly bills had gone as high as $1,700. Last month, the New Mexico Department of Justice announced it had received several complaints from residents across the state who saw their monthly bills skyrocket from their usual range of $150 to $200.
Staffers wrote in the Tuesday filing that they intend to investigate what caused the issue, whether PNM complied with applicable laws and regulatory requirements and whether there are regulatory measures available to prevent a situation like this from happening again.
They wrote that they would test meters in Alamogordo and Ruidoso, review PNM’s billing data and write monthly updates and a public report with their findings and recommended next steps.
In a statement to Source NM, PNM spokesperson Eric Chavez said the company stands ready to provide information to utility regulators.
“PNM understands the concerns surrounding this summer’s meter reading and billing issues and remains committed to supporting affected customers,” Chavez said. “We welcome the opportunity to provide the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission with information about what occurred, how customers were affected and the actions PNM has taken in response.”
The announcement comes nearly a month after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sent a letter to Don Tarry, the CEO of PNM and its parent company, informing him that residents across the state had filed complaints with the New Mexico Department of Justice over shockingly high PNM bills.
In his Sept. 9 letter, Torrez included complaints several residents had sent to his office, including one who wrote that a relative’s bill had suddenly jumped from $150 to $766 in one month. Another, written by an Otero County married couple, said that PNM didn’t read their meter in July.
“Though we completely understand staffing issues, an electric bill of over $1,000, when we have not had one over $200 in the last year, is absurd,” they wrote. “We cannot get any answers from PNM, even after asking to see usage patterns and asking about meter modifications. This is highly irregular, and we should not have to pay over a thousand dollars when PNM will not provide facts.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Cornell University case means we must redouble the fight for institutional change on campuses
description: The details are different. The university is different. But the questions students are asking are ones generations of us have asked before.
text:
IN 2012, while I was a student at Boston University, sexual assault allegations involving members of the men’s hockey team put campus sexual violence at the center of the conversation. Students were talking about it everywhere. The newly opened Center for Gender, Sexuality and Activism, where I became involved, was perfectly positioned to turn that outrage into organizing and demands for institutional change. 
I was part of yet another generation of feminist students demanding that our university do more to prevent sexual assault and support survivors. We organized to open a rape crisis center and mandatory consent and sexual violence prevention training for student organizations. We challenged a culture that treated sexual violence as an individual tragedy rather than an institutional responsibility. 
But even then, I knew our demands weren’t new, just as the problem wasn’t new. Students at Boston University had been advocating for many of these same changes since the 1970s. What was new was the moment we found ourselves in, and our ability to use the growing spotlight on campus sexual violence to push our university to act. We inherited decades of organizing by students, survivors, advocates, and activists before us, and our job was to build on it and use the opening we had to create change. 
Thirteen years after graduating, reading about the allegations at Cornell University feels painfully familiar. 
A former Cornell student has alleged in a civil lawsuit that seven fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her in 2024 and that the university failed to adequately protect her or respond afterward. A prosecutor has now reopened the criminal investigation, while New York’s attorney general is reviewing Cornell’s handling of the case. 
The details are different. The university is different. But the questions students are asking are ones generations of us have asked before: Who is responsible for preventing sexual violence? What happens when institutions fail? And why, after decades of student organizing, are young people still fighting so many of the same battles? 
At my alma mater, Boston University, the removal of Pride flags from campus offices earlier this year sparked protests and a debate about LGBTQ+ visibility and free expression. Nationally, the Trump administration has changed the federal landscape around Title IX and civil-rights enforcement, including returning to an earlier Title IX framework for handling sexual misconduct 
Programs focused on gender equity, LGBTQ+ students, sexual violence prevention, and student activism aren’t peripheral to higher education’s mission. They give students the tools, knowledge, relationships, and power to make their campuses safer. 
And student organizing works. 
The policies and resources students have today did not simply appear because institutions decided to create them. Generations of students organized for them. They held rallies, shared their stories, met with administrators, changed policies, educated their peers, and demanded accountability. 
Today, as executive director of Mass NOW, I get to work alongside a new generation of student organizers taking on many of these same fights. 
This fall, we launched the Feminist Campus Network to bring together students from colleges and universities across Massachusetts. We’re helping students connect with one another, organize on their campuses, share resources, and advocate with elected officials around a broader feminist policy agenda. 
At a moment when institutions may be pulling resources away from gender justice, we’re choosing to invest more deeply in the students organizing for it. 
That’s also why Mass NOW is joining forces with Jane Doe Inc to organize a Cornell Jane Doe Solidary Rally. On Thursday, October 8th, from 6 to 8 pm, students and community members will gather on Boston Common to demand a future in which preventing sexual violence is treated as an institutional responsibility, survivors have meaningful support, and students don’t have to keep relearning the same lessons generation after generation. 
More than a decade after graduating college, there are moments when it feels like we’re losing ground. Institutions we fought to change are retreating from commitments we thought we had secured. Students are being asked to fight battles that can feel frustratingly familiar. 
But when I look at the movement today, I don’t see us going backward. 
I see a movement getting smarter, broader, and more connected. I see young organizers building on what previous generations fought for while challenging our movement to be more intersectional and expansive. I see longtime organizers sharing lessons and resources instead of asking the next generation to start over. And I see people across generations recognizing that none of us owns this movement; we inherit it, contribute to it, and pass it forward. 
I came into feminist organizing because generations before me refused to go away. The students organizing today are part of that same lineage. And now, those of us who once organized from dorm rooms and student centers have the responsibility to stand beside them. 
Our institutions may retreat. Our movement won’t. 
Sasha Goodfriend is executive director of Mass NOW.

title: US Senate candidates in 9 key races quiet about Social Security benefits cliff
text:
WASHINGTON — Nearly all of the U.S. senators elected this year will be in office when Congress debates how to restructure Social Security to prevent an automatic drop-off in retirement benefits in 2032. Very few candidates in competitive races, however, have policy proposals on their campaign websites and many, when contacted by States Newsroom, declined to share details about which changes they’d support if elected. Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said even though Social Security’s financial woes have been discussed more during this year’s campaign cycle, most candidates have shied away from getting into the weeds. 

 






(Illustration by Getty Images)

“What's really disappointing is nobody is talking about a realistic suite of options that will fix it,” she said. “There are a few who will mention lifting the payroll tax cap, which is probably the most often cited policy, but that on its own won't fix the program.” Workers now pay a 6.2% tax that goes directly to Social Security, though that doesn’t apply to earnings above $184,500. MacGuineas said one upside to this year’s campaign cycle is more voters understand that a candidate promising not to touch Social Security guarantees the automatic benefit cut in 2032, which will worsen over time. But, she said, she understands why candidates would want to wait until they are actually elected to Congress to go into detail about something that was once widely considered the third rail of American politics. “It's been so long since politicians have been honest about what Social Security faces and what fixes will be required,” MacGuineas said. “An election cycle is not where you'd expect a 180-degree switch into a direct conversation. I think this is the first step, and hopefully, post-midterms, we are able to start having that conversation.”Two-way communicationShai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said candidates need to be honest with voters about the changes they’ll likely have to make to Social Security.At the same time, he said, politicians need to hear from Americans that they understand Congress must take some action in the years ahead.  “Until we get that two-way street working, it's going to be really hard to move anything into law,” he said. Candidates, and those who work for them, have plenty of resources to study up on Social Security’s financial problems and explore the numerous changes that could be combined to avoid a 22% reduction in benefits from taking place in 2032. “It's not like policymakers are entering into a novel problem that has unexplored solutions,” Akabas said. “They're walking on well trodden ground and it is more about finding the political will to put those solutions together to create a bipartisan reform package than it is creating solutions from scratch.” While Akabas said it’s important for candidates to discuss realistic solutions on the campaign trail, the job of fixing the program would be less fraught if undertaken in a bipartisan way.“If the two parties together hold hands and say, ‘Here's a reform that we're going to put in place, and yes, it has difficult decisions, but it's the right thing to do for the country,’ I think our polling shows that that could be reasonably well received,” he said. “If, on the other hand, a candidate is putting that proposal out by themselves, it is extremely easy for the other side to message, ‘This candidate just wants to raise your taxes’ or ‘This candidate just wants to cut Social Security.’”Here’s what politicians running in close Senate races say about Social Security on their websites and shared with States Newsroom when asked for which detailed policy changes they’d support if elected to Congress. Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s website says if elected she would “work to eliminate taxes on Social Security benefits for the nearly 95,000 seniors in Alaska.” A spokesperson wrote she “is in this race to fix the rigged system in DC and put Alaska first – that means putting more money in Alaskans’ pockets and ending federal income tax on Social Security.” Republican Dan Sullivan didn’t have any policy proposals on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information. IowaRepublican Ashley Hinson’s campaign website says she would preserve “Social Security and Medicare benefits that vulnerable Iowans depend on, while rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse that deplete these programs.” Campaign communications director Billy Fuerst wrote in an email that Hinson “will always protect Social Security for Iowa seniors, and she will work with anyone to ensure the long-term solvency of this vital program. Ashley has never and will never cut a penny from Social Security.”  Democrat Josh Turek’s website says he would strengthen “Social Security by ensuring billionaires pay their fair share” and raise “Social Security income and assets limits for disabled individuals.” A staffer for his campaign sent several examples of Turek talking about Social Security, including an article in the Iowa Capital Dispatch that quoted him saying it was “ridiculous” that wealthy Americans didn’t pay any taxes to Social Security on income above $184,500. Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton’s website states: “We need to protect social security and provide real solutions for seniors.” A campaign staffer sent an article from the Johnson County Post quoting Hamilton as saying, “Both parties have kicked the can down the road, and the only way this gets solved is if Republicans and Democrats act together. And there’s movement: Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, and Bernie Moreno, a Republican, are working on bipartisan legislation to lift the payroll tax cap. That’s where I’d start. Right now only the first $184,500 of income is subject to Social Security tax, so somebody making $50,000 pays that tax on every dollar they earn while a person making millions pays on a small fraction. Raising the cap is the best lever we have to keep the program solvent without cutting benefits. I think about my mom, who’s on Social Security now. A cut is not an option for her, and it shouldn’t be for anyone."  Republican Roger Marshall didn’t have any policy positions on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information. MaineRepublican Susan Collins’ campaign website has one paragraph mentioning her work enacting a law that increased Social Security benefits for millions of Americans who had pensions after working in government or other public-sector jobs. Her campaign didn’t send details about what policy changes she’d support in the future to avoid the benefit cliff.  Democrat Troy Jackson’s website says he would “protect” Social Security and notes he published an op-ed in the Bangor Daily News saying he would eliminate the $184,500 payroll cap and raise benefits. He wrote he would “never” vote to raise the retirement age or privatize the program. Campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad wrote in an email that, “Troy is committed to protecting Social Security from cuts and ensuring that Mainers receive the secure retirement and benefits they’ve paid into and earned.” She added that if elected, “he’ll work to scrap the cap and require millionaires to pay Social Security taxes on their income, allow Medicare to negotiate the price of every drug, eliminate profiteering and waste, and expand benefits—not raise the retirement age.” MichiganDemocrat Abdul El-Sayed’s website says he would “fight to close the Social Security payroll tax cap to make sure the rich pay their fair share so that Social Security stays solvent well into the future.” Campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak wrote in an email that El-Sayed would “ensure our seniors get the benefits they earned through a lifetime of labor.”  Republican Mike Rogers doesn’t have any policy details on this campaign website. But communications director Alyssa Brouillet wrote in an email that Rogers is committed to protecting the program since his “parents survived on social security, as do his wife, Kristi’s, parents.” Brouillet added that Rogers “is committed to protecting social security and Medicare for our seniors.” New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas’ campaign website says he “will never vote to cut benefits or force seniors to work longer for less. He has fought against efforts to raise the retirement age, slash Social Security benefits, and privatize the entire system, a move that would gamble Granite Staters’ hard-earned benefits in the stock market and benefit Wall Street. Chris is committed to shoring up and improving Social Security to ensure that current retirees and future generations can trust that their benefits will be there.” Republican John Sununu didn’t have any policy details on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information. North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper didn’t have any policy proposals on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information.  Republican Michael Whatley didn’t have any policy positions on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information.  Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown’s website says that because of the Social Security Fairness Act, a broadly bipartisan bill that became law in 2024, more than 2 million “former teachers, bus drivers, police officers, firefighters, and other workers are now receiving their full Social Security payments that previously were withheld by the federal government.” A campaign spokesperson didn’t provide any details about what types of policy changes Brown would support in the future to avoid the automatic benefit cut, responding to States Newsroom’s request for policy details with criticisms of Husted.  Republican Jon Husted didn’t have any policy details on his campaign website and staff didn’t respond to multiple requests for more information.  TexasRepublican Ken Paxton’s website doesn’t have any policy proposals related to Social Security. A campaign staffer responded in an email that Paxton “believes we must protect Social Security for the millions of seniors who spent their lives paying into the system and are counting on the benefits they earned.” The campaign staffer also said that Paxton “will continue to stand behind lowering taxes and ensuring Social Security remains protected for generations to come." The campaign didn’t explain how exactly Paxton would do that if he became a senator.  Democrat James Talarico’s website says he would support “eliminating the tax cap on those earning over $400,000 a year, and incentivize employer-sponsored pensions.” A campaign staffer wrote in an email that Talarico would eliminate the $184,500 payroll tax ceiling for Social Security. He would also “support creating a tax system in which every dollar of income over $400,000 is taxed to fund Social Security. This policy would include a tax ramp-up starting at $400,001 that grows with additional income. This would ensure the top 2% of American earners are doing their part to keep this program solvent, without increasing the tax burden on the middle class during a cost-of-living crisis.” The campaign staffer wrote that Talarico wouldn’t support increasing the retirement age at which Americans can begin collecting Social Security benefits or reduce scheduled benefits.

title: Hurricane expected to hit Coast this weekend, forecasters say
description: Most severe impacts from Isaias will be concentrated on the Coast, but heavy rain, flooding and gusty winds will be possible further inland, including Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Tropical Storm Isaias, which is expected to develop into the first Atlantic hurricane of the season by Thursday, may be on a path to hit the Mississippi Gulf Coast Friday evening, according to Wednesday projections from the National Weather Service.
“While most severe impacts will remain concentrated along the Coast, heavy rain, flooding and gusty winds will be possible further inland across the forecast area,” NWS Jackson posted on its Facebook page Wednesday morning. “Please continue to monitor forecast updates for further details.”

Mississippi’s Gulf Coast, from Bay St. Louis to the state’s eastern border, is under a hurricane watch. A watch means that hurricane conditions are possible, while a hurricane warning means those conditions are expected. 
The weather service added that there is a chance of flash flooding for a large swath of the state between Friday night and Saturday night. The projected impact area includes Hattiesburg, Jackson and Meridian, and stretches north into Greenwood and Columbus. 

CLICK HERE: Mississippi Today’s disaster guide
The Mississippi Emergency Management Agency told residents Wednesday to begin preparations now. 
“The threat is real, and now is the time to prepare,” MEMA executive director Stephen McCraney said. “We have seen how quickly tropical systems can impact Mississippi. Tropical Storm Arthur in June brought tremendous amounts of rain, flash flooding and significant damage.”
McCraney reminded Mississippians to have enough supplies to last the first three days after a storm hits. 
“Do not assume help will arrive immediately,” he said. “Your preparation today could make all the difference tomorrow.”
The agency gave the following preparation tips:

Check emergency supplies. Have at least three days of drinking water and nonperishable food for every member of your household. Make sure you have medications, a first-aid kit, flashlights, batteries, important documents and other essential supplies.
Charge electronic devices. Fully charge cell phones, portable battery packs and other essential devices before severe weather arrives.
Secure outdoor property. Bring outdoor furniture, grills, trash cans and other loose objects inside or secure them so they do not become dangerous in strong winds.
Clear drainage areas safely. Remove leaves and debris from gutters and storm drains where it can be done safely.
Know your flood risk. Never drive or walk through floodwaters. Remember: Turn around, Don’t drown.
Make an evacuation plan. Know where you will go, how you will get there and where you can stay if an evacuation becomes necessary. Make arrangements in advance for children, older adults, individuals with disabilities and pets.
Stay informed. Monitor local weather reports and emergency information. Make sure Wireless Emergency Alerts are enabled on your phone and have multiple ways to receive warnings, including NOAA Weather Radio and the MEMA mobile app.

title: Florida government gearing up for Tropical Storm Isaias
description: As of Wednesday afternoon, Tropical Storm Isaias was about 500 miles from the mouth of Mississippi River with 50 mph winds as Florida’s leaders said they were “prepared and ready to respond” for landfall, expected later this week. The storm, moving at about 8 mph, is expected to become a hurricane Thursday and “approach the […]
text:
Tropical Storm Isaias' wind speed probabilities as of Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. (Screenshot via National Hurricane Center)As of Wednesday afternoon, Tropical Storm Isaias was about 500 miles from the mouth of Mississippi River with 50 mph winds as Florida’s leaders said they were “prepared and ready to respond” for landfall, expected later this week.
The storm, moving at about 8 mph, is expected to become a hurricane Thursday and “approach the U.S. northern gulf coast on Friday,” the National Hurricane Center said.
The center issued a hurricane watch from Mississippi to Indian Pass in Gulf County, Florida. 
Gov. Ron DeSantis had made no public appearance as of Wednesday afternoon, although he posted to social media: 
“There will be impacts by Isaias to the Florida panhandle. Even if it makes landfall west of the panhandle the eastern, most dangerous side the storm will impact NW Florida. If you are in those communities make sure to execute your hurricane plan.” (Grammar directly copied from DeSantis’ post)
Tuesday night, DeSantis spoke at the Center for Education Reform’s annual summit in Philadelphia.
U.S. Sen. Rick Scott said he wouldl be in Pensacola Thursday “working with local leaders and emergency management officials to make sure families are prepared.”
“Storm season is not over. We still have weeks of storm season,” Florida’s Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said during a news conference unrelated to the story. Hurricane season runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.
“This is the first storm that we have seen in over two years, and the stat that is amazing to me is I think there is like 450,000 people that have moved to the great state of Florida who have never experienced a hurricane,” he said.
“That’s how blessed we have been. But, having said that, we knew that something like this was going to be inevitable and we are ready. We are monitoring the situation,” Ingoglia added.
State of emergency 
The last hurricane to touch Florida was Milton, a Category 3 that made landfall in Siesta Key in October 2024. 
The governor Tuesday declared a state of emergency for 25 panhandle counties.
As of Wednesday, the Florida Division of Emergency Management’s emergency response team was activated. “Our partners are working around the clock to support communities and ensure resources are positioned where they are needed most,” the division posted to social media. 
Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky notified all health insurers, managed care organizations, and other plans licensed by the Office of Insurance Regulation that they are required to allow customers in those 25 counties to fill in advance prescription medications (so long as there are active refills) and pay pharmacies for at least a 30-day supply. The mandate stays in place for as long as the emergency order is in effect.
“We will be boots on the ground there,” Ingoglia said, referring to his employees who work with insurance companies to assist Floridians. His office supervises the insurance office.
Ingoglia suggested Floridians take a video of the outside and inside of their homes to document the state of the properties in advance. 
“One of the best ways to help bring down insurance premiums is to help mitigate losses, and you do that by preparing people in advance,” Ingoglia said. 
Floridians can report price gouging to the attorney general’s office.
According to the University of Florida, this could be the latest first hurricane during an Atlantic hurricane season since 1905.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis schools takeover could begin once state takeover board is ready, judge says
description: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters A federal judge appears poised to allow the state takeover of Memphis schools to move forward as soon as the oversight board says it’s ready to seize control of Tennessee’s largest school district. U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw filed an […]
text:
U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw expressed skepticism Friday about Memphis-Shelby County Schools's argument that the state takeover violates students’ constitutional rights. Pictured: East High School in Memphis. Getty Images)
(Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)

This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
A federal judge appears poised to allow the state takeover of Memphis schools to move forward as soon as the oversight board says it’s ready to seize control of Tennessee’s largest school district.
U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw filed an order Monday indicating that he will soon remove a temporary block on the state-appointed board after months of delay. That came days after the first hearing on Memphis-Shelby County Schools’ lawsuit against the state takeover, where Crenshaw said he never intended the block to be long term.
Crenshaw ordered the oversight board chair to notify the court under oath once the board is “ready, willing, and able” to begin its work, a step that could allow the politically appointed board to assume control of the district within days.
Oversight board Chair Billy Orgel did not respond to Chalkbeat’s request for comment on whether or when he would file a statement of readiness with the federal court. Chalkbeat also reached out to the Tennessee Attorney General’s office, who is representing the oversight board, for comment.
The state board was set to start its four-year term on July 1. But Crenshaw issued a temporary block on the takeover the day before, in an early win for MSCS and Shelby County officials challenging the law passed this spring authorizing the takeover.
District officials argued then that the new governance structure had no processes in place to handle major financial decisions like maintenance contracts that could significantly affect school operations ahead of the new school year. Early meetings in June revealed the board did not have established state emails or even a set location to hold its meetings.
It’s unclear whether the board has been working behind the scenes this fall to establish those processes, given Crenshaw’s earlier order.
Under the state takeover, the new state board — which includes a former MSCS superintendent and statewide teacher of the year — would seize control over the district’s annual budget and staffing decisions.
During Friday’s hearing, Crenshaw expressed skepticism about MSCS’ argument that the state takeover violates students’ constitutional rights and partially ruled in favor of the state by dismissing Gov. Bill Lee and other state leaders as defendants in the lawsuit.
Both sides are expected to file further court documents this month as Crenshaw considers dismissing the lawsuit altogether.
The members of the state oversight board, appointed by Tennessee Republican leaders this spring, are:

Chair Billy Orgel, a local developer and former Memphis-Shelby County school board member
Vice Chair Shanea McKinney of Cigna, who is a member of the University of Tennessee’s board of trustees
Secretary Nisha Powers, who leads a Memphis civil engineering firm and has served on the Tennessee Board of Regents
Dorsey Hopson, a former district superintendent
Dedrick Brittenum Jr., a Memphis lawyer and former City Council member
Beverly Robertson, a marketing executive and former president and CEO of the Greater Memphis Chamber of Commerce
Tyrone Burroughs, a Memphis CEO who sits on the Tennessee Lottery Commission and the Youth Villages’ board of directors
David Mansouri, the sole board member who is not a Shelby County resident and the Nashville-based leader of one of Tennessee’s most influential education advocacy organizations
Karen Vogelsang, a former Memphis teacher and 2015 Tennessee Teacher of the Year who now runs a literacy nonprofit

Bri Hatch covers Memphis-Shelby County Schools for Chalkbeat Tennessee. Reach Bri at bhatch@chalkbeat.org.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

title: Los refugiados y los solicitantes de asilo perderán cobertura de Medicaid el primero de octubre

text:

A partir del primero de octubre, varios grupos de inmigrantes que residen legalmente en el país, entre ellos los refugiados y los solicitantes de asilo que no tienen un permiso de residencia  permanente, perderán cobertura de Medicaid (asistencia médica proporcionada por el gobierno) y del Programa de Seguro Médico Infantil, o CHIP, por sus siglas en inglés.  Estos cambios entrarán en vigor a raíz de la ley denominada One Big Beautiful Bill Act que promulgó el presidente Donald Trump el año pasado.  
Los expertos en la política de salud y las organizaciones que trabajan con los inmigrantes en Misisipi advierten que los cambios van a intensificar el temor que ya existe y que pueden forzar que los inmigrantes demoren buscar atención médica. A la larga, esto podría resultar en tratamientos médicos más costosos para enfermedades prevenibles y pueden crear más presión en un sistema de salud que ya está sobrecargado. 
“Estos grupos de inmigrantes quedarán con muy pocas opciones de cobertura médica a precios razonables,” dijo Drishti Pillai, la directora de La Politica de Salud para Inmigrantes de KFF, (antes conocida como la Fundación de la Familia Kaiser) una organización nacional e independiente dedicada a la política de salud.  La directora Pillai señala también las próximas restricciones a los planes subsidiados del Mercado de Seguros Médicos de la Ley de Cuidado de la Salud a Bajo Precio (Affordable Care Act Marketplace) y a Medicare.  A partir de enero, estas opciones quedarán limitadas únicamente a los tres grupos de inmigrantes que también seguirán reuniendo los requisitos para recibir Medicaid. 
¿Quiénes seguirán calificando y quiénes no?
Los titulares de una tarjeta de residencia permanente, también conocidos como residentes permanentes legales, seguirán reuniendo los requisitos para recibir Medicaid, el programa federal y estatal que proporciona seguro de salud gratuito o de bajo costo a personas de bajos ingresos. También conservarán el acceso a dichas prestaciones los inmigrantes procedentes de Cuba, de Haití y de las naciones insulares del Pacífico incluidas en el Pacto de Libre Asociación (Compact of Free Association, COFA, por sus siglas en inglés), un acuerdo internacional con los Estados Unidos. 
Sin embargo, varios grupos de inmigrantes en situaciones de vulnerabilidad van a perder acceso a la cobertura de Medicaid.  Ya no tendrán acceso a Medicaid los refugiados y los solicitantes de asilo que huyeron de sus países de origen por temor a la persecución y que han recibido protección humanitaria de los Estados Unidos.  Tampoco lo tendrán los supervivientes de violencia doméstica que tengan solicitudes de residencia permanente aprobadas o en trámite bajo la Ley de Violencia contra la Mujer (Violence Against Women Act, VAWA por sus siglas en inglés). Dicha ley creó una vía legal para obtener la residencia permanente para las mujeres que fueron víctimas de abuso por parte de quienes patrocinaban sus solicitudes de residencia.  
Los refugiados que llegan a los Estados Unidos están huyendo del terror y de la violencia en sus países de origen, afirmó Lorena Lewis-Quiroz, directora ejecutiva de la Alianza de Inmigrantes por la Justicia y la Equidad (Immigrant Alliance for Justice and Equity, IAJE por sus siglas en inglés), una organización de defensa de los derechos de los inmigrantes con sede en Jackson.
“Estas personas ya vienen de estas situaciones atroces y ahora perderán el acceso a la asistencia médica básica.  No puedo creer que esto esté ocurriendo. ¿Me explico?”, afirmó ella.  “Esto está desmantelando poco a poco el sistema de atención médica para los inmigrantes.”
De igual manera, entre los inmigrantes que van a perder la capacidad de solicitar la asistenica médica incluyen los víctimas de la trata de personas, tal como la trata sexual y laboral, y los que tienen una visa T aprobaba o pendiente.  Este estatus provisional les permite a los inmigrantes solicitar la residencia permantente.  Otros grupos que van a perder Medicaid son:  

Los inmigrantes a quienes se les concedió un permiso humanitario para permanecer en los Estados Unidos por un mínimo de un año;
Los inmigrantes a quienes se les concedió la suspensión de deportación;
Las personas nacidas en Canadá que son amerindios o miembros de tribus indígenas reconocidas por el gobierno federal;  
Las personas mayores a quienes se les concedió admisión condicional antes de que surtiera efecto la Ley de Refugiados de 1980 (Refugee Act of 1980), incluidas las personas que huyeron de países comunistas de la Unión Soviética y de la Europa Oriental, así como también algunos refugiados procedentes del sudeste asiático.

En Misisipi, también perderán acceso algunos niños y adultas embarazadas que residen legalmente en los Estados Unidos. Algunos estados han optado por continuar la cobertura de estos grupos bajo la Ley para la Mejora de la Salud Infantil para Inmigrantes de 2009 (Immigrant Children’s Health Improvement Act, ICHIA) la cual elimina el período de espera de cinco años que muchos inmigrantes deben cumplir entre la obtención de la residencia permanente y su inscripción en Medicaid. Desde enero, 38 estados han optado por proporcionar cobertura médica a los niños con presencia legal en el país y 32 estados han hecho lo mismo para las personas embarazadas.  Misisipi ha optado por no cubrir ninguno de los dos grupos. 
“Los cambios a Medicaid son brutales y pueden impedir que los niños que reúnen los requisitos reciban cobertura si sus padres ya no pueden presentar solicitudes en nombre de sus hijos ciudadanos dado el estatus migratorio de los padres,” escribió por correo electrónico Kathy Sykes, la directora ejecutiva de la Alianza de los Derechos de Inmigrantes de Misisipi (Mississippi Immigrants Rights Alliance, MIRA). Esta organización estatal proporciona servicios legales y sociales gratuitos a inmigrantes.  
“Hay tantos cambios provenientes del gobierno federal que pueden ser muy confusos y puede hacer que incluso las personas que califican para estos servicios decidan no solicitarlos,” dijo.    
Consecuencias más allá de la pérdida del seguro médico
A la directora Pillai le preocupan los efectos más amplios de perder el acceso a Medicaid y de los procesos de verificación—incluso para los inmigrantes que aún califican para recibir este programa.
Los estados deberán verificar el estatus migratorio de las personas cuya cobertura será cancelada. Esto se llevará a cabo a través de la base de datos Verificación Sistemática de Extranjeros para la Otorgación de Prestaciones (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, SAVE por sus siglas en inglés), del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional de los Estados Unidos (Department of Homeland Security, DHS por sus siglas en inglés) y de la base de datos del seguro social. Si la agencia estatal encargada de Medicaid puede confirmar que una persona reúne los requisitos para recibir cobertura, esta conserverá su cobertura de Medicaid.  Si las autoridades no pueden verficar el estatus legal con la información que tienen, se les van a pedir información adicional a las personas afectadas y se les dará un plazo de 90 días para contestar.


Khaylah Scott, administradora de programas de Mississippi Health Advocacy Program (una organización de defensa de políticas de salud de Misisipi), dijo que las normas para calificar para Medicaid están vigentes desde hace 30 años, desde la Ley de Reforma del Bienestar Social de 1996. 
“Cuando se recibe poca comunicación por parte de la División de Medicaid y la primera noticia sobre estos cambios llega mediante una carta, eso puede resultar bastante repentino,” afirmó Scott. “Me imagino la confusión, el miedo que puede sentir alguien con tan solo recibir esta carta por correo y saber, en el fondo, que la razón principal es su estatus migratorio.”
El proceso de verificación puede ser confusa para los inmigrantes, en particular para los que no hablan inglés o los que hablan solo un poco de inglés.  Pillai dijo que las investigaciones previas han demostrado que las cancelaciones de cobertura también pueden afectar a las personas que se han mudado de domicilio o que, por alguna otra razón, no pudieron completar la documentación requerida.
“Todo esto puede provocar cancelaciones de cobertura, no debido al derecho de estar en el programa, sino por razones administrativas,” dijo ella.
La División de Medicaid de Misisipi no respondió a la solicitud de comentarios de  Mississippi Today sobre cómo se van a implementar estos cambios.  Un aviso público emitido el 14 de septiembre sobre una propuesta de modificación al plan estatal de Medicaid señal que “se predice [que la enmienda] no tendrá efecto en el presupuesto ya que el número de individuos afectados es bajo”; no obstante, no proporciona un número aproximado de cuántos inmigrantes se verán afectados.  
Los inmigrantes que ya no califican para recibir Medicaid o el Programa de Seguro Médico Infantil todavía pueden recibir cobertura mediante el Medicaid de Emergencia en ciertas circunstancias, como la aparición repentina de síntomas graves, que si no se tratan, pueden resultar en graves daños. Por ejemplo, una mujer embarazada que entra en trabajo de parto tiene cobertura en todos los estados. Ya que Misisipi no ha ampliado Medicaid, los criterios para recibir esta cobertura se limitan a un grupo más reducido de categorías.  Un adulto  indocumentado de bajos ingresos que no esté embarazado, que no sea padre o madre dentro de una categoría elegible y que no reúna los requisitos por una discapacidad no puede depender del Medicaid de Emergencia, aun si llegara a tener un acontecimiento que normalmente le permitiría recibir esta cobertura.  
A la larga, dijo Pillai, esta pérdida de cobertura médica podría provocar peores resultados de salud ya que muchas personas tienen que esperar hasta que las afecciones se vuelvan insoportables.
“Si las personas no tienen seguro de salud, entonces no reciben examenes de salud rutinarios y la falta de cuidado consistente puede provocar que estas personas dependan más de las salas de urgencias,” dijo ella.  “Esto puede causar más presión en los centros de salud de las comunidades ya que estos centros atienden a todos los pacientes sin importar el estado de inmigración y sin importar la abilidad de pagar.”
Lewis Quiroz anticipa un efecto similar:  “Va a ser otro caso de, ‘Pues, ¿sabes qué?  Voy a esperar hasta que me dé una embolia.'”
Este reportaje se produjo con el apoyo de los fondos de Sarah Yelena Haselhort para el Periodismo de Salud.
Corección (30 de septiembre de 2026):  Este artículo se ha actualizado para mencionar a la Alianza por los Derechos de los Inmigrantes de Misisipi, MIRA, (Mississippi Immigrants Rights Alliance, MIRA, por sus siglás en inglés), la organización en donde Kathy Sykes es directora ejecutiva.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Animal health company awarded 2026 Governor’s Bioscience Award
description: LINCOLN — A global animal health company was named the 2026 recipient of the Governor’s Bioscience Award, which recognizes individuals or companies that make significant contributions to Nebraska’s bioscience industry. Phibro Animal Health Corp. sells products meant to help livestock producers, farmers and veterinarians responsibly care for their animals. Th[...]
text:
Bio Nebraska Executive Director Rob Owen presents this year’s 2026 Governor’s Bioscience Award. (Courtesy of Bio Nebraska)LINCOLN — A global animal health company was named the 2026 recipient of the Governor’s Bioscience Award, which recognizes individuals or companies that make significant contributions to Nebraska’s bioscience industry.
Phibro Animal Health Corp. sells products meant to help livestock producers, farmers and veterinarians responsibly care for their animals. The company has maintained a presence in Nebraska since 2009 after acquiring Baltzell Agri Products, and in 2016 it acquired Omaha-based livestock vaccine company MVP Laboratories, according to a press release from nonprofit trade association Bio Nebraska.
Nebraska Department of Agriculture Director Sherry Vinton, who presented the award to Phibro officials at a University of Nebraska event Tuesday, praised the company’s innovation, saying it has made life better for the state’s livestock raisers.
“As a lifelong livestock producer and rancher, I know how critical healthy animals and reliable tools are to the success of Nebraska’s farm and ranch families,” Vinton said. “Phibro Animal Health’s work strengthens the health and productivity of our livestock while advancing the food-safety standards that protect the people who depend on the high-quality protein we produce.”
