name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa.’s top election official urges voters to plan for upcoming deadlines
description: The last day to register before the Nov. 3 election is Oct. 19. The deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot is Oct. 27
text:
Poll workers wait for voters at the Saltsburg Borough Building in Saltsburg, Indiana County on Election Day May 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)As the deadlines to register to vote in the upcoming election and request mail ballots near, Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt is urging Pennsylvanians to make sure they have a plan to cast their ballots by election day.
The last day to register before the Nov. 3 election is Oct. 19. People can do so at their county election office or online at vote.pa.gov
The deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot is Oct. 27. Applications must be received by county election offices by 5 p.m.
“If you’re planning to vote by mail, please don’t wait,” Schmidt said at a press conference Wednesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mail-in ballots must be received by county election officials by 8 p.m. on election day. Voters can return their completed ballots through mail, at a dropbox if one is available, or at their county election office or temporary satellite office.
The Department of State has a list of locations voters can return their completed mail ballots by county.
After voters mark their selections, mail ballots should be sealed in a yellow secrecy envelope. That secrecy envelope should be sealed in a pre-addressed outer return envelope that voters must sign and date.
As it stands, more than 50 counties have ballots available at their election offices for on-demand mail ballot voting. That’s a process where voters apply for a mai ballot in person, fill it out on the spot and then return it to an election official. 
The Department of State has an online list of counties currently offering the service.
As the election nears, Schmidt also warned voters to watch out for attempts to mislead them. 
“The closer we get to the election, the more mis- and disinformation voters are likely to encounter,” he said. “We urge voters to rely on trusted, official sources of election information, such as their county election office website or the Pennsylvania department of state voter website.”
Schmidt also warned of phishing scams asking voters to check their registration status and enter personal information. If voters want to check their registration ahead of the Oct. 19 deadline, they should visit vote.pa.gov.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Lawmakers call on state Supreme Court to extend deadline for skill games
description: Recognizing the impact its June 15 ruling would have on skill game hosts and operators, the Supreme Court instructed that no law enforcement agency was to act on the decision for 120 days. That safe harbor period expires Oct 13.
text:
State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, where business owners and volunteer organizations urged lawmakers to pass legislation to legalize and tax skill games. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital Star) Four state lawmakers with pending legislation to tax and regulate skill games have asked the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to extend the stay on its  finding that the devices are illegal gambling machines. 
Sens. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) and Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) and Reps. Danilo Burgos (D-Philadelphia) and Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne) filed a petition Wednesday asking the justices to exercise the court’s “King’s Bench” power to give the General Assembly more time to pass legislation regulating and taxing skill games.
Recognizing the impact its June 15 ruling would have on skill game hosts and operators, the Supreme Court instructed that no law enforcement agency was to act on the decision for 120 days. That safe harbor period expires Oct 13.
The lawmakers requested an extension until Feb. 10. 
Miele Group, based in Muncy Township, Lycoming County, manufactures Pennsylvania Skill Games, which have been the subject of legislative efforts to regulate and tax the slot machine-like devices. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The high court ruled that skill games are subject to the Gaming Act and the Crimes Code. As a result, anyone operating a skill game machine is required to be licensed by the state Gaming Control Board.
Skill games are slot machine-like devices that have proliferated in the last decade across the commonwealth in corner stores, bars, gas stations and volunteer organizations such as fire halls and American Legion posts.
Pace-O-Matic, the Georgia-based company that produces software for the games, argued the machines differed significantly from slot machines because players are offered an opportunity to win their money back.
Attorneys for the commonwealth argued before the Supreme Court that few players actually make the effort to win their bets back and that the machines are functionally the same as casino slot machines. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Pennsylvania State Police and the state Attorney General’s Office have warned that skill games must be removed from establishments before the ruling takes effect.
Since June, business owners and volunteer groups that have come to rely on the machines have urged lawmakers to act. And despite bills passing in both chambers of the legislature, neither the House nor the Senate has concurred in the other’s legislation.
Speaking at a rally for skill game legalization Tuesday at the state Capitol, Yaw said he has been working on legislation for six years. His Lycoming County district is home to Miele Manufacturing, which produces Pace-O-Matic’s Pennsylvania Skill games.
Yaw is the prime sponsor of a bill that would establish a $500 per game monthly fee he estimated would generate $300 million in new revenue for the state. Other legislation has proposed taxes between 16% and 35%.
The commonwealth’s casino industry, which has lobbied heavily against skill games, is taxed at a hefty 55% and pushed for a comparable rate.
“I’ve told our leadership, put my bill up, run it,” Yaw said, adding. “If it fails, I’ll go away. I don’t think it will fail.” 
Pennsylvania Skill Games in a Delaware County convenience store. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Despite a range of options, the lawmakers said in their petition to the Supreme Court that “the legislative process will not be complete by Oct. 13.” After Wednesday, the House and Senate have five voting days left before the session expires
Allowing the ban to take effect before the legislature can act would complicate the process of licensing the machines, the petition says.
“Petitioners do not seek the extension because law enforcement agencies are unable to enforce existing law. They seek it because widespread seizure and impoundment of devices in the weeks before enactment would make prompt implementation of the legislation materially more difficult,” it says.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Four South Dakota counties will vote in November on new sales taxes to lower property taxes
description: South Dakotans in two counties will decide in the Nov. 3 election whether to implement a county sales tax for homeowner property tax reduction, while residents in two other counties will vote in special elections later in November. State lawmakers and the governor gave counties the authority during this year’s legislative session to implement their […]
text:
Brown County has offices in Aberdeen connected to the Brown County Courthouse, Sheriff's Office and jail. The county will vote Nov. 3 on a proposed sales tax to reduce homeowner property taxes. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakotans in two counties will decide in the Nov. 3 election whether to implement a county sales tax for homeowner property tax reduction, while residents in two other counties will vote in special elections later in November.
State lawmakers and the governor gave counties the authority during this year’s legislative session to implement their own sales taxes for the first time in state history, with proceeds going toward lowering homeowners’ property taxes. Counties are limited to a half-percent tax. Lawmakers and the governor also decided to use proceeds from next year’s increase in the state sales tax rate, from 4.2% to 4.5%, to reduce property taxes for homeowners statewide.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Brown County commissioners included a provision in their Aug. 18 ordinance requiring a public vote on Nov. 3. In Codington, Clay and Charles Mix counties, residents gathered enough petition signatures to refer the ordinances to voters.
Codington County will vote on the issue on Nov. 3. Because ballots were already printed when petitioners in Clay and Charles Mix counties submitted signatures, those counties will hold special elections Nov. 17. State law requires special elections to be held between 60 and 90 days after the submission of a validated petition.
Six other counties have adopted a sales tax without putting it to voters or being subjected to a referendum. Custer, Fall River, Lawrence, Lincoln, Meade and Pennington counties’ half-percent sales tax ordinances will be implemented in January.
Two more counties have passed ordinances that are still within the window for a potential referral.
Hughes County commissioners passed a half-percent sales tax ordinance that has a deadline of Oct. 14 for a referral petition. Yankton County commissioners passed a half-percent ordinance but intend to lower the sales tax rate to 0.25%, requiring a new ordinance, said Auditor Patty Hojem. Both counties missed the Oct. 3 deadline for a January implementation, so the taxes wouldn’t take effect until July 2027.

name: WyoFile
title: Fremont County data center part of larger $66B plan
authors: by Marit Gookin and Austin Beck-Doss, The Ranger
description:
Commissioners grapple with county’s “little ability to take action” amid prospect of more data centers.
The post Fremont County data center part of larger $66B plan appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
While little official information about the data center taking shape northeast of Riverton has been aired, a big price tag was revealed on Tuesday: The data center under construction near the unincorporated community of Lost Cabin is phase one of a much larger, $66 billion data center project.
Data centers are currently a hot topic in both Wyoming and across the country, as concerns about their water and power consumption compete with promises of economic growth and technological advancement. 


As those concerns have come to Fremont County, it’s become clear that the county’s lack of zoning regulations means that the county has little control over whether such projects will move forward. And the scale of the planned Lost Cabin site is far beyond the relatively small facility that originally prompted conversations within the county.
“The building that’s out there is a prototype building. I guessed $66 million,” Fremont County Commissioner Ron Fabrizius said.
“The building they’re building now is $16 million. That’s just the building getting ready. The electronics on top of that is another $22 million,” 
Fremont County Board of Commissioners Chair Larry Allen responded. “The one they are planning now, they will have $66 billion invested.”
Facility already built
Even as the county considers whether it should take steps to create regulations that could address data center development, the project has seemingly gone from plan to reality.
“Yesterday I took a tour of the current small data center that they’ve built,” County Planning Director Steve Baumann told county commissioners Tuesday morning. He noted that the building has already received approval from the state fire marshal’s office and from the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Air Quality Division for its backup generators; it expects to have power from High Plains Power commissioned by late October or early November.
Baumann described the current facility as a metal building divided into four parts, with a section of about 24 feet by 60 feet dedicated to servers.
“I asked specifically what their intentions were for this request. They hope to build several buildings,” Baumann explained. “Perhaps new construction will be phased in specific campuses and for power to be generated by natural gas reciprocating generators similar to a very large CAT generator — 500 megawatt generating capacity. It’d be a substantial amount of power, none of which would go onto the grid, for the purpose of running a new data center or group of data centers.” 
The project is likely large enough that it would require the approval of the Industrial Siting Council. Its proposal to generate its own power comes amidst serious conversations about whether Wyoming should relax some of its rules around third-party power generation that have often been occurring specifically in the context of data centers and their potential impacts for local residents.
Maps associated with the company’s air quality permit application show the data center as located on a lot associated with the address 67 Lost Cabin Road, neighboring the JB Okie Mansion and its caretakers Zane and Ginger Fross. However, Baumann told the commissioners Tuesday that the closest residents to the data center are about a mile away.
In a prior interview, Zane Fross told The Ranger that he is optimistic about the economic opportunity such a project may bring to the area.
Who’s behind the project?
Initially, the company or companies behind the project appeared somewhat mysterious. 
Eventually the name ETC DC OpCo emerged, a company organized in the state of Delaware which was registered just this year. 
However, while the project saw little in the way of permitting requirements from the county, its backup generators required it to apply for an air quality permit from the Wyoming DEQ — and more information could be found on those forms.
According to information within the air quality permit application, the contacts for the Lost Cabin data center project are Aethel Energy Senior Environmental Specialist John Wester and ETC DC OpCo Production Superintendent Dustin Miller. The company behind the data center project is registered as ETC DC OpCo, while Baumann confirmed Tuesday that the company he’s been in touch with about the project is Aethel.
Miller’s LinkedIn profile says that he works for Electio Technologies, a Houston-based “energy transformation company building the optimization layer for the AI era” that appears to have the same address as ETC DC OpCo. ETC is sometimes used as an abbreviation for energy transfer company.
The county map server, which warns it may not always be fully up to date, lists the owner of the parcel of land on which the proposed data center would be constructed as Contango Resources LLC. Aethel Energy acquired Contango’s Wyoming assets last year.
Aethel Energy and Electio Technologies are both backed by a venture capital operation called General Catalyst.
Commissioners contemplate regulations
“I’m done in two months, but any government would say ‘let’s do something about this’ because it’s going to get out of control. It will have problems in a sense concerning land, water, those migrating animals … it’s going to have an effect on cattle, and people,” Commissioner Clarence Thomas remarked, noting that despite the concerns the commissioners have heard from the community, the county currently has little ability to take action. 
“We’re not just talking one data center.  We’re talking about many others coming after that,” Thomas said. “It’s like weeds.”
The post Fremont County data center part of larger $66B plan appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘It’s torture’: Trans immigrant detainees allege experiencing abuse, medical neglect at Jena immigration detention center
authors: By Cris Seda Chabrier, Verite News
description: Three transgender women being detained at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena, Louisiana allege that they are experiencing abuse and transphobia at the facility.
text:
Three transgender women who have been detained for months at a male-only central Louisiana immigration detention center allege that they have faced abuse and transphobia at the hands of staff and other detainees.
In interviews with Verite News, they allege that they have been assaulted by officers, forcibly detransitioned, verbally harassed and kept in solitary confinement. 
“Everywhere they call us men, faggots, very offensive words,” Camila Toro de Paula, one of the detainees, told Verite News. The officers “let it happen. We don’t have a right to anything here; we trans women don’t have rights” at the facility, she added.
Two of the women — Estephany Rivas and Sofia — have spent months at Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena. The third, Camila Toro de Paula, has been there for more than a year. The three women are in protective custody, separated from other detainees. Verite is only using Sofia’s middle name because she is worried about the conditions at the detention center continuing or worsening.


Camila Toro de Paula, who was taken by ICE agents in New York. Credit: Courtesy photo Credit: Courtesy photo


Sofia, who was taken by Border Patrol agents in Mississippi and transferred to ICE custody before being sent to Central Louisiana. Credit: Courtesy photo


Estephany Rivas, who was taken by ICE agents in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Credit: Courtesy photo
The Trump administration forces trans women to be housed with men in detention centers. U.S. Immigration and Enforcement houses the women in solitary confinement for their protection, but the women say the isolation has not prevented them from enduring death threats, humiliating pat downs and physical abuse by staff.
The Jena facility is run by GEO Group — a for-profit corporation that is one of the country’s largest private prison operators — which has been criticized for its treatment of detainees. A 2024 report on ICE detention centers in Louisiana by Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and other leading human rights organizations recorded “systemic human rights abuses,” as they called it, at the facilities. At the Jena facility, they reported that there had been detainee deaths, people being shackled for more than 24 hours, contaminated food, filthy cells and bathrooms, physical abuse – such as spraying detainees with pepper spray, sexual harassment and assault, medical abuse and neglect, and the use of solitary confinement as retaliation.
Other organizations, such as Immigration Equality and Southeast Dignity Not Detention, have found similar conditions for detainees at the facility.
“There is nothing in the system that is built to recognize their full humanity as trans people, and now there’s no mechanisms in place to protect them from transphobic violence, from abuse of solitary confinement,” Mich González, a New Orleans-based immigrant rights attorney who has represented trans women in detention, said about the Trump administration ending protections for transgender detainees.
The three women had all been living in the U.S. for several years. Like most immigrant detainees, they do not have active criminal charges against them. Rivas had misdemeanor traffic offenses that were resolved before her detention, according to court records and her attorney Mauricio Sierra. Toro de Paula had one previous conviction for a low-level misdemeanor as well as two felony charges stemming from a 2025 arrest that were dismissed, according to her attorney and a New York Times report.
Border Patrol detains woman in Mississippi
Media reports and court records also show that Toro de Paula, who is Venezuelan, and Rivas, who is Honduran, were taken by ICE agents in New York and in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, respectively, then taken to Central Louisiana. Sofia was taken by Border Patrol agents in Mississippi and transferred to ICE custody before being sent to Central Louisiana.
They are seeking asylum in the U.S. after facing death threats and attempted rapes in their home countries due to being transgender, and at least one has been persecuted by cartels.
It is not uncommon for people to be detained for months in poor conditions, but as the experience of these detainees, which has been corroborated by legal documents, records from the detention facility, medical records, interviews with the detainees’ attorneys and emails from the attorneys to the facility indicate, LGBTQIA+ immigrants face additional discrimination on the basis of their sexual and gender identity — often the very reason they are seeking asylum in the United States. Transgender women in particular are at a high-risk of gendered and sexual abuse due to being housed in male-only facilities.
Verite News reviewed court documents, emails, medical records and incident reports from their time at the Central Louisiana facility, and spoke with the women and their attorneys.
“What they are doing to us is torture,” Toro de Paula said.
The women say that they’ve faced physical abuse because they have refused to undergo pat downs and strip searches that expose their bodies in front of male guards. 
According to a June 25 incident report, a group of guards — which included men and at least one woman — approached Rivas and asked her to stand up and submit to a pat down. It is not clear from the report why they were searching her. The female guard said she touched Rivas’ shoulder. The officer then alleged that Rivas “aggressively turned towards me swinging his arm around.” Rivas turned around, “swung the towel in his hand, striking my neck, and said ‘Don’t fucking touch me,’” according to the officer. The report refers to Rivas using he/him/his pronouns instead of her preferred pronouns.
The guard went on to say that another Correctional Emergency Response Team (CERT) member at the facility put her in the prone position and handcuffed her.
On June 26, a “Unit Disciplinary Committee Report of Findings and Actions” written by a member of the Unit Disciplinary Committee — tasked with investigating incident reports — detailed Rivas’ account of the incident. Verite News has part of the report and requested the full document from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which has yet to respond.
According to the report, Rivas “stated his shirt began to rise, that’s when he told the officer ‘Don’t touch me.’”  In an interview with the committee, Rivas said that she refused to be searched because there were several men present, and she denied that she ever hit the officer with a towel. Rivas said that “a view of camera footage” would show she never swung a towel.
‘They threw me to the ground’
“They threw me to the ground, and all the men were on top of me. (The female sergeant) tried to lift up my shirt to search me. And I told her, ‘No, no, don’t touch me — don’t touch me because I don’t want you to lift up my shirt,’” Rivas alleged in an interview with Verite News. 
Sofia also alleged she had previously allowed the same female guard to search her, but after Rivas was restrained, the guard pushed her against the wall again, taunted her and pulled her hair.
“After they punished (Rivas), she slammed me against the wall again and searched me once more,” Sofia alleged. “‘No touch you?’ ‘No touch you?’,” she’d say to me. She was kind of trying to make me angry to see if I’d do something so she could punish me too. And I told her, ‘It’s okay.’ I told her. And she grabbed my hair and pulled it.”
According to the disciplinary report document, the findings were based on the credibility of the officer, the investigation report and Rivas’ version of the incident. Although only Rivas’ testimony is available in the document, DHS said that “all staff provided the required documentation for the incident” and that a use of force review “was conducted by GEO and ICE Leadership and found to be justified.”
Verite News provided Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center Center, with the reports. Decker said that the description of Rivas’ arrest as her being “assisted to the prone position and handcuffed by another CERT member” was a “sanitized” way to describe a takedown — when officers use force to place someone face-down on the floor. 
“We’ve had a number of clients who have been beaten and permanently disabled by takedowns, so we routinely see that they’re not actually following the use of force guidelines; that they’re using an indiscriminate amount of force when they’re taking people down,” Decker said.
ICE’s own National Detention Standards handbook classifies a “take-down” as a “hard technique” and stipulates that “officers should first issue verbal commands” because it carries a high risk of injury. 
Decker also pointed out the CERT members, who handcuffed Rivas, typically have high-risk security training and are brought in for takedowns.
Rivas’ attorney Mauricio Sierra, who is challenging her detention and seeking her release through a habeas corpus lawsuit, confirmed her account.
“There was no justifiable reason to … attack my client, to confine my client in that way, ” Sierra said. Sierra added that when he met with her, she was in a yellow-colored jumpsuit, a change from her blue-colored jumpsuit, indicating that the facility was classifying her as a higher level threat to the guards at the detention center. DHS confirmed her uniform color was changed because the charge of “Assault on Staff” is more severe. 
Due to the conflicting allegations, Rivas was scheduled to have a hearing with an investigative panel on June 29. She alleges that the hearing never took place and that the video footage of the incident she requested was not handed over, while DHS says that the hearing did take place and she provided a verbal statement using the translator line. It is not clear from the documents available to Verite if there were additional findings as a result of the investigation. 
Decker added that, in her experience working on use of force cases at detention centers, it is extremely difficult for detainees to hold officers responsible.
“The accounts of the detained people are the most reliable source of information. The video footage is great, but you often can’t get it, and I think the officers’ accounts are just not accurate,” Decker said. Verite asked for the video but it was not provided at the time of publication.
Camila Toro de Paula shows a drawing of the cell where she’s kept in administrative segregation at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena, Louisiana. Credit: Courtesy photo
Protective custody
Beyond the allegations of physical abuse, the detainees said they have suffered emotionally from months of isolation.
At the detention facility in Jena, the women are confined in administrative segregation for their protection because they are transgender. It is the same unit as disciplinary segregation, where people are sent for infractions. Both administrative and disciplinary segregation are types of solitary confinement.
Experts, including the United Nations, say that any type of prolonged solitary confinement amounts to torture, despite its use being widespread in the U.S.
“They say that where they’re keeping us here for our protection, but this isn’t protection, it’s torture,” Sofia said.
Detainees in administrative segregation are supposed to have greater privileges to those who are there for disciplinary reasons, such as getting more time in the yard or being able to use a tablet, but court documents indicate they are still locked up for twenty hours a day.
And the women at the Jena detention center also allege that the few privileges they have are curtailed arbitrarily. According to medical records, Sofia once suffered a mental health crisis due to an officer cutting off time outside her cell.
“Sofia approached the sergeant with the intent to explain how she and other queer detainees felt this was discriminatory,” a psychologist who, in coordination with Humanitarian Outreach for Migrant Emotional Health, provided a mental health evaluation for Sofia’s asylum case. “According to Sofia, the sergeant told her to ‘shut up,’ followed by ‘shut your mouth.’”
“She went to her cell, grabbed a razor, and ‘cut (her)self, just to feel relief,’” the report continued.
“Sofia elaborated that the superficial ‘scratch’ relieved her frustration,” the psychologist wrote. “She believes there is a difference between clinical symptoms of depression and her experience of being ‘rightfully stressed for being (detained) so long under unfair conditions.’”
DHS responded that both Central Louisiana facility staff and medical staff deny the incident occurred, despite their own records showing Sofia had been transferred to a mental health hospital for self-harm. 
The The Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center is seen in this aerial photo in Jena, La., Tuesday, April 8, 2025. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert)
Jeremy Jong, a staff attorney with the immigration advocacy nonprofit Al Otro Lado, told Verite News that detention centers are not equipped to deal with detainees who have complex needs, and often opt to simply place people in solitary confinement.
Additionally, DHS responded that “recreation privileges have never been revoked, and that they are offered recreation daily,” but that the women have at times been moved from the general population yard to the Special Management Unit due to rules infractions.
Despite being in protective custody, the women have faced transphobic abuse and threats from other detainees, they allege. In emails reviewed by Verite News from November and December 2025, Laura Berger, an immigration staff attorney at The Legal Aid society representing Toro de Paula, repeatedly wrote to the Jena facility’s supervisory detention and deportation officer, Christopher Rabe, about a detainee who continually verbally harassed and threatened Toro de Paula.
“One of the other detainees in her unit attempted to assault her and loudly accused her of having AIDS. The detainee threatened to harm my client and said that he had killed people before,” Berger wrote in the email. Although the facility provides a way for detainees to make complaints, Berger says that staff either brushed off Toro de Paula’s complaints or are unable to understand the threats since they were made in Spanish.
When asked for comment, DHS responded that the allegations were “FALSE” and that “no staff at (Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center) witnessed the conduct being described by Toro de Paula’s attorney.” However, emails from Rabe to Berger acknowledge the facility had to separate the other detainee from Toro de Paula.
The agency also said that “staff cannot control what other detainees may verbalize,” but “they are trained to hold detainees accountable for misconduct should it occur with internal disciplinary reports.” 
Forced detransition and medical neglect  
All three women say they are being denied treatment for medical ailments like stomach aches, blood in their urine and skin rashes, and are also denied trans health care.
When asked for comment, DHS responded that detainees “have been sent to see a urologist on multiple occasions and other specialists as part of their care plan.” The agency added that it “is the best healthcare many aliens have received in their entire lives” and that “meals are certified by dieticians.” The women also allege that the food is contaminated, undercooked and inedible.
The facility had at least two deaths that were due to an improper medical response, according to a 2017 investigation by the DHS’ Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties.
The three transgender women allege to Verite News that they have been denied medical care, including access to hormone replacement therapy that they were taking before being detained by ICE. Credit: Illustration by Bethany Atkinson/Deep South Today
While medical neglect is widespread in detention facilities nationwide, specifically denying trans health care fits into a nationwide trend of forced detransition in detention centers.
At Central Louisiana, Sofia and Rivas say that they are being denied hormone replacement therapy, which they both were taking before they were detained. According to a DHS statement to Verite News, DHS segregates the women by biological sex because of Trump’s 2025 executive order. The order also explicitly states that the Bureau of Prisons and federal funds cannot be “expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The women also say that they are also being denied feminine clothes and makeup, both of which would help them feel more comfortable in their bodies.
“They don’t let us wear makeup, so what we do is use a pencil to paint on our faces. Just because we do that, they get mad and report us. What harm are we doing to them by” using pencils to replace makeup, Rivas said.
DHS says the allegations that undergarments have been changed is false. Regarding their use of colored pencils as makeup, DHS says that “detainees are not permitted to utilize colored pencils outside their intended use” because it is considered contraband.
“(Detention) is now encouraged because mistreating people puts them in a more desperate situation, to then seek voluntary departure and under duress give up legal rights they may have to stay in the country,” Nora Ahmed, who is ACLU of Louisiana’s legal director, told Verite News.
Transgender immigrants in detention
The women at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center who are alleging transphobic harassment, physical and emotional abuse aren’t the only ones in Louisiana in recent years.
In 2023, Vicky, a transgender woman who was detained in Pine Prairie ICE Detention Center — also operated by the GEO Group — filed a civil rights complaint describing the culture of the facility. In a press release announcing the filing of the complaint, the group Immigrant Justice said the facility had a “culture of transphobia, harassment and medical negligence.”
In September 2025, the ACLU of Louisiana, Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and the National Immigration Project filed complaints on behalf of four immigrants who were detained at the South Louisiana ICE Detention Center in Basile — also run by the GEO Group. The complaints alleged that two trans men and one nonbinary person, all housed in a female-only facility, were subject to sexual abuse, forced labor, retaliation and denial of medical care. 
And this type of alleged mistreatment is happening in other states as well. A 2016 Human Rights Watch report that included interviews with former trans detainees, found that they were subjected to abusive strip searches in front of male guards, and a peer-reviewed study that analyzed ICE audits found that strip searches of transgender detainees occurred in violation of ICE policy from 2014 to 2019 in at least three states: Washington, Arizona and California.
Yet, it is difficult to estimate how many people are affected by transphobic abuse in immigrant detention centers. 
Under the second Trump administration, ICE is excluding the number of transgender detainees from constitutionally-mandated detention center reports. The last report issued by the Biden administration in January 2025 recorded that there were 47 transgender people in immigration detention. But according to the Vera Institute of Justice, the government is not counting transgender people due to the administration’s hostility towards trans people’s lives and rights.
The 2025 executive order that President Donald Trump signed equated gender with biological sex and mandated federal agencies to remove “all statements, policies, regulations, forms, communications, or other internal and external messages” which recognized transgender and gender non-conforming people. The order also prohibited trans women from being housed in women’s prisons or detention centers. In effect, they can only be housed in male facilities. 
Shortly after, the 2015 “Transgender Care Memorandum” was taken offline. It was last available in February 2025 from ICE’s website, according to the Internet Archive. The memo — signed by Tom Homan, then the executive director for ICE under the Obama administration — established basic care requirements for transgender detainees. (Homan is now Trump’s “border czar.”) For example, it mandated limiting solitary confinement to 72 hours, to consider placing a detainee in housing consistent with their gender identity, and to conduct strip searches in private, among other rules. Additionally, contracts with some detention facilities had their transgender care requirements removed. 
While past complaints indicate that these transgender care requirements were often violated by facilities, the memo still gave trans detainees a degree of recognition, as well as a way to challenge discriminatory treatment. 
“We know that the government is making it impossible to even be yourself in prison,” Déa Thatcher, an organizer with Trans & Queer Community Fund, a mutual aid group that provides commissary support for trans immigrant detainees, said. “When I tell you the amount of times I’ve gotten on a video with someone and they have put their hands over their face because they don’t want me to see their beard, it’s like they are being forced to look a certain way and present a certain way.”
‘I am practically signing my death warrant‘
According to Rivas’ habeas corpus petition, she is seeking asylum due to being targeted by the Honduran Los Zetas cartel, who she claims murdered her brothers after she refused to traffic drugs for them. She had been harassed by them for years due to being transgender, the petition says. Mexican cartel members later kidnapped and assaulted Rivas on her journey to the U.S.-Mexico border. 
“If I go back to my country, I am practically signing my death warrant,” Rivas said. 
Sofia and Toro de Paula are also seeking asylum after being subjected to transphobic physical violence in their home countries. They both had their asylum petitions denied and are appealing the decision.“In general, trans women had a shot at winning (asylum) because of how our asylum laws are written and because trans people are targeted in many countries for being trans,” Jong told Verite News.
But immigration detention makes it harder for their legal team to prepare an asylum case or an appeal because they can only meet with detainees for a few hours each week, making it more difficult to prepare a strong case.  It is then much more likely that they will lose their case and be deported. 
“You have to collect all this evidence, where your main person to help you is locked up, with little to no access to the outside world, and where everyone outside is grappling with their absence,” immigration attorney Mich González said. He added that immigrants have cases that could determine life or death, yet are being tried in an administrative court inside a facility that is actively harming people.
The women could be detained indefinitely. The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to review a case determining whether immigrants can be denied bond and kept in detention while they challenge their removal. If the court rules in favor of the Trump administration, the women will have no clear path out of immigration detention, barring deportation or being allowed to legally remain in the country. 
“We want them to treat us with dignity and to treat the next trans people who come to this center well, with respect,” Rivas said.

title: Beshear asks Trump to reconsider federal changes to Head Start
description: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has asked President Donald Trump to reconsider proposed changes to the Head Start program that he said would “destabilize early education systems that we have developed over decades.”  This summer, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced an intent to change policies governing the program, which provides free educ[...]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has asked President Donald Trump to reconsider proposed changes to the Head Start program that he said would “destabilize early education systems that we have developed over decades.” 
This summer, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced an intent to change policies governing the program, which provides free education and services to children from birth to age five in low-income families. The program was launched as a pilot in 1965. 
Trump administration threatens to gut Head Start rules

“Over time, the delivery of these crucial services became unnecessarily encumbered by onerous regulations,” the proposed changes memo reads. “Eliminating these restrictive Federal regulations would also empower small and local businesses, freeing them to focus on excellence in service delivery rather than bureaucratic compliance.” 
The proposed changes include a prioritization of the English language, edits to the performance standards described by the Trump administration as “detailed and prescriptive” and more. 
Beshear sent a letter to the president on Tuesday, which was the deadline for public comment, and said the changes would “cut funding, increase class sizes, weaken curriculum standards, and make our kids less safe.” 
He also said he signed a second letter with representatives from 24 other states asking for the same reconsideration.
During his Wednesday press conference in Frankfort, Beshear said the proposal “makes no sense.” 
“My hope,” said Beshear, “is that the president reads the letters, rolls back these proposed changes and puts the American people, especially our kids, first.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gov. Laura Kelly backs Kansas Democrat for U.S. House, wades into Iowa governor’s race
description: Outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly endorses a Democrat in Kansas' 2nd District congressional race and she taunts the Republican gubernatorial nominee in Iowa.
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly, the two-term Kansas governor, endorses Democrat Don Coover in the 2nd District congressional race and declines to endorse Iowa gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn, a registered Kansas voter until October 2024. This June 26, 2026, image of Kelly is from a Kansas Reflector interview with the governor. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Gov. Laura Kelly issued the anticipated endorsement Wednesday of a fellow Kansas Democrat campaigning for U.S. House and unexpectedly ventured into the Iowa gubernatorial contest to oppose one of her “constituents.”
The two-term governor from Topeka urged voters Nov. 3 to support Don Coover, a U.S. Army veteran, veterinarian and rancher from Galesburg. He’s campaigning for the 2nd District seat held by Republican U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt.
“Kansans deserve leaders who work hard, listen to Kansans and show up ready to get to work on day one, and that’s Don Coover,” Kelly said. “He’ll put Kansans first, not special interests or big donors, and work with both parties to get things done.”
Coover said he was honored to receive Kelly’s blessing and admired her record of placing Kansans ahead of partisan politics.
“I’ll take that same approach to Washington,” he said.
Schmidt celebrated an endorsement by the Kansas State Lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police, which represents thousands of law enforcement officers. He was previously endorsed by Kansas Farm Bureau, Kansas Livestock Association and National Rifle Association.
“In Congress, I’ll continue working to give law enforcement the tools and resources they need, protect those who protect us and keep Kansas communities safe,” Schmidt said.
Meanwhile, Kelly took to social media to support Democrat Rob Sand, who is competing against Republican Zach Lahn in the race for Iowa governor. A point of contention has been a revelation that Lahn voted in Kansas elections during 2018, 2020 and 2022 before registering in October 2024 to vote in Iowa. Another campaign topic has been Lahn’s frequent trips to visit his children in Kansas.
“Imagine my surprise when I learned that one of my constituents is running for governor,” Kelly said. “Not here in his home state of Kansas, but two states over in Iowa. Now, generally, I support Kansans. I was even proud to see Zach Lahn voted here in ’18, ’20 and ’22. I hope he voted for me in the Kansas governor’s race. But in the Iowa governor’s race, I’m supporting the Iowan.”
“Zach, there are no hard feelings, but it is time to come back to Kansas,” she said. “As they say, there’s no place like home.”
Lahn graduated from high school in Iowa before attending college in Colorado and working on political campaigns in Colorado and Montana. During the gubernatorial race in Iowa, Lahn said his official residence was a farm near Belle Plaine, Iowa.
He moved to Wichita nearly a decade ago to help launch a private school financed by the son and daughter-in-law of billionaire Charles Koch. With millions of dollars from the Koch family and backing of Chase and Annie Koch, the school opened in 2018. Annie Koch and Lahn divorced their spouses and married each other, which coincided with signs of financial stress at the school known as Wonder. The Lahns loaned the school at least $4.5 million.
Lahn said he returned to Iowa in 2023, but children in his blended family stayed in Wichita. The Des Moines Register reported that Lahn, a licensed pilot, flew from Iowa to Kansas 37 times from October 2025 to May 2026.
During the Tuesday debate in Iowa between Lahn and Sand, the issue of Lahn’s residency was raised.
“I have a blended family, and they split time,” Lahn said. “And I’m gonna tell you right now, I am not going to be intimidated on this.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Lincoln Party puts out statement of principles, which foe calls ‘bare minimum’
description: After facing criticism for lacking any policy platform, Indiana’s fledgling Lincoln Party released Wednesday what it called a statement of principles.
text:
The Lincoln Party logo.After facing criticism for lacking any policy platform, Indiana’s fledgling Lincoln Party released Wednesday what it called a statement of principles.
The Lincoln Party’s platform is at issue because it will gain automatic statewide ballot access for its nominees if its secretary of state candidate, former Republican Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, tops 2% of the vote in this fall’s election.
Lincoln Party Chair Nathan Gotsch says the party’s creation is aimed at making it easier for independent candidates to run for office without having to gather petition signatures to appear on election ballots.
Gotsch, who is Ballard’s campaign manager, said in a statement that all Lincoln Party candidates and party officials will be required to sign and uphold the statement of principles.
Indiana Lincoln Party Chair Nathan Gotsch (Courtesy photo)
Those include broad strokes such as “ensuring that government protects the rights of all people equally” and meeting “standards for governing in the public interest.”
“The Lincoln Party will be built around principles, not a platform that tells candidates where they have to stand on every issue,” Gotsch said. “That doesn’t mean our candidates won’t have clear positions on issues. Quite the opposite. It will be their job to tell voters where they stand and what policies they want to advance to solve the problems facing their communities.”
Republican candidate Max Engling has faulted Ballard and the Lincoln Party for a lack of stances on taxes, social issues and other policies.
Engling’s campaign did not immediately comment Wednesday on the Lincoln Party’s announcement. 
He previously criticized the Lincoln Party as presenting voters a blank slate of future support for what it regards as “high-quality candidates” without any stated ideology.
“To me, that says nothing about what they stand for,” Engling said.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh’s campaign declined to comment Wednesday.
The Libertarian Party has retained automatic ballot access by topping the 2% mark in secretary of state voting every four years since 1994.
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings knocked the Lincoln Party statement as “establishing a bare minimum standard.”
“What the Lincoln Party released is a code of conduct,” Shillings said. “It’s nice, but it isn’t a policy platform, and I don’t think it’s news. Pretty much every political party, every elected or appointed official and anyone else who holds an office job already adheres to something very similar.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: US Wind pulls out of wind turbine manufacturing at Sparrows Point
description: US Wind, the company behind a proposed offshore wind farm off the coast of Ocean City, no longer plans to develop components for wind turbines at Sparrows Point — at least not for now — turning its lease over to Anduril Industries to build a shipyard there.
text:
US Wind CEO Jeff Grybowski outside the U.S. District Court in Baltimore on Dec. 10, 2025, after a hearing on the Trump administration's plans to reconsider the permit issued for its Maryland wind farm. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)US Wind, the company behind a proposed offshore wind development off the coast of Ocean City, no longer plans to develop components for wind turbines at Baltimore County’s Sparrows Point — at least not for now.
The Baltimore-based company turned over its lease at the Tradepoint Atlantic site in Sparrows Point to Anduril Industries, the shipbuilding company whose arrival was heralded on Tuesday by a visit from President Donald Trump (R).
It comes as US Wind’s only offshore wind project, planned for Ocean City’s coastline, continues to face legal headwinds and roadblocks from the Trump administration.
At the tail end of President Joe Biden’s (D) administration, the US Wind project received its last federal permit, but the town of Ocean City challenged it shortly thereafter. And after Trump’s inauguration, the federal government that once defended the permit permit for the project signaled its intent to revoke it, spurring a new round of legal wrangling.
Sparrows Point shipyard could bring thousands of jobs, promises billions in investments

In a statement issued Tuesday, US Wind CEO Jeff Grybowski said his company “jumped at the opportunity” to bring “near-term” jobs to the Sparrows Point site as US Wind faces delays. The site will be taken over by Anduril, which plans to invest $3.7 billion at the former home of Bethlehem Steel to construct a new shipbuilding facility, Arsenal-2, that is expected to bring an estimated 3,100 permanent new jobs to Maryland.
“Our offshore wind plans, like many other similar projects in the U.S., are delayed due to legal disputes and uncertainty created by federal agencies. So, we are shifting our focus to helping Anduril build a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility at Sparrows Point,” Grybowski’s statement said. “This new development ensures that job creation and economic development can proceed apace at [Tradepoint].”
The facility at Tradepoint had been expected to fabricate steel components for wind turbines, including towers and monopiles, and create hundreds of manufacturing jobs. Last year, the Trump administration pulled back $47.4 million in grant funding that had been awarded during the Biden administration for the steel facility, called Sparrows Point Steel, but US Wind said at the time that it planned to move forward with the steel fabrication site anyway.
In a statement on Wednesday, Rebecca Rehr, the director of climate policy and justice at the Maryland League of Conservation Voters, bemoaned the news about Sparrows Point Steel, calling it another negative effect of Trump administration policies on clean-energy companies.
“Maryland faces rising energy demand and electricity bills. We have been consistently disappointed that the Trump administration doesn’t see the value across the supply chain for the clean energy industry, and continues to single out wind when wind is working,” Rehr said.
“We are seeing job and growth opportunities across clean energy sectors, yet this administration continues to block these projects, which are the fastest and cheapest to deploy,” her statement said.

text:
Van Ingram, longtime director of the Kentucky Office of Drug Control Policy is retiring after 22 years. (Screenshot)Help is available to Kentuckians living with addiction. For resources, visit https://findhelpnow.org/ky. In physical emergencies, call 911. For mental health crises, call or text 988. Locate free Naloxone (Narcan), which can reverse overdoses, near you here. 
Van Ingram, the longtime head of Kentucky’s Office of Drug Control Policy, is retiring at the end of 2026, Gov. Andy Beshear announced Wednesday. 
Tara Hyde, the CEO of People Advocating Recovery who is in long term recovery, will step into the role of executive director. 
Ingram has been with the office since 2004, when Ernie Fletcher was governor of Kentucky. 
Before that, he worked with the Maysville Kentucky Police Department for 23 years, including six as chief of police, according to the Justice and Public Safety Cabinet. Ingram was named executive director of the office in 2008. 
“There are caring people all over state government, in every cabinet and every agency, that have worked to bring this problem under control, as well as the Administrative Office of the Courts, the General Assembly, have all played a big part in our success,” said Ingram. 
During Ingram’s time with the Office of Drug Control Policy, overdose deaths took a downward turn. The 2025 Drug Overdose Fatality Report showed overdose deaths are down nearly 23% from 2024, following a four-year downward trend. 
Tara Hyde. (Sam Foree)
“It’s this work that led governor after governor, both Republicans and Democrats, to reappoint him to this position,” Beshear said during a Wednesday press conference in Frankfort. 
Hyde, a longtime advocate for policy to help people in recovery, has herself been in recovery since 2011. 
“Since being in recovery and overcoming addiction, I’ve found a real passion for helping people, for getting people access to services and for creating new services when they didn’t exist,” Hyde said. “That’s why I’ve made it my life’s work to support recovery services as well as individuals who are actively seeking help.” 
She added: “I look forward to stepping into this role to support my fellow Kentuckians who are fighting addiction and going through substance use disorder treatment, recovery support services, looking for housing and gaining access to meaningful, passionate lives — because that’s what we all deserve.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s housing crisis needs bold answers
description:
Homelessness has become ordinary in Vermont. And that is extraordinary.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s housing crisis needs bold answers.
text:
This commentary is by David Bond, who taught at Bennington College from 2013 to 2026. He now runs the Center for Environmental Justice at Georgetown University. 
Vermont is not an easy place to be homeless. Winters are unforgiving, and this rural state has minimal infrastructure to support unhoused people. Shelters are few and far between, and most were built when the loss of housing was a temporary setback tied to house fires or fleeing domestic abuse.
Personal tragedy is no longer the trigger of homelessness in Vermont. Today, a social catastrophe rips all manner of residents from their homes with ruthless indifference. Yet our government seems incapable of reckoning with this unfolding disaster.
Last year, I taught a class on the housing crisis at Bennington College. My students and I read every report we could find and interviewed shelter staff, local journalists and housing advocates who all describe the same horror story: a system overwhelmed by desperation. 
Ten years ago, the median price of a home in Vermont was $200,000. Today, it’s $438,000. Home prices have nearly doubled over the past decade while salaries increased at half that rate, with most wage growth accruing on the higher end of the income ladder. A newly constructed home in Vermont now has a median price of $620,000, a sticker price out of reach for, by my calculation, 80% of the state’s population. 
Rents have also risen while the income of most renters has flatlined at $43,000. In some Vermont communities, the median fair market rent has almost doubled in the past five years. And today, half of all renters in Vermont have slipped into what the Department of Housing and Urban Development defines as cost-burdened as rent eats up more and more of their paychecks. 
The human wreckage of these numbers gathers in parking lots crowded with occupied cars each night, in tattered encampments in the woods and under the overpass, and in the long lines outside public libraries and recreational centers each morning waiting for the privilege of a bathroom: rural homelessness.
While the actual number of homeless people in Vermont may seem minor in comparison with states like California and New York, the rate of increase in homelessness in Vermont outstrips every other state.

READ MORE

And in contrast with those states, the homeless in Vermont are not pouring in from elsewhere nor willfully rejecting society. By and large, unhoused people have deep roots in the Green Mountain State. And a great number of them are working full-time or are seniors living on the fixed income of retirement.
In Vermont, housing costs have achieved escape velocity from the economic fundamentals of place. What working residents can afford is no longer a gravitational force holding mortgages and rents within the realm of reason.
For Vermonters losing their grip on housing, few accord the crisis any academic explanation. It’s a full-time job that no longer adds up. It’s a sickness that bankrupted a family. It’s retirement that never factored in inflation. It’s student loans when no one is hiring. It’s a divorce that cut a paycheck in half. It’s a minor setback that spirals into total loss.
Three converging trends offer a provisional explanation of the housing disaster in Vermont.
First, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many cooped-up residents in Boston and New York City bought second homes in Vermont. Many of those homes now operate as vacation rentals in a state with the second-highest share of seasonal homes in America. Vacation rentals limit housing available for residents and skew pricing away from local wages and toward weekend wealth.
Second, private equity has elbowed its way into single-family home markets. A recent study found that Vermont has witnessed a 60% rise in corporate investor purchases of single-family homes, catapulting the state into the top 10 for growth of private equity in residential markets. 
And third, global investors, having amassed more wealth than can be profitably held in checking accounts or stocks, now turn to U.S. real estate. Their outsized investments in luxury properties may have started in big cities, but their telltale signs ripple outward into rural areas: surging prices with high vacancy rates. 
This all shines a rather unflattering light on high-minded talk of supply and demand as the most sensible solution to the housing crisis. Simply unshackling private developers to build, build, build may only construct more vacation homes and investment opportunities for elites from elsewhere.
Vermont was founded as an armed animus to absentee landlords. Where are the bold visions now to meet this housing crisis at scale? Where are the radical policies and programs that can place housing costs back within reach of working Vermonters?
In my class, students brainstormed how Vermont might seize shuttered colleges and factories to remake public housing for the 21st century. We explored how Vermont might look to Red Vienna or Mexico’s National Housing Fund or even American labor unions’ unrealized plans for mutual housing as models to meet this crisis at scale. And we imagined how Vermont might become a beacon for young talent eager to get to work building a more just, sustainable and dignified world.
When Gov. Phil Scott’s executive housing team visited our class, students jumped at the chance to ask about their visions for public housing. The deputy secretary of the Agency of Human Services, Kristin McClure, responded to the premise by saying, “Vermont is not looking to become more of a landlord.” Reflecting on the quarter-billion dollars Vermont spent on emergency housing in the past few years, she added, “We did the math, and we could have housed every single homeless person had we built new units with that money.”

text:
DMACC and Ankeny Community School District have partnered to put high school students in a professional early childhood education environment. (Photo by Lourdes Balduque/Getty Images)Des Moines Area Community College is helping high school students get a jumpstart on their early childhood education training through a partnership with the Ankeny Community School District.
The Ankeny-based community college announced in a news release Wednesday it is expanding its relationship with the school district through a program allowing high school students to attend early childhood education courses at Terrace Learning Center, which houses the district’s preschool program.
According to the release, this initiative is two years in the making and transforms courses previously offered online only through the community college’s online career academy into in-person instruction and on-the-job observation of professionals.

Students who enroll in the Introduction to Early Childhood Education and Childhood Health, Safety and Nutrition courses will be taught on-site by a DMACC instructor and have opportunities to complete observation and clinical work.
“Offering the courses through DMACC faculty allows traditional college students to enroll in the same sections alongside high school students,” said DMACC early childhood education program chair Katie Champlin in the release. “As a result, both groups experience a more authentic college classroom environment while high school students benefit from learning alongside current college students.”
With this partnership, students will gain a more complete picture of what working in early childhood education looks like beyond any assumptions that having only classroom work can create, Champlin said in the release, aiding them in building confidence and establishing their “professional identities as future early childhood educators.”
The overarching goal of the district and community college’s work is to help high school students earn a certificate in early childhood education, with 13 required credits, before they earn their diploma. This certificate satisfies the education requirement for the Child Development Associate credential as well.
“Ultimately, the partnership creates a pathway,” Champlin said in the release. “An opportunity to explore the profession, develop practical skills, earn college credit and credentials, and see a clear pathway toward continued education and employment in (early childhood education).”

title: Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints
description: Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints New public portal gives Delawareans a direct way to report fraud, waste, corruption and misuse of state resources DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s Office of the Inspector General has launched a public website and complaint hotline, giving residents, state employees and others a direc[...]
text:
Delaware inspector general launches website, hotline for fraud and abuse complaints
New public portal gives Delawareans a direct way to report fraud, waste, corruption and misuse of state resources
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s Office of the Inspector General has launched a public website and complaint hotline, giving residents, state employees and others a direct way to report suspected fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and misuse of state government resources.
The launch marks another step in establishing the independent watchdog office created by the General Assembly in 2025 and now led by Delaware’s first inspector general, Robert P. Storch.
The new website provides information about the office, its responsibilities and how it operates. It also includes an online form for submitting complaints and concerns to the inspector general.
Complaints and inquiries are kept confidential to the greatest extent possible, according to the office, and people filing reports may choose to remain anonymous.
“The public launch of the new OIG website and Hotline mark an important milestone in the development of our office,” Storch said in an announcement reported by Delaware news organizations.
Storch said the office is continuing to hire staff while giving the public more information about the agency and how concerns can be reported.
New avenue for government complaints
The Office of the Inspector General was established as an independent, nonpartisan state agency responsible for detecting and deterring fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuses of government resources that harm the public interest.
State law allows the inspector general to investigate the management and operations of state agencies and to begin investigations either on the office’s own initiative or after receiving a complaint.
Complaints may be submitted by individuals or organizations.
The law also requires the office to maintain a telephone number, website, email address and mailing address for complaints and inquiries.
The inspector general is required to remain neutral and impartial and is not intended to serve as an advocate either for the person filing a complaint or for the state agency involved.
Delaware’s first inspector general
Gov. Matt Meyer signed Senate Bill 4 in August 2025, creating the Office of the Inspector General following years of discussion about establishing an independent statewide government watchdog.
Storch was sworn in May 8 as Delaware’s first inspector general.
At the time, state officials said the office was intended to strengthen accountability, transparency and public confidence in state government.
Storch previously served as inspector general for the U.S. Department of Defense and as the first Senate-confirmed inspector general of the National Security Agency. He also held senior positions in the U.S. Department of Justice Office of Inspector General.
One of Storch’s early priorities was establishing a public website and complaint hotline so Delawareans would have a direct way to bring concerns to the new office.
What the office can investigate
The inspector general’s jurisdiction includes allegations involving fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuses of government resources.
The office may examine the management and operations of state agencies and investigate complaints involving the public interest.
The law also limits the office’s role in routine employment disputes involving state workers unless those complaints are connected to fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption or another abuse of government resources.
The inspector general also is expected to coordinate with the Delaware Department of Justice, auditor of accounts, Public Integrity Commission and other investigative or law enforcement agencies when appropriate.
State law generally requires the inspector general to issue public findings and recommendations following completed investigations.
The office also must issue an annual report outlining complaints received, investigations opened and completed, significant investigations and unresolved recommendations or concerns.
The launch of the website and hotline gives Delawareans a direct point of access to an office created specifically to investigate concerns about how state government operates and how taxpayer resources are used.
TO GO: Delaware Office of the Inspector General

Website: https://oig.delaware.gov/
Online complaint form: https://complaint.oig.delaware.gov/
Hotline: 1-855-OIG-6998
Local phone: 302-244-DOIG
Email: OIG_Hotline@delaware.gov
Mailing address:
60 Loockerman Plaza
Dover, DE 19901
Confidentiality: Complaints and inquiries are kept confidential to the greatest extent possible. People filing complaints may also choose to report anonymously.
What it does: Investigates allegations of fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption and other abuse of Delaware government resources.
Who can file a complaint: Individuals and organizations may submit complaints.
What can be reported: Suspected fraud, corruption, misuse of taxpayer resources, serious mismanagement or other government conduct that may harm the public interest.
What it generally does not handle: Routine state employee workplace disputes unless they involve fraud, waste, mismanagement, corruption or misuse of government resources.

title: Alert: Mississippi Blood Services seeks donors to ease shortage
description: A Mississippi Blood Services employee collects blood at the organization in Flowood on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Blood Services is calling on all eligible donors to give blood as it struggles with a severe supply shortage.
Donors of every blood type are needed.
Kasey Dickson, Mississippi Blood Services director of marketing and public relations, explained that it’s normal for donations to drop during the summer. However, MBS isn’t sure what’s causing the ongoing slowdown.
Mississippi’s blood shortage is part of a national problem. The American Red Cross, America’s Blood Centers and the Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies released a joint statement in July calling for more donations to help the nation’s strained blood supply.
MBS needs 250 blood donations and 40 platelet donations daily to maintain a healthy supply. Dickson said the amount of donations it currently receives daily is “not anywhere near that.” 
“Blood cannot be made in a tube,” Dickson said. “The only way that blood can be provided to other individuals in need is if individuals themselves donate it.”
Mississippi Blood Services provides blood products to over 50 hospitals statewide, as well as ambulance and helicopter services that transport to rural communities. This includes whole blood, platelets and more.
MBS collects products at facilities in Flowood, Oxford and with mobile collection units. 
Eligible donors can walk in or schedule an appointment. People can find information on eligibility on MBS’ website and by calling 601-981-3232. 
MBS recommends donors prepare by eating a healthy meal and drinking plenty of fluids. Donors will be given an onsite health screening, which includes a questionnaire and a mini-physical. 
Once blood is collected, it gets tested for its blood type, red blood cell antibodies and undergoes nucleic acid amplification testing. It’s also screened for infections, including HIV-1 and hepatitis B. After testing and processing, it’s ready to be delivered to hospitals in need.
MBS has been spreading the word about the need for donations, as well as holding special promotions. For Breast Cancer Awareness Donor Appreciation Week, people who donate at the Flowood and Oxford centers can receive a free T-shirt and car magnet while supplies last through Friday.
