name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Future of Mass Save in limbo as Legislature stalls on energy bill
description: A political backlash to Mass Save, amid a rising tide of angst over soaring utility bills, has taken root in the Bay State.
text:
IMAGINE THAT YOU’RE part of a team charged with crafting the next iteration of one of the largest energy efficiency programs in the country, the budget of which exceeds that of the University of Massachusetts system. 
Now add in the fact that the 200 elected officials in the Massachusetts Legislature, could — and very well may — come in at any point between now and January 5, 2027, and blow it all up.  
That’s what’s currently playing out. 
Mass Save is a program that provides low or no-cost energy efficiency upgrades to homes and businesses around the state with the goal of reducing energy usage and, therefore, monthly bills. To do that, electric and gas customers pay a surcharge to fund the program, which offers home energy assessments, improved insulation, smart thermostats and, increasingly, electric heat pumps to warm and cool buildings.  
But a political backlash to Mass Save, amid a rising tide of angst over soaring utility bills, has taken root — and spread to influential members on Beacon Hill. After the House advanced a plan to slash next year’s Mass Save budget by $1 billion and the Senate rejected that proposal, lawmakers are now negotiating whether the program’s budget should be cut, capped, or left to program officials to figure out as it works through a sprawling energy bill that aims to lower prices for ratepayers.  
Meanwhile, as that contentious legislative debate lingers, there’s something else happening under the radar: Planning for the next three-year Mass Save cycle is already well underway. 
Utilities that administer the program are preparing to submit by the end of March a draft plan that will chart the course for what Mass Save will seek to accomplish between 2028 and 2030.  
There’s just one problem. It’s entirely unclear whether and how the Legislature will wade into Mass Save’s budget through the energy bill, threatening to upend all the planning, modeling, stakeholder discussions, and consultant reports that have already been completed to shape the future of the program, which is overseen by the Energy Efficiency Advisory Council.  
“This is one great big exercise in holding your breath,” said Steven Miller, founder of LabReNew, a company that helps research and scientific labs reduce their carbon footprint, and a member of the EEAC. 
Gov. Maura Healey, who is seeking reelection this year, has also offered little clarity on whether she’s on board with the proposed Mass Save cut and what future direction she wants the program to take.  
At a press conference on Monday in Everett where she announced new home heating assistance, Healey demurred several times after being pressed on her stance on the program and her role in legislative negotiations. Instead, she touted her “all of the above” approach to energy to lower prices and “strongly” urged the Legislature to pass the energy affordability package she filed 18 months ago. Her version of that bill left the current Mass Save budget intact, but she did embrace a cap on the program in the future this past summer.  
Mass Save’s budget has grown from roughly $3 billion between 2019 and 2021 to $4.5 billion for the current three-year cycle, increasing the fee on customer bills. That’s after the Department of Public Utilities (DPU), which has to approve the plan, decided to reduce the budget proposal for the current Mass Save cycle by $500 million in February 2025, an initial signal of the wariness among some in state government of the burden on ratepayers. 
But now, the politics around energy affordability at large and the specific discussions underway in the Legislature have forced those involved in the program’s future to consider the need to recalibrate and prepare for tighter fiscal limits despite looming climate commitments and rising power demand.  
“There are new constraints on the budget, and I think that has set up some boundaries for the discussion this time,” said Brooks Winner, Boston’s director of community energy programs who serves on the EEAC. “Obviously, it’s different than it was three years ago. In some ways it’s helping us all be laser focused on what is worth investing in. It’s required us to sharpen our pencils and be really clear about what our priorities are.” 
Mass Save has evolved significantly since it first launched in 2008, starting as an initiative mainly designed to conduct home energy assessments, distribute LED lightbulbs, and ensure homes and businesses are weatherized and well-insulated.  
It was also fairly agnostic as to how buildings were heated and cooled: Reducing the amount of energy required to keep a home comfortable is good for both the individual customer’s wallet and everyone else because it lowers energy demand for the whole system. 
But it’s morphed into a much larger program, which has made it a prime focus for elected officials eager to pull a quick lever to lower energy costs in a state that has among the highest in the country. Mass Save has become one of the few tools available to the state to drive decarbonization for a sector of the economy that accounts for 35 percent of greenhouse gas emissions in Massachusetts. 
In addition to weatherization efforts, the program now also aims to switch households from their oil or gas heating system to an electric heat pump — technology that is much more expensive than a traditional insulation job — and expand rebates and incentives toward renters, moderate-income customers, and customers living in designated equity communities — populations that have historically been left out even though they also pay into Mass Save.  
“We will continue to advocate for a focus on lowering the energy bills of low- and moderate-income communities, improving delivery of services, and cutting administrative costs,” Lauren Diggin, a spokesperson for the Department of Energy Resources, said in a statement. “We are committed to ensuring a cost-effective program that efficiently delivers to customers.” 
The debate inside the EEAC as it prepares Mass Save’s next three-year planessentially boils down to breadth versus depth.  
The state could embark on a plan that places more emphasis on traditional weatherizations and insulations with some focus on heat pumps — a narrower effort that may reach more homes by eating up less of the program’s budget but deliver fewer emissions benefits. It could also aim to simply bring as many households into the program as possible without regard for income level or renter status.  
Or, the state could more aggressively pursue costlier heat pump and solar panel installations and deepen targets baked into the current plan to reserve a set amount of benefits for lower- and middle- income customers. That would continue the effort to work toward greater equity within the program and potentially provide greater emissions benefits but likely reach fewer customers overall.  
For the current program cycle, program administrators developed a list of 21 designated equity communities in cities like Brockton, Worcester, Springfield, and several Boston neighborhoods including Roxbury and Mattapan. Customers there have been offered no-cost weatherizations regardless of income. And they set out to install heat pumps in an additional 87,000 homes between 2025 and 2027 — more than what Mass Save had done cumulatively since 2019. 
For Mass Save proponents, cutting support for energy efficiency — something entirely in the state’s control, unlike the barrage of actions taken by the Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects — is the ultimate self-own.  
Limiting the projected rise in energy demand reduces both the amount of electricity and infrastructure that utilities would need to purchase and pass on to customers. A 2026 analysis by environmental nonprofit Acadia Center found that $8.4 billion in ratepayer investments in Mass Save between 2016 and 2024 yielded $16 billion in savings. The report also found that a $1 billion cut to the program would cost customers $4.5 billion in lost benefits.   
And on the hottest day of 2025, the program generated more than $2.6 million in savings in a single hour by lowering peak energy demand, according to the Department of Energy Resources. 
An outright cut to the current program budget limited to 2027 alone as proposed by the House would save people some money upfront and wouldn’t directly bleed into the next Mass Save cycle, but there would still likely be spillover effects and trigger a scramble inside the EEAC to quickly scale back the program significantly. 
Projects with household and business customers would need to be put on pause, jeopardizing their viability, and contractor jobs would be severely curtailed unless funding ramps back up. Customer trust that has been building — 81 percent of respondents view Mass Save as a trusted resource, up from 69 percent a year ago, according to a survey of 400 Massachusetts residents completed this past May — would likely decline.  
Mass Save is “one of the best ways you can take control of the energy usage in your own home, in your own business, and have more control over your bills and your own financial situation,” said Kate Peters, Eversource’s director of residential energy efficiency. 
A potential legislative compromise to keep the program’s current budget in place but cap or dial back future budgets could limit the upfront costs for ratepayers and provide a useful boundary for Mass Save administrators to understand the direction that Beacon Hill wants to take. But it also risks limiting energy savings down the line and how fast the state can cut emissions.  
Rep. Mark Cusack, chair of the House energy committee (center) presides over a hearing alongside Sen. Michael Barrett, head of the Senate energy committee.  (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
If there are cuts, the utilities and those overseeing the program on the EEAC would have at least a couple of months to digest any legislative reforms made to Mass Save before turning in a draft plan at the end of March — and even longer before they submit a plan to the DPU for review by the end of next October. 
But either way, contingency plans are under discussion regarding what initiatives might need to be scaled back with less funding. 
“Ultimately, it’s going to have to be decided: Who gets voted off the island?” said Larry Chretien, executive director of the Green Energy Consumers Alliance, who opposes the proposed Mass Save cut. 
Others, though, are skeptical that the program, while laudable, is delivering the tangible benefits that justify the more than $1 billion it currently collects from ratepayers each year. 
The majority of the advantages of Mass Save are no longer directly connected to financial benefits for ratepayers, argues the Massachusetts Coalition for Sustainable Energy (MCSE), which consists of business groups across the state. The DPU said as much itself in its approval in 2024 of the current plan, in which the regulators wrote that Mass Save benefits are now mostly derived from emissions reductions that “may not be evident to customers on their bills.”  
Plus, the focus on more expensive heat pumps in the program only reduces emissions if electricity is generated by carbon-free sources. Roughly half of power in New England is still generated by natural gas, while electrification progress has proven “painfully slow,” leading to a program that features “ballooning costs” that are “resulting in very little direct cost savings to ratepayers,” according to letters that the MCSE sent to lawmakers over the summer. 
That’s especially problematic if increased gas-to-heat pump conversions simply lower customers’ gas bills while their electric bills grow — a dynamic that means that “bill savings for program participants can no longer be assumed,” the DPU wrote, though special winter heat pump rates can make the technology more financially feasible. 
“We’ve come to a point where we’ve gone too far,” said Bill Rennie, senior vice president at the Retailers Association of Massachusetts, a member of the MCSE. “Our members are all for renewables, green energy sources, and trying to continue on that path, but to get there, we need to be able to afford to still keep the lights on and keep the heat on. We need a reset.” 
It’s true that Mass Save’s budget has grown substantially and, with it, both what customers pay into the program and the savings that they get out. It’s far and away the largest program of its kind among Northeast states; Mass Save was about $1.5 billion larger than New York’s energy efficiency program last year even though New York has more than double the population of Massachusetts. 
The rate at which Mass Save has grown as a percentage of the typical utility bill, though, is still much less than the overall increase in energy costs in recent years.  
As policymakers hash out how much is too much with respect to what burden ratepayers should bear in funding energy efficiency, there’s one macroeconomic shift that could meaningfully change the Mass Save calculus: The war in Iran that has sent oil prices surging.  
Diesel is now an unprecedented $6.30 per gallon on average nationwide, according to AAA, with heating oil costing an average of $6.12 per gallon in Massachusetts. 
About 1 in 5 households in the Bay State, mostly in the western part of the state, heat their homes with heating oil, one of the highest rates in the country. Heating oil prices are up 74 percent compared to last year, state data show. 
The price spike could lead some lawmakers to feel even more bullish about the need to lower energy bills right away, including through a cut to Mass Save. 
But others hope the geopolitical landscape further strengthens the case for Mass Save and to get off volatile fossil fuels. 
Last winter, state officials forecasted that the cost to produce heat was relatively close between heating oil and heat pumps, with the assumption that oil would cost $3.10 per gallon — without the special heat pump rate factored in. 
That modeling would likely look much different when heat pumps are compared to oil now at roughly double the cost. 
“This is more essential than ever,” said Kyle Murray, Massachusetts program director at Acadia Center, an environmental nonprofit. “It just lays bare that this is the economic pain that we are vulnerable to by not making these investments.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Advance Fact Check: Tom Barrett’s voting record and Will Lawrence’s goals for healthcare
description: Voter Guide: 2026 Michigan General Election U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s congressional and his time in the Michigan Legislature came under fire during the first televised debate between him and Democratic nominee Will Lawrence, as did the challenger’s claims regarding the feasibility of his healthcare plans and the various attacks he lobbed against Barrett on Tue[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Charlotte, left, and Democratic nominee for U.S. House William Lawrence, right, face off in their first head-to-head debate at WKAR's studios in East Lansing, Mich., on Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/WKAR-MSU)Voter Guide: 2026 Michigan General Election

U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s congressional and his time in the Michigan Legislature came under fire during the first televised debate between him and Democratic nominee Will Lawrence, as did the challenger’s claims regarding the feasibility of his healthcare plans and the various attacks he lobbed against Barrett on Tuesday in a forum organized by WKAR-TV.
The debate recorded at the station’s studios on the campus of Michigan State University also included attacks on Barrett (R-Charlotte) for being lockstep with President Donald Trump’s economic, military and immigration agendas, while Barrett hit Lawrence for his past social media commentary on various political issues throughout the years.
Michigan Advance fact-checked the candidates’ biggest claims and compared them with available evidence.
 
CLAIM: Recent gas price increases were due to the war in Iran and that the economy would recover as the war winds down, Barrett said.
While much of the strain on fuel prices stems from fallout of the Iran war, prices were already high going into Trump’s second term in the Oval Office. Fuel price data shows that it was only slightly lower this time last year. The current average price for a gallon of gasoline in Michigan is $4.40 per gallon of regular unleaded, according to AAA. 
The war with Iran started in late February of this year. In October 2025, AAA reported the average Michigan gas price as being $3.09 a gallon. Gas prices in Michigan were at an average of $3.14 per gallon of regular unleaded when Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.
 
CLAIM: Barrett voted against authorization for Trump to continue waging the Iran war and has separated himself from Trump’s decision to start hostilities.
Barrett was adamant during the debate that he had separated himself from Trump on his determination to wage war with Iran, and that his decision to do so began after Trump’s 60-day window, as dictated by the War Powers Act, closed. 
The U.S. House of Representatives roll call votes show that Barrett voted against a resolution in March put forward by U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) to end the war per Section 5C of the War Powers Act. The vote failed 212-219.
A resolution to end the war under the same section of the act was put forward by U.S. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) in June, which Barrett voted for — one of only four Republicans to vote for the measure, which passed 215-208. It also passed the U.S. Senate 50-48, but it was derailed by Trump after a meeting with Senate leadership.
ABC News also noted that the measure that passed both chambers of Congress did not carry the force of law and only indicated symbolic opposition.
A measure that would have effectively given congressional authorization and potentially ended the war — known as a formal Authorization for Use of Military Force — was introduced by Barrett in May. The legislation would have carried the force of law as opposed to the resolutions passed throughout the year. It would have defined, set limits on and detailed a plan to end the war in Iran. His legislation would have ended the war by July 30, if passed. 
Barrett is the only House Republican to have issued an AUMF. The U.S. House has not voted on Barrett’s legislation, and it still sits in the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.
 
CLAIM: Single-payer health care as promoted by Lawrence was just “Medicare for All” repackaged, and would cost $40 trillion for taxpayers and the nation, Barrett said. 
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services concluded in 2017 that healthcare spending in the U.S. would reach nearly $6 trillion by 2027 and that consumers could spend over $42.9 trillion on healthcare over the next decade.
Lawrence has supported a single-payer healthcare system that mimics other progressive Democrats’ call for Medicare for All as a way to not only rein in those costs but devise a healthcare system that would provide better access.
Lawrence faults Barrett over Medicaid cuts, renews Medicare for All push

Various studies and analyses by universities and policy think tanks have offered differing conclusions about the true cost of switching to a single-payer system.
The American Action Forum, a center-right policy institute, has said that the fiscal burden of the switch would be too great and that lawmakers should rule it out. Both U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and former Vice President Kamala Harris issued plans for the same kind of system when they ran for president over the last decade, respectively. Harris’ platform was expected to increase federal spending by $43.9 trillion.
Yale University’s School of Public Health and the University of Maryland, Baltimore both found in a July study that there could be savings with single-payer healthcare. That said, the Scientific American, which leans left in the AllSides media bias chart, noted that those studies were not peer reviewed. Still, the magazine did note that the money and lives saved with such a system could mean $1.04 trillion in savings.
Yale, as it separately analyzed Sanders’ plan from 2020, also found that a Medicare for All system could save 68,000 lives by increasing healthcare access, and that it could shrink healthcare spending by 13%, or $450 billion a year.
Lawrence, like Sanders and Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, also believes that his healthcare plan would see end users pay less.
 
CLAIM: Barrett has rejected corporate PAC contributions from the health insurance industry.
Both The ’Gander Newsroom and American Journal News — two left leaning and progressive news outlets — have noted this year that Barrett’s claims of never taking health insurance PAC contributions was half true: He had accepted contributions but had returned some of that money. One contribution that he hadn’t returned was a $1,000 contribution made to his reelection campaign in June from UnitedHealth Group PAC.
That said, Barrett has accepted more than $20,000 in contributions from the pharmaceutical industry during his time in office, particularly in his 2022 and 2024 campaigns, according to both American Journal News and OpenSecrets, a campaign finance tracker.
 
CLAIM: Barrett voted against the reauthorization of warrantless surveillance.
The Advance reported in September. that Barrett co-sponsored the Protection Against Mass Surveillance Act, put forward by U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), which bars federal agencies from purchasing and deploying automated surveillance systems like Flock cameras. 
The bill would also bar state, local and tribal governments from using federal funds to purchase and operate automated surveillance technology.
As he reiterated in Tuesday’s debate, Barrett has repeatedly said that he was willing to break with his party — and Trump — on the issue of mass surveillance as a way to protect individuals’ Fourth Amendment rights.
However, the House has not moved on Burchett’s bill, and it still sits in the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
CLAIM: Barret said local control on the siting of large scale energy projects, and potentially data centers, was stripped away by Lansing Democrats in pursuit of a Michigan Green New Deal.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in November 2023 signed Public Act 233 into law, which allows for the Michigan Public Service Commission to circumvent local ordinances when it comes to the siting of large renewable energy projects. The legislation was a priority for the Democratic-led trifecta in the Michigan Legislature — a time when the party controlled both the state House and Senate with Whitmer in office as the executive.
The projects can include large scale solar or battery storage projects, but the law says nothing about AI data centers.
The worry from some township leaders, like Fabius Township Supervisor Dan Wilkins, is that Whitmer also in 2024 signed PA 181 and PA 207, which offered tax incentives to data centers in Michigan. 
That has some like Wilkins worried about residents not being able to opt out of MPSC control over decisions on data centers with state incentives in play. It was not just Democrats, however, who pushed for an uptick in the state’s renewable energy portfolio, as Wilkins notes in a July blog post on the Fabius Township website. 
Former Gov. Rick Snyder, a Republican, signed PA 341 of 2016, which sought to increase that portfolio standard from 10% to 15% by 2021. The law did not directly call for new green projects, but it did help spur additional wind and solar energy production in Michigan.
 
CLAIM: Barrett voted to block state-based AI regulations for data centers and gave $80 billion in tax breaks to corporations interested in building data centers, Lawrence said.
The Center for American Progress reported that Barrett had voted for a version of Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act that had included a 10-year ban on enforcing state and local AI regulations. That provision would have barred enforcement of local laws and regulations that could have restricted or regulated AI models and systems, the organization said.
Barrett pushes for international AI agreement as health professionals back Doctors Not AI Act

Barrett said after the debate that was false. The words “data centers” were never mentioned in the language of the bill, Barrett said, and he noted that the language spoke of artificial intelligence only “as a broad technology” like other telecommunications systems. Barrett said the concern was for a potential patchwork of regulatory frameworks across the nation when AI technology, systems and its data could cross state lines. Barrett said he believed the federal government should take the lead on regulations and that states could add on to that framework.
American Century Investments, an investment and financial success firm, wrote a September 2025 blog post analyzing the impacts of the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act on Big Tech. The firm’s accountants noted that the act gave billions in tax breaks to major AI companies and laid the groundwork to build data centers. Those same companies are projected to save $14 billion to $18 billion a year in taxes due to Trump’s bill.
Barrett both supported and championed the bill. He also voted for the SPEED Act, which helped speed up data center construction and federal permitting, and was widely praised by the data center industry, according to CNBC.
 
CLAIM: Fentanyl deaths were down since Trump retook office and implemented sweeping immigration action via U.S. Border Patrol and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Barrett said.
Like Barrett, The White House this year said that Trump’s targeting of nations he deemed as supporting “narco-terrorism,” his tariffs on nations like Mexico in response to alleged drug trafficking and his use of ICE against supposed gangs like Tren de Aragua, have contributed to steep declines in overdose deaths — 14% between 2024 and 2025. Trump’s administration also noted that fentanyl deaths had dropped 22% in that same period.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported in February 2025, just one month after Trump returned to office, that it had provisional data to show that there was a 24% decline in total drug overdose deaths in the United States. That said, the CDC noted then that multiple factors contributed to the drop, and that shifts in the illegal drug supply was just one factor.
Yet The Inter-American Dialogue, a non-profit policy think tank dedicated to Western Hemisphere issues, noted that the U.S. had likely “turned the corner on the fentanyl crisis” before Trump even took office. The think tank’s data shows that, instead, fentanyl overdoses began to significantly drop in mid-2023 and at the end of 2024 — when President Joe Biden was still in office.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: State-supported quantum computing hub opens in New Haven
description: Officials gathered in one of New Haven’s new bioscience towers to cut the ribbon on a the QuantumCT innovation hub.
text:
Officials gathered in one of New Haven’s new bioscience towers to cut the ribbon on a tech innovation hub — and on a dream for our state’s future as a quantum version of Silicon Valley.
The ribbon-cutting Tuesday evening marked the opening of a 4,500 square-foot center for researchers, students and entrepreneurs run by QuantumCT, a nonprofit formed to jump-start quantum computing research and company hatching. (Or, in policy parlance, to build out the quantum “ecosystem.”)
The hub is on the first floor of 101 College St., the second of three Carter Winstanley-constructed bioscience lab-office buildings transforming a stretch of downtown atop the former Route 34 Connector.
The goal is for Yale and University of Connecticut quantum computing researchers to share ideas at the hub and make connections with students looking to enter the field and with businesses looking to incubate new companies. Network. Train. Research. Maybe make deals. Actual companies would be housed in the third building, recently approved to be built down the block at 2 Church St.
The broader dream is to make this stretch of New Haven the epicenter of Connecticut’s emerging quantum computing sector — Quantum Alley, say, or the Quantum Corridor — and to make the state a national leader in a projected $200 billion industry by 2040.
[RELATED: CT is trying to kickstart a quantum computing sector]
Quantum computing — quantum physics-based technology that can conduct computations at super-speeds and on multiple levels at once rather than based on binary, yes-no answers — promises to revolutionize fields from health care (like personalized medicine) and drug discovery (cure for cancer, perhaps?) to aerospace to finance.
“We want to make Connecticut the quantum center of the nation,” QuantumCT Interim CEO Vivek Ramakrishnan declared at the formal part of Tuesday’s event.
“A global leader,” said another pre-ribbon-cutting speaker.
The 101 College Street building in New Haven, Conn. Credit: Paul Bass / New Haven Independent
Connecticut isn’t alone in seeking to seize the moment to become the next Silicon Valley. Greater Chicago, Boulder/Denver, Santa Barbara (California) and College Park, Maryland, already have similar efforts underway. 
The betting money at Tuesday evening’s event was that the transition from research to the first wave of market-ready lucrative “real-world applications” and company-building will happen fast over the next two years. Then we’ll see which regions emerge as the winners.
In informal conversations before and after Tuesday evening’s ceremonial snip, as they checked out the new QuantumCT hub space and volunteered to try to explain quantum computing to reporters and politicians who never majored in physics, officials and investors offered a more nuanced version of the dream.
They spoke of how Connecticut can become one of the new quantum Silicon Valleys, rather than the one new hub. 
For instance, state Economic and Community Development Commissioner Dan O’Keefe played up the “global leader” dream in his formal remarks to the crowd of 100 or so community leaders and techies gathered at 101 College. In a conversation afterwards, he played down competition among different U.S. regions. He, like others interviewed, spoke of how we have unique strengths based on which we can carve a leading role.
Our advantage would be based on the two decades of leading quantum research already conducted at Yale and University of Connecticut; and on the presence of leading financial/insurance, military contracting and pharmaceutical firms here that will become prime customers and partner developers of quantum innovations.
UConn President Radenka Maric said Yale’s researchers have led the field in the processing-information end of quantum computing, while her university’s 65 (soon to be 70) quantum researchers have carved out a specialty in quantum sensors. (One definition of the latter: devices that “exploit properties of matter at the smallest scales — like those of electrons and atoms — to measure quantities such as temperature, distance and magnetic fields with unprecedented sensitivity and precision.”) The strength of that two-campus combination is at the heart of the emerging state hub’s competitive strategy, she said.
Money has already poured into the effort: The state committed $50.5 million to the emerging New Haven life sciences-quantum corridor, including creation of QuantumCT here (as part of a broader $121 million “quantum revolution” investment). It won a competitive $15 million National Science Foundation grant to seed that hub, with the possibility of an additional $145 million over the next decade.
Private investment has begun flowing as well. For instance, Florida-based D-Wave this year plunked down $550 million to buy a 65-member Yale-hatched start-up called Quantum Circuits. D-Wave’s Luke Harvey, on hand Tuesday evening, said the company made a bet on the quality of Yale research in picking the emerging New Haven corridor for expansion at what he sees as the transition point from quantum research to commercial applications.
“Innovation is happening so quickly in the quantum space,” said Harvey, the company’s senior director of advanced computing business. “Key breakthroughs will happen in the states nurturing the ecosystems.” He said D-Wave is looking to invest in the New Haven ecosystem and double Quantum Circuits’ workforce here.
Tuesday’s event attracted a representative from at least one European company (who declined to be publicly identified in an article) impressed with Connecticut’s efforts and considering expanding its U.S. operations here.
Quantum Circuits is located across town at 25 Science Park, which developer Carter Winstanley filled up a generation ago in an earlier wave of tech-sector development. Winstanely jumpstarted the city’s biosciences/tech boom at the time by also transfoming the former SNET headquarters at 300 George St. into a health and life sciences center. His firm is now building the three downtown bioscience towers fueling the city’s quantum leap into a more ambitious economic bet. He didn’t give a speech before the crowd Tuesday evening; a steady stream of government and business leaders gravitated to him instead for one-on-one confabs.
This story was first published Oct. 7, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia doubles ‘distinguished’ schools as state accountability results show major gains
description: Forty-four percent of Virginia schools earned the “distinguished” rating for exceeding state expectations in growth, achievement, and readiness, an 11% performance leap from last year, as the state continues efforts to support more than 1,000 schools that fell short. On Wednesday, the Virginia Department of Education released its accountability results, show[...]
text:
A carpet designed with Virginia and the rest of the United States lies inside a classroom. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Forty-four percent of Virginia schools earned the “distinguished” rating for exceeding state expectations in growth, achievement, and readiness, an 11% performance leap from last year, as the state continues efforts to support more than 1,000 schools that fell short.
On Wednesday, the Virginia Department of Education released its accountability results, showing how schools are performing against state expectations. The data will be used to identify schools that need additional support. 
The results mark the second release under Virginia’s new School Performance and Support Framework, which replaced the state’s previous accountability system.
Most Va. schools meeting new state expectations, Va. education department reports

 State results

Virginia’s share of distinguished schools jumped from 23% to 44%, while the number of schools labeled “needs intensive support,” meaning they are not meeting any of the state’s expectations, dropped from 11% to 7%.
The number of schools labeled “meets expectations” fell from 43% to 26%, while schools “approaching expectations” rose from 22% to 23%.
An agency spokesperson told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday that improvement, particularly in elementary schools, resulted from progress in the growth component, as shown by their gains in reading and math assessments. Along with growth, the accountability system measures school performance through four components: mastery, readiness and graduation.
Federal law requires states including Virginia to identify and support their lowest-performing schools. The accountability tiers are labeled “targeted support and improvement,” “additional targeted support and improvement,” and “comprehensive support and improvement.”
Schools under the federal Comprehensive Support and Improvement status, the most significant level of support and monitoring, contributed to the largest single-year decrease in Virginia. 
Data shows that 16 of the 49 eligible schools exited, with six schools moving out of federal identification entirely and 10 moved into targeted support. Most of the schools had been among the lowest-performing 5% of Title I schools for all students since the first year they were identified in 2018.
VDOE also shared that 99.7% of schools are fully accredited, up from 96.8% in the fall of 2025.
Virginia also improved its chronic absenteeism rate, dropping to 11.5% from 13.3%, which is still above the pre-pandemic rate of 10.7%.
Student absences for 10% or more of the academic year — a period equal to 18 or more days — are classified as chronic absenteeism, one of the factors in determining whether a school meets the state’s educational standards. 
 What’s next

The agency said changes to the framework will continue over multiple years, with all changes approved by summer and implemented for the 2028-2029 school year.
Changes to the framework are tied to House Bill 643, which requires the Board of Education to consider a broader set of changes after the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission’s December 2025 review of the framework.
JLARC proposed the board create clearer performance labels and new scoring thresholds that better compare schools across grade levels.
The changes would also adjust how some student achievement measures are scored, account for schools with fewer English learners, and evaluate whether the state’s school improvement program is actually helping schools improve.
The agency said it is reserving $26 million for schools labeled needing “additional targeted support and improvement” and “comprehensive support and improvement.”
VDOE said it will also pilot a new improvement network for schools that need  “targeted support and improvement,” and increase its focus on supporting educators serving students with disabilities in all schools.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Where do Alaska’s gubernatorial candidates stand on the gas pipeline and energy?
description: All four of the candidates in Alaska’s gubernatorial election this year support construction of a trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline and increased, state-backed drilling for natural gas in Cook Inlet. But in a pair of forums held Sept. 21 and Oct. 2 in Anchorage, the four differed on a variety of other topics pertaining to the […]
text:
Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson speaks at a gubernatorial candidate forum on Sept. 16, 2026, while former Attorney General Treg Taylor, Anchorage business owner and talk-show host Bernadette Wilson and former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins listen. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)All four of the candidates in Alaska’s gubernatorial election this year support construction of a trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline and increased, state-backed drilling for natural gas in Cook Inlet.
But in a pair of forums held Sept. 21 and Oct. 2 in Anchorage, the four differed on a variety of other topics pertaining to the state’s energy policy, and one said he plans to borrow hundreds of millions of dollars in order to invest in projects that could pay off over decades.
Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson, together with Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins are each competing to replace Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and cannot run again.
With Southcentral Alaska facing a shortage of cheap natural gas-fired electricity and rural Alaska continuing to experience high utility costs, the cost of energy is likely to be a major issue over the next four years. 
All four candidates participated in the first forum, hosted by the Renewable Energy Alaska Project, while only Bronson and Kreiss-Tomkins attended the second forum, hosted by the Alaska Power Association.
“The difference between prosperity and decline in Alaska is often measured in cents per kilowatt-hour. That’s the bottom line,” Taylor said at the REAP forum. “Without affordable, reliable energy, Alaskan families are going to struggle.”
Absentee voting by mail and fax is underway, and early voting in person will begin Oct. 19. Election Day is Nov. 3. 
Cook Inlet natural gas
Southcentral Alaska relies on natural gas for electricity and heating, but production from oil and gas deposits beneath and near Cook Inlet hasn’t kept up with demand.
After a cold 2025-2026 winter, utilities are worried that regionwide supplies could run short. Even if this year’s winter passes without incident, the long-term production trend is downward, and utilities are planning to import natural gas as soon as the end of the decade.
“I think we need to immediately incentivize more exploration and capital projects in the Cook Inlet,” Taylor said on Sept. 21. 
“We’ve also got to prepare — because of where we’ve put ourselves — for importing LNG, and that’s a horrible place to be when you’re an energy-rich state,” Taylor said. 
Currently, the state of Alaska is directly and indirectly subsidizing natural gas production. The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority — the state’s development financer — has provided loans to HEX, a company drilling in the region, and the state is foregoing royalties on gas leases in the area.
“I think it is appropriate for the state to offer royalty relief to Cook Inlet natural gas producers, as is currently the case,” said Kreiss-Tomkins at the APA forum, adding that he believes “getting every last molecule out of the Cook Inlet natural gas basin is a state priority.”
Speaking after Kreiss-Tomkins, Bronson said the state needs to somehow encourage a second jack-up drilling rig in Cook Inlet to allow the drilling of more wells in Cook Inlet.
“The most important stuff is natural gas production in the near term, to provide our immediate needs as we plan on more generation and transmission going forward,” he said. 
Wilson said she believes structural changes are needed to boost Cook Inlet gas.
“We most certainly need to incentivize production in Cook Inlet,” she said on Sept. 21. 
“Yes, whatever we can do to incentivize HEX, whatever we can do to incentivize Hilcorp,” she said, referring to two of the three companies currently drilling for gas in Cook Inlet.
In the room at the time of the debate were some sitting state legislators who supported a proposal to raise business taxes on Hilcorp, HEX and other privately owned oil and gas firms.
Wilson said she believes the threat of a tax increase deterred those companies from drilling. 
“We have to pay very close attention that when we complain and — quite frankly —  bitch and moan about the gas shortage, who has brought this on? We brought it upon ourselves, and we have to change the outlook,” she said.
On the gas pipeline
If Cook Inlet natural gas is the answer for the immediate future, Bronson said on Oct. 2, “for the long-term future, it is the gas line.”
The proposed Alaska LNG project envisions a pipeline from the North Slope to Cook Inlet, bookended by a pair of industrial processing plants. The project would bring abundant gas to Southcentral and to foreign customers via an export terminal. 
According to official estimates, the project is expected to cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion, but skeptics — including some state legislators — believe it will cost $65 billion or more.
For now, it isn’t certain how that project will be funded, who would sell natural gas into it, or who will buy that natural gas. 
“We definitely need to have a sustainable energy system. But what we can do right now — what we have to do — the first three things we’re going to do is build a gas line, build a gas line, build a gas line,” Bronson said on Sept. 21.
Earlier this year, the Alaska Legislature took up — but failed to pass — a tax cut that would have benefited the project. 
“I strongly support the natural gas pipeline and support restructuring property taxes for the state of Alaska if it helps us get to yes,” Kreiss-Tomkins said on Oct. 1. 
Taylor said he thinks that on energy, the state needs to “think big, like the Alaska gas line, for example, a $50 billion project that would put a lot of Alaskans to work and solve a lot of our energy needs along along the Railbelt, and with the potential to export that energy to our our allies.”
Wilson said she ultimately hopes Alaska will be able to boast about having the lowest energy prices in the country.
“A gas line obviously is front and center of that conversation,” she said on Sept. 21.
“For 40 years, we have debated if we were going to make enough money from a gas line, and in 40 years, we have made precisely $0 from a gas line, because we’re debating on ‘Are we going to get our fair share?’ Enough,” she said. 
A pipeline isn’t currently expected before the end of the decade, and the first phase of the project involves building a gas import facility that would later be turned around to export gas.
“I think it’s pretty much inevitable that there are going to be LNG imports in Cook Inlet and the Railbelt. That’s obviously incredibly unfortunate,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Borrowing for power
Speaking about energy more broadly, Kreiss-Tomkins said that if elected, he would ask the Alaska Legislature for permission to borrow money for projects across the state.
“I believe we need to pass a statewide energy bond in Alaska and make a generational investment in energy infrastructure and transmission infrastructure,” he said on Oct. 1.
When it comes to picking which projects would be funded by that bond, Kreiss-Tomkins said he would consult experts. 
“I think we can take some big swings in some projects that can set up Alaska for the next 50 to 75 years,” he said on Sept. 21. 
The Democrat said he believes Alaska is too reliant on natural gas alone and wants to see the state adopt a variety of power sources. 
“Diversification is a key principle I have,” he said on Oct. 2, explaining that he believes the state should be funding projects through its existing renewable energy fund. He also wants to preserve the $1 billion trust fund that subsidizes rural prices through a program known as Power Cost Equalization.
Taylor said he also supports diversification but didn’t endorse Kreiss-Tomkins’ idea of borrowing money to build projects. 
“We have to approach this problem with an all-of-the-above approach. We have to pursue all the avenues, and then let the market decide the winners and the losers,” Taylor said on Sept. 21.
Taylor said he believes the state needs to think big, with both the gas pipeline and the long-shelved Susitna-Watana hydroelectric project, which would put one of the largest dams in the United States between Anchorage and Fairbanks. 
While the project would have a large up-front cost, the federal government is offering large tax credits for hydroelectric projects that begin construction before 2033.
Taylor said what he’d like to see is “a unified electric grid with a dispatcher to dispatch the lowest-cost energy to Alaskans along the Railbelt.”
It was a sentiment echoed by Kreiss-Tomkins, who said, “we need to coordinate our utilities.”
Wilson did not specify her plans for rural energy or energy in general but reiterated that she wants to see fewer restrictions on development and construction.
In both forums, Bronson said he supports the construction of large-scale computing data centers because he believes they will bring their own electricity generators. 
“They’ll create their own electricity. They’ll deal with the cooling and the noise problems, and I think that’ll be good for us,” Bronson said on Sept. 21.
If the state requires datacenter owners to produce more power, that electricity could be sold locally, Bronson said.
“That’s how you drive down the cost of electricity. Let private enterprise come in and invest, and you compel them to produce more than they actually need,” he said.
In the short term, he believes the state should fund the replacement of older diesel generators in rural Alaska.
“A lot of the diesel generators out there are older than the people that maintain them. I think that’s unacceptable, and the cost of electricity with the newer-generation diesel generators goes down considerably,” he said on Oct. 1.
“I’m not a big fan of wind because it’s not reliable. It’s not base load electricity. Solar isn’t either,” Bronson said.
In the longer term, Bronson said he wants to see small-scale nuclear power plants in rural Alaska away from the Railbelt. The U.S. military is already planning so-called “microreactors” at some of its Alaska bases.
Kreiss-Tomkins didn’t agree with Bronson on nuclear power.
“I think micro-nuclear is compelling … but I think by any measure, it’s still an immature technology and not anything that we can bank on,” he said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: State engineer denounces ‘outrageous’ federal waiver of New Mexico water laws to build border wall
description: The chief lawyer for New Mexico’s Office of the State Engineer told legislators this week that the state is pushing back against  the Trump administration’s announcement of a “waiver” of all the state’s laws and regulations regarding the use of groundwater to aid construction of a border wall.
text:
The New Mexico Office of the State Engineer’s general counsel on Oct. 6, 2026, said New Mexico border water wells that the federal government is using, including the one pictured above, are illegal and are potentially hazardous. (Photo courtesy OSE)The chief lawyer for New Mexico’s Office of the State Engineer told legislators this week that the state is pushing back against  the Trump administration’s announcement of a “waiver” of all the state’s laws and regulations regarding the use of groundwater to aid construction of a border wall. 
U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced Friday in the Federal Register, an official repository of federal announcements, that he had unilaterally decided to waive all New Mexico laws and regulations bearing on water wells being used to build the border wall. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The waiver announcement potentially upended all ongoing lawsuits and challenges the state has mounted in recent months aiming to apply state laws and regulations to at least eight water wells that the U.S. Customs and Border Patrol agency and its contractors have drilled to help suppress dust and build roads as part of the border wall effort. 
The Office of the State Engineer in early August threatened to revoke the licenses of two Arizona-based contractors who drilled the wells. The office later that month also sued the federal border agency over the wells. 
But Mullin in the Friday announcement wrote that suspending all state laws and regulations is legal and necessary due to an “acute and immediate need to construct additional physical barriers and roads in the vicinity of the border of the United States in order to prevent unlawful entries into the United States.”
Nathaniel “Nat” Chakeres, the Office of the State Engineer’s general counsel, told lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Tuesday that Mullin’s announcement is “outrageous” and “unconstitutional.” 
He said the move violates New Mexico residents’ property rights and also the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which enshrines states’ rights to regulate publicly owned water. 
“We’ve always regulated the use of water on federal lands,” he said, offering examples of national laboratories or military installations being subject to state law. 
New Mexico sues feds, contractors over water wells drilled to aid border wall construction

“There is not a lot of groundwater to be had, and the New Mexicans who rely on that water for their livelihood…they’re worried,” Chakeres said.
The Office of the State Engineer has already drafted paperwork asking a federal judge to order the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency to immediately cease using the water, Chakeres said. The office estimates the federal agency has already drawn millions of gallons from the aquifer. 
In addition to being unauthorized, Chakeres said the wells were poorly constructed. He shared an image of an open well casing that sat roughly six inches above pooled surface water. The next rain storm could send oil, gas or construction chemicals into the groundwater, he said. 
“That is bad. That is a direct conduit down into the aquifer. Anything can fall down in there,” he said. “It’s appalling. We were shocked when we came out and saw this. No New Mexico drillers drill wells like this.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New York governor declares measles emergency
description: Kathy Hochul’s decision to declare a “state disaster emergency” comes amid the nation’s worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years.
text:
NEW YORK — Facing a surge of measles cases in New York state’s rural counties, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul issued an executive order on Monday allowing paramedics, pharmacists, midwives and other non-physicians to administer vaccines.
Hochul’s decision to declare a “state disaster emergency” comes amid the nation’s worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years and an eruption in neighboring Pennsylvania that is the largest that any single state has experienced since the early 1990s.
As of Oct. 3, New York had reported 108 total cases, its highest number since 2019. Pennsylvania has recorded more than 1,000 cases this year, and state officials there have attributed five deaths to the disease (so far the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only confirmed two of them.) There have been no deaths in New York.
As of October 1, the CDC had recorded more than 3,887 confirmed cases this year in the United States.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test,” Hochul said in a news release.
Also on Monday, New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, announced that the state would join 15 other Democratic-led states in suing the Trump administration over its decision to scale back the childhood vaccination schedule. Joining in the lawsuit are the state attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin, and the governor of Pennsylvania.
Measles is a respiratory virus that leads to symptoms of fever and rash, and can cause serious health complications, such as pneumonia and even death. It’s highly contagious and can be contracted through exposure to contaminated air or surfaces. It is entirely preventable, however, with the two-dose MMR, or measles, mumps, and rubella, vaccine.
Children under a year old, who are typically too young to receive the first dose of the vaccine, are highly susceptible.
Through a robust vaccination campaign, measles was declared to be effectively eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, according to the CDC. But during the COVID-19 pandemic, anti-vaccination sentiment began to rise, and measles cases have surged over the past  two years.
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is an outspoken vaccine skeptic and has opposed vaccine mandates. Under Kennedy, the agency has called into question the safety and efficacy of vaccines and recommended fewer vaccines for children. The move has prompted most states to unlink their vaccine guidance from federal recommendations and form their own health alliances and standards.
Combined with efforts by Republican-leaning states to weaken vaccine mandates, the federal shift has contributed to a decline in the vaccination rate among kindergarteners and a resulting increase in measles cases.
According to health policy research group KFF, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccination for the 2025-2026 school year, compared with 95% in the 2019-2020 school year. During the last school year, 39 states had MMR vaccination rates below 95% — the minimum considered necessary to prevent community spread, according to KFF.
Katrine Wallace, an epidemiologist at the School of Public Health at the University of Illinois Chicago praised governors for taking action to stop the spread of measles. But Wallace said it’s critical that the federal government encourage people to get vaccinated to slow the spread of the disease.
“There really isn’t a national promotion of ‘Hey, we’re having an outbreak right now. Please vaccinate your kids. The MMR is safe and effective, and it prevents measles.’ That’s not being pumped out on social media. That’s not being put on TV,” Wallace said. “So this administration is not promoting the best tool that we have to prevent severe disease from viruses.”
Nationally, the CDC reports that 352 people have been hospitalized this year due to measles. Of the 3,887 confirmed cases, 61% are people younger than 19 and 95% were not vaccinated or had an unknown vaccine status.
According to CDC data, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Wisconsin, Texas, and Virginia are experiencing the highest number of cases.
The rise in cases under Kennedy’s leadership has prompted Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro to call for the secretary’s ouster.
“He’s making it harder for governors to be able to keep people safe in our communities. I’m actually shocked that the president is letting him get away with this,” Shapiro said in a recent NBC News interview. “I don’t know why he’s still allowing him to even serve in the role”.
This story was first published Oct. 6, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Nevada Current
title: 2 real estate agents vie to close sale with North Las Vegas voters.
description: Sherry Strothers, a Navy veteran supported by labor and progressive groups, will face planning commissioner Esmeralda Villeda, who is backed by industry groups and sitting councilmembers, in the North Las Vegas Ward 1 race to replace a termed-limited incumbent. Term-limited incumbent City Councilman Isaac Barron, who served since 2013, has backed Villeda as[...]
text:
Sherry Strothers, Esmeralda Vellida. (Candidate photos)Sherry Strothers, a Navy veteran supported by labor and progressive groups, will face planning commissioner Esmeralda Villeda, who is backed by industry groups and sitting councilmembers, in the North Las Vegas Ward 1 race to replace a termed-limited incumbent.
Term-limited incumbent City Councilman Isaac Barron, who served since 2013, has backed Villeda as his replacement. 
Three candidates ran during the June primary election to replace Barron. Villeda came in first with 40% of the vote, or 1,575 votes, while Strothers obtained 35%, or 1,384 votes. 
Because none of the candidates obtained more than 50% of the vote, the race advanced to the general election. 
Villeda had a massive fundraising lead over Strothers according to July 15 campaign finance reports. 
Strothers, whose campaign has been overwhelmingly self-funded, raised about $35,000 with about $3,000 on hand at the time. 
Villeda, who has received financial support from various industry groups including real estate and developers as well as the significant backing from the North Las Vegas Fire Fighters Local 1607, raised $64,000 in the second quarter of the year. She had $48,000 on hand at the time.  
Villeda, a real estate agent, serves as the vice chair of the City of North Las Vegas Planning Commission, which makes recommendations to the City Council on matters of planning and zoning.
Strothers has also worked as a real estate agent in North Las Vegas after retiring from the navy. 
Nevada Current interviewed Strothers and Villeda ahead of the primary election. 
Strothers, who is homing in on housing affordability and revitalization of aging neighborhoods, said at the time that Ward 1 had been neglected and left out of revitalization plans. 
Her top housing priorities include reviving a Veteran-Housing Initiative, a 112-unit housing project that was proposed to be developed on a vacant land that was previously blocked due to zoning issues, and converting vacant properties into affordable housing. 
Strothers said she also supports a policy that prevents high rental increases, similar to a 5% limit on rent increases pushed by the Culinary Union in 2022. 
There were conflicting views on whether the union received the necessary amount of votes for the ballot initiative to qualify. In a 4-1 vote, the city council ultimately killed the ballot initiative. 
“I don’t want to kill industry,” Strothers previously told the Current.  “I want business to still be attracted to North Las Vegas, but we do need something that minimizes the ability for large landlords to just arbitrarily raise their rent.” 
Villeda said she wanted to build on the work she has done on the planning commission.
“I’ve been on the planning commission for three years now,” she told the Current earlier this year. “I see where the city is going. I see the momentum. I’m already working with our council members, with our mayor, making sure that we continue to keep that momentum going.”
In addition to affordability, she wants to address proximity to amenities like grocery stores and parks. 
“We want to make sure that residents don’t have to drive 10 to 15 minutes to a grocery store or 10 to 15 minutes to a community park,” Villeda said. 
One of her top priorities is to bring long-overdue improvements to streets and parks in the ward, according to her campaign website. 
Both candidates were asked by The Nevada Independent whether North Las Vegas should implement a data center moratorium. 
Strothers said she strongly agreed saying “projects should demonstrate measurable community benefits before moving forward.” Villeda didn’t respond. 
When asked about whether the city should enter into a 287(g) agreement with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Strother told the Independent that it “would undermine community trust and make residents less willing to report crimes.” Villeda declined to answer. 
In addition to Barron, Villeda is endorsed by current North Las Vegas Councilman Scott Black, who is running for mayor, and out-going mayor Pamela Goynes-Brown. 
Labor groups including SEIU and Teamsters Nevada endorsed Strothers. She is also backed by veterans groups including Nevada Veterans Caucus, as well as the Nevada Black Legislative Caucus, Make the Road Nevada Action and Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada Action.
Both candidates received dual endorsements from the Culinary Union.

name: Nevada Current
title: Attorney seeks to oust incumbent in Clark County District Court race
description: Judge Veronica Barisich is seeking a second term in Clark County District Court Department 5.  She faces a challenge from Tracy Hibbetts, a prosecutor who is making her second run for the bench.  Barisich, who attended Thomas M. Cooley Law School in Michigan, and has been admitted to the Nevada Bar since 2005, says the […]
text:
Veronica Barisich, Tracy Hibbetts. (Candidate photos)Judge Veronica Barisich is seeking a second term in Clark County District Court Department 5. 
She faces a challenge from Tracy Hibbetts, a prosecutor who is making her second run for the bench. 
Barisich, who attended Thomas M. Cooley Law School in Michigan, and has been admitted to the Nevada Bar since 2005, says the most unexpected aspect of her first term on the bench is the caseload. 
“My docket has been all civil, including two specialty courts, which are medical malpractice and probate,” Barisich told the Current. “I’m one of the nine medical malpractice judges and one of only three probate judges. What has surprised me the most is just the amount of cases that I’ve been given and that I’ve maintained,” 
Barisich adds she reads “everything that comes through the door.” 
Hibbetts says she chose to challenge Barisich for several reasons.
“When it’s a low-information, low-turnout election year, where the top of the ballot is the governor and constitutional offices, you tend to want to be on the top of the ballot as much as you can, so voters don’t get ballot fatigue,” she observed, adding that Barisch’s name “doesn’t really pop up in the community.” 
Hibbetts also cited Barisich’s “high reversal rate on appeal” as a reason for challenging her. 
Of 52 cases appealed in her first term, appeals courts found Barisich to be in error a third of the time, according to Our Nevada Judges, which tracks judicial data. 
“When a case is appealed, it comes with the opportunity to learn,” Barisich said. “If my decision and my analysis was correct, then that’s just fermented. If it was half correct or half not correct, then we learn something about the law. And there are some cases that are issues of first impression that we don’t have specific case law on. It’s very valuable when we can receive case law.”
Being a judge, she says, “is always a learning experience.”
Of the 145 attorneys who participated in her evaluation in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 survey, 73% recommended Barisich be retained. Her highest scores were for integrity while her lowest scores were for legal ability. 
The judge notes she didn’t find the feedback to be helpful, adding she wasn’t provided with the comments. “All I gleaned is that I’m here to do my job, and I keep on trying to do it better.”
Barisich raised $317,000 and had $245,000 on hand as of July. 
She’s endorsed by a dozen law enforcement associations; a variety of labor unions, including Laborers 872, SEIU Nevada, Southern Nevada Building Trades, Teamsters Nevada; and community organizations such as Independent Black Voters and Hispanics in Politics. 
She’s also endorsed by the Third Branch PAC, an organization that bills itself as nonpartisan but is funded solely by the Nevada Republican Club.   
Hibbetts earned her law degree at California Western School of Law. She’s been a member of the Nevada Bar since 2012. 
This is Hibbetts’ second run for the bench. She came in third in a four-way primary race in 2022 for Las Vegas Justice Court Department 6, a seat won by Jessica Goodey in the general election.
Since then, she left her job as a public defender to become a prosecutor, a move she says has given her “a more well-rounded understanding of the criminal justice arena.”  
While she worked for civil firms before law school, the bulk of her experience is in criminal law. The seat she is seeking hears civil cases. 
“Each department’s assignment is not permanent,” she notes. “It is based on the person elected into the seat. If I’m elected, I’m not necessarily inheriting an all civil docket,” she said, adding that when you run for the bench “you jump in knowing that you may have to do something that’s outside your arena. “
Hibbetts’ husband Brian is a retired Las Vegas Metropolitan Police sergeant and a Republican state assemblyman. 
“It would be silly to say that we don’t talk about work at home, but obviously we have different party affiliation because I believe that judicial candidates should remain neutral,” Hibbetts says, adding she’s registered as nonpartisan.  
Hibbetts serves on the board of the Clark County Law Foundation as well as the Asian Bar Association of Nevada, in addition to volunteering in the community. 
She’s endorsed by Culinary Local 226, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, and several law enforcement associations, including the Clark County Prosecutors Association, the Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers, and the Clark County District Attorney Investigators Association.
Hibbetts raised $142,000 as of July and had $128,000 on hand. She says raising money is easier for District Court, because that’s where more civil law attorneys practice. 
Early voting begins Saturday, Oct. 17. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Former Missouri AG Andrew Bailey makes appearance in Columbia after leaving FBI post
description: Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri attorney general who left his post at the FBI last week, told fellow Republicans Tuesday night that he vowed to continue holding wrongdoers, whether criminal or political, to the letter of the law. “The cornerstone of prosperous communities is the criminal justice system and holding wrongdoers accountable,” Bailey said. “It[...]
text:
Former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey speaks on Tuesday at American Legion Post 202. Bailey served as the co-deputy director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation before resigning last week (Nolan Henry/Missourian).Andrew Bailey, the former Missouri attorney general who left his post at the FBI last week, told fellow Republicans Tuesday night that he vowed to continue holding wrongdoers, whether criminal or political, to the letter of the law.
“The cornerstone of prosperous communities is the criminal justice system and holding wrongdoers accountable,” Bailey said. “It doesn’t have to be mean, doesn’t have to be mean-spirited, but it means that if you do wrong, you pay your debt to society.”
Bailey was the keynote speaker for the Columbia and Boone County Pachyderm clubs at American Legion Post 202. It was the among the first public appearance he has made since leaving Washington.
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins also spoke at the event.
Bailey served as the Missouri attorney general from 2023 to 2025 and was appointed by President Donald Trump a year ago to serve as co-deputy director of the FBI. He resigned Thursday, saying he wanted to return to Missouri and spend more time with his family.
“I remember being on the phone with my wife and talking to her about these incredible accomplishments,” Bailey said. “She said, ‘Hey, that’s great. You need to get on home because your kids need you.’ And so I stepped down.”
At the meeting Tuesday night, Bailey reflected a Republican message, saying blue states are “lying, cheating and stealing elections.”
“We’ve got more we can do to make sure our elections are secure,” he said. “We can’t let blue states like California and New York cheat by allowing criminal aliens to vote, double counting Democrat votes and thereby suppressing your constitutional right to vote.”
Bailey also paid respect to Charlie Kirk, labeling the political activist, who was shot and killed last year, as a civil rights leader of the current generation. He encouraged fellow Republicans to honor Kirk’s legacy by following Bailey’s efforts to produce indictments, arrests, prosecutions and sufficient prison time for offenders.
“We can’t let them silence our constitutional right to express our beliefs, worship as we see fit, keep and bear arms, participate in elections and oversee our law enforcement to include immigration enforcement,” Bailey told the audience. “That’s how you fight socialism, using the enforcement mechanisms provided under innocent people.”
Bailey also shared a personal connection to Amendment 3, which prohibits abortion and gender transition procedures for minors. He said he and his wife suffered the loss of a daughter in 2018.
“We named her Grace because, by the grace of God, I got to hold her for one hour before the good Lord took her home,” Bailey said. “But that hour I got to spend with my daughter taught me that all life has value. Period. I will never surrender, never retreat.”
Although he has stepped down from his FBI position, Bailey said he will continue to fight for Republican objectives in the state.
“I didn’t ever ask to be a politician, but I am a public servant, and I knew I wanted to serve the people of the state of Missouri,” Bailey said. “I knew we could do more. We can always do more.”
Bailey also reinforced his role as a public servant, not a politician, saying he would not be stepping into a role in public office.
“I am not a politician,” he said. “I am not a candidate for public office.”
Like Bailey, Hoskins talked about local issues he believes Missouri Republicans should consider when voting in November.
“Here in Boone County, they have a queer-led children’s story hour for toddlers and preschoolers, with books celebrating and pushing kids to dress in drag,” Hoskins said. “And I said not on my watch, and I put their funding on notice.”
He was referring to a letter he wrote to the Daniel Boone Regional Library staff in July about “Rainbow Story Time,” an LGBTQ+ themed event planned in Columbia. The library held the event despite the backlash.
Hoskins has also been involved in the debate over the congressional maps to be used in the November elections. After a high-profile legal battle that included several lawsuits and court decisions, the 2022 map will be used instead of the gerrymandered 2025 map that he preferred.
Hoskins did not back down Tuesday in the face of his apparent defeat.
“Any Tom, Dick or Harry can file a lawsuit against anyone,” Hoskins said. “And by golly, the liberal left, funded by their out-of-state East Coast sugar daddies, sure has sued me a lot, as many times as possible for following the law and doing my job.”
Hoskins ended his speech with a promise to uphold his responsibilities as secretary of state.
“I will protect Missouri elections,” Hoskins said. “I will protect life. I will protect our Second Amendment. I will protect our men and women serving in the military. I will stand up and fight for everyone in this room, and I will never forget where I came from and the hardworking men and women in this room that elected me secretary of state.”
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah needs a ‘Code Red’ policy to protect the homeless from extreme heat, report says
description: University of Utah researchers have released a new report looking at how heat impacts people experiencing homelessness — and offering recommendations for lawmakers to help address a lack of cooling resources during summer months.  For the report released Monday researchers interviewed 24 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness in the Salt Lake Valley ab[...]
text:
A person and a dog lay in the grass outside the City-County Building in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, March 26, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)University of Utah researchers have released a new report looking at how heat impacts people experiencing homelessness — and offering recommendations for lawmakers to help address a lack of cooling resources during summer months. 
For the report released Monday researchers interviewed 24 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness in the Salt Lake Valley about how they navigate extremely hot temperatures in public spaces, along with how city and private business policies impact their ability to cope. 
“They reported heat exhaustion, dehydration, sleep disruption, and emotional strain, with limited access to shade, water, and restrooms,” the report says. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Eight people experiencing homelessness who participated in the study also used GPS-enabled smartphones and backpack-mounted weather monitors to track their locations and temperatures over six summer days. 
According to the data collected by those monitors, they “routinely experienced hazardous conditions, including prolonged exposure” to moderate and high-risk heat thresholds (temperatures greater than 91 degrees Fahrenheit and 102.9 degrees Fahrenheit, respectively). 
Researchers also looked at how Salt Lake City businesses respond to people experiencing homelessness, who may use their storefronts as a way to escape the heat. When cooling resources are lacking, businesses “frequently become de facto heat refuges,” researchers wrote in the report. 
However, “their capacity is limited and their practices are too variable to substitute for coordinated public cooling infrastructure,” the report says. 
Of about 30 business employees, managers and owners who agreed to do interviews for the research, about 77% reported no restrictions on who could enter their storefront and 73% reported no set customer time limits. However, “half of policies governing access and interactions” with people experiencing unsheltered homelessness “were informal and case-by-case,” the report says. 
A research assistant in the Department of Parks, Recreation, and Tourism at the University of Utah hands out temperature monitors at Liberty Park in Salt Lake City to understand the impact of extreme temperatures on unsheltered populations. (Photo courtesy of the University of Utah)
Only 30% of the businesses reported corporate guidance, and 37% changed their practices during extreme weather. Some offered water or allowed people to cool off indoors, while others “expressed concern that doing so might attract more” people experiencing homelessness. 
A majority of the businesses (60%), mentioned they had “personal guidelines for engaging and communicating” with people experiencing homelessness. 
“Most responded with statements like ‘treat everyone the same,’ ‘treat them kindly, ‘treat them with respect,’ and ‘treat them with empathy,’” the report says. “Only one said that her rule was to keep her distance and not engage.”
Altogether, the findings pointed to “thermal equity as both an infrastructure and governance issue,” researchers wrote in the report. 
Exposure to heat “can be intensified by limited access to shade, water, sanitation, indoor cooling, and secure places to rest.” However, at the same time “interventions can work against one another: displacement from a shaded location can force someone into hotter conditions; restricted bathroom or water access can increase health risks; and informal business policies can make cooling opportunities unpredictable.” 
The researchers included a list of recommendations for policymakers, including: 

Set a “Code Red” policy for extreme heat.
Treat water, bathrooms, shade and cooling as integrated heat infrastructure by maintaining functional drinking fountains, extending summer bathroom access and providing shaded seating.
Expanding cooling center locations and hours.
Expand and protect the tree canopy where people experiencing unsheltered homelessness spend time.
Establish protected shaded rest areas during extreme heat. 
Include people experiencing unsheltered homelessness in climate health planning.
Engage businesses as partners — not substitutes — for public infrastructure.
Support community and peer-led adaptation by incorporating existing networks people experiencing homelessness use to share water, food, information and warnings about enforcement. 

In recent years, Utah lawmakers considered bills that would create a statewide “Code Red” policy, similar to the state’s existing Code Blue Alert that expands homeless shelter capacity when temperatures drop to dangerously low levels. 
But those bills haven’t passed. 
In 2025, lawmakers considered a bill sponsored by Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, that would have flexed shelter capacity by up to 35% during dangerously hot weather. That bill failed in the House on a 21-49 vote. 
Earlier this year, another bill sponsored by Rep. Steve Eliason, R-Sandy, would have allowed certain shelters to expand their capacity if local temperatures reach or exceed 105 degrees fahrenheit, but that bill also failed in the House on a 34-37 vote. 
“Ultimately, housing remains the most effective long-term protection from extreme heat, but housing alone does not address immediate risk,” researchers noted in the report. “Expanding equitable access to trees, water, sanitation, cooling, and secure public space can reduce preventable heat exposure while creating a more inclusive urban climate-adaptation system.”
