name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Transit summer train cancellations rose in 2026
description: NJ Transit canceled 1,715 trains between June and August, a slight increase from the summer of 2025. The agency blames intense heat and severe storms.
text:
NJ Transit canceled 1,715 trains between June and August, a slight increase from the summer of 2025. The agency blames intense heat and severe storms. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersy Transit’s summer train cancellations edged up to 1,715 this year amid aging equipment, inclement weather, some staffing issues, and recurrent disruptions from Amtrak.
The 1,715 trains canceled between June 1 and Aug. 31 mark a slight increase from the 1,646 canceled over the same period last year. The difference was driven entirely by intense heath and severe storms that caused a surge of weather-related cancellations in July.
“There was major unprecedented heat in July along with extreme storms that took down trees throughout the system,” said Jim Smith, a spokesperson for NJ Transit.
Smith said the agency’s Morris and Essex line was especially hard hit, seeing more than 50 trees toppled during just one severe storm.
Summer has often been a difficult season for NJ Transit over the last decade as heat degrades the performance of some rail infrastructure, adding to other performance woes at an agency that was underfunded for much of this millennium.
The agency reported 657 cancellations due to unpreventable issues, the category that captures weather-related incidents. 
NJ Transit reported only 288 unpreventable cancellations last year, and this year’s total is the highest since 2020, when a tropical storm stopped trains across multiple NJ Transit lines, sometimes for days.
Mechanical issues from New Jersey’s aging fleet of trains were the second leading cause of cancellations. Those prevented 459 trains from running over the three-month period, down from 634 the prior year. They numbered just 174 in 2019.
Tom Haas, chair of the NJ Transit Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen, said degrading performance was to be expected of trains that have been in service for decades, including some that have been on the tracks for about half a century.
“Simply put, it’s getting old,” Haas said. “Just like a car that had 300,000 miles on it, it may still be a good car that’s normally reliable, but that advancing age is going to start to take its toll, and maintenance issues are going to become more and more frequent.”
The age of the agency’s existing rolling stock can add other wrinkles. Some of the trains’ manufacturers have gone out of business or stopped producing certain parts, making repairs harder, Haas said.
Some of the trains in NJ Transit’s fleet have been in service for decades. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
NJ Transit is in the process of replacing its entire rail fleet through the purchase of 374 new multilevel train cars, the first of which are expected to arrive and be put into service sometime this year.
For NJ Transit commuter Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Union), those train cars can’t come soon enough, and repeated delays to their delivery have become something of an irritation.
New Jersey ordered the first of its new Multilevel III rail cars in 2018, but pandemic supply chain disruptions pushed back their original 2023 delivery date. A later timeline that would have put the first of the new cars into service in mid-2025 was also missed.
“NJ Transit has made a big investment in addressing this one piece of the problem, so let’s bring that investment to fruition. Looking at past experience, the trains are very, very late in terms of being completed and delivered,” said Macurdy.
Smith, the NJ Transit spokesperson, said the agency still expects the first of the new trains to come into service this year.
Amtrak-related cancellations surged back to 164 this summer after plummeting into the low double-digits last year. The quasi-public corporation owns tracks and other infrastructure used by some NJ Transit train lines, most notably the northeast corridor, the nation’s busiest commuter rail line.
Problems with the catenary wires from which trains draw power were the main cause of issues, Smith said. Those wires can sag and malfunction during extreme heat. Still, Amtrak performance far exceeded some past years. Amtrak was responsible for 527 cancellations in the summer of 2024.
Crew- and engineer-related cancellations — a leading source of disruptions early in former Gov. Phil Murphy’s tenure — declined slightly to 231 but remained significantly elevated over levels seen in summers between 2021 and 2024.
Haas, the engineers’ union president, said retirements had thinned the ranks of NJ Transit’s locomotive engineers some, adding that while the agency had moved to restore their ranks, engineers’ 20-month training regimen meant progress took time.
“We just do not have that reserve right now. That’s in large part because of how long it takes for a candidate, a trainee, to go through the training program to become a fully qualified locomotive engineer,” he said. “It’s almost two years.”
Though World Cup service restricted outgoing commuter rail at some specific stations on some days, the event did not affect NJ Transit train performance overall, Smith said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Charter school in Canton opened with a STEM focus but no full-time STEM teachers. It has had many more problems
description: Mississippi Today reviewed more than 500 pages of memos, financial and academic records, and more than 10 hours of recorded meetings with state regulators, employees and parents to better understand the financial trouble of SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, a charter school in Canton.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
CANTON — Kristen Williams was excited to co-lead Mississippi’s first charter school geared toward the sciences.
When SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy opened in 2023, she became the inaugural provost. She told Chief Executive Officer and Founder Tamu Green she wanted to create something like the ACME Academy in Vicksburg, a public school where students take classes in architecture and engineering. She pictured Canton students competing nationwide in robotics competitions and engaging classroom experiments such as troubleshooting a circuit board or chemical reaction.
But as the months passed, more and more employee proposals to bring interactive whiteboards and virtual reality workshops into classrooms went ignored.
Despite SR1 CPSA being a STEM school — focused on science, technology, engineering and math — its leaders hadn’t hired a STEM teacher as of February 2026, according to an email a former administrator provided to Mississippi Today. According to a former employee who assisted in staff training and resigned in September, the school still hasn’t hired one.
Green would sometimes have STEM experts visit the school, Williams told Mississippi Today, but no full-time instructor. “The vision was there, but it was not clear,” she said.
Williams was discouraged to see students share old laptops and old iPads for state-mandated testing. She was also not provided a school budget or given the opportunity to weigh in on it, she said.
Green also ignored requests to pay for staff professional development, she said. 
Williams left the school at the end of the academic year in 2024. 
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, confers with Dorlisa Hutton, chief operations officer and vice president for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I just really believed in their vision,” Williams said about Green and his wife, Dorlisa Hutton, a school administrator who served as the school’s chief operating officer. “I believed in what they were trying to do before I stepped into the role.”
Now, the school may lose its charter. In October 2023, the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board sanctioned Green for requesting money to serve 150 students but only enrolling 12. School leadership spent about $816,725 that year, or about $68,060 per student, which is more than five times what the average Mississippi school district spends.  
Green did not answer questions sent through multiple emails and messages left with receptionists about the financial health of his school and whether he operated outside the laws on child nutrition services and accounting. Hutton didn’t respond to questions in multiple calls, text messages, voice messages, emails as well as in-person.
Mississippi Today reviewed more than 500 pages of memos, financial and academic records, and more than 10 hours of recorded meetings with state regulators, employees and parents to better understand the school’s financial trouble. 
Mississippi Today also talked to 13 former employees of the charter school and SR1 (Scientific Research), Green’s Ridgeland-based nonprofit organization, about business concerns at the school and with Green’s leadership. Four of them spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear that speaking publicly would affect their current or future employment.
Heavy oversight is needed when spending tax dollars
Some of Green’s spending remains a mystery due to a lack of documentation. Green has failed to provide financial documents and information for some school vendors. The authorizer board has been waiting since Dec. 22 for statements of economic interest from every board member and school official.
Green and other charter school operators are not required to provide regulators the same financial information as traditional public school leaders. Charter schools are publicly funded but independently managed, and they aren’t subjected to the same scrutiny as traditional public schools. 
In Mississippi, charter schools are given license to operate and be monitored by the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, which is composed of political appointees and managed by an executive director the board appoints. 
Students head to waiting vehicles and school buses after classes end for the day at SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Reports and disclosures from regulators at the authorizer board helped tell the story of the school’s organizational dysfunction and money woes. They show that Green hasn’t been forthcoming with information on school spending. He denied the charter authorizer board’s requests for records last year and claimed the financial documents belong to his nonprofit organization, SR1 (Scientific Research), according to Dillon Pitts, the board’s attorney. Green argued the organization’s financial documents are not under the board’s purview. 
Even if regulators are granted access to financial records for SR1 (Scientific Research), it could be difficult to parse the nonprofit’s information from the school’s. SR1 has not submitted financial audits to the federal audit clearinghouse for three of the last six years, which contributed to SR1 losing a federal grant administered by the Mississippi Department of Human Services in May.
Read More: Board presses for a recommendation on Canton charter school’s fate
The relationship between SR1 and the charter school is more entwined than Green has acknowledged in authorizer board meetings. A 2025 audit shows SR1 (Scientific Research) provides vital funding to the charter school, paying 21% of its operating costs through in-kind donations and supplying transportation, rent, utilities and telecommunication services. 
Nonprofit organizations such as SR1 serve the primary function of signing the contract with the authorizer board, which allows for the charter school to open. That makes the organization’s role as a vendor for SR1 CPSA for some services unusual when compared to the relationship other Mississippi charters have with their nonprofits that authorize them.
Without a clear picture of spending at either institution, compliance with federal grant requirements remains a mystery, making it difficult to ensure that  taxpayer money makes it to the classroom. 

But in an unsigned statement, which Mississippi Today received by email, SR1 (Scientific Research) referred to a request for comment as part of a disruptive pattern of “third party information gathering,” which distracts from its mission of educating children. The response also included a summary of the nonprofit’s grant activity, including an after-school program and the charter school. 
The statement denied any impropriety in their funding structure, and denied claims that SR1 and the charter school are organizationally connected. However, past audits for the charter school indicate that SR1 CPSA received significant support from SR1.
Regulators in Mississippi struggle to get information on some charter schools’ purchases, which traditional public schools must disclose to the public. But they are not alone: Charter school executives around the country have been allowed to operate in secrecy while mismanaging public dollars meant to subsidize an alternative to traditional public schools. 
Financial and academic challenges have festered into crises in these charter schools around the U.S., leaving regulators, parents and local leaders in the dark. In recent years, charter schools have been forced to close due to long concealed money woes and, in an example in Texas, attempts to hide a school executive’s exorbitant salary. Others have operated with lower academic standards than public schools.
“You really need a heavy level of oversight to ensure that, essentially, the public dollar is not being used to subsidize private profit,” said Frank Adamson, an education professor at San Francisco State University who has published peer-reviewed research on charter school finance.
A lack of consistent support
Former SR1 CPSA employees said they didn’t have the resources or support staff needed to ensure student success.
At a February 2026 meeting, staff complained about the school’s lack of STEM instruction, former kindergarten teacher Niccori Thomas recalled. Three former employees said the only STEM instruction at the school occurred when Vickie Liou, a STEM teacher who works for the SR1 nonprofit, visited three times in April and May.
“The STEM room has tons of STEM resources in it, but there’s no STEM teacher at all,” Thomas said.
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, listens as Letitia Johnson, finance director for the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, answers questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
One former administrator, who did not want to be identified publicly because he fears jeopardizing his job search, said Green misled him about his job title and responsibilities. He was an office manager, according to his first contract, but subsequent contracts and documentation referred to his role as operation manager. The role became more custodial than clerical, he said.
He said Green and other staff in the Ridgeland office retaliated against him when he brought incorrectly filled out paperwork to their attention or when safety procedures weren’t followed. He was threatened with more responsibilities.
That former administrator, who had experience managing shifts and paperwork for a hospital,  said he had to clean toilets and bathroom floors as well as handle student files and paperwork that state and federal regulators required. Later, he had to track school bus routes.
“I didn’t sit down from when I got there at 6:30 a.m. until I left at 4 p.m.,” he told Mississippi Today. “I was trying to give them the benefit of the doubt. I thought maybe they are overloaded and they are still learning. But as time moved on, I realized that’s not it.”
The inspectors are coming
Former employees said they were left alone to answer inspectors’ questions about missing purchases and paperwork. Government agencies such as the secretary of state’s office and the Mississippi Department of Education inspected the school and SR1 headquarters in the past year. Meanwhile, the charter authorizer board investigated financial mismanagement and the child nutrition department. 
Another former administrator, who fears jeopardizing his job search, said Green never showed up to hear the authorizer board inspector’s findings from its child nutrition department inspection. Regulators found that portion sizes, food temperatures and nutritional composition did not comply with federal guidelines, Pitts, the attorney for the authorizer board, said during a May 14 hearing.
School employees, including an administrator, were preparing food brought to the school from the Ridgeland headquarters, according to a September 2026 inspection by authorizer board Executive Director Lisa Karmacharya. The Mississippi Department of Education expressed similar concerns about the child nutrition program, she told the board on Sept. 21.
Lisa Karmacharya, executive director of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, listens during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The same former administrator, who fears jeopardizing his current job, described a mad dash after charter board inspectors arrived to inventory technology and furniture at the school in March. He said there was a push to make it look as if purchased supplies were for the charter school.
Employees from the SR1 Ridgeland headquarters arrived the next day with tablets, chairs and desks and stuck SR1 CPSA stickers on some items. Something similar happened twice before, two other former employees said.
Questions about spending at the charter school came up during an authorizer board hearing in May. Pitts questioned Green about previously undisclosed credit cards, noting several Amazon purchases that lacked backup documentation like invoices and receipts.
Williams, the former provost, told Mississippi Today the school lacked documentation for school supplies, which were ordered from Amazon and dropped off by SR1 employees. Green and other executive staff did not provide invoices or receipts for those purchases despite requests to do so, she said.
“In my old districts, we’d have to do a requisition. You had to put everything on there, and that way you can document what line item it needs to come from as far as how you’re paying for it.”
‘My integrity is too important’
Missing financial documents and turnover in its business office were the reasons for inaccurate accounting, according to the school’s 2025 audit. Three former business office employees said they were forced to sift through disorganized piles of receipts and invoices left on their desks. They said Green provided little to no context on purchases.
A photo submitted to Mississippi Today shows a security camera in a workspace at SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy. Former employees who were on the charter school’s finance team described being under constant surveillance by either Chief Executive Officer and Founder Tamu Green or Dorlisa Hutton, Green’s wife and a school administrator who served as the chief operating officer. 
A former SR1 employee gave Mississippi Today a recording of a May 2024 staff meeting where Green compared the charter school’s accounting paperwork to a student who procrastinates on a paper until the day before it is due. Green called members of the charter authorizer board “Karens,” a disparaging slang term used to describe certain aggressive white women, for asking for the source of the money for school supplies.
One lead accountant, who fears retalliation at her current job, began looking for another job as a business manager within a month of working at SR1. She and another finance team member described being under constant surveillance by either Green or Hutton. A security camera was pointed at their desks. 
The former lead accountant said Green and Hutton told her to pay bills without any explanation. She saw deposits from federal agencies, but never got answers as to whether they were tied to a specific grant. 
“I mean my unwritten rule was we just spent, but we didn’t know you were supposed to make everything look really good (in June 2025),” Green said during the charter board hearing. He then explained he was looking to show regulators the best possible financial snapshot of his organization. (The charter school’s audit was 29 days late in 2025 and 126 days late in 2024, according to the authorizer board.) 
Tamu Green, chief executive officer and founder of SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy in Canton, told a hearing officer in May that the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board’s expectations around the school’s finances and recordkeeping were “a guessing game.”
Mississippi Today confirmed through bank documents and payroll records provided by former employees that money allocated to SR1, the parent organization, for an antipoverty grant initiative in Scott County, which has since been discontinued, partially paid the salary of at least three school employees, including an administrator.
“I’m a stickler when it comes to accounting work done correctly because that could cost me my livelihood. I don’t understand why they didn’t have the same fear,” a former finance team member said of Green and Hutton.
School leadership painted ‘pretty picture’ to mask issues
As the authorizer board moved closer to deciding whether to revoke the school’s charter, parents and staff pressed Green for answers about the school’s fate. Thomas, who was a charter school teacher and parent, struggled for months to get in contact with Green about whether the state would close the school. She wanted to know if she had to find a different school for her child and another job.
She emailed Green in December, and he responded in April. He offered no clear answer.
Students attending SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy board a school bus at the end of classes, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
She also has concerns about the charter school building. The school, housed in a daycare facility, now enrolls students in grades K-4. The students’ toilets are sized for toddlers.
Thomas said her child received fewer services at the charter school than he would at the local public school. She said she had to call the Madison County Library System for a mobile library unit because the school lacked one. She said there were no extracurriculars or electives except recess and music. 
Past administrators, many of whom worked in traditional public schools, said they’re concerned about Green’s apparent disregard for state and federal guidelines. Some removed the charter school from their resumes, fearing it would hurt employment chances at other schools. 
Leadership changes continue to fuel dysfunction on campus. A provost hired in August tendered plans to resign at the end of September. The school has cycled through at least four school leaders since it opened in August 2023. There have been at least two business managers in the past year.
“They paint this pretty picture,” a former administrator who left in July said of his time at the charter school. “That’s how they get people. They paint this pretty picture. They go all out in left field. If you ask them a question, they’re not going to answer it directly.”
“And then once you come on board, you’re going to see it for yourself. You’re going to see the issues.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Noncitizens trying to vote? Vanishingly rare.
description: Last week the Trump administration announced to much fanfare that a grand jury had indicted 10 Minnesotans on charges of falsely claiming American citizenship to vote in recent elections. At a news conference in Washington, D.C., Attorney General Todd Blanche said the indictments show that voter fraud is rampant and prove the need for tough […]
text:
Election officials perform an accuracy test on voting machines ahead of the August primaries Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (Photo by Ria Gupta/Minnesota Reformer)Last week the Trump administration announced to much fanfare that a grand jury had indicted 10 Minnesotans on charges of falsely claiming American citizenship to vote in recent elections. At a news conference in Washington, D.C., Attorney General Todd Blanche said the indictments show that voter fraud is rampant and prove the need for tough new elections legislation now pending in Congress.
But viewed in context — a period when Minnesotans cast millions of votes — the findings should actually bolster rather than undermine confidence in our elections. They show what countless careful studies have concluded: Actual voter fraud is vanishingly rare. They also put the lie to President Donald Trump’s claim that he won here three times, as well as the ceaseless barking from MAGA that noncitizens are swinging elections.
Consider what it took to round up these 10 cases. A recent report by ProPublica details how the Trump administration scrambled to find voter fraud in Minnesota and other states, assigning scores of agents from Homeland Security Investigations to fan out across the country and deploying a vast federal database of citizens’ personal information. The agents were so ill-informed and the database so error-prone that a federal prosecutor called the effort “dysfunctional.”
Despite this massive effort, all it produced was 10 cases of alleged fraud over two election cycles, a period when Minnesotans cast 5.8 million votes. An additional 1.3 million votes were cast during primary elections in that period. 
Moreover, these are just allegations — and court records show that most people charged with voter fraud in Minnesota are never convicted. Considering the Trump administration’s record of failed indictments — from the sandwich thrower to the reflecting pool vigilante and all the Minnesotans wrongfully detained during Operation Metro Surge — we should be skeptical that even these 10 indictments will produce convictions.
It’s really no surprise that Trump’s team could find so little voter fraud in Minnesota. In the two general elections from 2018 to 2020, Minnesotans cast roughly 6 million votes.
Court records show there were just 40 convictions for registering or voting illegally in those years. That’s just 20 convictions in each cycle — or 0.00067% of votes cast.
The same pattern holds true nationally. After the 2016 election, the Brennan Center at New York University studied voting data from 42 jurisdictions in 12 states. They found 30 cases of suspected noncitizen voting out of more than 23 million votes cast. 
Also in 2016, the New York Times surveyed elections and law enforcement officials in 49 states. They documented just a handful of cases of noncitizen voting out of 137 million votes cast.
Indeed, the way to reinforce Minnesotans’ confidence in our elections isn’t with intrusive new rules that threaten to disenfranchise thousands of voters, as with the Republicans’ proposed SAVE Act. 
Instead, just tell people the facts. 
In Minnesota, for example, the people who actually run polling places are not party insiders or faceless bureaucrats — they’re your friends and neighbors. They’re the same people you run into at church or the grocery store, and it’s not unusual to walk into a neighborhood polling place and recognize the folks handing you a ballot. Anyone can volunteer to serve on Election Day, and most step up precisely because they believe in our democracy. Moreover, state law requires that every polling place have election judges from both major political parties.
What about corrupted voting machines? Minnesota law requires every city to test its voting equipment at least three days before an election — and the public and the press are invited to watch, along with a representative of each major party. On Election Day, political parties can appoint observers to watch voting in every precinct and challenge suspect voters.
Why is noncitizen voting so rare in the real world? Think about it for a moment. If you’re living in the United States without proper documents, the last thing you want to do is attract the attention of law enforcement. Why would you risk getting your family deported to cast one vote? 
Why is voter ID fraud so rare? Think another moment. Would you risk five years in prison and a $10,000 fine because someone asked you to vote with a fake ID?
Once voters understand how rare election fraud actually is, they’ll understand why there’s no need for drastic federal legislation that election experts say would throw thousands of Americans off the voter rolls.
Of course, if you want to defend our democracy and our elections, you don’t have to scour voting statistics or become an election judge. All you have to do is get out and vote on Election Day.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesotans: We can trust our neighbors who run our elections
authors: The Rev. Marilyn K. Levine, Nancy McLean, Toni Kay Mangskau, Sherri Brown
description: Our stomachs have settled from the State Fair, school buses are back on the roads and the leaves are starting to turn. Our transition from summer to fall is officially underway. Which also means early voting has officially started in Minnesota! We lead the nation in voter turnout, and are proud of our record. From […]
text:
Voting signage points to Knox Presbyterian Church in Minneapolis, Minnesota during the primary election Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Our stomachs have settled from the State Fair, school buses are back on the roads and the leaves are starting to turn. Our transition from summer to fall is officially underway. Which also means early voting has officially started in Minnesota! 
We lead the nation in voter turnout, and are proud of our record. From now until Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3, Minnesotans can make their plan to vote early. 
As each of us makes our plan to vote, we’d like to share an important reminder with our fellow Minnesotans: Our elections are run by our neighbors, not strangers. 
Each election season Minnesotans from every corner of our state — from both major parties, as well as people with no affiliation at all — serve as the election judges who help run our elections. 

These are the same people we see at church, at school drop-off and the playground with their kids. 
What could neighbors who live in different corners of our state from Beltrami, Washington, Olmsted, and Anoka counties possibly all have in common? 
We believe that in Minnesota, no matter what you look like, how you pray, or what language you speak, that each of us deserves a say in shaping our future. Whether you are an 18-year-old voting early for the first time, or an election judge planning to cast your 50th ballot, we know we’re stronger when more of our voices are represented, not fewer. 
That’s why we’re joining with our neighbors, alongside Minnesotans in 20 counties across our state, from St. Louis to Hennepin and Sherburne to Le Sueur, to call upon our county commissioners to sign our Freedom to Vote Protection Pledge. 
Our pledge calls upon all of our local, state and federal officials — especially those who help administer our elections and certify the results — to publicly commit to three things. 
First, that they will abide by the U.S. Constitution and state election laws. 
Second, that they will refuse to comply with any unlawful executive orders or data requests from the Department of Justice that seek to restrict voting. 
Third, a commitment to faithfully play their role to certify and seat the rightfully elected winners of our elections this November, regardless of party affiliation.

 But not everyone shares our vision for a democracy where all of us have a voice. 
This federal administration continues to sow doubt about our elections and drive division among our neighbors. Their vision for our future is one where it’s more difficult to cast your vote at the ballot box, so ultimately, less of us have a say. 
That’s why they tried leaning on the postal service to make it harder for us to return our mail-in ballots. That’s why they’ve gutted the Voting Rights Act that generations before us marched and bled to pass. The president has even gone so far as to encourage his supporters to “cheat like hell” during midterm elections.

This federal administration wants us to feel small, alone and afraid so we stay home this election season. Fear is the oldest tool in the book, and we are watching them reach for it again. Invent a crisis. Pour fuel on fear. Aim it at a neighbor, the immigrant, the Muslim family next door, our Black neighbor down the street. 
They want us to be afraid of each other because neighbors who trust each other are harder to frighten, divide and keep home this election season. But Minnesotans know a good neighbor doesn’t believe the worst about the family next door just because a billionaire-backed politician points a finger. 
Protecting our elections isn’t something we do once every four years. It’s ongoing work that happens county by county, community by community, 365 days a year. This work happens in every corner of our state, led by neighbors like us. 
We’re proud of our neighbors who run our elections. Across Minnesota, we decide our future, choose our leaders and will continue voting with our neighbors to make our voices heard at the ballot box. In every corner of our state, from Mankato to White Earth, Hermantown to Winona, our elections are run by us, for us.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Rural Klickitat County faces surge in data center proposals
description: Rural Klickitat County has just 24,000 residents. Developers are eyeing it for up to six data centers drawing enough power for 6 million homes.
text:
The Columbia River in Klickitat County, looking downstream from one of the sites of a proposed data center in the rural area. (Photo by Emma Renly)
Klickitat County stretches for more than 80 miles along the Columbia River, speckled with small towns along the waterfront and within its agricultural lands. It’s here that at least six hyperscale data centers are being proposed.
The rural county, best known for wine vineyards and agriculture, has just 24,000 residents. But public records show that data center developers have asked the Bonneville Power Administration and Klickitat Utility District for access to up to 5,655.5 megawatts of power. That’s enough to power up to six million homes or about 15 cities the size of Seattle.
Directly surrounding counties — Skamania, Benton, Yakima and Hood River — all unanimously approved data center moratoriums this year, but Klickitat County commissioners did not.
A growing petition in Klickitat County is circulating online, asking county commissioners to enact a moratorium. Begun by White Salmon resident Jenn Sharp and other community members, the petition has nearly 800 signatures as of Oct. 6.
“The process to finalize a comprehensive and robust ordinance which can withstand the legal pressures massive corporations will exert can take several months or even years to complete,” Sharp wrote in an email, using the county’s pending ordinance regulating solar and battery energy storage systems as an example.
She hopes the petition shows elected officials that residents want a moratorium as a guardrail while a proposed data center ordinance is finalized.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Before the petition went online, County Commissioner Todd Andrews proposed a six-month data center moratorium at the commission’s meeting on Sept. 8, but his motion died without a second.
Commissioners Lori Zoller and Ron Ihrig argued Andrews’ proposal came up without prior notice. They also said the county should focus on developing a permanent ordinance to regulate data centers.
Zoller, who’s seeking reelection to the Klickitat County Commissioner District 2 seat this year, said moratoriums only provide a short pause for proposals and cannot kill projects.
“Mr. Ihrig and I are working hard on this issue for the County and the public, and we are confident we can address the subject,” Zoller said. “That is what we were elected to do. Not to hide behind a moratorium.”
The draft for a proposed data center ordinance became available online for public comment on Sept. 22 to “establish regulations for the siting, permitting, and operation of industrial-scale data center operations.” It specifically lists facilities of 20 megawatts or more.
Zoller described the document as a “living document” that would remain open to public feedback. It might not be ready until Oct. 20 for board approval, pending legal review.
As the ordinance draft currently stands, it still allows data centers, but applicants must meet zoning requirements. The biggest change would be a one-mile setback from homes.
Data center tax break close to getting zapped by WA Legislature

Still, residents worry a data center application will be submitted before the ordinance is finalized.
Klickitat County
The data center debate has also spilled into the reelection of the commissioner position at Klickitat Public Utility District.
The PUD submits the power requests to Bonneville after receiving a completed form and application fees.
Residents have criticized the PUD members for signing non-disclosure agreements with the developers. Since then, PUD commissioners — Doug Miller, Rodney Colton, and Dan Gunkel — released a joint statement on Sept. 22 saying they are advising the PUD to discontinue NDAs, but that “existing agreements will remain in effect through their current terms.”
Gunkel, who represents District 3, is also up for reelection this year.
While a power request is part of the data center building process, it does not guarantee that the facility will be built. Each project in Klickitat County is at a different stage of development. Some have identified land, water and power sources, while others remain in preliminary feasibility stages.
However, no site permits have been submitted to the county planning department. No construction has begun.
If a site plan is submitted, the application goes to the Planning Commission and Board of County Commissioners. Officials say, however, the review is largely technical and, under current county rules, their power to say no is limited.
“We’ll review it, but all we’re going to be reviewing is for setbacks, height limitations, parking requirements to ensure all the standards are code,” said Klickitat County Planning Director Scott Edelman. “There’s no question as to whether they can do it. It’s simply — are you meeting the standards?”
Previously, the county’s only policy guiding data centers is from 2023, which allows them to be built in industrial parks without requiring a conditional use permit from the county Board of Adjustment, which would involve a public hearing on the project.
Residents say allowing data centers on industrial land with so little review eliminates their voice on the topic.
“Because our population is so small, as well as surrounding populations, that could be a reason to target the area … How many people does it take to stop something like this?” Dallesport resident Liz Mutch said.
The initial 2023 policy also says that Klickitat is a good market for data centers, and would strengthen and diversify the economy.
Chelsey Jones, an economic development specialist for Klickitat County, said that taxes generated from data centers could provide revenue to local services and taxing districts.
“These include fire, EMS, recreation, hospital and school districts as well as regional libraries and the county itself,” she said, adding that construction can support around 3,000 temporary workers and once completed, each facility can employ anywhere from 25 to 75 people.
Where are the data centers?
A former aluminum smelting factory sandwiched between the Columbia River and Highway 14 is the location for a data center being developed by Blue Owl Capital on land owned by NSC Smelter. The closest town is eight miles away, Goldendale.
Itʻs the only power request thatʻs reached a formal agreement through Bonneville, providing for 160 megawatts of power.
Downstream of the aluminum smelting plant are two additional data center proposals in the town of Dallesport, with a population of 1,300 — one on an active orchard owned by Tom Webster and the other on a cliff above the Columbia River, owned by Lakeside Industries. Both facilities plan on using power from Bonneville.
Lakeside Industries and partner Avison Young did not respond to a request for comment. Power application documents say that the data center would have emergency standby generation through diesel generators.
As demand for AI rises, so do power thirsty data centers

Erica Diaz, executive assistant to Webster’s The Fruit Company, said that Webster is continuing to evaluate the property for “data center development and advanced chip manufacturing opportunities.”
“No developer, buyer, or end user has been selected, and no final development plan or decision regarding the future use of the property has been made,” Diaz added.
The exact locations of the other three data centers are unknown, though documents show Shell Energy and its subsidiary, Savion, a renewable energy developer, are behind the applications.
The three titles are Energizer Data Center and Expanded Capacity, for large-scale computer servers and computing infrastructure;  Energizer II,  an AI data center, and Vines Rest DC.
Spokane County reverses course, approving four-month data center pause

Unlike the other data centers, documents show that Vines Rest DC and Energizer II would uniquely start at full power capacity, which would not be possible if using power from Bonneville alone. An external power source would be needed. The transmission line is on private property owned by Rob Mercer, a vineyard on Klickitat’s eastern border.
When contacted, Mercer confirmed that a “small portion of the property has an easement for a potential tie-in at the Bonneville power line for a nearby solar project.” But it is not the direct location of a data center.
The nearby solar project is Savion’s River Turn Energy Center, a large-scale solar farm with a battery.
However, Kelly Cooper, a spokesperson for Savion, said, “While preliminary feasibility work is underway, there is currently no defined Vines Rest project … River Turn and Vines Rest are separate development evaluations.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Trump administration urges states to allow on-road dyed diesel
description: Dyed diesel is a tax-exempt fuel typically allowed in off-road machinery only.
text:
President Donald Trump authorized highway use of dyed diesel fuel and some states are following suit. Fuel prices shown here are from June 23, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said Tuesday in Iowa that she is urging state governors to follow the president’s move to suspend penalties on the unrestricted use of dyed diesel, a tax-exempt fuel typically allowed in off-road machinery only.
President Donald Trump announced Monday evening at a rally in Nebraska he would authorize highway use of dyed diesel fuel and defer the federal excise tax on the fuel to provide relief from the steep diesel prices which have hit record highs of more than $6 per gallon, nationally.
The move from Trump followed actions from several states, like Ohio, to suspend state fuel taxes or to allow dyed diesel fuel. After Trump’s Monday-night executive order, more states, including Iowa, have leveraged similar state-level suspensions.
Rollins, speaking with reporters at a stop in Iowa Tuesday, said she is “on the phone constantly with other governors, trying to get them to do the same.”
Rollins said 13 governors, including Democratic Gov. Josh Stein in North Carolina, have followed suit.
“I’m working on a lot of the other Democrat governors, saying … this will really help your constituents and your farmers.”


About dyed diesel
Dyed diesel fuel is a tax-exempt diesel fuel used in off-road equipment for farming, construction and heating. The diesel is dyed red so that law enforcement can identify the fuel and enforce penalties when it is used on roads.


According to the executive order from the president, the federal suspension could save drivers as much as $100 per trip to the fuel station.
In his announcement Monday evening, Trump said the order would allow “anyone” to purchase red-dyed diesel fuel “for any reason.” Trump’s executive order runs through the end of the calendar year.
Rollins said Tuesday that in addition to the executive order on dyed diesel, an influx of 100 million barrels of oil from the Group of Seven, or G7, countries have “already” caused the price of diesel to decline. The G7 announcement was made Friday. According to AAA fuel price data, the national average price of diesel was about $0.13 per gallon lower Tuesday than a week prior.
“There’s a lot of really good things that are being deployed right now,” Rollins said.
Fuel prices have risen sharply due to the ongoing war in Iran and closures in the Strait of Hormuz, a prominent trade route for products like oil and fertilizer, combined with continued conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
In his rally speech in Nebraska, Trump said the situation in Iran is “going to be over with very soon.” Rollins echoed the sentiment Tuesday when asked about the war and said the government of Iran “cannot have” a nuclear weapon and that the war was “so important for the future.”
“He has said that we’re moving quickly, that we will and should be out of it very soon,” Rollins said. “When that happens, all of the fuel prices, everything will absolutely go down significantly.”
Rollins said the current situation “is exactly why” the administration is “working so hard” to increase domestic energy production.

title: Missouri voters sent a message. Will their leaders listen?
description: In early August, Missouri voters decisively rejected two efforts to rewrite some of the basic rules of state government. Although Republicans hold supermajorities in the Senate (24-10) and House (111-52), Amendment 4 would have required citizen-led constitutional amendments to win both statewide and in all eight congressional districts. Voters also rejected[...]
text:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).In early August, Missouri voters decisively rejected two efforts to rewrite some of the basic rules of state government.
Although Republicans hold supermajorities in the Senate (24-10) and House (111-52), Amendment 4 would have required citizen-led constitutional amendments to win both statewide and in all eight congressional districts.
Voters also rejected Amendment 5, which would have required lawmakers to phase out the individual income tax as revenues grew and allowed them to expand sales taxes to replace some of the lost revenue. Critics argued the shift would fall more heavily on lower- and middle-income Missourians. Amendment 4 lost 80% to 20%; Amendment 5 lost 83% to 17%.
A month later, the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the Legislature’s 2025 congressional redistricting plan was subject to a referendum and that Secretary of State Denny Hoskins could not block the public vote.
Such clear messages have done little to settle the underlying political fights. Rep. Alex Riley, R-Springfield, concluded after the August elections that Republicans needed to “go back to the drawing board a little bit.” This is like Napoleon Bonaparte interpreting his disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812 as a minor setback.
Many of us who have left Missouri for work remain Missourians at heart. I grew up in St. Louis, but also lived in Kansas City and Columbia and, as a young journalist, in Perryville, giving me a good sampling of the state’s citizenry. I have lived on the East Coast, in the South and now on the West Coast, and a standout feature of most of the Missourians I have known is authenticity. This allowed them to engage others despite significant differences, and to do so with a decency and even friendliness that made room for the compromise needed for community-based problem solving and a true representative democracy.
Over the past 20 years, unfortunately, like many native Missourians who now live outside the state, I grew reticent to share my roots because my home state became increasingly associated with America’s culture wars. It became fertile ground for conflict entrepreneurs, people skilled at inflaming and exploiting natural divisions for personal fame and profit, and “rage entrepreneurs,” experts at bending collective frustration and resentment toward their own ambitions. Such entrepreneurs have made enormous amounts of money and gained unprecedented political and cultural influence by sowing distrust, anger and even hatred.
Instead of “going back to the drawing board a little bit,” Missouri leaders should reconnect themselves with their “Show Me” roots. That unofficial slogan has long been associated with a skeptical, noncredulous streak — a demand for evidence rather than rhetoric. It also reflected a traditionally conservative temperament. But the conservatism I remember in Missouri had little in common with the anger and absolutism that dominate so much of contemporary politics.
It more closely resembled the conservatism described by Russell Kirk in The Conservative Mind. In Kirk’s tradition, a conservative recognizes an enduring moral order that humans must respect if they are to flourish. Such conservatism embraces virtue, tradition and continuity while accepting that change is inevitable. Progress requires prudence, and grand efforts to reshape society according to an elite vision deserve skepticism.
What I most admired about Missouri was its ability to live with the tensions inherent in democracy’s messy process of change. Consider its history. Missouri remained a slave state in the Union during the Civil War, even as a rival Confederate-aligned state government claimed legitimacy. Records document more than 300 escapes from Missouri involving more than 1,500 enslaved people seeking freedom.
The 1857 Dred Scott decision, arising from a Missouri case, became one of the Supreme Court’s most infamous pre-Civil War rulings. In 1948, the Missouri case Shelley v. Kraemer produced a landmark Supreme Court decision barring state courts from enforcing racially restrictive housing covenants. From 1904 through 2004, Missouri voted for the winning presidential candidate in 25 of 26 elections. It took the nation’s pulse and mirrored the American people’s conflicted growth into the country’s founding principles.
I once witnessed a remarkable example of Missouri’s Show Me character at a town hall with U.S. Sens. Thomas Eagleton and John Danforth. In the 1980s, I was a chaperone for a group of students from north St. Louis who journeyed to Washington, D.C., to experience the democratic process. Both senators, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, addressed hundreds of Missourians for hours on many contentious issues.
Partisan passions were intense. But Eagleton and Danforth modeled passionate disagreement while also demonstrating decency, mutual respect, empathy, a search for common ground and, most importantly, an insistence on informed argumentation.
They offered a master class in the values implied by Missouri’s unofficial “Show Me” slogan, not to mention its official motto: “The welfare of the people shall be the supreme law.”
If Missouri reclaims this tradition, perhaps more Missourians — including those of us who now live elsewhere — will once again recognize the state we remember.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Unusually high number of Oklahoma House incumbents face November reelection challenges
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Dozens of incumbent Oklahoma lawmakers are facing challengers in November due in part to a push by Democrats to recruit more candidates and growing frustration with legislative actions.  Experts say the unusually high number of contested legislative races could fuel voter turnout, but is unlikely to result in Republicans losing control of […]
text:
Lawmakers' desks on the Oklahoma House floor are pictured June 1, 2026 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Dozens of incumbent Oklahoma lawmakers are facing challengers in November due in part to a push by Democrats to recruit more candidates and growing frustration with legislative actions. 
Experts say the unusually high number of contested legislative races could fuel voter turnout, but is unlikely to result in Republicans losing control of the lower chamber.
Of the 101 Oklahoma House seats, 55 will have contested races on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. During the 2024 general election, only 32 House seats were on the ballot. 
The vast majority of these involve an incumbent lawmaker hoping to be reelected for another term.
Rep. Carl Newton, R-Cherokee, is one of the 43 incumbent lawmakers facing a reelection challenger. He said he decided to seek reelection for what would be his final term because he “owes it” to his constituents. 
“I feel like both parties should have a chance to have somebody on the ballot, that’s their right to have those so it doesn’t surprise me,” he said of an increase in challengers this year. “I think that the Democratic Party has been big on trying to make sure there are some challenges in every race, as many races as they can.” 
And, part of the job of a state representative is working with new people every two years, Newton said.  
Erin Brewer, chair of the Oklahoma Democratic Party, said they actively focused on encouraging more candidates to run to give voters a choice at the ballot box and drive voter participation. 
In the past, many Oklahoma elections have been decided during June’s primary or August’s runoff elections, both of which are closed and partisan. Oklahoma also has some of the lowest voter turnout in the country. 
Brewer said her party made an effort to recruit more candidates to run in elections across the state, she said. They’ve also been able to do more this year to help candidates with campaign websites and materials. 
“Oklahoma is one of the lowest voter turnout states in the nation, but part of that is because we simply haven’t been having as many competitive races as we should have in general elections,” she said. 
Oklahomans are ready for a “different kind of leadership,” she said. 
“We know that we’re going to flip some seats in November, and part of that is because of the sheer number of candidates we have on the ballot,” Brewer said. “But part of it is because they’re really strong quality candidates and they’re doing the work.”
Another incumbent being challenged, Rep. Daniel Pae, R-Lawton, said competition brings out the best in elections, and he hopes it will lead to higher voter turnout. He is facing Democrat Blake Munoz in November. 
“The thing learned over the years, even going back to when I was running for student council at Lawton High, you should never be complacent when it comes to campaigning so I always campaign as if I’m 15, 20 points down,” he said. 
Allyson Shortle, a political science professor at University of Oklahoma, said she doesn’t think Oklahoma will see lots of seats flipped, but the races will be more competitive – even if the Republican candidate ends up on top. 
“But it certainly will get the Democrats in the state very enthusiastic in a way I don’t think we’ve seen in many, many years, if not decades,” Shortle said. 
First time candidates
Linda Pedro, a member of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, is challenging Rep. Dick Lowe, R-Amber, for his seat representing House District 65. 
Pedro, a Democrat from El Reno, said she’s making her first run for public office because she’s seen her community struggling with housing, homelessness and affordability issues. 
“I’d like to be a voice for the people to say, ‘Hey, you know, that’s gonna affect these people, cause I’m one of them,’” she said. 
Pedro said she feels good about her chances in the election because her communities and district know who she is and what’s important to her. 
Seth McKee, an Oklahoma State University political science professor, said voter turnout could aid Democratic candidates as the people angriest with President Donald Trump’s administration are likely to vote against Republicans. 
The president’s approval ratings have dropped across the country, including in Oklahoma, as war with Iran continues and everyday costs continue to rise. 
“That coalition is going to be overwhelmingly Democratic in terms of the people who show up, and of course it’s going to vary across states,” McKee said. “It’s not going to be as Democratic in Oklahoma, but it’s all going to have that same bias to it. And so, if you look in Oklahoma, it’s going to be a much lighter red coalition than you would normally see.”
Tony Oliva, an independent, said he doesn’t expect to win his race against incumbent Rep. Meloyde Blancett, D-Tulsa. He said he just has his name on the ballot to give people another choice but isn’t spending money or campaigning. 
Oliva said he launched his first bid for office because he is frustrated with his representation and the two-party system. 
Open seats
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said, this election will mark the largest incoming class of lawmakers since 2018, regardless of the outcome of the incumbents’ races.
A dozen seats will not have a returning representative either due to term limits or a legislator not seeking reelection. 
Two of these seats are vacant following lawmaker resignations. 
Rep. John Waldron, D-Tulsa, resigned effective Oct. 1 after admitting to using artificial intelligence to make a GIF of him and a potential election candidate kissing. He’ll be replaced by Democrat Kristina Gabriel, who defeated him in the primary.
Rep. Ajay Pittman, D-Oklahoma City, also resigned this year after pleading guilty to forgery-related charges. Democrat Herschel Brown and Republican Melvin Latham are vying to fill the House District seat 99, which represents parts of Nichols Hills and northeast Oklahoma City. 
Democrat Andrea Biscardi, of Owasso, said she is running for public office for the first time to represent House District 9, which includes parts of Claremore and Owasso. Rep. Mark Lepak, R-Claremore, currently holds the seat and cannot run for reelection because of term limits. 
It’s her first time running for any political office and she chose to do so because the seat is “almost always uncontested.” 
Biscardi said she’s passionate about healthcare and public education. 
“I’ve seen a lot of issues with people just getting the benefits that they already deserve,” Biscardi said. “You know, it takes two months to get on this or two years to get on disability, two hours to get someone on the phone to get SNAP benefits turned back on. There’s a lot of social services that could use help in Oklahoma.” 
She’s set to face Republican Scotty Stokes in November.

name: WyoFile
title: The mountain elite: Jackson Hole’s Catherine Cullinane hung with the Stonemasters, pioneered diabetes education
description:
She was guiding the Grand Teton when she was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes, so made a career treating others who had the disease.
The post The mountain elite: Jackson Hole’s Catherine Cullinane hung with the Stonemasters, pioneered diabetes education appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Catherine Cullinane had climbed with the Stonemasters in Yosemite Valley, a loose-knit group of hard men that pushed the limits of rock climbing, and was working in the Tetons for Exum Mountain Guides when she got the news.
“I had been guiding the Grand all year, and I got really skinny,” she said. A nurse, she understood that she exhibited “all the classic symptoms of having Type 1 diabetes.”
But because the disease didn’t run in her family, the ailment wasn’t on her radar.
“It was quite shocking,” she said of her diagnosis. “If someone knew you had diabetes, they always wanted to tell you about their great uncle that had their leg amputated or lost their vision — a lot of negativity.
“I became obsessed,” she said, thinking “that’s not going to happen to me.”
She had big goals as an outdoors woman and wanted to ensure she could continue to follow her calling.
“I must have been born to be outside most of my life,” she said.
Goal one was to climb Denali, North America’s highest peak, ice-clad and soaring to 20,310 feet in the Alaska Range.
“Climbing Denali helped me think that I could do pretty much anything,” she said after her successful climb. The “anything” she next wanted was a baby.
“You have to have your blood sugars in perfect control, in total normal range, the whole time you’re pregnant,” Cullinane said. “I was already 34, 35 [years old] at that point, so I was sort of anxious [to] try to be in perfect control.”
Daughter Jane Jackson was born in 1991. Earlier this year, Jackson climbed Cerro Fitz Roy, a giant granite spire in Argentina’s Patagonia region, one of the toughest summits on the planet.
“Climbing Denali helped me think that I could do pretty much anything.”Catherine Cullinane
Cullinane never considered herself an athlete. The daughter of a banker and special ed teacher, she grew up backpacking with her family in the Sierra Nevada mountains.
“My mother would pack breakfast, lunch and dinner for six or seven days, and then my dad would pack it up on the burros, and we would all start walking with our little Sierra Club cups on our belts.”
The mountain bug bit her. “I became quite obsessed with the whole [American] Everest 1963 expedition,” devouring National Geographic’s coverage, she said.
After high school, she took a gap year and moved to Yosemite Valley where she got a job in a cafeteria and began climbing “with some of the famous old rock climbers.
“My parents were horrified.”
“People would take me out climbing, and I was good at it, for whatever reason. Crack climbing kind of came natural to me. All the Stonemasters and the other men climbers, most of them were totally psyched if they took us climbing and we could do the route. Really good crack climbers definitely showed me the technique.”
Her forte was climbing hand and fist cracks — vertical fissures common in rock walls and on many peaks. To grip a two-inch wide vertical crack, a climber reaches up as if to shake, then slots her hand vertically into the gap. Then, “you bring your thumb down and you kind of flex your whole thumb and palm area.”
A hand jam isn’t as secure as an open-palm grip on a feature like a pull-up bar, but works when properly applied. A similar technique allows a climber to twist her toes into the fissure to ascend.
Cullinane climbed The Nose on El Capitan, the sheer Northwest Face of Half Dome and other big walls.
“Leading was the hard part back in the day.” To protect herself with a running belay as she ascended, she used artificial chockstones called Hexcentrics, which took some art, to place correctly in the crack.
“It was terrifying compared to now,” Cullinane said, comparing old-school gear fumbling to the ease of placing today’s spring-loaded camming devices.
She met a test one summer on the West Face of Yosemite’s Sentinel Rock. Cullinane drew the lead for the last pitch, a hand crack then rated 5.10, the most difficult.
“I think now it’s 5.11a or something,” she said. “At that time, you couldn’t hang on anything,” she said of the free-climbing ethos that shunned grabbing only the rock. “You wanted it to be perfect, pure — just climbing.”
She made a runout — “way above my protection,” and got to the anchor at the top of the pitch.
“I was so pumped that I couldn’t even clip in,” she said. “So I took a big whipper. I went about 30-35 feet.”
She wasn’t wearing a helmet and was tied in with a three-inch waistband only — no leg loops.
That fall “kind of limited my leading,” she said.
Cullinane worked through her climbing fears and also pursued her education in nursing school. Her father, “pretty set in his ways,” had never encouraged her to be a doctor, proposing she become a nurse or teacher.
One summer she came to the Tetons and was hired by Exum to help on easy climbs where guides would take perhaps 15 kids at a time. “I would be sort of the helper, checking knots, encouraging the kids.”
She began carrying loads up to the Lower Saddle of the 13,775-foot-high Grand Teton, then tied on to Exum parties as a junior guide. After a few years, she was the leader of her own team with her own set of clients.
“So I took a big whipper. I went about 30-35 feet.”Catherine Cullinane
After graduating from nursing school in 1983, Cullinane was tapped for a 1986 expedition to the north side of Everest. No American woman had yet been on top.
It was not to be. Weather set in. “The jet stream lowered and we lost a Sherpa in an avalanche, which was horrible.” She reached about 24,500 feet on the 29,031-foot-high Sagarmāthā or Jomolangma.
Cullinane became a diabetes educator, started an entire program at St. John’s Medical in Jackson, and worked at San Francisco General Hospital. She melded her medical and Himalayan interests through a neighbor in Kelly, Dr. David Shlim, and the Canadian International Water and Energy Consultants Travel Center Hospital in Nepal. Asked to review the staff in Kathmandu, she found nurses up to snuff on medical protocol, but unfamiliar with insulin pumps, which Cullinane explained.
These days Cullinane spends some months in Utah where rock climbing diehards, even the older set, keep up their craft. Two years ago, a handhold broke on a climb and she fell 10 feet and hit a ledge before her rope caught her. She broke five bones.
“It was ugly,” she said. 
“I was in a wheelchair for two months, and then I had a boot on my right leg for 16 weeks, and on my left leg for 12 weeks.”
At 71, her latest transition is “learning to age gracefully while still trying to climb.
“I love climbing and I don’t want to give it up. So I have to learn how to push back, bring the level down, the bar down a little bit, so I can still do it and not get too frustrated with my injuries.
“I didn’t think I was an athlete,” she said of her pioneering days. “I didn’t think I was particularly strong. I feel like I’ve had an ordinary but extraordinary life. I just go about my day.”
Cullinane said she’s amazed at the young women athletes in her valley. “What they’re doing in the Tetons [is] kind of crazy.”
All sorts of Equality State women stand out too, whether they’re on a ranch, in the saddle or even in court “fighting for healthcare freedom for women in Wyoming,” she said.
“I think there’s roadblocks that are intrinsic in our society, which is a total bummer,” she said of the state of equality. “But I think in Wyoming there’s a lot of potential for women to do what they want to.”

name: WyoFile
title: Proposition 1 is not self-reliance
description:
A self-imposed cut to property taxes means fewer services and more reliance on volatile funding sources, writes guest columnist Jerry Obermueller.
The post Proposition 1 is not self-reliance appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
This November, the people of Wyoming will decide whether or not to reduce residential property taxes by 50%.

Opinion

At the heart of this decision is whether we want to assume the risks associated with fewer of the services property taxes currently cover. “Assuming the risk” is not about self-reliance since the services impacted absolutely require pooled resources, not individual effort. The risk is less safety for your family on roads, less fire protection, fewer first responders and law enforcement, and less aid in distress. 
Here is some context about property taxes. Eighteen of our 23 counties currently do not collect enough property tax to self-fund schools, and all counties and towns fall short of self-funding operations. The Wyoming Legislature currently fills the gap with other statewide revenue sources. That is why we don’t already notice disruption of services due to the lack of property taxes. Can those backup plans also cover a tax cut so that there is no loss of services? This is a blind spot and part of the overall risk. Proposition 1 ignores this risk — a real deal breaker.
The backup revenue streams are highly volatile. Sales taxes, mineral severance taxes, federal mineral royalties and investment income, which represent the other major revenue sources working alongside and in support of property taxes, are all affected by factors beyond our control and often beyond our borders. 
We can’t guarantee severance taxes by forcing energy companies to drill. We can’t rely on the federal government’s commitment to leasing federal lands for exploration of minerals, providing the state with federal mineral royalties. We can’t predict the future success of the stock market to safeguard Wyoming’s investment income.
What we can control is paying property taxes and contributing to sales tax revenue, the only general revenue sources that look like “self-reliance.” If we give ourselves a tax cut, it increases our dependence on other revenue sources, weakens our core value of self-determination and increases the risk of losing our status as a modern rural state. 
A “no” vote on Proposition 1 means we know the importance of taking a personal stake in the future of Wyoming through pooled resources. A “no” vote shows our continued support for the value of small communities which depend on receiving a share of property taxes from higher property-value counties. It is one of our great historical achievements that rugged individualism and shared community values, self-interest and altruism, exist together in a dynamic balance. As a result, we have avoided the downward spiral of many rural areas around the country. We still have livable towns and cities and real tangible economic value in our communities, our businesses and our homes. Proposition 1 puts our modern rural state and personal properties at risk of systemic devaluation, a self-inflicted wound. 
Self-reliance and self-determination in Wyoming include shared responsibilities to uphold our communities and neighbors in our “one community with long streets.” It’s the Wyoming Way.

title: Tenn. Republicans: Legislature to investigate other execution methods after failed lethal injections
description: Republican leaders in Tennessee’s legislature say they will investigate the reliability of lethal injection as an execution method after the state failed to execute two death row inmates in the span of five months. Gov. Bill Lee stopped the May execution of Tony Carruthers after a physician unsuccessfully attempted to insert intravenous lines to begin […]
text:
Death row offender Christa Pike was taken taken by ambulance to a hospital for treatment after two failed lethal injections on Sept. 30. Republican leaders say the Tennessee General Assembly will investigate the failure and consider alternative execution methods in an upcoming legislative session. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Republican leaders in Tennessee’s legislature say they will investigate the reliability of lethal injection as an execution method after the state failed to execute two death row inmates in the span of five months.
Gov. Bill Lee stopped the May execution of Tony Carruthers after a physician unsuccessfully attempted to insert intravenous lines to begin the lethal injection process for over an hour. Death row inmate Christa Pike survived two failed rounds of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol on Sept. 30 before the execution was halted. Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, is receiving medical care in a Nashville hospital. 
Lee ordered a third-party review and issued a pause on all executions in the state until the end of the year.
Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, a Franklin Republican and candidate for Senate Speaker, told conservative radio show SuperTalk 99.7 WTN Monday that he supports Lee’s decision to defer executions while the investigation takes place.
“I’m inclined … that if we’re having this much trouble with this particular means of execution, we need to take it off the table and go to something that’s far more reliable and predictable,” Johnson said, listing the electric chair or a firing squad among other potential options. 
Gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn said she favors reinstating the electric chair as the state’s primary execution method.
“If we’re having this much trouble with this particular means of execution, we need to take it off the table and go to something that’s far more reliable and predictable,” said Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, A Franklin Republican, of using lethal injection for death penalty executions. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“My colleagues in the General Assembly, if we come to the conclusion that the lethal injection as a means of execution is not reliable enough, and we need to take that off the table, I would like for us to be able to contemplate that before another person is set to be executed,” Johnson said.
Lethal injection has been Tennessee’s primary execution method since 2000. Offenders who were sentenced to death prior to Jan. 1, 1999 can request electrocution as an alternative. Lee paused executions in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and again in 2022 after officials failed to test lethal injection chemicals for endotoxins, a chemical contaminant, before the execution of Oscar Smith, prompting Lee to pause the execution and order an investigation and protocol review.
In 2023, Rep. Dennis Powers, a Jacksboro Republican, introduced a measure that would allow death row inmates to choose to be executed by firing squad as well as by lethal injection or electric chair. The bill failed.
Johnson said he is awaiting legal advice regarding the state’s options for contemplating other means of execution.
House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, told SuperTalk 99.7 WTN that he is in favor of “looking at all alternatives,” including the electric chair, firing squad or hanging, which Tennessee used as its method of execution until 1913.
State Senate Minority Leader Raumesh Akbari, a Memphis Democrat, and state Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat and the party’s House caucus chair, called for the legislature to bring back legislative oversight of state agencies.
Johnson and Sexton said Tennessee’s Republican supermajority has no intention of moving away from capital punishment.
Sexton said lawmakers would do their own investigation into the failed executions. He also said the general assembly will “look at speeding up” the appeals process for death row offenders.
Tennessee governor orders third-party review, pauses all executions for the rest of the year

“The problem is in the 1970s and 80s, we had the U.S. Supreme Court that put in a lot of parameters and a lot of things that I don’t think are needed, and allowing them to file appeal after appeal and drive up the costs and try to force states not to execute,” Sexton said. “That’s not what we’re going to do.”
The U.S. Supreme Court struck down capital punishment statutes nationwide in 1972 in Furman v. Georgia, finding such statutes imposed in an “arbitrary and capricious” way violated the Eighth Amendment protection against cruel and unusual punishment. Four years later, the court upheld a new set of more specific capital punishment statutes with narrowed eligibility in Gregg v. Georgia.
Johnson said Slemmer’s family waited 30 years for Pike’s sentence to be carried out, and the state failed them.
“I certainly think there should be an appeals process,” Johnson said. “It doesn’t really need to take 30 years.”
Both Johnson and Sexton indicated they expect legal challenges to any changes made to the state’s execution protocol.
“We are going to work with the (Attorney General), with the White House, with others to figure out how to do this effective, efficiently and swiftly,” Sexton said. “And if we need (it) to be challenged in the court system, then let’s go challenge it. Let’s see what the new U.S. Supreme Court says and then we’ll go from there.”
Adam Friedman contributed.
