name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Government must deliver for renters
description: Campaign rhetoric on affordability feels out of touch is because most politicians are ignoring the needs of renters.
text:
Life is hard for a lot of people right now. That’s not anything new. Paying bills, keeping up with housing costs, and making ends meet have become increasingly difficult for people across Connecticut. We are living through an affordability crisis.  
In this election cycle, Connecticut residents are once again hearing plenty of promises about affordability. Candidates are offering plans, proposals, and long-term solutions. Those conversations are important. But we also need to ask a more immediate question:  
What can we do for people who are struggling right now?  
Part of why the current campaign rhetoric on affordability feels so out of touch is because most politicians are ignoring a massive group of people who are deeply weighed down by the cost of living: renters. 
The Connecticut General Assembly has an opportunity to begin answering the need for action by prioritizing a rent affordability agenda in 2027. Doing so would not only help people survive now but build faith in government. 
One in three people in Connecticut rent. And when asked, renters named housing costs as their number one affordability concern. But our state has done little for them.
It’s true that Connecticut has passed significant housing legislation intended to increase supply. Those efforts are worthwhile and important for the long term, but they do not put money back into a family budget today, especially for people who rent. And our state has to offer both long- and short-term solutions to give people hope. 
Neither major party candidate for Governor has an explicit, direct rent affordability plan. Both have ideas about housing overall, focused on increasing supply – which is a worthy goal and may decrease costs years from now, but won’t do anything for the approximately 230,000 Connecticut renters who are housing-cost burdened today. 

Tyler Mack

If someone is struggling to pay their rent this month, telling them that housing supply may improve years from now does not make today’s rent any more affordable.  
If a family is struggling to make ends meet, a promise of future relief can feel a lot like no relief at all.  
Long-term solutions matter. But so does helping people survive long enough to benefit from them.  
Over the last two years, voters have gone to the polls hoping that the people they elect will make their lives more affordable. They have voted for candidates from both parties. But when the bills keep coming and the financial pressure doesn’t let up, people understandably begin to question whether government is working for them. That is where the problem becomes bigger than affordability. It becomes a problem of trust.  
When people hear promises but don’t see results in their own lives, they can lose faith in their elected leaders. Some stop voting. Others conclude the system is rigged against them. That should concern all of us. 
Renters contribute to the property tax system, even though they don’t receive a property tax bill themselves. On average, around 20% of people’s rent pays property taxes. Property taxes are part of the cost of housing, and renters ultimately help pay those costs through their rent. Yet when we talk about property tax relief, renters are often treated as though they are not part of the equation. 
They should be. 
We need a renter’s affordability agenda for Connecticut. This agenda should include a renter’s tax credit to provide direct relief to people who need it. It should also include just cause eviction protections to make sure good tenants have stability and security, and prevent new landlords from creating skyrocketing rent hikes when they buy a building. And it should prevent astronomical security deposit fees that keep people from being able to move out of bad situations, even if they can afford the rent on a better place.  
This renter’s affordability agenda would not solve Connecticut’s affordability crisis, including its housing crisis, and it wouldn’t be a silver bullet. But it would be a tangible way for our state government to say to renters: We see you. We understand that you are struggling. And we are willing to do something about it. 
People should not have to choose between believing in government and believing what they see in their own lives.  
We cannot keep talking about affordability while forgetting the people living through it. This legislative session, let’s give renters meaningful, direct relief while we continue working on the long-term challenges that make housing and everyday life so expensive. 
Let’s pass the renter’s affordability agenda. Let’s show people that government can deliver.
Tyler Mack is a policy and advocacy strategist for the Connecticut Project Action Fund.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand, Lahn trade attacks on residency, family at first Iowa gubernatorial debate
description: Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn accused each other of lying about their residency and family wealth Tuesday while answering questions on the state budget and education during the first 2026 Iowa gubernatorial debate. The debate, hosted by KWQC, was held by at St. Ambrose University in Davenport. It is the first of multiple […]
text:
Democratic Auditor Rob Sand and Republican businessman Zach Lahn are competing to become Iowa governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn accused each other of lying about their residency and family wealth Tuesday while answering questions on the state budget and education during the first 2026 Iowa gubernatorial debate.
The debate, hosted by KWQC, was held by at St. Ambrose University in Davenport. It is the first of multiple debates scheduled between Sand and Lahn in the weeks before the Nov. 3, 2026 general election.
Moderators presented the two candidates a series of questions on issues including Iowa’s economy, education system and high cancer rates. While Sand and Lahn shared some of their plans to tackle these issues if elected governor, much of the time was spent arguing over talking points brought up on the campaign trail through criticisms and political advertisements.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lahn, a businessman who owns a farm in Belle Plaine, spent a significant amount of time in the debate saying Sand was falsely presenting him as not an Iowa resident, and claimed his opponent was attacking his family and children by making this issue prominent in the gubernatorial campaign.
Since becoming the GOP nominee in a contentious June gubernatorial primary, Lahn has faced scrutiny over his state residency. According to the Kansas Reflector, he registered to vote in Iowa in 2024 and met the state’s two-year residency requirement for his 2026 Iowa gubernatorial run, but previously lived in and was a registered voter in Kansas, where he worked on a private pre-K through 12th-grade school named Wonder. The Des Moines Register reported in April he regularly flew his personal airplane between Iowa and Kansas because he had a blended family with some children based out of Wichita, Kansas. He told the Register, “but if I’m elected governor, it would be a different arrangement, and we’d work it out. Because, you know, we’d be in Iowa as much as humanly possible.”
After Lahn claimed the first year Sand was state auditor, he “overspent his budget, had to get bailed out by the governor,” Sand retorted that, “I don’t know how the Kansas State Auditor’s Office works, but we are funded in large part by payment from our clients at the local level. … My predecessor burned through the state’s accounts in the auditor’s office, and we righted that within our first year.”
While moderators attempted to refocus candidates on the initial question asked — about public school funding and the state’s Education Savings Account program providing public funds for private school tuition and associated costs — Lahn argued he should get the opportunity to respond directly to Sand’s comments about his residency.
The Republican said the claim that he is a Kansas resident was “a central lie of Rob Sand’s campaign.” He also said he believed the position of Iowa governor was a “full-time job, and I’m here for it.”
“I’m gonna tell you this right now, this issue is about one thing. It’s about my children. That’s it,” Lahn said. “I have a blended family, and they split time. And I’m gonna tell you right now, I am not going to be intimidated on this. I will spend whatever effort necessary to defend my children from people who’d like to exploit them like you. And my promise to the voters of Iowa, I will also defend your children from people who’d like to exploit them like Rob Sand. I won’t put up with it.”

More debates this week
This week, “Iowa Press” will host two debates on Iowa PBS. Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek square off for a U.S. Senate debate on Wednesday, Oct. 7. Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James, candidates for the 2nd Congressional District seat, will debate on Oct. 8. Both debates will take place at 7 p.m.

Earlier Tuesday, Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, released a video calling for Lahn to “come back to Kansas.”
“Generally, I support Kansans,” Kelly said in the video. “I was even proud to see Zach Lahn voted here in ’18, ’20, and ‘22. I hope he voted for me in the Kansas governor’s race. But in the Iowa governor’s race, I’m supporting the Iowan. Zach, there are no hard feelings, but it is time to come back to Kansas. As they say, there’s no place like home.”
Lahn claimed Sand also traveled frequently, citing properties owned by the family of his wife, Christine Lauridsen Sand, who is the CEO of the Lauridsen Group, Inc., a business that operates six food and health products companies. The Republican candidate claimed Sand regularly “traveled to Aspen, Colorado, to their $77 million mansion there,” referencing a Wall Street Journal article stating the mansion was sold by an LLC “linked to the headquarters of the Lauridsen Group,” alongside a “multimillion dollar home in Northwest Iowa.”
These residential properties are not owned by Sand, but by family members of his wife. He did not directly respond to these claims by Lahn during the debate — the only statement he made about the Lauridsen Group, Inc. was in response to a statement from Lahn who claimed Sand’s in-laws helped fund his campaign using money that “in part, came from selling high nitrate fertilizer.”
“My in-laws’ business doesn’t sell nitrate fertilizer,” Sand said.
Though there was significant back and forth about campaign attacks during the debate, the candidates also answered questions on issues like the $1.4 billion in tax incentives approved by state lawmakers during a special legislative session and signed into law by Gov. Kim Reynolds Friday for a proposed $15 billion steel mill project in Lee County.
Sand said if the project comes to Iowa, it will play a positive role in improving Iowa’s economy — but he said there are legitimate reasons why some Iowans are concerned about the tax incentive package. He pointed to similar propositions like Wisconsin providing tax incentives for the company Foxconn despite not ultimately building the initial proposed project. He also brought up problems Mesabi Metallics, the company proposing to build the Iowa steel mill, have faced in opening an iron ore mine in Nashwauk, Minnesota.
“I think what’s most important here is making sure that this deal is rock solid and actually going to work for Iowans,” Sand said. “We want to make sure, for example, that what happened in Minnesota doesn’t happen here. We don’t want to see a lot of upfront incentives. Instead, we should make sure that this company is making the investments, improving the infrastructure in Iowa — actually building here — and after meeting benchmarks, then seeing incentives come in after that to make sure that actually something is being provided to Iowans.”
Republicans supporting the law passed during special session said the increased tax incentives to Mesabi Metallics available through the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program are contingent on the project’s completion. The law states the 10% tax credit, remitted over the course of a decade, will not be issued to a business until the business begins operations, or until “a designated portion of the project” has been placed in service, and until at least half of created jobs — which must meet a qualifying wage threshold — associated with the project or a designated portion have been added to the payroll.
Sand added, “this is encouraging, and hopefully, we see it out, and hopefully, it becomes real.”
Lahn expressed less skepticism about the project, saying it represents a vital opportunity for southeast Iowa, an area he said was “an economically depressed part of the state.”
“We talking about thousands of new jobs, we’re talking about billions of dollars in investments,” Lahn said. “And my role as governor is to be the chief negotiator for the state, the person that’s going to bring these businesses in.”
While Lahn has emphasized supporting local Iowa businesses and workers during his campaign, he said he believed the project by  Mesabi Metallics — a Minnesota company owned by the India-based Essar Group — was “one of those opportunities that’s transformational to the state” that a governor must advocate for.
“We can’t sit on the fence, we can’t sit on the sideline, we have to prioritize economic growth in the state,” Lahn said. “But the bigger issue here with economic growth is that we have to be prioritizing our rural communities as well, which this project does. It gives the opportunity for rural growth. We’ll see hospitals reopen in the state, we’ll see more houses being built, we’ll see people coming here.”
There are three more gubernatorial debates scheduled. Sand and Lahn will debate Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 7 p.m. in Sioux City hosted by KTIV-TV4;  on Wednesday, Oct. 21 in Des Moines for an “Iowa Press” debate and Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 6:30 p.m. on Cedar Rapids, hosted by KCRG-TV9 / The Gazette.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson, James tackle affordability, federal relations at first gubernatorial debate
description: GRAND RAPIDS – The relationship between Michigan and the federal government — especially when it comes to the tariffs levied by the Trump administration — was central throughout the first general election debate of Michigan’s gubernatorial election between Democrat Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) on T[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, left, stands with with Rep. John James, R-Mich, Republican gubernatorial candidate during a televised debate on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at WOOD-TV, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)GRAND RAPIDS – The relationship between Michigan and the federal government — especially when it comes to the tariffs levied by the Trump administration — was central throughout the first general election debate of Michigan’s gubernatorial election between Democrat Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) on Tuesday night. 
Benson was specifically critical of James’ record in the U.S. House and what she said is a refusal of James to stand up to President Donald Trump on the issue of tariffs, especially those levied against Canada.
“They are costing Michigan $5,600 each household, more than any other state in the nation. And anyone who’s supposed to go to Washington to fight for us should be fighting to drive down those tariffs, push back on those tariffs. But he has not,” Benson said. 
But James responded that he has “actually never voted to increase tariffs on Canada, despite what she says, and I’ve actually called out the administration specifically, talking with the trade ambassador and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back, protect our industry.” 
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, left, debates Rep. John James, R-Mich, Republican gubernatorial candidate on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at WOOD-TV, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Benson also proposed, as she has said in the past, that she plans to negotiate a subnational trade agreement between Michigan and Canada, in which goods going directly between those are not subject to tariffs and costs. 
Asked by reporters after the debate how exactly the agreements would work, Benson said that “States have the sovereignty to actually engage in subnational agreements like this, and there’s plenty of examples of this,” citing New York Gov. Kathy Hochul as having already made such an agreement, though it was not clear from research that New York state has any such agreement in place with Canada. “We’re going to work to make sure that these are legally enforceable agreements to protect the people of Michigan, drive down costs, and protect our jobs.”
James also pushed back against the actual efficacy of those agreements, saying that in the past, subnational agreements have failed to bring jobs to Michigan. 
“The fact of the matter is, there are six states that have higher export percentages than Michigan. Five of them are run by Republican governors. Two of them are in the top five overall, and all of them are doing better,” he said. “Each of the states that we’re looking to for guidance on where we can be and what we can do economically are run by Republican governors.”
Rep. John James, R-Mich, Republican gubernatorial candidate talks during a debate with Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at WOOD-TV, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
James also said that he introduced a bill Tuesday called the Trade Act “to make sure that we protect our jobs and lower costs, because I’m dedicated to bringing solutions and doing things, and not just pointing the fingers and complaining. Michigan’s lost too many jobs.”
He first proposed the bill at a forum at the Detroit Economic Club, but because Congress is not in session, the bill has yet to be introduced, and details of the specific relief that the legislation would promise are not available publicly. 
They also discussed how to respond to other federal actions — including immigration agents’ presence in the state. 
James emphasized cooperation with federal law enforcement within Michigan’s communities.
“We’re going to make sure that we’re prioritizing violent offenders, and we’re going to make sure that we enforce the law,” he said. “Frankly, I don’t believe we’re going to need ICE presence in the state of Michigan because we are going to be enforcing the law. So again, prioritizing violent offenders, working and abiding by federal law, and coordinating closely with our communities.”
Benson, meanwhile, asked about the presence of immigration agents in schools, said that she often saw the use and abuse of federal authority to “terrorize” communities. 
“It requires a governor who is willing to and ready to stand up to the President of the United States and use every legal tool in my toolbox, which other governors have done, and we’ve seen that do that successfully to protect the people of Michigan from the encroachment of ICE and the harm that they are creating in communities across our state,” Benson added after the debate. “I’ll proudly do that as governor, just as I’ve stood up to the president to protect our elections in this state. I’ve honed that ability to be unafraid to stand up to anyone, anytime, anywhere who would try to infringe upon the constitutional rights and freedoms of our citizens.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, talks during a televised debate with by Rep. John James, R-Mich, Republican gubernatorial candidate on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at WOOD-TV, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Affordability in Michigan was also paramount at the debate — and both candidates said that they supported a potential suspension of both state and federal gas taxes to lower prices at the pump as gas prices reach some of the highest levels in the nation. 
Those high gas prices have come as the war in Iran continues — and Benson claimed that James has supported, through votes in Congress and loyalty to his party, the continuation of that war and as such the continued high gas prices. 
But James emphasized during the debate, as well as to reporters after, that he has told the president privately and publicly that he supports a swift end to the war. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I applaud the administration for using every economic and every diplomatic resource at their disposal. Iran cannot have a nuke, but we need to wrap this thing up like, yesterday,” he said. “As somebody who’s been to war and actually been shot at, I understand the toll and the price of war.”
Benson also focused on lowering costs of electricity through continued diversification of Michigan’s energy grid with clean energy, something that James has said he would seek to roll back from policies put in place under the Whitmer administration. 
“I live in Detroit. Every month, I see my electricity bills go up and my outages increase as well,” she said. “I know the next governor of Michigan must ensure we are ending profit-driven rate hikes that have gotten us here, where our electricity bills are going up in some cases more than many other states, and also invest in clean energy infrastructure because frankly, that is the only thing that will reduce our energy costs in the long term.”
Meanwhile, James proposed addressing policies that he said increase costs for housing developers by more than $100,000 before they even put a shovel in the ground. 
“We also need to increase our workforce development. We need to make sure that we’re getting more labor to the front,” he said. “We need to reform our laws and make it more difficult to grow opportunity and jobs and have everybody assess them. These are the types of things that leadership brings and a governor will bring to make sure that everybody can experience prosperity as well as better housing prices.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, left, is joined by Rep. John James, R-Mich, Republican gubernatorial candidate during a televised debate on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at WOOD-TV, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Both also pitched plans to make healthcare more affordable — Benson through reforms to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, including a prescription drug affordability board, and James defending his votes on federal Medicaid policy, stating, “Medicaid will not be taken away from people who are working at least 80 hours.”
Both candidates also pitched themselves as candidates of change and reform — Benson as a foil to Trump, and James as a shift from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. 
They also each worked to tie each other to the respective current leader of their own party, in Trump and Whitmer, something that both candidates also pushed back on.
“I’ve stood up to the president many times. I’ve said that I can group the president without worshiping him. I can disagree without attacking him, and I always put Michigan first,” James said. “The fact of the matter is, she is holding me to a double standard when she has never, not once, stood up to Gretchen Whitmer before she needed a campaign issue.”
“The choice in this race is simple. Who do you want the next governor to work for? I will work for you, and my opponent has already shown us that he won’t. Because as governor, he’ll do exactly what he did in Congress: raise your prices, get rich, and do everything Donald Trump asks him to do,” Benson responded. “So, if you like gas pushing $5 a gallon, our mortgage rates over 7% or tariffs taxing just about everything we pay for, then John James is your guy.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley calls for constitutional amendment on abortion rights
description: Democratic candidate David Crowley committed to advocate for a constitutional amendment that would allow voters to decide whether access to abortion and reproductive healthcare is a right protected by the state constitution.  At an event in Milwaukee on Tuesday, Crowley said that it is good that the state Supreme Court ruled that an 1849 law […]
text:
David Crowley, who in July restarted his campaign 10 days after he dropped out, said Gov. Tony Evers, who endorsed him, was his campaign’s “secret weapon.” (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Democratic candidate David Crowley committed to advocate for a constitutional amendment that would allow voters to decide whether access to abortion and reproductive healthcare is a right protected by the state constitution. 
At an event in Milwaukee on Tuesday, Crowley said that it is good that the state Supreme Court ruled that an 1849 law that was interpreted as a nearly absolute ban on abortion is unenforceable. But, he said, “other restrictions remain, and future legislatures can change that law.” He appeared at the event with U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin and his runningmate, lieutenant governor candidate Sarah Godlewski. 
For a proposed constitutional amendment to go before voters, the Wisconsin Legislature has to pass the proposal in two consecutive sessions. The governor does not have a role in signing off on the proposals. 
“Right now, women’s rights are only safe as the next election, and I don’t think Wisconsin’s women should have to hold their breath every four years,” Crowley said. “This amendment will establish a fundamental right to make and carry out decisions about reproductive health, including contraception, fertility treatment, pregnancy, miscarriage care and abortion. It will keep medical judgments about viability and necessary care with treating healthcare professionals, and it will prevent the state from penalizing anyone who is seeking healthcare or helping another person seek the care that they need.”
During the Milwaukee event, Crowley criticized Republican candidate Tom Tiffany as being “an anti-abortion extremist who backed their plan to ban abortion nationwide at zero weeks with no exceptions for rape, incest, or the life of a mother.”
Tiffany previously supported legislation to restrict abortion access during his time in the state Legislature and in Congress. He voted in 2015, when he was a state senator, for the state’s ban on abortion after 20 weeks. In Congress, he has cosponsored legislation that would have made it a crime for doctors to perform abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy.
Tiffany said during a campaign event on Tuesday that he would uphold the state’s current 20-week ban. 
“David Crowley wants unlimited abortion all the way up to nine months, and I just don’t think that’s where most Wisconsinites are,” Tiffany said.
A recent lawsuit filed by Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin seeks to repeal several laws in Wisconsin that restrict abortion, arguing that they are unconstitutional because of a constitutional right to abortion. There is no language in the state constitution that directly addresses abortion, but the lawsuit argues the passage that guarantees that “all people are born equally free and independent and possess inherent rights, including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness” covers a right to abortion.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Audit: Minnesota public defenders shoulder high caseloads even by 30-year-old standards
description: Minnesota public defenders are struggling under heavy caseloads to fulfill their constitutional obligation to represent every person accused of a crime who can’t afford a lawyer, according to a report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor released on Tuesday. The state’s roughly 600 public defenders represented people in more than 135,000 cases in 2025,[...]
text:
Getty Images.Minnesota public defenders are struggling under heavy caseloads to fulfill their constitutional obligation to represent every person accused of a crime who can’t afford a lawyer, according to a report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor released on Tuesday.
The state’s roughly 600 public defenders represented people in more than 135,000 cases in 2025, ranging from disorderly conduct to murder. That’s 225 cases per lawyer, though caseloads vary based on the seriousness and complexity of cases.
For the entire five-year period analyzed in the evaluation, average caseloads have exceeded state standards meant to ensure attorneys can meet their ethical duty to provide “prompt, competent, and diligent representation.”
What’s more, the Office of the Legislative Auditor found the governing body overseeing public defense still hasn’t updated the state’s caseload standards despite being advised by a similar audit in 2010 that the standards were outdated.
The standards, which were last updated in 1995, don’t take into account the significant increase in material that defense attorneys need to review, such as bodyworn camera footage.
Without an accurate assessment of how much time it takes to represent people accused of various crimes, the governing body that oversees Minnesota public defense cannot effectively estimate the resources it needs and how to deploy them.
The report’s authors stated bluntly the Board of Public Defense “has not provided effective leadership.”
In response to the audit, the board’s leaders noted they established a workgroup that is revising standards. That workgroup was formed two years ago.
While public defenders say caseloads are overwhelming and leading to burnout, the vast majority say they continue to meet their obligations to clients.
More than 80% of public defenders said they were meeting their obligations, though only about half said they could spend sufficient time with their clients and return phone calls within one working day, according to a survey by the Office of the Legislative Auditor.
Caseloads have come down significantly in recent years thanks to a massive infusion of cash from the Democratic-controlled state Legislature in 2023, which increased funding for public defense by $42 million a year — or about 40%.
The additional funding has allowed the state to increase public defense staffing by 22% in recent years, while the number of cases has increased about 14% since 2021.
Attorneys in 5 out of 10 public defense districts did have average caseloads under the state standard in 2025, though many surveyed said their workload was too high.
The budget increase came after a hard-fought campaign by rank-and-file public defenders, who nearly went on strike in 2022 for the first time in state history, decrying high caseloads and low pay compared to prosecutors.
Public defenders, who are unionized with the Teamsters Local 320, negotiated historic pay raises in 2023, ranging from 26% to 72% depending on seniority, which brought them close to parity with prosecutors.
The auditor’s office also found the Board of Public Defense’s resource allocation procedures are outdated, and that it has not adequately evaluated key leaders’ performance. Auditors report that the board has not set performance measures even after the Office of the Legislative Auditor advised it to do so in 2010.
That will not surprise rank-and-file public defenders. The board reappointed State Public Defender Bill Ward in 2022 after an overwhelming vote of no confidence by public defenders.
Board leaders said they would examine how they evaluate the state public defender and noted a new one starts next month.
The report found managers completed “very few” performance evaluations as required, which managers attributed to their own high caseloads limiting their ability to carry out their supervisory duties.
The board’s leaders took issue with the recommendation to determine the proper balance of caseloads and supervisory responsibilities for managers, noting they already have standards but they’re difficult to meet at current funding levels.
“We are deserving and needing of a large funding increase,” Ward told lawmakers after the report was presented on Tuesday, pointing to funding cuts during the Great Recession nearly two decades ago.

description: Gov. text:
5-day watches/warnings forecast cone for Tropical Depression No. 9. (Source: The National Hurricane Center and Central Pacific Hurricane Center )
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed an executive order Tuesday night declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties in advance of a rapidly developing tropical depression heading toward northwest Florida.
“This order will allow the Florida Division of Emergency Management to stage critical preparedness resources and ensure Florida is ready to respond,” DeSantis said in a news release. “Floridians should take this time to get disaster plans in place and ensure their hurricane supply kit is stocked.” The governor said residents should visit FloridaDisaster.org for a review of disaster plans.
The tropical depression is officially known as Tropical Depression 9. The state of emergency is in effect for: Baker, Bay, Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gilchrist, Gulf, Hamilton, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Leon, Liberty, Madison, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Wakulla, and Washington counties.
“Impacts are expected to extend beyond the point of landfall, with heavy rainfall, strong winds, coastal flooding, and isolated tornadoes possible across North Florida,” DeSantis said. “Additional precipitation could further saturate soils and increase the potential for flash flooding following the state’s recent significant rainfall.”
Meanwhile, state emergency response teams began mobilizing Tuesday to support storm preparation efforts. Resources, such as fuel, generators, flood barriers, pallets of water bottles, tarps, sandbags and shelf-stable meals, are being staged in both Leon and Santa Rosa counties to ensure they can be sent quickly to communities in need.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: In first debate, Collins and Jackson blame each other for Mainers’ struggles
description: Sharing the stage for the first time Tuesday night, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson directly blamed each other for Mainers’ struggles and called each other corrupt.   Tuesday night’s debate, hosted by CBS News 13/ WGME, is the first of four debates over the next two weeks for the Senate […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson met for the first time on the debate stage on Oct. 6, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of WGME-TV)Sharing the stage for the first time Tuesday night, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson directly blamed each other for Mainers’ struggles and called each other corrupt.  
Tuesday night’s debate, hosted by CBS News 13/ WGME, is the first of four debates over the next two weeks for the Senate race, which could decide the balance of power in U.S. Congress. Polls have the candidates in a virtual tie. 
Collins, the five-term incumbent, wasted no time getting to what has consistently been her key pitch to Maine voters — touting the federal funding she has been able to secure for the state in her opening remarks.  
Before getting into his own background, Jackson, former Maine Senate president and logger, used his opening remarks to condemn Collins for her vote on this day eight years ago to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. This is Collins’ first reelection campaign since Kavanaugh helped overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. 
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said. 
Their closing statements later summed up how they each would approach the job. 
“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority, and relationships,” Collins said. 
Meanwhile, Jackson said, “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything.”
The economy 
Collins blamed Jackson for Mainers’ high cost of living. 
“If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta,” Collins said. 
In turn, Jackson blamed Collins.
“It’s because of Sen. Collins not being willing to stand up to Donald Trump, voting with him 96% of the time,” Jackson said, noting her vote to advance Trump’s signature spending package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which is projected to slash Maine’s Medicaid funding by billions over the next decade. 
Collins pointed out that she ultimately voted against the final package. 
“If I had not allowed the bill to go to the floor, I would never have been able to author the $50 billion fund to help rural healthcare,” Collins said, referring to a mitigation effort she got tacked on to the law.  
Jackson equated that approach to “an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out.” 
Corruption
Jackson and Maine Democrats have been accusing Collins of corruption after ProPublica reported last month about her alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme, which she has denied.
She did so again Tuesday night. “These allegations are completely false and they are very offensive,” Collins said.  
Collins’ staff has said the FBI has not contacted them since 2021, when it was investigating her donor, Martin Kao, the former CEO of defense contractor Navatek, who pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions involving a pro-Collins super PAC. No one in Collins’ orbit was charged as a result of the investigation then.
But ProPublica reported that the FBI was looking into the senator again in recent years — that was until Donald Trump returned to office for a second term and the probe died as part of his purge of the bureau. Among many claims, Kao said in the ProPublica story that Collins wouldn’t meet with him until he donated to her campaign.
Ahead of the debate Tuesday, Collins’ staff held a press call to share a document showing  Collins supported a joint University of Maine and Navatek project at the university’s request in 2017. Her staff also shared a photo of the senator meeting with Kao months before a donation was made. 
How Mainers are weighing the pay-to-play allegation involving Susan Collins

Maine Democrats said in response Tuesday that they still believe the paper trail points to a pay-to-play scheme and noted the incomplete recent probes into the senator. 
Jackson was also given a chance to respond to pro-Collins ads calling out his son for working as a lobbyist while he led the Maine Senate.
“My son didn’t do anything wrong,” Jackson said.
Collins criticized the former Senate president for getting travel to his home in Allagash reimbursed during his tenure, even though he also had a house in Augusta. The Maine Ethics Commission declined to pursue that same residency complaint made by a Republican state lawmaker back in 2023. It is common for Maine legislators who live in districts far from the State House to stay in long-term rentals or hotels during session. 
“I was in the House five days a week, and I went home on the weekend, just like every other legislator,” Jackson said. 
Questioning each other
The moderator allowed the candidates to ask one question of the other. 
Jackson focused again on Collins’ vote to confirm Kavanaugh, asking: “What will it take for you to admit that you were wrong?” 
Collins said she evaluates U.S. Supreme Court nominees based on their qualifications and experience. She added, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me,” referring to Jackson’s opposition to abortion early on in his time as a state legislator. 
Collins asked Jackson how he thinks he will get things done in a closely divided Senate as the most junior senator, citing governors vetoing dozens of his bills and some of his proposals not making it out of committee.
Jackson rebutted that she does not understand how the state legislative process works. 
“Multiple people put in the same bill. I am a team player,” Jackson said. “I let other people go forward with bills because I felt it was more important for them to get the recognition than me.” 
Is fraud a problem?
When asked if fraud is a problem, both said yes, though Jackson said only if it is true and Collins unequivocally said there already is a “terrible problem” with fraud in healthcare programs.  
“Taxpayer money is always needed to be taken care of, spent wisely,” Jackson said. However, he qualified, “Having people come from D.C. just to score political points, I don’t agree with. Let’s have an independent investigation go in and find out for sure.” 
Pointing to an independent investigation under former President Joe Biden, Collins said the inspector general found $42 million in improper payments and fraud in Maine’s Medicaid program, as well as noted other recent allegations. 
Maine’s health department has stressed that that federal audit did not contain any allegations of fraud.  The state has suspended payments to five providers who billed MaineCare for services they did not provide as it investigates improper payments and independently reviews the findings of the federal audit.
On Trump and socialism 
Collins did not answer when asked if she would join Trump if he comes to Maine to campaign. 
“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” Collins said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Jackson was asked if his support for Medicare for All was because he is a socialist. 
Ignoring the latter, Jackson responded, “I support Medicare for All so that people that I know across the state have healthcare.”
Well known stances
The candidates also reiterated their well known stances on several issues. 
Jackson supports Medicaid for all, while Collins said Big Government taking over healthcare is not the solution. 
They also disagreed on whether to keep sending military aid to Israel. Collins said she thinks the current level of military aid to Israel is good. Jackson said he doesn’t want “any more offensive weapons going to murder people in Palestine” and called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a war criminal. 
Jackson supports abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while Collins opposes getting rid of the agency and called for reform. 
Collins added that she and independent U.S. Sen. Aungus King wrote to Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey asking for permission for his office to be involved in the federal investigation into the fatal ICE shooting in Biddeford. She also said the federal inspector general is investigating, however, family members and local officials have previously said that they had not been contacted by the federal government.
There were a few points of agreement Tuesday night. Both candidates said there should be federal guardrails on Artificial Intelligence and data centers and that they support federal protections for access to medical abortion drugs.

title: USDA to increase research into U.S. seed stores, partner with DOJ to investigate seed industry
description: PRAIRIE CITY – The U.S. Department of Agriculture launched a program Tuesday to increase research and sequencing of the country’s seed collection and announced it was “strengthening” its agreement with the Justice Department to investigate competition in the seed industry.  Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins made the announcement Tuesday at a farm near[...]
text:
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, center, at a farm near Prairie City, Iowa, Oct. 6, 2026 speaking about USDA seed sovereignty program alongside Iowa Reps. Zach Nunn, front left, and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, right. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) PRAIRIE CITY – The U.S. Department of Agriculture launched a program Tuesday to increase research and sequencing of the country’s seed collection and announced it was “strengthening” its agreement with the Justice Department to investigate competition in the seed industry. 
Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins made the announcement Tuesday at a farm near Prairie City, following a roundtable discussion with Iowa farmers. 
USDA’s Seed Sovereignty initiative will invest in the National Plant Germplasm System, to sequence the country’s existing seed stores in an effort to “unlock the tremendous potential of the plant genetic resources the United States holds and identify critical gaps,” according to a USDA release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rollins said the U.S. has “significantly invested” in international seed collections, but has failed to invest in its own “robust” seed collection of more than 600,000 seeds from over 16,000 species. 
She said the research will “protect” the genetic resources that underpin the food system “while also paving the way for new breakthroughs that are vital for our food security.” 
Scott Hutchins, the USDA undersecretary for research, education and economics, said researchers will use the USDA funding and artificial intelligence to “quickly” sequence all of the seeds in the nation’s germplasm system. Sequencing the seeds, he said, will give the department a better understanding of its genetic resources.
“If we know what we have, we also know what we don’t have, and we know what kind of dependency we might have with seeds from outside the United States,” Hutchins said. “That’s why we refer to it as seed sovereignty.” 
He estimated that currently about 10% of the U.S. seed collection has been sequenced. 
Hutchins said once the germplasm, or the genetic material, is understood, researchers can then see what traits those seeds hold – like drought or pest resistance – that can be helpful to farmers. 
He said USDA will also use the Genesis AI initiative from the U.S. Department of Energy to “quickly find those traits and put them to work for our farmers.” 
“While we do have treaties around the world to share seeds, those treaties do not extend to the sequencing and the genome information,” Hutchins said. “We intend to make that United States intellectual property, make it available to United States farmers for the benefit of United States agriculture.”
Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper said seed technology is “at the very core of modern agriculture.”
“Investing in research helps ensure Iowa farmers remain sustainable and profitable, while ensuring they have access to a competitive market to purchase their seed genetics,” Kuiper said.
In August, USDA also announced it planned to fund several new research facilities, including the National Plant Germplasm System Centralized Distribution Center in Ames, toward which the USDA directed $12 million. 
Investigating seed pricing 
Rollins was joined by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, to announce an expanded memorandum of understanding between USDA the U.S. Department of Justice with a “new focus on seed markets.” 
“The Department of Justice will be shining an even brighter light on seed pricing practices, on seed licensing, on seed relabeling and on barriers facing independent seed companies,” Rollins said. “So again, working very very hard to do everything we can to support our farmers and ranchers.” 
Last year, the two departments announced they were working together to “protect competition in key agricultural markets such as feed, fertilizer, fuel, seed, equipment, and other essential goods.” Farmers, lawmakers and independent agribusiness operators have said consolidation in these industries is one of the elements driving up input prices for farmers. 
The Federal Trade Commission confirmed in May it had launched an antitrust investigation of the fertilizer industry and ag leaders, including the USDA deputy secretary, have been soliciting information from farmers and local dealers to help build the case. 
FTC recently reached a $35 million settlement with Corteva over the seed and pesticide company’s loyalty program which the suit alleged meant the company was not fairly competing with other brands and generics. 
Woodward noted the previous work of the DOJ, including a settlement to keep egg companies from coordinating to inflate prices. Woodward said in addition to bringing down prices for farmers, “Americans deserve answers” to how prices in the industry have risen. 
USDA secretary urges states to allow on-road dyed diesel

According to USDA data, the average price of crop seeds increased more than 270% between 1990 and 2020, at a rate “significantly faster” than the price that farmers received for their commodities. The USDA report shows that corn, soybeans and cotton seeds, which are typically genetically modified seeds, rose at an even faster rate, with an average increase of 463% in the 30-year time frame.  
Rollins, citing the report, said “there’s got to be a reason for that.” 
“It’s time to figure it out; and it’s time to do better for our farmers; and it’s time to look at the consolidation in the industry; it’s time to understand why we rely on China for a lot of our seeds,” Rollins said. “It’s time. And I’m honored to hopefully help lead that.” 
Hutchins said the Seed Sovereignty initiative intends to make the information it gathers on the U.S. seed stores available to companies “on a licensing basis” and not an exclusive basis. 
“It should open up more competition in that context, but the companies themselves have to be able to exist and be able to create an opportunity to put that germplasm into their portfolio,” Hutchins said. 
Rollins said she was also announcing a $6 million grant to Iowa State University to expand its Energy Agriculture Innovation Lab. The funding is part of $125 million allocated in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for research facilities at land grant universities. Rollins said the grant would ensure that “ISU will remain a leader in cutting edge research and technology.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Amazon’s Walla Walla data center plan sparks tension between protesters, local officials
description: WALLA WALLA, Wash. — More than four hundred Washingtonians across 19 locations took to the streets Sunday to demand a statewide moratorium on data centers.  In Walla Walla, where a $4.8 billion Amazon data center project is planned, the tension among opponents and local officials was palpable. “Some of you standing here today have been […]
text:
Roughly 40 people waved signs, chanted and marched during a Walla Walla demonstration demanding a data center moratorium. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)WALLA WALLA, Wash. — More than four hundred Washingtonians across 19 locations took to the streets Sunday to demand a statewide moratorium on data centers. 
In Walla Walla, where a $4.8 billion Amazon data center project is planned, the tension among opponents and local officials was palpable.
“Some of you standing here today have been called extremists and communists for standing with us,” Ben Mattice, co-founder of the Walla Walla Anti-Data Center League said to a crowd of about 60. “You are not extremists for wanting transparency. You are not extremists for wanting clean drinking water.”
The state, home to 130 data centers, offers tax breaks on labor and new computer equipment for data center operators. Washington ranks 10th in the country for the number of data centers in operation. 
“It is our job to call on officials … to protect our communities and to, at the very least, put a pause on hyperscale data centers,” Mattice said.
Shortly after the rally, roughly 40 people waved signs, chanted and marched to the office of Melissa Shumake, the county’s community development director. Shumake, who has served as director for less than a year, has the sole authority to require Amazon to submit an environmental impact statement regarding their proposed construction of 16 data center buildings.
Members of the league say that Amazon’s development has been shrouded in secrecy. They’re fearful that Amazon will use more water than they’re allowed to, or worse, pollute aquifers. They point to what happened in Morrow and Umatilla County just across the Oregon border where earlier this year Amazon agreed to pay more than $20 million to settle a lawsuit alleging the company’s data centers contaminated groundwater with nitrate. 
Meanwhile, local officials are growing frustrated, saying Amazon has “outright” permission to develop its data centers in the Wallula Gap Business Park, some 30 miles west of Walla Walla. It’s been estimated that the project will bring in $5 million a year in personal property taxes for the county.
It wasn’t until February that the Walla Walla Port Commission announced that Amazon Web Services was behind the 2024 purchase of some 500 acres in the business park. 
The port commissioners, according to Executive Director Patrick Reay, signed a non-disclosure agreement with Amazon back in March 2023 – more than a year before Advance Phase LLC, a company owned by Amazon, purchased the land from the port. The agreement barred commissioners from stating the company’s involvement until this year, Reay said. 
It seemed like the kind of deal the port couldn’t pass up. Nearly $5 billion of private capital investment would produce over 700 jobs throughout the four-phase development of the project, according to a 2024 report on the sale agreement. By comparison, the total assessed value of properties in Walla Walla County was around $10 billion that year. 
“Where else could your assessed value raise by approximately 50% on 554 acres?” Reay said. “It was a real estate transaction for us that met our mission.”
During each phase of development, Amazon has planned to construct four data center buildings, each about 215,000 square feet, according to the 2024 report, though the specifics listed are subject to change as the project develops, Reay said. 
Amazon is currently jumping through the bureaucratic hurdles of permitting. The county has entered a public comment phase running through Oct. 12 on behalf of Amazon’s permit application. 
Amazon said it is constructing three, not four, data centers in this first phase, which it anticipates building out over the next three years, according to a State Environmental Policy Act document submitted to Walla Walla County. 
Amazon also stated its estimated annual water use is “considerably lower” than previous agriculture operators on the property. Annually, it’s estimated to use 18 million gallons of surface water for cooling computer equipment and 6 million gallons of groundwater for domestic use. 
Amazon did not disclose how much energy will be needed to operate the data centers. 
Back in August, after hearing local opposition, Amazon deliberately submitted an incomplete permitting application to the county so that it could “engage directly with the community,” according to a Frequently Asked Questions document Amazon made public regarding its Walla Walla data center project. It hosted an open house that drew around 300 attendees in Burbank. 
“Since 2010, Amazon has invested over $400 billion in Washington including infrastructure and compensation to employees and has over 95,000 employees in the state,” according to a statement from Amazon. The company “is committed to responsible development and being a long-term, positive presence in the Walla Walla community.”
The FAQ document said the company will annually use 14 million gallons of water to cool its server equipment, but in its SEPA checklist submitted to the county, it estimated using 18 million gallons. When asked about the difference between the two figures, Amazon did not immediately respond.
Amazon recently launched the “Built Together” initiative, a program dedicated to serving communities near their data centers. It will fund community college and workforce development, energy efficiency upgrades for K-12 schools and other needs specific to the community.  
Growing opposition
Data center projects have become flashpoints in recent months at all levels of government. In Washington, for example, Seattle and Spokane passed data center moratoriums. Skamania, Benton, and Yakima, counties also enacted moratoriums, while neighboring Klickitat County, with just 24,000 residents, is seeing a growing movement against new development after six projects requested enough power to energize up to 6 million homes.
Major data center projects in Utah and New Mexico have generated national headlines as they spawned large protest movements. In Washington D.C., the issue is scrambling usual party lines as the president backs data centers and a bipartisan coalition in Congress is calling for restrictions.
Washington lawmakers tried but failed to pass a sweeping data center regulation bill in the last session. The bill’s sponsor Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, plans to bring the bill back next year with a provision to ban local officials from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers.

A moratorium is “a short-term solution,” Doglio said. “I’m far more interested in putting in place guardrails to not only address future development of data centers, but also do a look back and make sure utilities have contracts in place that protect ratepayers.” 
Ben Mattice, co-founder of the Walla Walla Anti-Data Center League, said the group’s strategy is to “make this entire county unpalatable for Amazon.” (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)
Over the summer, the Walla Walla Anti-Data Center League garnered nearly 1,900 signatures on two separate petitions for a data center moratorium. Members of the league host town halls, meet with local stakeholders, table at community events and file public records requests to local government agencies, Mattice said. 
The strategy is to “make this entire county unpalatable for Amazon,” Mattice said. The group is “[doing] as many things as we can to put rocks in the gears to slow the thing down in hopes that either the bubble bursts and they don’t need it anymore or they go elsewhere.”
Each week, members of the league attend county commissioner meetings to ask for a moratorium and an environmental impact statement. 
The county commissioners haven’t acted. Todd Kimball, one of three, said that even if the county placed a moratorium on data centers, it wouldn’t stop Amazon’s development. 
“They have an application in. It grandfathers them into the old rules,” Kimball said. 
Kimball, who has been in office for 10 years, has grown frustrated with some of the group’s claims about the county, saying it has been more transparent than ever.
“We’ve done more to educate the public with this project than any other ever in Walla Walla County,” Kimball said. “The application is online, which we’ve never posted before.”
Amazon’s 550-acre project is located in the heart of the Wallula Gap Business Park, an industrial-zoned property adjacent to Highway 12 and the Columbia River. The park offers electricity, potable water, natural gas and sewer lines to industries operating on its grounds. 
The anti-data center group is pointing to Shumake, the county’s development director, to ensure an environmental impact statement is prepared, but she doesn’t think it will be necessary. 
“If I determined that somehow there are impacts that cannot be mitigated, then I would potentially require them to do a full EIS,” Shumake said.
“This is an industrial zone with a project that ultimately has a smaller impact than other projects in the same industrial zone,” Shumake said. 
“We have to have data centers somewhere,” Shumake added. “And in an industrial zone without population centers nearby, where there’s existing water rights. Like, I can think of a lot worse places where this might go.”
Earthjustice, an environmental law firm tackling data centers across the country, disagrees. The permitting application that Amazon submitted lacked specific details that are required to exempt an environmental impact statement, attorney Jan Hasselman wrote in a public comment to the county.
